questions.stem: A marketing associate asks Claude to "make this product page better" and gets a rewrite that changes the tone, the length and the calls to action all at once. None of it is what the team wanted.
options: The request never defined what better actually meant, so Claude guessed which dimension to optimise
Claude ignored the instruction because product copy sits outside what it handles reliably
The page was pasted as plain text, and formatting loss caused the tone to shift in the rewrite
The request was too short, and any prompt under a paragraph produces unfocused output
questions.why: Vague evaluative words like "better" name a direction without naming a dimension. Improving clarity, shortening, and raising conversion are different edits that pull against each other, so the model picks for you.
questions.traps: Length is not the problem and a short prompt can be perfectly precise. Blaming the paste or the model's competence skips the actual defect, which sits in the instruction.

questions.stem: A recruiter wants a rejection email drafted. They tell Claude the candidate's name and the role but nothing else, and the draft comes back warm, long and full of feedback the recruiter cannot legally give.
options: Ask for three drafts and pick whichever of them happens to avoid the legal problem
Tell Claude that it is a legal document so it applies a more cautious register throughout
Provide the candidate's full interview notes so the draft has enough grounding to be accurate
Specify the constraints that matter: length, what may not be said, and the tone the company uses
questions.why: The model defaults to helpful and complete. Anything you cannot include has to be stated as an exclusion, because there is no way to infer your legal constraints from a name and a job title.
questions.traps: More source material makes the feedback problem worse, not better. Sampling three drafts leaves the same gap to luck, and relabelling the register does not encode a specific prohibition.

questions.stem: An operations lead prompts Claude with "summarise this report" and receives a summary that is technically accurate but omits the budget variance their director specifically asked about.
options: Increase the requested summary length so more of the report's content survives the cut
Name the audience and the decision the summary serves, so the model knows what to keep
Ask for the summary twice and merge the two versions to improve topic coverage
Request bullet points instead of prose, since bullets preserve detail more faithfully
questions.why: A summary is a set of choices about what to drop. Without knowing who reads it and why, the model optimises for general coverage, and a specific figure a director cares about is not general.
questions.traps: A longer or bulleted summary still drops the wrong things. Merging two general summaries gives you more general summary, not the budget variance.

questions.stem: A consultant asks Claude to "review my slide deck for issues" and gets typo corrections when they wanted to know whether the argument holds together.
options: Upload the deck as a file rather than pasting the text so structure is visible to the model
Ask for a longer review, since a thorough pass eventually reaches the argument level too
Say which layer to review: argument, structure, or surface wording
State that the audience is a board so the model applies a higher standard of scrutiny
questions.why: "Issues" spans everything from a comma to a broken premise. Naming the layer is what turns a generic review into the one you needed, and the layers genuinely trade off against each other.
questions.traps: Length does not reorder priorities, and raising the stakes without naming the layer makes the model more thorough at the wrong level. File upload changes fidelity, not focus.

questions.stem: An analyst asks Claude to explain a quarterly variance to "the team". The result assumes deep finance knowledge, and half the team who read it are engineers.
options: Ask Claude to write at a lower reading level so the technical terms are automatically avoided
Request a glossary appended to the explanation so unfamiliar terms can be looked up
Split the request so finance readers and engineers each receive a separately written version
Describe who the readers actually are and what they already know before asking for the explanation
questions.why: "The team" carries no information about prior knowledge. Naming the readers lets the model pitch the explanation once, correctly, rather than defaulting to the subject's native register.
questions.traps: A reading-level instruction blunts the prose without fixing which concepts need unpacking. A glossary patches symptoms, and two versions is real work to solve a problem one sentence would have prevented.

questions.stem: A support manager wants Claude to draft replies to angry customers. The drafts are polite and correct but read as though the company has no policy on refunds.
options: Instruct Claude to be more apologetic, which softens the reply enough to defuse the complaint
Ask for shorter replies so there is less room to imply commitments the company cannot keep
Give Claude the actual refund policy in the prompt so drafts stay inside what is offered
Tell Claude to avoid mentioning refunds at all and route every such case to a human
questions.why: Policy is external knowledge the model cannot infer. Supplying it is what lets a draft be both empathetic and accurate about what the customer will actually receive.
questions.traps: Tone changes do not add policy. Shortening reduces exposure without adding correctness, and routing every refund mention to a human discards most of the value of the drafting.

questions.stem: A pharmaceutical firm's comms team gets consistently over-cautious drafts from Claude. Every sentence hedges, and the copy reads as though nothing can be claimed at all.
options: Explain the regulatory context and name the claims that are already approved for use
Ask Claude to write with more confidence and remove hedging language from the final draft
Lower the stakes described in the prompt so the subject reads as less regulated than it is
Draft the copy without Claude and use it only for a proofreading pass at the end
questions.why: Undirected caution is what a model produces when it can tell a domain is risky but cannot tell where the line sits. Naming the approved claims converts vague hedging into specific, defensible statements.
questions.traps: Stripping hedges leaves unsupported claims. Understating the regulatory context invites exactly the copy that gets rejected in review, and abandoning drafting forfeits the gain.

questions.stem: A project manager pastes a long email thread into Claude and asks for "the next steps". Claude returns steps that were already completed two weeks earlier in the thread.
options: Paste only the most recent message, since older messages are what caused the confusion
State today's date and which parts of the thread are already done
Ask Claude to sort the thread chronologically first and then extract the outstanding items
Request the steps as a numbered list so completed items are easier to spot and remove
questions.why: A thread contains proposals, completions and reversals with no reliable markers of state. The model needs to be told where "now" is, because the text does not encode it unambiguously.
questions.traps: Truncating to the last message throws away the context that makes the steps meaningful. Sorting and numbering both organise the same ambiguity without resolving it.

questions.stem: A finance team needs Claude to convert messy expense descriptions into a fixed set of eight category labels. Descriptions are inconsistent, and Claude keeps inventing near-miss categories.
options: Describe the eight categories in more detail so the boundaries between them are clearer
Ask Claude to list its categories first, then apply them to the expense descriptions
Instruct Claude to use only the eight labels, repeating the instruction at the end
Show worked examples mapping several messy input lines onto the exact set of allowed labels
questions.why: Examples pin down both the label set and the judgement calls at the boundaries. Descriptions of categories leave the edge cases open; a worked mapping shows what you actually do with an ambiguous line.
questions.traps: Richer descriptions still leave interpretation to the model. Self-generated categories drift by design, and repeating a constraint does not teach where a borderline expense belongs.

questions.stem: An associate supplies three examples of the tone they want in customer emails. All three examples happen to be complaint responses, and Claude now writes every email, including welcome notes, as though defusing a complaint.
options: The examples were unrepresentative, so the model generalised the wrong pattern from them
Three examples is too few, and the model needs a substantially larger sample to be reliable
The examples were too long, which caused the model to overweight their content over their tone
Tone cannot be taught by example and has to be described in explicit adjectives instead
questions.why: Examples teach whatever they have in common. When every example shares a situation, the model cannot tell whether you meant the tone or the situation, and it copies both.
questions.traps: The count is not the defect — three well-chosen examples work. Tone is very teachable by example, and length is unrelated to the wrong generalisation.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude to extract five fields from supplier invoices. Most invoices work, but ones missing a purchase order number produce invented numbers rather than a blank.
options: Add an instruction saying that purchase order numbers must be accurate and never guessed
Ask Claude to flag its confidence for each extracted field so low-confidence values are visible
Include an example invoice with no purchase order and show the blank output it should produce
Extract the four reliable fields and have a person key in purchase order numbers by hand
questions.why: The failure is on the missing-data path, so the examples have to cover it. Showing the empty case teaches that a blank is a legitimate output, which the model otherwise treats as a task it has failed.
questions.traps: An accuracy instruction does not tell the model what to emit instead. Confidence flags add review work without changing behaviour, and manual keying gives up on the field entirely.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude for a competitor comparison. Each run returns a different shape — sometimes prose, sometimes a table, once a set of nested bullets — which breaks the script that consumes it.
options: Ask for a table each time and restate that instruction at both the start and end of the prompt
Supply an explicit template with the exact columns and the rule for unknown values
Break the comparison into one competitor per request so each response stays small and uniform
Raise the specificity of the analysis itself, since a precise analysis implies a precise format
questions.why: Format drift is underspecification. A template removes the model's discretion about shape, and covering the unknown-value case removes the one branch where it would otherwise improvise.
questions.traps: Repetition emphasises an instruction that was never precise. Splitting the request multiplies calls without fixing shape, and analytical depth does not constrain layout.

questions.stem: An associate needs Claude's output to drop straight into a spreadsheet, but the responses keep arriving with a friendly sentence before and after the data.
options: Copy the response and delete the extra sentences manually before pasting into the sheet
Request a shorter response overall so there is less room for surrounding commentary
Ask for the data only, with no preamble or closing commentary, and specify the delimiter
Ask Claude to place the data at the end so the extra text can be cut in one action
questions.why: Conversational framing is the default register. It goes away when you rule it out explicitly and say what the payload should look like on its own.
questions.traps: Manual cleanup repeats forever. Shortening and repositioning both accept the commentary instead of removing it, and neither survives a long batch.

questions.stem: A compliance officer wants Claude's risk write-ups to always carry the same five headings, but roughly one in five responses merges two of the sections together.
options: Give the five headings verbatim and instruct that each appears even when a section is empty
Number the headings in the prompt so their separateness is more strongly signalled
Ask for longer write-ups, since more content makes merging adjacent sections less likely
Generate each of the five sections in its own separate request and assemble them afterwards
questions.why: Sections merge when the model judges one to be thin. Stating that an empty section still gets its heading removes that judgement call, which is the actual source of the variance.
questions.traps: Numbering and length both nudge without deciding. Five separate calls do guarantee the shape but at five times the cost for a problem one clause fixes.

questions.stem: A sales lead asks Claude to "shorten this proposal" and the result loses the pricing table, which was the part the client most needed to see.
options: Specify a percentage reduction rather than a vague instruction to shorten the document
Say what must be preserved as well as the target length, because shortening deletes
Ask Claude to shorten only the narrative sections and leave everything else untouched
Shorten the proposal manually, because automated cutting cannot judge client priorities
questions.why: Cutting requires knowing what is load-bearing. A length target tells the model how much to remove but nothing about what survives, so it trims by prose density rather than importance.
questions.traps: A percentage is still only a size. Naming the sections is closer but brittle across documents, and doing it by hand discards a task the model handles well once told the constraint.

questions.stem: A nonprofit asks Claude to write a grant application. The draft is fluent but describes a generic organisation, because the prompt described the grant and not the applicant.
options: Ask for a longer draft so there is more room for the organisation's details to appear
Request several variations and choose the one that happens to fit the organisation best
Tell Claude the application is competitive so it writes with more distinctive language
Supply the organisation's programmes, outcomes and history as source material
questions.why: Specificity comes from supplied facts. A model with no information about your programmes can only produce the shape of a grant application, which is exactly what it did.
questions.traps: More length and more variation both scale generic content. Signalling competitiveness changes the prose style without adding a single verifiable detail about the organisation.

questions.stem: A team's examples for a summarisation task are all excellent, but each one is roughly a page long while real inputs run to thirty pages.
options: Increase the number of one-page examples so the pattern is reinforced more strongly
Ask Claude to process thirty pages in one-page chunks so each matches the example length
Use examples drawn at the real input length, or state the length difference in the prompt itself
Note in the prompt that inputs are longer and rely on the model to scale the approach
questions.why: Examples set expectations about the whole task, including scale. A page-long example demonstrates a compression ratio and a level of selectivity that do not transfer to thirty pages.
questions.traps: Reinforcing a mismatched pattern strengthens the mismatch. Chunking changes the task into something else, and a bare note is weaker than showing the real case.

questions.stem: An associate asks for a table of risks with owners and dates. Claude produces the table, but invents plausible owner names for rows where the source document named nobody.
options: State that unknown fields must be left blank and never inferred from surrounding context
Ask Claude to mark invented entries in a different style so they can be identified later
Remove the owner column, since the source document does not reliably contain that data
Request a shorter table so there are fewer rows in which invention can occur
questions.why: A table has cells and the model treats an empty cell as an incomplete job. Explicit permission to leave a blank is what makes the honest output available to it.
questions.traps: Self-marking invention is unreliable for the same reason the invention happened. Dropping the column loses real data, and fewer rows means proportionally the same problem.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to research a market, build a financial model, and write the board memo in a single prompt. The memo is fine but the numbers do not reconcile with the research.
options: Ask for the same three deliverables but request that Claude show its working throughout
Reorder the request so the memo is written first and the research is used to support it
Provide more detail about the market so the research step has less room for error
Run the three as separate steps, checking the output of each before it feeds the next
questions.why: Chained work compounds errors silently. Separating the steps creates the checkpoints where a wrong figure gets caught before it is written into a conclusion for the board.
questions.traps: Shown working helps a reviewer but only if someone stops to read it, which a single-shot request discourages. Reordering and enrichment leave the chaining problem exactly where it was.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude for "a few ideas" for a campaign and receives twenty, most of which are outside the budget they never mentioned.
options: Ask Claude to rank the twenty ideas so the impractical ones sort to the bottom
State the budget, the channel and how many ideas are wanted
Request a second pass in which Claude removes any idea that seems expensive to execute
Accept the twenty and filter them by hand, since constraints vary case by case
questions.why: Constraints have to be in the prompt to shape generation. Filtering afterwards spends the model's effort on options that were never viable and leaves you doing the elimination.
questions.traps: Ranking and second passes both ask the model to guess a budget it still has not been given. Manual filtering works but is the cost you were trying to avoid.

questions.stem: A legal assistant uploads a contract and asks a question about indemnity. Claude answers confidently using general contract knowledge rather than the clause in the uploaded file.
options: Ask the question again with more specific wording so the relevant clause is easier to locate
Upload the contract a second time to be certain the file was successfully attached
Request that Claude quote the entire indemnity section before offering any interpretation
Instruct Claude to answer only from the document itself, and to say so when the document is silent
questions.why: Grounding is an instruction, not an automatic consequence of attaching a file. Without it the model blends the document with what it already knows, and the blend is invisible in the answer.
questions.traps: Rewording helps retrieval but not the blending. Re-uploading addresses a failure that did not occur, and demanding a full quote is a heavier version of the right idea without the crucial silence clause.

questions.stem: An associate dislikes a draft and replies "no, not like that, try again". The next draft is different but wrong in a new way, and the loop repeats four more times.
options: Say which specific aspect failed, and what should be kept from the draft you rejected
Start a fresh conversation each time so earlier rejected drafts stop influencing the output
Ask for several drafts at once and choose from them rather than iterating one at a time
Provide a finished example of the target so Claude can match it
questions.why: Undirected rejection carries no gradient. Naming the failed aspect and the parts worth keeping turns a random walk into a correction, which is what iteration is supposed to be.
questions.traps: Fresh starts discard the progress already made. Batch drafting and finished examples are useful techniques but neither addresses the habit of rejecting without saying why.

questions.stem: A researcher asks Claude to "find the problems" in a study design and gets a list dominated by minor statistical quibbles, while the sampling flaw they suspected goes unmentioned.
options: Ask the question again in a new conversation to see whether a different answer surfaces
Request more problems in the list so the sampling issue is more likely to be included
Ask specifically about the areas of concern and what would undermine the conclusion
Supply the study's raw data so the analysis rests on evidence
questions.why: An open request returns a broad, shallow sweep. Asking what would most undermine the conclusion forces prioritisation, which is the judgement you actually wanted from the review.
questions.traps: Resampling and lengthening both play the odds. Raw data deepens a statistical review but does not redirect it toward design, which is where the suspected flaw lives.

questions.stem: A team lead asks Claude to mediate a written disagreement between two colleagues by summarising both positions. The summary favours the colleague whose message was longer and more detailed.
options: Ask for a shorter summary so the length imbalance in the source has less influence
Ask for the strongest version of each position at comparable depth
Instruct Claude to be neutral and to avoid taking sides in the disagreement
Summarise each position in its own separate request and place the results side by side
questions.why: Length in the source becomes emphasis in the summary unless you say otherwise. Asking for comparable depth makes the balance an explicit requirement rather than a hoped-for side effect.
questions.traps: A neutrality instruction does not correct for asymmetric input. Shortening compresses the imbalance rather than removing it, and separate requests still inherit each message's own depth.

questions.stem: An associate needs meeting notes in a fixed template that includes a decisions section. When a meeting made no decisions, Claude fills the section with discussion points instead of leaving it empty.
options: Move the decisions section to the end of the template so it is less likely to be padded
Ask Claude to review its own output and remove anything that is not strictly a decision
Use a different word than decisions, since the term invites broad interpretation by the model
Say explicitly that an empty section should read as none rather than being filled with related content
questions.why: A blank looks like failure to a model trying to be complete. Naming the empty case, and what to write in it, is what makes "none" a valid and available answer.
questions.traps: Reordering does not change the padding instinct. Self-review repeats the same judgement that caused the problem, and renaming the section shifts the ambiguity rather than resolving it.

questions.stem: A team supplies two examples of the analysis they want. Claude follows the structure exactly but also reproduces a factual error that appeared in one of the examples.
options: Two examples is an unstable number and the model averaged them into an incorrect result
Examples teach form and content together, so anything in them must also be correct
The error was in the second example, and the model weights later examples more heavily
Factual errors in examples are ignored, so the mistake must have originated elsewhere
questions.why: An example is a demonstration of a good answer in full. The model has no way to know which parts you meant as structure and which as substance, so it copies both.
questions.traps: Position and count are not the mechanism. The claim that errors in examples are ignored is precisely backwards and is the misconception this scenario exists to correct.

questions.stem: A communications team asks for a press release and specifies a 400-word limit. Claude returns 620 words, and asking again returns 550.
options: Ask for 300 words instead, so the overshoot lands closer to the real target
Break the release into sections with a word budget for each of the sections
State the limit as a hard constraint, then verify the count before publishing
Accept the longer draft and trim it by hand, since precise counts are not achievable
questions.why: Length targets are approximate for a language model, so the reliable pattern is to state the constraint firmly and then check the number yourself rather than trusting it.
questions.traps: Deliberately under-asking is a workaround that misses in both directions. Sectioning helps but still needs verification, and giving up on the constraint discards a target that matters for the channel.

questions.stem: An associate uploads six research papers and asks for the consensus view. Claude produces a confident synthesis, but two of the six papers actually contradict the stated consensus.
options: Ask for the position of each paper before asking what they collectively support
Ask for the consensus again and check whether the second answer matches the first one
Upload the papers one at a time so each is processed with the model's full attention
Request that Claude cite page numbers so the synthesis can be verified after the fact
questions.why: Synthesis flattens disagreement. Extracting each source's position first makes the contradiction visible as data, so the consensus claim is built on something you can inspect.
questions.traps: Repeat runs test stability, not accuracy. Sequential upload does not change the flattening, and citations help verification only after a misleading synthesis has already been produced.

questions.stem: Each round of feedback fixes the problem raised but reintroduces an issue that was resolved two rounds earlier. The associate is now on the seventh revision.
options: Start over with a single prompt containing every requirement gathered so far in the process
Ask Claude to remember the earlier corrections and avoid repeating them in future drafts
Maintain a running list of settled requirements and restate it with each new round of feedback
Accept the current draft and fix the recurring issue by hand in the final version
questions.why: Constraints established conversationally compete for attention as a thread grows. Carrying them forward explicitly is what keeps a settled decision settled across revisions.
questions.traps: Asking the model to remember relies on the same fading attention that caused the regression. A full restart discards useful progress, and manual patching leaves the process broken for next time.

questions.stem: A team needs Claude's output in a strict format for a downstream tool. It works in testing, but in production about three percent of responses include an explanatory note before the payload.
options: Increase the strictness of the wording in the prompt until the explanatory notes stop appearing
Specify the format precisely and validate every response before it reaches the downstream tool
Test with a larger sample so the three percent failure rate is caught before production use
Ask Claude to review each response for format compliance before it is returned to the tool
questions.why: Prompt instructions reduce a failure rate; they do not make it zero. Anything feeding a downstream system needs a validation step, because the remaining percent will otherwise break it.
questions.traps: Stronger wording chases an asymptote. More testing measures the rate without handling it, and self-review inside the same response is not an independent check.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to read fifty customer interviews and identify themes. The themes are plausible but shallow, and clearly weighted toward the interviews mentioned first.
options: Ask for more themes so the later interviews are represented in the longer list
Reverse the order of the interviews and run the analysis a second time for comparison
Ask Claude to weight all fifty interviews equally when identifying the common themes
Extract the points from each interview first, then find themes across the set
questions.why: Two-stage analysis gives every source equal footing, because the second stage works on a uniform extract rather than on fifty documents competing for attention in one pass.
questions.traps: Asking for equal weighting states the goal without providing the mechanism. Reversing order reveals the bias, and more themes dilutes rather than rebalances.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to write onboarding documentation and specifies that it must avoid jargon. The result avoids technical terms but replaces them with vague phrases that are harder to act on.
options: Give a short list of terms that remain acceptable despite the restriction
Remove the jargon constraint, since technical accuracy matters more than accessibility here
Ask for the jargon version and a plain version, then let readers choose between them
Instruct Claude to define each technical term the first time it appears in the document
questions.why: A blanket ban removes vocabulary without supplying replacements, so the model reaches for imprecision. An allowed list keeps the words that carry real meaning.
questions.traps: Dropping the constraint abandons the readers it was for. Two versions doubles maintenance, and defining terms inline is a reasonable alternative but does not repair a ban already in force.

questions.stem: A policy team asks Claude a question about a 90-page handbook they uploaded. The answer is correct but cites section 4.2, while the relevant text is actually in section 7.1.
options: Ask Claude to double-check its citation before accepting the answer as final
Re-upload the handbook, since a section numbering error suggests the file parsed badly
Ask the question differently so the model locates the correct section on the second attempt
Treat the citation as unverified and check that section reference against the handbook itself
questions.why: A correct answer with a wrong pointer is the characteristic failure here, and it is why locators get checked separately from content. The answer being right is not evidence the citation is.
questions.traps: Self-checking a citation uses the same process that produced it. A parsing fault would corrupt content too, and rewording may move the error rather than reveal it.

questions.stem: An associate writes prompts that work well for them but produce poor results when a colleague reuses them, because the colleague works on a different product line.
options: Ask the colleague to write their own prompts, since prompts do not transfer between contexts
Add more detail about the original product line so the prompt becomes more thorough
Make the product context an explicit input to the prompt rather than assumed knowledge
Have Claude rewrite the prompt to be more general before the colleague reuses it
questions.why: Prompts that rely on implicit shared context break the moment the context changes. Naming the variable and passing it in is what makes a prompt reusable across a team.
questions.traps: More detail about the wrong product entrenches the problem. Generalising strips the specificity that made it work, and abandoning reuse forfeits the point of sharing prompts at all.

questions.stem: An associate has spent forty minutes refining a prompt for a one-off task that would have taken twenty minutes to do by hand. They are close but not quite there.
options: Recognise that prompt refinement pays off on repeated tasks, so finish this one by hand
Continue refining, since the prompt will be reusable for similar tasks in the future
Ask Claude to write the prompt, since prompt engineering is itself a task it handles well
Lower the quality bar for this task so the current version of the prompt is acceptable
questions.why: The economics of prompting depend on repetition. Refinement is an investment amortised over runs, and for a genuine one-off there are no future runs to amortise it against.
questions.traps: Assuming future reuse is what the scenario has already disproven for this task. Meta-prompting does not change the arithmetic, and quietly lowering the bar trades quality for a sunk cost.

questions.stem: A training coordinator asks Claude to "make a quiz" about a new policy and receives ten questions, all of which test whether the reader can recall the policy's wording rather than apply it.
options: Ask for harder questions so the difficulty rises above simple wording recall
Specify that questions must test application rather than recall
Provide the policy in full so the questions have more material to draw on
Request more questions so that some of them happen to test practical application
questions.why: Recall and application are different question types, and recall is the default when a source text is supplied. Naming the cognitive level is the instruction that changes what gets generated.
questions.traps: Difficulty is not the same axis as application — a hard recall question is still recall. More material and more questions both scale the same default.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to "clean up" a dataset description and it silently corrects two figures that were unusual but correct, because they looked like typos.
options: Ask Claude to list its changes afterwards so the corrections can be reviewed and reverted
Provide the dataset itself so the unusual figures can be verified before editing
Ask for a lighter edit so fewer changes are made to the original description overall
Say which kinds of change are permitted, and that factual values must be left untouched entirely
questions.why: "Clean up" licenses unbounded editing. Bounding the permitted change types is what protects content the model would otherwise read as an error worth fixing.
questions.traps: A change log helps only if someone audits it every time. Supplying data enlarges the task, and asking for less editing reduces the rate without removing the licence.

questions.stem: A team receives an analysis from Claude that answers a slightly different question than the one they asked, but does so thoroughly and convincingly.
options: Accept the analysis, since a thorough answer to a related question is usually still useful
Restate the question and ask directly whether the analysis answers it as it was asked
Ask for a longer analysis so the original question is covered somewhere within it
Rephrase the question with simpler wording and run the whole analysis again
questions.why: A fluent answer to the wrong question is a recognised failure mode precisely because fluency masks the mismatch. Checking answer against question is the habit that catches it.
questions.traps: Accepting it embeds the drift into your work. Length buries the original question further, and rerunning without diagnosing the mismatch may reproduce it.

questions.stem: An internal comms draft written by Claude lands badly with staff because it uses the optimistic register of an external press release for an announcement about a hiring freeze.
options: Ask for a more serious tone so the optimism is reduced in the final version
Shorten the announcement so there is less room for inappropriate framing to appear
Tell Claude who the readers are and what register the situation calls for
Have Claude write three versions in different tones and pick the most suitable one
questions.why: Register follows from audience and stakes. Naming both is what lets the model choose a tone that fits, rather than defaulting to the promotional voice most announcement text is written in.
questions.traps: A vague tone instruction narrows the range without grounding it. Shortening and sampling both work around a gap that one sentence of context would close.

questions.stem: A consultant asks Claude to critique a client's strategy. The critique is sharp and well-argued, but assumes resources the client does not have.
options: State the client's real constraints before asking for the critique
Ask for a gentler critique so the recommendations feel more achievable to the client
Request that Claude focus on strengths as well as weaknesses in the strategy document
Ask for the critique to be shorter so only the most feasible points survive
questions.why: A critique implies alternatives, and alternatives are bounded by resources. Without the constraints, the model compares the strategy to an idealised option set the client cannot reach.
questions.traps: Softening changes delivery, not feasibility. Balance and brevity both leave the recommendations resting on resources that do not exist.

questions.stem: A multinational team gets Claude to draft a policy summary. It is accurate for the head office jurisdiction but wrong for two regions, neither of which was mentioned in the prompt.
options: Ask Claude whether the summary applies internationally after reading the initial draft
Name the jurisdictions in scope and ask for the differences between them to be called out
Request a more general summary that avoids jurisdiction-specific claims altogether
Have each region review the summary and correct the parts that do not apply to them
questions.why: Jurisdiction is a scoping input. Asking for the differences up front turns an invisible assumption into explicit content that regional reviewers can actually check.
questions.traps: A follow-up question invites a post-hoc rationalisation of a draft already written. Generality removes the useful detail, and regional review is a fallback rather than a fix.

questions.stem: An associate provides one example of a well-written status update. Claude matches it closely, including a project-specific abbreviation that means nothing on other projects.
options: Explain the abbreviation so Claude uses it correctly in future status updates
Ask Claude not to copy anything specific from the example it has been given
Provide two or three varied examples so the pattern is separable from the specifics
Write the example in a more generic style so nothing project-specific appears in it
questions.why: Variation is what separates signal from incident. With a single example, every feature looks essential; with several, the shared structure stands out and the incidental details fall away.
questions.traps: Explaining the abbreviation preserves it. A blanket instruction not to copy specifics is vague enough to lose the pattern too, and a sanitised example is weaker than a varied set.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude to score support tickets from one to five for urgency. Their examples cover scores of one, three and five, and the model rarely produces a two or a four.
options: Instruct Claude to use the whole scale including the intermediate values
Ask for a score with one decimal place so intermediate judgements have somewhere to go
Reduce the scale to three points, since the model is effectively using three anyway
Add examples at the intermediate scores so the full range is demonstrated
questions.why: Demonstrated values become the usable range. Unexemplified points read as unavailable, so the fix is to show the model what a two and a four actually look like.
questions.traps: An instruction to use the range does not say where the boundaries sit. Decimals and rescaling both redesign the measurement rather than teaching the one you have.

questions.stem: An associate includes six examples in every prompt for a simple two-way classification. The task works, but each call is slow and costs more than the team expected.
options: Test whether fewer examples hold the accuracy on this task
Keep the six examples, because accuracy is more important than the cost per call
Move the examples into a project so they do not need to be sent with each request
Combine several classifications into one call so the examples are amortised across them
questions.why: Example count has diminishing returns, and a binary decision usually saturates within two or three. Measuring where accuracy plateaus is how you find the cheap point without guessing.
questions.traps: Assuming six are needed skips the test. Batching and reuse both reduce cost per item but neither asks the prior question of whether the examples earn their place.

questions.stem: A team asks for a summary "in bullet points" and receives eleven bullets, several of which run to four lines and read as paragraphs with a marker in front.
options: Ask for fewer bullets so each one carries proportionally more of the content
Request that Claude use sub-bullets to break up the longer points in the summary
Ask for a table instead, since tables impose more structure than bullet lists do
Specify a maximum count and a maximum length per bullet so the format constraint is real
questions.why: A bullet is a shape, not a size. Constraining count and length is what makes the format do the compression work that was the point of asking for bullets.
questions.traps: Fewer bullets makes each one longer. Sub-bullets add structure to sprawl, and switching to a table changes the artefact rather than fixing the brevity.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to produce a document with a specific heading hierarchy. It looks right on screen but the levels are inconsistent when pasted into the company template.
options: Ask Claude to use larger text for the top-level headings so the hierarchy is clearer
Paste as plain text and apply the company's heading styles by hand afterwards
State the exact heading levels wanted, then check the structure after pasting
Request that Claude describe the intended hierarchy in a note above the document
questions.why: What looks like a heading and what is tagged as one are different things, and only the second survives a paste into a styled template. Stating levels and verifying is the reliable path.
questions.traps: Font size is presentation, not structure. Manual restyling works but repeats forever, and a descriptive note leaves the actual document unchanged.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to produce a 30-page handbook in one request. The result is thin in the middle sections and repeats itself between chapters four and seven.
options: Ask for the handbook again and specify that repetition should be avoided throughout
Generate an agreed outline first, then write sections against it one at a time
Request a longer handbook so the thin middle sections receive more coverage
Write the middle sections separately and splice them into the single-pass draft
questions.why: A long single pass loses track of what it has already covered. An outline gives each section a defined job, which is what prevents both the thin patches and the overlap.
questions.traps: An anti-repetition instruction does not give the model a map. More length spreads the same problem, and splicing patches symptoms without an organising structure.

questions.stem: An associate chains three Claude steps in a manual workflow. Step two occasionally produces output in the wrong shape, and step three fails confusingly when it does.
options: Validate step two's output against its expected shape first
Combine the three steps into one prompt so there are no handoffs that can fail
Add an instruction to step three telling it to handle unexpected input gracefully
Rerun the whole chain whenever step three produces a confusing result
questions.why: Chains need contracts at the boundaries. Checking shape at the handoff turns a confusing downstream failure into a clear, local one you can actually act on.
questions.traps: Merging the steps hides the failure rather than removing it. Graceful handling in step three masks bad input, and blind reruns treat a deterministic shape problem as noise.

questions.stem: A brand team tells Claude to write "on brand" copy. The output is competent but generic, because the brand guidelines were never supplied.
options: Ask Claude what it understands the brand to be before requesting the copy
Name a comparable brand and ask Claude to write in a similar style to that one
Ask for several versions so at least one is likely to land near the brand voice
Supply the actual guidelines, or several examples of copy the team considers on brand
questions.why: "On brand" is a pointer to a document the model cannot see. Supplying the guidelines or exemplars is what converts the phrase into something actionable.
questions.traps: Asking the model what it thinks your brand is invites invention. A comparable brand imports someone else's voice, and sampling hopes for a hit.

questions.stem: An associate needs a summary that a specific executive will read in under two minutes, but keeps specifying the constraint as "keep it brief".
options: Say that the reader is busy so Claude applies stronger compression to the summary
Give the constraint in measurable terms, such as a word count or a point count
Ask for the shortest possible version and expand it if too much has been lost
Provide the executive's job title so Claude can judge the appropriate length
questions.why: Brief is relative and the model has no anchor for yours. A number is checkable by both of you, which is what makes it a constraint rather than a preference.
questions.traps: Signalling busyness is another relative cue. Shortest-possible overshoots in the other direction, and a job title implies nothing reliable about reading time.

questions.stem: An analyst asks Claude to compare two uploaded contracts. The comparison is detailed but treats a clause as differing when the two contracts use different wording for the same obligation.
options: Ask Claude to compare the contracts again and focus only on substantive differences
Upload the contracts in the same format so wording differences are less prominent
Ask for the obligation each clause creates rather than how each is worded
Request that Claude quote both clauses so the wording can be compared side by side
questions.why: Contract comparison is about effect, not text. Asking what each clause obliges shifts the analysis to the level where a difference actually matters.
questions.traps: A vague instruction to be substantive does not define the level. Format normalisation and side-by-side quotes both keep the comparison at the wording layer.

questions.stem: A team uploads a 200-page manual and asks a narrow question. The answer is correct, but the same question asked an hour later returns a slightly different and less complete answer.
options: Ask a more specific question naming the section or topic
Ask the question several times and take whichever answer appears most frequently
Split the manual into smaller documents so each question searches less material
Accept the variation, since answers over long documents are inherently non-deterministic
questions.why: Retrieval over a long document varies with how the question is framed. Narrowing the question is the lever you control, and it makes the relevant passage far easier to land on.
questions.traps: Majority voting spends three calls to paper over framing. Splitting the manual is real work with maintenance cost, and accepting variance abandons a fixable problem.

questions.stem: An associate keeps asking Claude to "make it punchier" and the copy gets shorter each round until important qualifications have been removed.
options: Stop after two rounds, since further requests reduce quality more than they improve it
Name what must survive the edit alongside the stylistic direction that is being requested
Ask for punchier language but the same length so nothing is lost in the process
Restore the qualifications by hand once the punchy version is finished
questions.why: Stylistic instructions without preservation constraints compound. Each round removes what the previous round left, so the constraint has to be carried alongside the direction.
questions.traps: A round limit is arbitrary and stops mid-way. Fixed length invites padding, and manual restoration undoes work the model was asked to do.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to revise a document and it rewrites sections that were already approved, because the request did not distinguish them from the sections under review.
options: Ask Claude to revise the document more conservatively across all of its sections
Paste only the sections that need revision and reassemble the document afterwards
Ask Claude to explain which sections it changed so unwanted edits can be reverted
Mark the approved sections as fixed and name only the sections open for revision
questions.why: Scope has to be marked or everything is in scope. Declaring the fixed sections is what protects approved text while keeping the whole document available as context.
questions.traps: Conservatism is a degree, not a boundary. Pasting fragments loses context, and post-hoc change logs put the burden on review rather than preventing the edit.

questions.stem: A team's prompt asks for JSON. It works most of the time, but occasionally Claude wraps the JSON in an explanation of what the fields mean.
options: Ask Claude to stop explaining its output in the instruction at the top of the prompt
Request that the explanation appear after the structure so it can be truncated
Say the response must contain the structure alone, and parse defensively
Use a simpler structure so there is less about it that invites explanation
questions.why: Instruction plus validation is the durable pattern for machine-consumed output. The instruction lowers the rate and the parser handles what gets through, which no wording alone will eliminate.
questions.traps: A single instruction leaves the residual failures unhandled. Repositioning and simplifying both reduce the odds without protecting the consumer.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to "check this for accuracy" against a document they did not upload, and receives a general plausibility assessment they mistake for verification.
options: Supply the source and ask for a claim-by-claim check against it
Ask Claude to state its confidence in each claim so weak points can be identified
Rephrase the request as a fact-check so the model applies a stricter standard
Ask Claude to search for supporting evidence for each claim in the document
questions.why: Accuracy is relative to a source. Without one, the model can only assess whether claims sound plausible, which is a different and much weaker thing than checking them.
questions.traps: Confidence and stricter framing both operate without a reference. Searching introduces a source but not the one the document is supposed to match.

questions.stem: An associate asks for a technical explanation "for a beginner" and gets an accurate piece that still assumes the reader knows what an API is.
options: Ask for a simpler explanation and repeat until no unfamiliar terms remain in it
Say what the reader already knows and what they do not, rather than using a relative label
Request that every technical term be defined the first time it is used in the text
Ask for an analogy-based explanation so no technical vocabulary is needed at all
questions.why: Beginner is relative to a field. Stating the actual knowledge boundary is what lets the model pitch correctly on the first attempt rather than converging through rounds.
questions.traps: Iterating to simplicity is slow and can overshoot. Inline definitions and pure analogy are both reasonable techniques that still need to know where the reader starts.

questions.stem: A team's classification prompt includes eight examples, seven of which are the common category. The model now labels almost everything as that category.
options: Add more examples of the rare categories until the total example count reaches twenty
Tell Claude that the rare categories are important and should not be overlooked
Balance the examples across categories rather than mirroring the real-world frequency
Run the rare cases through a separate prompt built specifically for those categories
questions.why: Example distribution reads as a prior. Mirroring real frequency in a small set pushes the model toward the majority label, so balance is what keeps the minority categories reachable.
questions.traps: Padding the count without balancing keeps the skew. An importance instruction fights the demonstrated pattern, and a separate prompt needs the classification that is failing.

questions.stem: An associate wants a comparison table but keeps getting a narrative that describes the comparison in prose instead.
options: Specify the columns and rows wanted rather than simply naming a table
Ask more firmly for a table and state that prose is not acceptable in the response
Provide an example of the table filled in with placeholder values for the model to match
Ask for the prose version first and then request that it be converted to a table
questions.why: Naming the artefact is weaker than specifying its structure. Columns and rows define the table concretely enough that prose stops being a plausible response.
questions.traps: Firmness does not add structure. An example works but is more effort than naming the columns, and the two-step conversion doubles calls for the same result.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to draft a report and check its own figures in the same request. The figures are checked, but the check confirms the numbers Claude itself produced.
options: Ask Claude to be more rigorous when checking the figures within the same response
Request that Claude show its calculations so the checking step is easier to follow
Ask for the check first and then have the draft written around the verified figures
Separate the drafting and the checking into two requests
questions.why: A check inside the same pass validates the model's own reasoning against itself. Independence is the property that makes verification meaningful, and it needs a separate step.
questions.traps: Rigour instructions do not create independence. Shown working helps a human reviewer, and reordering still leaves both steps inside one generation.

questions.stem: A legal team asks Claude to summarise obligations from a contract and specifies that nothing should be added. The summary is faithful but omits an obligation buried in an appendix.
options: Ask for a longer summary so more of the document's content is represented in it
Request that Claude count the obligations so the total can be checked against expectations
State that appendices and schedules are in scope, since obligations hide outside the main body
Ask the question a second time focusing specifically on the appendices of the contract
questions.why: Scope in a structured document includes its attachments, and they are easy to treat as supplementary. Naming them as in scope is what brings them into the analysis.
questions.traps: Length does not redirect attention to a section treated as peripheral. A count reveals a discrepancy only if you know the true number, and a second pass is a fix after the fact.

questions.stem: An associate asks a question about an uploaded spreadsheet and gets an answer based on the column headers rather than the values underneath them.
options: Convert the spreadsheet to a document format before uploading it for analysis
Ask a question that requires the values and say the answer must come from the rows
Ask Claude to describe the spreadsheet's structure before answering the question
Reduce the number of columns so the relevant data is easier to identify
questions.why: Headers are salient and self-describing, so a loosely framed question can be answered from them alone. Requiring the answer to rest on the rows forces the model into the actual data.
questions.traps: Reformatting and trimming columns both change presentation without changing what the question demands. A structural description is a useful preliminary but not the fix.

questions.stem: A team has a prompt that works at 85% accuracy. Three rounds of refinement have each moved it by less than a percentage point, and one round made it worse.
options: Accept that the prompt has plateaued and address the rest another way
Continue refining, since accuracy improvements compound over enough iterations
Revert to the original prompt and begin the refinement process again from the start
Add more instructions covering each of the specific errors that still occur
questions.why: Refinement has diminishing returns, and a plateau is a signal to change approach rather than to push harder. The remaining errors usually need review, validation, or task redesign.
questions.traps: Continued refinement is the sunk-cost path the plateau argues against. Restarting rediscovers the same ceiling, and stacking error-specific instructions makes prompts brittle.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to write "a short professional bio" without saying where it will appear, and gets a version that is wrong for the conference programme it was meant for.
options: Ask for a more formal bio, since conference materials call for a professional register
Provide the person's full career history so the bio has more material to select from
Ask for several bios of different lengths and choose whichever fits the programme
State the destination and the conventions that go with it
questions.why: Destination determines length, person, and what gets emphasised. Naming it supplies all three constraints at once, which no amount of source material or formality does.
questions.traps: Formality is one dimension of several. More history expands the input without narrowing the output, and sampling lengths guesses at conventions.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to explain a delay to a customer. The draft is honest and clear but reveals an internal supplier dispute the company does not want disclosed.
options: Ask for a vaguer explanation so the sensitive details are less likely to appear
State what may not be disclosed, because a candid explanation uses whatever it knows
Remove the supplier information from the prompt before asking for the explanation
Review each draft before sending and remove any sensitive content that appears
questions.why: Confidentiality is a constraint the model has no way to infer. Naming the off-limits material lets it write candidly about everything else, which vagueness would sacrifice.
questions.traps: Vagueness costs the clarity the message needs. Withholding context weakens the explanation, and per-draft review is a safety net rather than an instruction.

questions.stem: A team writes examples showing the reasoning they want, but only the final answers appear in the examples, and Claude's outputs skip the reasoning too.
options: Include the reasoning in the examples themselves, not only the answers
Ask Claude to explain its reasoning in addition to matching the example format
Provide more examples so the underlying reasoning pattern becomes apparent
Ask for the reasoning in a follow-up request after the answer has been produced
questions.why: Examples demonstrate the shape of a complete response. If the reasoning is absent from them, the demonstrated shape is answer-only, and that is what gets copied.
questions.traps: An added instruction competes with the demonstrated pattern. More answer-only examples reinforce it, and a follow-up produces reasoning constructed after the answer.

questions.stem: An associate needs consistent date formatting across a generated report. Dates appear correctly in most places but drift to a different convention inside tables.
options: Ask Claude to use a consistent date format throughout the whole document
Convert all dates to text so the model does not reformat them automatically
Generate the tables separately with their own formatting instruction attached
State the date format explicitly and check it inside the tables
questions.why: Local conventions inside structured elements are a known drift point, so the reliable approach is an explicit format plus a targeted check where drift concentrates.
questions.traps: A general consistency instruction has already implicitly failed. Text conversion fights the model, and separate generation adds steps to solve a formatting detail.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to both find the problems in a process and design its replacement. The replacement is elegant but solves only the problems listed first.
options: Ask for the design again and specify that every listed problem must be addressed
Ask for several designs so between them all the problems are likely covered
Complete and review the problem list before asking for a design
Request that the design include a table mapping each problem to its solution
questions.why: Diagnosis and design in one pass lets the design's momentum truncate the diagnosis. Separating them makes the problem list a reviewable artefact before it constrains a solution.
questions.traps: Insisting on coverage of a list still generated in the same breath does not fix it. Multiple designs and mapping tables both organise an incomplete list.

questions.stem: A team asks for social posts and specifies a character limit. The posts fit, but the limit was applied before hashtags and links were added.
options: State that the limit includes hashtags and links, since the model counts what it is told
Ask for shorter posts so there is headroom for the hashtags and links to be added
Add the hashtags and links by hand once the posts are within the character limit
Ask Claude to count the characters and report the total for each post it produces
questions.why: Limits need their boundaries defined. Saying what counts toward the total is what makes the constraint match the platform's own measurement rather than the model's assumption.
questions.traps: Headroom is guesswork. Manual addition works but repeats, and a reported count measures the same wrongly-scoped total.

questions.stem: A researcher asks Claude to extract every mention of a term from a long document. The extraction is accurate for the term itself but misses the places where a synonym was used.
options: Ask for a second pass over the document to catch anything the first pass missed
List the synonyms and variants that count as the same concept here
Ask Claude to search for the concept rather than the exact term in the document
Reduce the document length so the model can attend to all of it at once
questions.why: Extraction follows the definition it is given. Enumerating the variants converts a string match into a concept match with boundaries you control rather than ones the model infers.
questions.traps: A second pass repeats the same definition. Asking for the concept without enumerating it leaves the boundary to the model, and shortening does not address vocabulary.

questions.stem: An associate needs a competitor analysis covering eight companies across five dimensions. A single prompt returns a matrix where the later companies are described in noticeably less detail.
options: Ask for the matrix again and specify that all eight companies deserve equal treatment
Reduce the analysis to three dimensions so all eight companies fit comfortably
Ask Claude to start with the companies that were previously covered least thoroughly
Handle the companies in batches and combine the results once each batch is complete
questions.why: Attention thins across a long generation, so later items get less. Batching gives every company a comparable share of a fresh pass, which an instruction inside one pass cannot manufacture.
questions.traps: Equal-treatment instructions do not change how generation degrades. Cutting dimensions loses analysis, and reordering moves the thin end rather than removing it.

questions.stem: A team pipes Claude's summary of a meeting into a second prompt that drafts follow-up emails. When the summary misreads an action item, the emails commit the company to it.
options: Ask the email step to verify the action items against the original transcript
Combine both steps so the emails are generated directly from the meeting transcript
Review the summary before it feeds the email step
Add an instruction telling the email step to be cautious about commitments it makes
questions.why: The severity of an error rises at each stage of a chain. A review gate at the point where a mistake is still cheap is what stops it becoming an external commitment.
questions.traps: Verification inside the email step re-reads a transcript it was not given. A merged step removes the checkpoint entirely, and caution does not detect a misread.

questions.stem: An associate splits a large task into six Claude steps. Each step works well alone, but the end-to-end result is incoherent because each step made different assumptions about the audience.
options: Fix the shared context once and pass it into every step so the assumptions cannot diverge
Add a final step that rewrites the combined output into a single consistent voice
Reduce the pipeline to three larger steps so there are fewer places to diverge
Ask each step to infer the audience from the output of the step before it
questions.why: Decomposition creates independent contexts, and anything not passed explicitly gets re-invented per step. Pinning shared context at the top is what keeps six outputs describing one thing.
questions.traps: A rewrite step papers over divergent substance with consistent tone. Fewer steps reduces the count of divergences, and chained inference compounds drift.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to analyse survey results and write recommendations. The recommendations are sensible in general but do not follow from anything in the survey data.
options: Ask for the recommendations again with an instruction to ground them in the data
Provide more of the survey data so the recommendations have more to draw on
Ask for the findings first, then ask for recommendations that cite specific findings
Request that the recommendations be ranked by how strongly the data supports them
questions.why: Recommendations generated alongside analysis default to domain common sense. Requiring each one to cite a finding creates a link you can check, which is what grounding means operationally.
questions.traps: A grounding instruction without a citable artefact is unenforceable. More data and confidence ranking both operate on the same ungrounded generation.

questions.stem: An associate gives Claude feedback in a long paragraph covering six separate issues. The next draft fixes two of them well and ignores the rest.
options: Repeat the feedback paragraph until all six issues have been resolved in the draft
Give the feedback as a numbered list so each issue is a discrete item to address
Give the feedback one issue at a time across six separate rounds of revision
Ask Claude to list the issues it identified in the feedback before revising the draft
questions.why: Prose feedback buries items; a list makes each one a countable obligation. It also makes it obvious to you which were skipped, which a paragraph does not.
questions.traps: Repetition retries the same unstructured input. Six rounds works but is slow, and asking for a restatement adds a step without changing the structure of the request.

questions.stem: A team keeps a very long conversation going while refining a document. Recent instructions are followed well but a constraint set at the start is now regularly violated.
options: Start a new conversation whenever the current one becomes difficult to steer
Ask Claude to summarise all constraints agreed so far before each new revision
Move the constraint to the end of each message so it appears most recently
Restate the standing constraints as the thread grows
questions.why: Earlier instructions compete with a growing conversation. Restating what must remain true keeps a standing constraint in effect rather than trusting it to survive.
questions.traps: A fresh start loses the accumulated work. A self-summary can omit the same forgotten item, and position alone does not make a constraint durable across turns.

questions.stem: An associate asks for a rewrite, likes it less than the previous version, and cannot easily get back to what they had.
options: Keep the versions you liked outside the conversation so a good draft is never lost
Ask Claude to reproduce the earlier version from its memory of the conversation
Scroll back and continue the conversation from the point before the rewrite
Ask for both versions to be produced side by side in every future revision
questions.why: Iteration is lossy and drafts are cheap to store. Keeping good versions outside the thread makes reverting trivial instead of dependent on reconstruction.
questions.traps: Reproduction from memory is approximate. Scrolling back helps within one session but not across them, and side-by-side output doubles length every round.

questions.stem: A team's refinement process improves the prompt for their test cases, but performance on new cases has quietly got worse over the last several rounds.
options: Add the new failing cases to the test set and continue refining against the larger set
Refine for fewer rounds so the prompt does not become too closely fitted
Hold back a set of cases not used during refinement and check against them periodically
Test on more cases from the same source so the measurement becomes more stable
questions.why: Tuning against the cases you measure on inflates the measurement. A held-back set is the only way to see whether gains are real or specific to the examples you optimised toward.
questions.traps: Absorbing failures into the tuning set removes the independent check. Fewer rounds and more same-source cases both leave the measurement contaminated.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude for "options" for restructuring a department and receives three, all of which involve redundancies the leadership had ruled out.
options: Ask for more options so that some avoid redundancies among the larger set
State the ruled-out options up front so alternatives are available
Ask Claude to assess each option's feasibility after it has been generated
Rephrase the request to emphasise growth rather than restructuring the department
questions.why: Exclusions shape generation only if stated. Ruling out the obvious answer is what pushes the model into the space of options you can actually consider.
questions.traps: More options resamples the same space. Post-hoc feasibility filters what should not have been generated, and reframing the goal changes the question being asked.

questions.stem: An associate specifies "no more than five recommendations" and gets five, but three of them contain two recommendations joined by "and".
options: Ask for three recommendations instead so there is less pressure to combine them
Ask Claude to split any compound recommendations after the list is produced
Request that recommendations be short so there is no room to combine two
Say that each item must be a single action
questions.why: A count is a weak constraint when the unit is undefined. Defining what one item is prevents compression from smuggling extra content past the limit.
questions.traps: Lowering the count increases the pressure to compound. Post-hoc splitting and brevity both address the symptom without defining the unit.

questions.stem: A team tells Claude to avoid mentioning a competitor by name. The copy complies, but describes the competitor so specifically that any reader would know who it is.
options: State that indirect identification is also out of scope, not just the literal name
Ask Claude to avoid comparisons altogether so no competitor can be identified
Review the copy and remove any description that identifies the competitor
Replace the competitor's name with a generic placeholder throughout the copy
questions.why: Constraints are read literally. If the intent is that the competitor not be identifiable, that is the constraint to state, because a name ban only bans the name.
questions.traps: Removing comparisons discards useful content. Manual review is a check rather than an instruction, and a placeholder still carries the identifying description.

questions.stem: An associate stacks eleven separate constraints into a single prompt. The output satisfies most of them, but two are violated in every attempt and they happen to conflict with each other.
options: Add emphasis to the two violated constraints so they receive more attention
Split the constraints across two prompts so each carries a smaller set
Identify the conflicting pair and decide which of them takes priority
Accept the violations and correct the two constraints by hand afterwards
questions.why: Persistent violation of the same two constraints across attempts points to a contradiction rather than inattention. No amount of emphasis satisfies two incompatible requirements at once.
questions.traps: Emphasis cannot resolve a conflict. Splitting distributes the contradiction across calls, and manual correction leaves the specification broken for next time.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to answer from an uploaded FAQ. It answers correctly but adds two extra tips that are sensible and not in the FAQ.
options: Ask Claude to mark which parts of its answer came from the document
Instruct Claude to answer strictly from the document alone
Ask a narrower question so there is less room to add supplementary advice
Remove the extra tips manually before the answer is published to customers
questions.why: Helpfulness adds content unless bounded. A strict-grounding instruction is what keeps the answer traceable to a source you have approved.
questions.traps: Source marking is self-reported and unreliable. Narrowing reduces the surface, and manual removal is a repeated cost rather than a control.

questions.stem: An analyst asks about trends in an uploaded dataset covering 2019 to 2024. Claude's answer describes a trend continuing into 2025, which is not in the data.
options: Ask for the trend analysis again with an instruction to be conservative
Add the 2025 data to the upload so the projection can be verified
Ask Claude to label any projection so it is distinguishable from observed data
Instruct Claude to confine claims to the period covered
questions.why: Extrapolation reads as a natural completion of a trend. Stating the boundary of the data is what keeps described trends inside what was actually observed.
questions.traps: Conservatism is vague. Adding data moves the boundary without defining it, and labelling relies on the model recognising its own extrapolation.

questions.stem: A team uploads meeting minutes and asks who is responsible for a decision. Claude names the person who spoke most about the topic rather than the person assigned to it.
options: Ask the question again using the word accountable rather than responsible
Upload a document listing team roles so the assignment can be inferred correctly
Ask specifically for explicit assignments, and for a blank where none has been recorded
Ask Claude to list everyone who discussed the topic and choose from that list
questions.why: Prominence in a transcript is a strong but wrong signal for ownership. Asking for explicit assignment, and allowing a blank, prevents inference from filling the gap.
questions.traps: Synonyms do not change the inference. A roles document invites a different wrong inference, and a discussion list restates the same conflation for you to resolve.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to compare an uploaded policy against a regulation that was not uploaded. The comparison is fluent and cites regulation clauses that do not exist.
options: Ask Claude to state its confidence in the regulation clauses that it cites
Ask the question again to see whether the same clause numbers are produced
Ask Claude to note where its knowledge of the regulation may be out of date
Upload the regulation, since a comparison needs both sides present
questions.why: A comparison against an absent document is generated from recollection, and specific clause numbers are the least reliable part of that. Supplying the text is what makes the comparison checkable.
questions.traps: Confidence, repetition and staleness notes all operate on recalled content. Repetition in particular can reproduce the same fabricated numbers consistently.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to write a proposal and then, in the same request, to critique it and produce a final version. The critique is mild and the final version barely changes.
options: Run the critique as a request of its own
Ask for a harsher critique so more substantive changes appear in the final version
Ask for the critique to be written before the proposal is drafted
Request that the critique list a minimum number of specific problems
questions.why: Self-critique in the same pass inherits a commitment to the draft. Separating it removes the authorship stake that makes the critique gentle.
questions.traps: Harshness and quotas force volume rather than independence. Critiquing before drafting has nothing to critique.

questions.stem: An associate asks for content "suitable for LinkedIn" and gets posts with a promotional tone that does not match how their team actually writes there.
options: Ask for a less promotional tone so the posts sound more natural to readers
Describe the tone and conventions your team uses
Provide the company's other social content so the tone can be inferred from it
Ask for several tonal variations and select the one closest to the team's voice
questions.why: A platform implies a format more than a voice, and the model's default for it is the most common register. Describing your conventions is what replaces that default.
questions.traps: A negative instruction removes one thing without specifying a target. Inference from other channels and sampling both approximate what a sentence could state.

questions.stem: A team's reviewer sends feedback like "this section feels off" and the resulting revisions are unpredictable, sometimes better and sometimes worse.
options: Pass the feedback through unchanged, since the model can interpret informal language
Ask Claude to propose several interpretations of the feedback and pick one
Ask the reviewer to revise the section themselves rather than describing the problem
Translate impressionistic feedback into a specific defect before passing it to the model
questions.why: Impressionistic feedback names a symptom without a cause, and interpreting it is the reviewer's job or yours. Passing the ambiguity to the model makes the outcome a coin flip.
questions.traps: Interpretation by the model is exactly the unpredictability described. Multiple interpretations moves the guess, and asking the reviewer to write it themselves discards their role as reviewer.

questions.stem: A team automates a three-step process. Steps one and three are reliable, but step two involves a judgement call that the team disagrees about internally.
options: Automate step two anyway and correct the outputs when they are wrong
Ask Claude to make the judgement and explain its reasoning for later review
Keep step two with a person until the team agrees on the rule
Have Claude apply the most common interpretation used within the team
questions.why: An unsettled judgement cannot be specified, and an unspecified step cannot be automated correctly. The disagreement is a prerequisite to fix, not something a model resolves.
questions.traps: Automating an undefined rule produces confidently wrong outputs. Explanations and majority interpretation both encode a position the team has not actually agreed.
