questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to summarise an uploaded report's conclusions. The summary is accurate but presents a tentative finding with the same certainty as a confirmed one.
options: Ask for a longer summary so the hedging language has room to survive
Ask for the strength of evidence alongside each conclusion
Ask Claude to quote the conclusions directly rather than paraphrasing them
Read the conclusions section yourself rather than relying on a summary
questions.why: Summarisation compresses hedges first because they read as filler. Making evidential strength an explicit requirement keeps the distinction that matters most for decisions.
questions.traps: Length does not protect hedges specifically. Direct quotes avoid the problem by avoiding summarisation, and reading it yourself forfeits the task.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude for a risk register and specifies ten risks. The list includes several near-duplicates because the count was treated as a target to fill.
options: Ask for the risks that genuinely apply, with the count as a ceiling
Ask for twenty risks and remove the duplicates from the longer list afterwards
Ask Claude to check the list for duplicates once it has been generated
Specify categories so each risk comes from a different area of the business
questions.why: A fixed count is a quota, and quotas get filled. Framing the number as a ceiling lets the honest answer be fewer, which is what stops padding.
questions.traps: A longer list has proportionally more duplication. Self-checking applies after padding, and categories constrain shape without removing the quota pressure.

questions.stem: An associate refines a prompt while testing on a single example. It now handles that example perfectly and fails on the second example they try.
options: Refine further using the second example until both cases work correctly
Write separate prompts for each type of example the team encounters
Test against several varied examples during the refinement rather than a single one
Ask Claude to generalise the prompt so it covers cases beyond the first example
questions.why: Tuning against one case optimises for its particulars. A varied test set is what distinguishes a general improvement from an accommodation of one example.
questions.traps: Adding the second case one at a time repeats the pattern more slowly. Separate prompts multiply maintenance, and asking the model to generalise does not test whether it did.

questions.stem: A team uploads a slide deck and asks what the presenter concluded. Claude answers from the slide text, missing that the final slide's conclusion was contradicted in the speaker notes.
options: Ask for a longer answer so more of the deck's content is included in the response
Ask whether the speaker notes and the slides actually agree with each other
Upload the speaker notes as a separate document from the slide content
Ask Claude to read the final slide more carefully before answering the question
questions.why: A deck is a layered document and the layers can disagree. Asking about agreement makes the discrepancy the object of the question rather than something to be smoothed over.
questions.traps: Length and closer attention to one slide both stay inside a single layer. Separating the files removes the very relationship you need to examine.

questions.stem: An associate breaks a task into steps but finds that step four regularly needs information that was discarded after step two.
options: Ask step four to request the missing information when it needs it
Merge steps two and four so the information does not need to be carried between them
Repeat the original input at every step so nothing is ever discarded
Design the steps around what each one needs downstream
questions.why: Decomposition boundaries should follow information dependencies. Working out what each step consumes is what prevents a later step starving for detail an earlier one dropped.
questions.traps: A step cannot request what is not in its input. Merging distant steps distorts the structure, and repeating everything defeats the purpose of decomposing.

questions.stem: A team asks for a customer email that is "friendly but professional" and gets drafts that swing between casual and formal across different attempts.
options: Give a concrete anchor, such as an example email
Ask for a tone exactly between friendly and professional in the instruction
Ask for several drafts and choose the one that lands in the right place
Define friendly and professional in the prompt so the terms are unambiguous
questions.why: Two abstract tone words define a region, not a point. An exemplar fixes the position concretely, which is why tone is more reliably shown than described.
questions.traps: Asking for a midpoint restates the same abstraction. Sampling leaves consistency to chance, and defining the adjectives adds words without adding an anchor.

questions.stem: A team improves their prompt every time an error occurs. After twenty such fixes the prompt is two pages long and new instructions no longer seem to have much effect.
options: Continue adding fixes, since each one addresses a real error that occurred
Split the two-page prompt into several shorter prompts run one after another
Move the older instructions to the end so the newer ones take precedence
Rebuild the whole prompt around the general rule that all of these fixes share
questions.why: Case-by-case accretion produces a prompt where instructions compete and dilute. Consolidating around the underlying rule restores the leverage each instruction has.
questions.traps: Continuing accretion is what created the plateau. Splitting and reordering redistribute a bloated instruction set without simplifying it.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to find inconsistencies between two uploaded documents. It reports four, of which one is a real conflict and three are differences in emphasis.
options: Ask Claude to rank the four by severity so the real conflict stands out
Define what counts as an inconsistency here before asking for the comparison
Ask for the comparison again and request only the most significant inconsistencies
Ask Claude to explain each inconsistency so the false ones can be identified
questions.why: Inconsistency spans everything from a contradiction to a different framing. Defining the threshold is what makes the output actionable instead of something you have to triage.
questions.traps: Ranking, filtering and explaining all sort a list generated against an undefined standard, leaving the definitional work with you every time.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to keep an announcement "positive" and it omits a change that affects staff pay, because mentioning it would undercut the tone.
options: Separate what must be included from how it should be framed
Ask for a positive tone and a complete announcement in the same instruction
Ask Claude to list what it left out after producing the announcement
Ask for a neutral tone instead so nothing is omitted for tonal reasons
questions.why: A tone constraint applied to an unbounded scope becomes an editorial filter. Fixing required content first, then asking for framing, keeps the two decisions independent.
questions.traps: Adding completeness as a second adjective leaves the conflict unresolved. A post-hoc omissions list is unreliable, and switching to neutral abandons a legitimate goal.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to review thirty CVs against a role. The reviews are consistent for the first ten and become terser and less specific after that.
options: Ask for the review again with an instruction to keep quality consistent throughout
Shorten the role description so more attention is available for each CV
Process the CVs in small batches of five or six
Review the last twenty a second time and use those results instead
questions.why: Depth degrades over a long generation. Batching restores a full attention budget for each group, which is a property of how the work is chunked and not of the instruction.
questions.traps: A consistency instruction cannot allocate attention. Shortening the criteria weakens every review, and re-running the tail creates two different standards.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to improve a document. The result is better written but the specific technical claim they were unsure about has been rephrased into something vaguer.
options: Ask Claude to improve the document without changing any of its meaning
Check the technical claims after each revision and restore them when altered
Ask for a list of suggested improvements rather than a revised document
Ask for improvements to the writing while marking the technical claims as fixed text
questions.why: Rewriting is lossy at exactly the points where the source was uncertain, because vagueness is the path of least resistance. Marking those spans as fixed protects them.
questions.traps: A meaning-preservation instruction is too broad to bind. Post-hoc checking catches the loss late, and a suggestions list is a different deliverable.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude a yes-or-no question about an uploaded policy. It answers yes with a clear explanation, but the policy is genuinely ambiguous on the point.
options: Ask the same question again to see whether the answer is stable across attempts
Ask for a confidence level alongside the yes-or-no answer that is given
Ask what the policy actually says on the point and whether it is clear
Ask a more specific version of the question so the ambiguity is avoided
questions.why: A binary question format forces a binary answer even when the source does not support one. Asking what the document says lets ambiguity appear as the finding it is.
questions.traps: Repetition may return a consistent answer to a question the source cannot settle. Confidence scores are self-reported, and narrowing may miss the ambiguity entirely.

questions.stem: An associate asks for "a summary and any concerns" and receives a summary with no concerns section, because the model judged there were none worth raising.
options: Ask whether there are concerns as a separate follow-up question after the summary
Ask for the concerns section with an explicit none when there are none
Ask for at least two concerns so the section is always populated
Ask for the concerns before the summary so the section is not skipped
questions.why: The word "any" makes a section conditional, and the model resolves the condition silently. Requiring the section plus an explicit none is what makes its absence informative.
questions.traps: A follow-up works but splits a single deliverable. A minimum quota manufactures concerns, and reordering does not remove the conditional.

questions.stem: A team's process has Claude generate a draft, a human edit it, and Claude polish the result. The polish step regularly undoes the human's edits.
options: Tell the polish step which changes were deliberate
Ask the polish step to make only minimal changes to the document it receives
Have the human edit after the polish step rather than before it
Ask Claude to compare the polished version against the human's edits afterwards
questions.why: A later step has no way to distinguish a deliberate edit from an artefact of the draft. Marking the human's changes as intentional is what makes them survive.
questions.traps: Minimal-change instructions are a degree without a target. Reordering leaves the human's work unpolished, and a post-hoc comparison detects the loss late.

questions.stem: An associate has two prompt versions that both look reasonable. They pick the one that produced the better answer on the example they happened to try.
options: Choose the more detailed prompt, since detailed prompts generally perform better
Combine the two prompts so the strengths of each are represented
Ask Claude which of the two prompts it expects to perform better
Compare them across a whole set of varied cases before choosing between the two
questions.why: A single comparison is within the noise of ordinary variation. A set of cases is what turns a preference into a measurement you can rely on.
questions.traps: Detail is not a reliable proxy for performance. Merging produces a third untested prompt, and asking the model to predict is not evidence about outputs.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to "analyse" a customer churn dataset summary. The response describes the data accurately but never says what is driving the churn.
options: Ask for a deeper analysis so the underlying drivers are eventually reached
Ask the specific question you need answered rather than naming an activity like analysis
Provide more of the dataset so the analysis has additional material to work with
Ask Claude to analyse the data from a business perspective instead of a statistical one
questions.why: Naming an activity leaves the model to choose the question. Description satisfies "analyse", so the fix is to ask the actual question you want answered.
questions.traps: Depth and volume both extend a description. A business framing shifts vocabulary without specifying what is being asked.

questions.stem: An associate needs a numbered checklist where each step is independently actionable. Claude returns a numbered list, but several steps depend on decisions made in the surrounding prose.
options: State that each step must be complete on its own without outside reference
Ask for more steps so each one covers a smaller and more actionable unit of work
Request that the prose be removed so only the numbered steps remain in the output
Ask Claude to review the checklist and flag steps that are not independently actionable
questions.why: Independence is a property you have to require. A numbered list looks actionable while still leaning on context, so the constraint has to name the property directly.
questions.traps: Granularity does not create self-containment. Deleting prose leaves steps that referenced it, and self-review repeats the judgement that failed.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to write documentation for a process, giving it the current process description. The documentation describes the process as it should ideally work rather than as it does.
options: Ask for a more accurate version of the documentation in a follow-up request
Provide examples of the workarounds so they appear in the documentation
State that the documentation must describe current practice
Ask Claude to document the process without making any improvements to it
questions.why: Models normalise toward the well-formed version of a process. Naming current practice, workarounds included, is what keeps documentation descriptive rather than aspirational.
questions.traps: A vague accuracy request does not define the target. Supplying workarounds helps but does not stop idealisation elsewhere, and "no improvements" is ambiguous about what counts.

questions.stem: An associate's examples show short inputs producing short outputs. When a genuinely complex case arrives, Claude produces an equally short answer that omits necessary detail.
options: Instruct Claude to write longer answers when the input is more complex than usual
Remove the examples so the model is not anchored to any particular output length
Ask Claude to assess the complexity of each input before producing an answer
Include an example where a complex input produces a correspondingly fuller answer here
questions.why: Examples set an implicit input-to-output ratio. Demonstrating the complex case is what teaches that output length should scale with what the input requires.
questions.traps: A length instruction competes with a demonstrated ratio. Removing examples loses the pattern entirely, and a complexity assessment does not change the response norm.

questions.stem: A team's prompt says to "be concise". Claude produces short answers, but it also drops the caveats that made earlier answers trustworthy.
options: Say what conciseness applies to, and name what must be kept regardless of length
Ask for concise answers that are also complete in a single instruction
Remove the conciseness instruction, since accuracy matters more than brevity
Ask for a concise answer followed by a longer version with the caveats included
questions.why: A global brevity instruction applies to everything, including the parts that carry the reliability. Scoping it, and protecting the caveats, keeps both properties.
questions.traps: Stacking "complete" against "concise" leaves the trade-off unresolved. Dropping the instruction abandons a real need, and two versions doubles the output.

questions.stem: An associate asks for a plan with no dependencies on other teams. The plan complies but is significantly slower, and the constraint was a preference rather than a requirement.
options: State the constraint more softly so Claude knows it is only a preference
Distinguish hard requirements from preferences in the prompt
Ask for two plans, one with the constraint applied and one without it
Remove the constraint and rely on review to catch unwanted dependencies
questions.why: Everything stated as a constraint is treated as binding. Labelling the softer ones is what lets a plan spend a preference to buy something more valuable.
questions.traps: Softer phrasing is still undifferentiated. Two plans is a workable fallback at double the cost, and removing the constraint loses the signal entirely.

questions.stem: A team receives Claude's output in the right structure, but the field values use inconsistent capitalisation that breaks a downstream lookup.
options: Ask Claude to be consistent with capitalisation throughout the output
Convert everything to lower case after receiving the output from the model
Specify the exact casing, then validate before the lookup
Provide a list of the permitted values so Claude can match them exactly
questions.why: Machine-consumed values need an exact specification plus a check. Casing is presentation to the model and load-bearing to the lookup, so it has to be stated and verified.
questions.traps: A consistency instruction has no defined target. Blanket lower-casing may break valid values, and a permitted list helps matching without guaranteeing form.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude for advice on a decision, describing only the option they favour. The advice supports that option and never considers the alternative they had rejected.
options: Ask Claude to play devil's advocate against the option that has been described
Ask for the risks of the favoured option in addition to the advice given
Ask the question again in a neutral tone so the preference is less apparent
Describe the alternatives as well, since advice is fundamentally a comparison here
questions.why: A single option leaves nothing to weigh. Supplying the alternatives is what makes advice a comparison rather than a justification of the option presented.
questions.traps: Devil's advocacy critiques one option without introducing the other. Risks and neutral phrasing both stay inside a single-option frame.

questions.stem: An associate uploads three quarterly reports and asks how a metric changed. Claude gives a clear trend, but has read one of the figures from a chart caption rather than the table.
options: Ask for the trend again and specify that figures should come from the tables
Ask which source each figure came from so the basis of the trend can be checked
Upload only the tables so there is no ambiguity about where figures come from
Ask Claude to show the three figures before describing the trend between them
questions.why: Provenance is what makes a derived number checkable. Asking where each figure came from surfaces the mixed sourcing that a clean trend statement hides.
questions.traps: A table-only instruction is reasonable but unverifiable without provenance. Stripping the documents loses context, and listing figures without their sources leaves the same gap.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to plan a project and estimate its duration in one request. The plan is well-structured and every task is estimated at a suspiciously round number of days.
options: Ask for the plan first, then estimate each of the tasks separately
Ask for more precise estimates so the round numbers are replaced with realistic ones
Ask Claude to explain how it arrived at each of the duration estimates
Ask for a range for each task rather than a single duration figure
questions.why: Estimation generated alongside planning is filler that maintains the plan's rhythm. A separate pass with stated assumptions turns each number into something you can argue with.
questions.traps: Precision instructions produce less round filler. Explanations and ranges dress up numbers that were never derived from anything.

questions.stem: An associate finds that adding "think carefully" to their prompt improved results once, so they now add it to every prompt regardless of the task.
options: Keep the phrase, since encouraging careful reasoning cannot make results worse
Add stronger versions of the phrase to prompts that are still underperforming
Test whether the phrase helps on each separate task type
Remove the phrase entirely, since single observations are not reliable evidence
questions.why: A single observation on one task is not evidence about others. Testing per task type is what distinguishes a real technique from a superstition carried forward.
questions.traps: Assuming it cannot hurt skips measurement on tasks where verbosity is costly. Escalating and blanket removal both act without evidence.

questions.stem: A team specifies that a document must be understandable by a non-specialist. It is, but it is now three times longer because every concept is explained from first principles.
options: Ask for a shorter version once the accessible version has been produced
State the length budget alongside the accessibility requirement so both are constrained
Accept the length, since accessibility was the more important of the two goals
Ask Claude to explain only the concepts that a non-specialist would not know
questions.why: Accessibility without a length budget expands indefinitely. Constraining both is what forces the model to choose which explanations earn their space.
questions.traps: A shortening pass cuts after the fact. Accepting the length gives up a real constraint, and asking it to judge unfamiliarity restates the same open-ended requirement.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to "fix" a section of a report. It rewrites the section fluently, but the section was not broken; it was the surrounding argument that did not connect to it.
options: Describe the symptom you observed rather than the fix you assume
Ask Claude to fix the whole report rather than just the one section
Ask Claude what it thinks is wrong with the section before fixing it
Ask for a more substantial fix so the underlying problem is addressed
questions.why: Asking for a fix at a location asserts a diagnosis. Describing the symptom lets the model locate the problem, which in this case sits outside the section named.
questions.traps: Widening the scope invites unnecessary rewriting. Asking for its opinion on the wrong section keeps the wrong frame, and a bigger fix compounds it.

questions.stem: A team includes examples in their prompt that were written two years ago. The outputs match the examples closely, including a product name that has since been retired.
options: Add a note to the prompt saying the product name in the examples is out of date
Ask Claude to update any outdated details it notices in the examples
Reduce the number of examples so there are fewer opportunities for stale content
Review the examples whenever the underlying facts change
questions.why: Examples are a form of supplied knowledge and go stale like any other. Reviewing them on change is maintenance the pattern requires, not an optional extra.
questions.traps: A correction note competes with a demonstrated pattern. Asking the model to spot staleness assumes knowledge it may not have, and fewer stale examples are still stale.

questions.stem: An associate needs output that a colleague will paste into a presentation. Claude's response uses formatting that renders as literal characters when pasted into the slide tool.
options: Ask the colleague to strip the formatting characters after pasting the content
Ask for shorter output so there are fewer formatting characters to deal with
Specify the plain output the destination tool accepts
Ask Claude to describe the formatting it wants rather than applying it directly
questions.why: Formatting is only meaningful where it renders. Specifying what the destination accepts is what makes output paste cleanly instead of carrying markup as text.
questions.traps: Manual stripping is a repeated cost. Brevity reduces incidence, and a description of intended formatting leaves the colleague to apply it.

questions.stem: A team runs a two-step process where Claude classifies a request and then drafts a response based on the class. Misclassifications produce confident responses in the wrong register.
options: Ask the drafting step to check whether the classification looks correct for the request
Surface the classification so a person can catch a wrong class before the draft is written
Combine the two steps so classification and drafting happen in a single response
Ask for a confidence score on the classification and review the low-confidence cases
questions.why: Making the intermediate visible is what turns a silent pipeline error into a catchable one. The classification is the decision that determines everything downstream.
questions.traps: Self-checking downstream uses the same signal that produced the class. Merging hides the decision entirely, and confidence scores catch only cases the model already doubts.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to write a response to a complaint, giving the complaint text only. The response addresses every point raised but concedes something the company disputes.
options: Ask for a more neutral response that avoids conceding anything to the complainant
Ask Claude to identify the disputed points before drafting the response
Supply the company's position on the disputed points before asking for the response
Review each response and remove concessions before it is sent to the customer
questions.why: The complaint is one side's account. Without the company's position, the model treats every claim as established fact, and a responsive reply concedes them.
questions.traps: Neutrality avoids all positions including the ones you want to state. Asking it to identify disputes without your position is guesswork, and review is a net rather than an input.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to check whether an uploaded proposal meets a list of criteria. It reports that all criteria are met, including one the proposal only partially addresses.
options: Ask for the evidence supporting each of the criteria listed
Ask Claude to be stricter when assessing whether the criteria have been met
Ask for a score against each criterion instead of a simple met-or-not judgement
Ask the question again for each criterion separately in its own request
questions.why: A binary judgement rounds partial evidence to the nearest verdict. Requiring the supporting text makes the strength of each match inspectable.
questions.traps: Strictness moves a threshold without exposing it. Scores are still unexplained judgements, and per-criterion requests repeat the same binary framing.

questions.stem: An associate asks for a rewrite that keeps the document "roughly the same length" and receives a version that is the same length but has traded detail for adjectives.
options: Ask for the rewrite again with an instruction to avoid unnecessary adjectives
Specify an exact word count so the length constraint is more precisely defined
Ask Claude to list what it removed so the lost detail can be restored
Say that the substantive content must be preserved
questions.why: Length is a container, not its contents. Constraining what must survive is what prevents an equal-length rewrite from swapping substance for prose.
questions.traps: Banning adjectives targets one symptom. A precise count tightens the wrong constraint, and a removals list arrives after the loss.

questions.stem: A team gets a good result from Claude once and cannot reproduce it, because the prompt was typed in the middle of a long conversation that has since been lost.
options: Try to recall the wording and reconstruct the prompt from what the team remembers
Ask Claude to reproduce the prompt that generated the earlier result
Capture prompts that work as reusable text outside the conversation where they were written
Accept the variation, since good results are partly a matter of chance
questions.why: A working prompt is an asset and a conversation is not durable storage. Capturing it outside the thread is what makes a good result repeatable.
questions.traps: Reconstruction from memory is lossy. The model cannot recover a prompt from a lost thread, and attributing it to chance discards a real technique.

questions.stem: An associate needs three sections in a fixed order. Claude produces all three with the right content, but reorders them so the conclusion appears first.
options: Ask Claude to reorder the sections after generating them in whatever order it chose
Number the sections so their intended sequence is clear from the content itself
Generate each section separately and assemble them in the correct order
State the required order explicitly rather than leaving it to the model
questions.why: Presentation order is a choice the model makes on rhetorical grounds unless it is specified. Stating the sequence removes the discretion.
questions.traps: A reordering pass is an extra call for a constraint one clause supplies. Numbering is a hint rather than a requirement, and separate generation is heavier than needed.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to identify "the main risk" in a plan and receives one risk, when in fact three risks of comparable severity exist.
options: Ask for the main risk again and then ask whether there are others
Ask for the risks that meet a stated severity threshold
Ask for the top five risks so a broader set is returned each time
Ask Claude to rank all risks it identifies by their severity
questions.why: Asking for one forces a ranking the situation does not support. A threshold lets the true number surface, which is the finding that matters here.
questions.traps: A follow-up recovers the others only if you think to ask. A fixed count of five over-collects, and ranking still starts from a singular framing.

questions.stem: An associate's prompt works well in their own account but produces different results for a colleague, and neither can identify anything different about how they are asking.
options: Compare the project settings and instructions on each account
Assume the difference is normal variation and use whichever output is better
Ask the colleague to retype the prompt in case of a copy-paste difference
Run the prompt several times in each account and compare the average results
questions.why: Account-level configuration is invisible in the prompt but present in every request. Comparing project instructions and settings is where an otherwise identical prompt diverges.
questions.traps: Attributing it to variance skips a systematic cause. Retyping tests a formatting theory, and averaging measures the difference without explaining it.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude to follow a specific reasoning method. They describe the method in detail, but outputs follow it loosely and skip steps under time pressure in longer inputs.
options: Describe the method in more detail so each step is unambiguous to the model
Ask Claude to confirm it will follow the method before it begins the task
Show the method applied end to end on a real case rather than describing the steps
Break the method into separate prompts, one for each step of the process
questions.why: Procedures are followed more reliably when demonstrated than when described, because a worked case shows what each step produces rather than what it is called.
questions.traps: More description is more of what already underperformed. A confirmation is not a behaviour, and one prompt per step is heavier than a single demonstration.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to review a document for five different concerns at once. The review covers all five but treats the most serious concern in a single sentence.
options: Ask for a longer review so each of the five concerns receives more attention
List the concerns in priority order so the most serious is addressed first
Ask Claude to weight its review toward the most serious of the five concerns
Run the serious concern as a dedicated review pass of its own
questions.why: Combined reviews split attention roughly evenly regardless of stakes. A dedicated pass is what gives a serious concern the depth it warrants.
questions.traps: Length raises the floor for all five. Ordering and weighting instructions nudge allocation inside a single pass without changing that it is shared.

questions.stem: A team tells Claude the output must be "suitable for external publication". The draft is polished but includes a forward-looking statement that the company's counsel would not approve.
options: Ask for a more conservative draft that avoids making any claims about the future
Name the specific categories of statement not permitted
Have counsel review each draft before it is published externally
Ask Claude what it thinks counsel would object to in the draft
questions.why: A general suitability standard is not something the model can apply to your legal environment. Naming the prohibited categories converts it into a checkable constraint.
questions.traps: Blanket conservatism removes legitimate content. Counsel review is a necessary control but not a prompting fix, and asking the model to predict counsel is speculation.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to summarise customer feedback from an uploaded file. The summary reflects the written comments but ignores the numeric ratings in the same file.
options: Say which parts of the mixed file should be used
Ask for a longer summary so the ratings are more likely to be included in it
Split the file so the comments and the ratings are uploaded separately
Ask Claude whether it used the ratings after reading the summary it produced
questions.why: Mixed-content files need their parts named. Prose is the salient content for a summarisation request, so the numeric data has to be brought into scope explicitly.
questions.traps: Length does not redirect to a different content type. Splitting the file breaks the link between rating and comment, and a follow-up question is a check rather than an instruction.

questions.stem: A team asks for a report with an executive summary. Claude writes one, but it summarises the report's structure rather than its findings.
options: Ask for a longer executive summary so the findings have room to appear
Ask Claude to write the executive summary after the report is complete
Ask for the summary to be written for an executive audience specifically
Say the summary must state the conclusions and what they actually imply for readers
questions.why: Describing structure is the default reading of "summary" applied to a document. Naming conclusions and implications as the required content is what changes it.
questions.traps: Length expands the description. Writing it last does not change what a summary is taken to mean, and an audience label does not specify content.

questions.stem: An associate is happy with Claude's draft but their manager rejects it for reasons the associate cannot articulate beyond it not feeling right for the company.
options: Collect examples the manager considers right, and use those as the target
Ask the manager to be more specific about what is wrong with the draft
Ask Claude to rewrite the draft in several different styles for the manager to choose
Ask Claude to guess what the manager might be objecting to in the draft
questions.why: Tacit standards are best captured by exemplars rather than descriptions. Collecting approved material turns an unarticulated preference into something a prompt can carry.
questions.traps: Pressing for articulation often fails precisely because the standard is tacit. Sampling styles and guessing both search blindly.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude for a recommendation and gets a balanced discussion of options with no recommendation at the end.
options: Ask for the recommendation again and specify that it must be stated clearly
Ask for a single recommendation that the trade-offs then support
Ask for the discussion first and then request a recommendation separately
Ask Claude to pick an option at random if it cannot decide between them
questions.why: Balanced analysis is the safe default. Asking for a decision, with the analysis in a supporting role, is what makes the model commit rather than survey.
questions.traps: A clarity instruction does not require commitment. A second request works but splits the task, and a random pick discards the judgement entirely.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to draft talking points for a difficult conversation, describing only what they want to say and not how the other person is likely to respond.
options: Ask for more talking points so a wider range of responses is covered
Ask Claude to predict how the conversation is likely to unfold in practice
Describe the other person's likely position first
Ask for the points to be written in a more persuasive style
questions.why: Talking points for a difficult conversation are shaped by the resistance they meet. Supplying the other position is what makes them responsive rather than a monologue.
questions.traps: More points on one side is more monologue. Prediction without information is speculation, and persuasiveness assumes the objections are already known.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to avoid technical terms in a customer-facing document, but the product's own feature names are technical and must appear.
options: Ask Claude to define the feature names when they appear in the document
Exempt the product's own feature names from the restriction when you state it
Apply the restriction and add the feature names back in manually afterwards
Ask for a version with and without technical terms and merge the two
questions.why: Blanket restrictions need their exceptions stated or the model applies them everywhere. Exempting proper product vocabulary is what keeps the document usable.
questions.traps: Definitions address comprehension but not the naming conflict. Manual reinsertion and merging both fix by hand what a clause would have prevented.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to identify action items from an uploaded transcript. It returns eight, two of which were suggestions someone raised and the group explicitly declined.
options: Ask for the items that were agreed, excluding rejected proposals
Ask for a shorter list so only the clearest action items are included
Ask Claude to review the transcript a second time for accuracy
Ask for the action items with the name of whoever proposed each one
questions.why: A transcript records proposals and their fates in the same prose. Defining the inclusion criterion as agreement is what separates a decision from a suggestion.
questions.traps: A shorter list drops items by salience, not status. A second pass repeats the same criterion, and attribution does not encode acceptance.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to both summarise a long document and answer three specific questions about it in a single request. The summary is good and the answers are shallow.
options: Ask for a shorter summary so more of the response is available for the answers
Ask the three questions first and request the summary afterwards
Ask for the answers to be expanded in a follow-up request
Ask the three questions in their own separate request
questions.why: Combining a broad task with specific ones splits the same budget between them. Separating gives the questions a full pass over the source instead of a remainder.
questions.traps: Rebalancing within one response still divides attention. Reordering shifts which task gets the fuller treatment, and an expansion pass elaborates a shallow answer.

questions.stem: An associate's examples all show Claude declining to answer when data is missing. Now it declines on cases where the data is present but formatted unusually.
options: Reduce the number of declining examples so the behaviour is less strongly reinforced
Instruct Claude to decline only when data is genuinely absent from the input
Add examples showing unusual but valid formats being handled
Ask Claude to explain why it declined so the false declines can be identified
questions.why: The examples demonstrated a decline boundary that the model generalised too widely. Showing valid-but-odd inputs being handled is what redraws the boundary where you want it.
questions.traps: Removing examples weakens the behaviour without relocating its edge. An instruction competes with demonstration, and explanations diagnose after the fact.

questions.stem: An associate receives a market summary from Claude citing a named consultancy's 2025 forecast with a specific growth percentage. The figure fits their expectations and the report is due in an hour.
options: Ask Claude whether it is confident the figure is accurate before including it
Use the figure with a note saying it is approximate and subject to confirmation
Search for any source reporting a similar figure and cite that one instead
Locate the consultancy's forecast and confirm the figure before it enters the report
questions.why: Named source plus precise number is the shape a fabricated citation takes, and matching your expectations makes it less likely to be questioned. Checking the primary source is the only step that settles it.
questions.traps: Self-reported confidence tracks fluency, not truth. An approximate label still publishes the number, and finding a similar figure elsewhere validates a different claim.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude about a regulation's notification deadline and receives a clear answer of thirty days. A colleague recalls it being different but is not certain.
options: Ask Claude again in a new conversation and see whether it repeats thirty days
Check the regulation text, which settles a disagreement between two recollections
Ask Claude to explain its reasoning for the thirty-day figure in more detail
Go with thirty days, since a specific number suggests a specific source behind it
questions.why: Two unreliable recollections do not average into a fact. The regulation is the authority, and consulting it is faster than reasoning about which memory to trust.
questions.traps: Repetition tests consistency, and a model can be consistently wrong. Explanations rationalise the stated number, and specificity is not evidence of provenance.

questions.stem: Claude produces a literature review citing eight papers. Six are real and correctly described. Two have plausible titles, real author names, and journals that exist, but the papers themselves do not.
options: Verify every one of the citations individually rather than the unfamiliar ones
Verify the two citations that seem least familiar and accept the rest of the list
Ask Claude which of its citations it is least confident about before checking
Note that the review is largely accurate and flag it as needing later verification
questions.why: Fabricated citations are constructed from real components, so they look exactly like the genuine ones. Nothing distinguishes them at a glance, which is why the check has to be exhaustive.
questions.traps: Familiarity is not a reliable filter. Self-identified uncertainty misses the confident fabrications, and deferring verification means publishing unverified claims.

questions.stem: An associate notices Claude's answer contains a quotation attributed to a well-known executive. The quotation captures the executive's known views closely.
options: Accept the quotation because it is consistent with the executive's documented positions
Ask Claude for the date and venue of the quotation to establish its provenance
Treat the quotation as unverified until located in a primary source
Paraphrase the quotation so attribution accuracy matters less in the final text
questions.why: Quotations are generated to fit context, and fitting well is what makes a fabricated one persuasive. Only locating it in a source establishes that it was said.
questions.traps: Consistency with known views is exactly what a plausible fabrication has. Asking for date and venue invites more invented detail, and a paraphrase still attributes a position.

questions.stem: A team checks four of twenty figures in a Claude-generated analysis. All four are correct, and the deadline is close.
options: Conclude the analysis is reliable, since a twenty percent sample found no errors
Check four more figures and accept the analysis if those are also correct
Ask Claude to confirm that the remaining sixteen figures are accurate
Recognise that four correct samples do not establish anything about the other sixteen
questions.why: A clean sample raises confidence slightly but bounds nothing. Prioritising the figures that carry the decision is how limited checking time gets spent well.
questions.traps: A clean sample of four is weak evidence about sixteen. Doubling the sample helps marginally, and asking the model to confirm its own figures is not an independent check.

questions.stem: An associate spot-checks ten claims in a document and finds one error. They correct it and consider the document verified.
options: Treat the whole document as unverified, since one error in ten shows errors exist
Correct the error and check ten more claims to establish whether others exist
Conclude the error rate is ten percent and adjust the document's confidence accordingly
Ask Claude to find and correct any other errors of the same kind
questions.why: Detecting an error establishes existence, not density or location. One finding in ten is a signal to verify systematically rather than a measurement to extrapolate from.
questions.traps: A second sample of ten is the same weak instrument. A ten percent rate from one finding is not a stable estimate, and self-correction shares the process that produced the error.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to review its own analysis for errors. It reports the analysis is sound. The team treats this as verification and publishes.
options: Accept the self-review, since the model examined the analysis specifically for errors
Recognise a self-review shares the reasoning that produced the analysis itself
Ask Claude to review it a second time to see whether the verdict is stable
Ask Claude to review it while adopting the role of a sceptical external reviewer
questions.why: Independence is what makes a check meaningful, and a model reviewing its own output has none. The same reasoning that produced an error will endorse it.
questions.traps: A repeat run reproduces the same blind spot. A sceptical persona changes tone rather than access to different information.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude how confident it is in each of five claims. It reports high confidence in four and moderate in one. The moderate claim turns out correct and one high-confidence claim is wrong.
options: Verify only the moderate-confidence claim, since the model flagged it as uncertain
Ask for numerical confidence scores so the ranking becomes more precise
Treat stated confidence as weakly informative and verify by stakes
Ask Claude to explain the basis for each of its confidence assessments
questions.why: Self-reported confidence correlates loosely with accuracy and cannot be relied on to direct verification. Consequence is the better guide to where checking time goes.
questions.traps: Trusting the flags is what failed here. Numerical scores add precision to an unreliable signal, and explanations rationalise the assessment.

questions.stem: Two associates disagree about whether a Claude-drafted policy summary is good enough to circulate. Both have read it carefully and reached opposite conclusions.
options: Ask a third colleague to read it and settle the disagreement by majority view
Ask Claude to assess the summary's quality and use that as a tiebreak
Circulate it with a note asking readers to flag anything unclear or wrong
Agree what the summary has to achieve for its readers, then judge it against that
questions.why: Disagreement about quality usually means the standard was never stated. Defining what the artefact must accomplish converts an argument about taste into a checkable question.
questions.traps: A third opinion adds a vote without a standard. Model self-assessment is not independent, and circulating an unresolved draft pushes the judgement onto readers.

questions.stem: A team judges Claude's outputs by how polished they read. Over three months, several polished outputs turn out to have contained significant factual errors.
options: Ask Claude to write in a plainer style so polish stops influencing the team's judgement
Introduce a rule that outputs must be at least a certain length to be accepted
Separate the fluency of the writing from the accuracy of its claims when judging quality
Ask Claude to flag its own factual claims so they can be identified more easily
questions.why: Fluency is the property a language model optimises most directly and is uncorrelated with truth. Separating the two axes is the habit that keeps polish from standing in for correctness.
questions.traps: Plainer prose does not make claims true. Length rules measure the wrong thing, and self-flagging depends on the model recognising its own errors.

questions.stem: An associate receives a competitor analysis covering pricing, features and market position. It is accurate throughout. The competitor's recent acquisition is not mentioned anywhere.
options: Check the output against what you already know should be covered
Ask Claude whether there is anything important it left out of the analysis
Ask for a longer analysis so more of the relevant material is included
Accept the analysis, since everything it does contain has been verified as accurate
questions.why: An omission leaves no trace in the text, so it can only be found by comparison against an external expectation. Verifying what is present says nothing about what is absent.
questions.traps: Asking the model about its own gaps assumes it knows them. Length does not target the specific missing item, and accuracy of the present content is a different property.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude for the risks of a plan. The list is thorough on operational and financial risks and silent on reputational ones, which is where the real exposure sits.
options: Ask for more risks so the reputational category eventually appears
Ask about each specific risk category by name
Ask Claude whether it has considered every category of risk
Rank the risks and investigate whichever category is least represented
questions.why: An open request returns the categories most represented in ordinary discussion of plans. Naming the categories is what guarantees each gets considered.
questions.traps: Volume samples the same distribution. A self-check on coverage is unreliable, and ranking works on a list that already omits the category.

questions.stem: Claude produces a summary table where the individual figures are correct but the total at the bottom does not equal their sum.
options: Ask Claude to recalculate the total and use the corrected figure
Ask Claude to show its working so the arithmetic can be followed
Check derived figures independently of the model that produced them
Accept the individual figures and remove the total from the table
questions.why: Totals and other derived numbers are produced as text rather than computed, so they need an independent check. Doing the sum yourself is trivial and conclusive.
questions.traps: A recalculation by the same means can repeat the error. Shown working still needs checking, and deleting the total loses information the table should carry.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to convert a set of figures between currencies. The conversions are internally consistent but use an exchange rate from an unstated date.
options: Ask Claude which exchange rate it used and note it alongside the figures
Ask Claude to use the current exchange rate for all of the conversions
Convert the figures yourself, since currency conversion is straightforward arithmetic
Supply the exchange rate you want used, since an unstated rate is unverifiable
questions.why: Conversion is only meaningful relative to a stated rate. Supplying it makes every output figure reproducible and puts the rate choice where it belongs.
questions.traps: Asking afterwards may get an invented rate. Requesting the current rate assumes live data access, and doing it manually forfeits the task unnecessarily.

questions.stem: A team receives an analysis with a section that reads as established consensus. No sources are cited and the team is unsure whether the claims come from the uploaded documents or elsewhere.
options: Ask which claims come from the supplied documents and which do not
Ask Claude to add citations to the analysis it has already produced
Assume the claims come from the documents, since those were provided as context
Ask for the analysis again with an instruction to cite sources throughout
questions.why: Blended output is the default when documents are supplied alongside a model's own knowledge. Asking for the split is what makes the boundary visible and checkable.
questions.traps: Retrofitted citations may be attached to claims that did not come from the sources. Assuming provenance is the error, and a rerun loses the analysis you already have.

questions.stem: A team publishes Claude-drafted content after a proofread. Three months in, two factual errors have reached customers, both of which read perfectly well.
options: Ask the proofreader to be more careful when reading the drafted content
Add a factual review step alongside the proofread
Ask Claude to fact-check its drafts before they go to the proofreader
Reduce the volume of drafted content so each piece can be read more slowly
questions.why: Proofreading and fact-checking are different activities with different inputs. A well-written false statement passes a proofread by design, so the missing step has to be added.
questions.traps: Care does not supply the sources a proofreader was never given. Self-fact-checking is not independent, and slowing down does not change what is being checked.

questions.stem: An associate is checking a Claude-generated summary of a meeting they attended. Everything matches their recollection, so they approve it.
options: Check the summary against the recording or notes, since recollection is itself unreliable
Approve the summary, since a participant's memory is a reasonable check on accuracy
Ask another attendee to confirm the summary matches their recollection too
Ask Claude to highlight the parts of the summary it is least certain about
questions.why: Memory reconstructs and is particularly weak on detail and sequence. Where a record exists, checking against it is both easier and more reliable than recall.
questions.traps: One recollection is a weak check and two correlated ones are barely stronger. Model uncertainty does not address the reviewer's own limitation.

questions.stem: A team notices that Claude's output includes a specific statistic with no source. When asked for the source, Claude provides one that looks authoritative.
options: Accept the statistic, since Claude was able to identify where the figure came from
Ask for a second source to corroborate the first one that was provided
Read the source independently, since one produced on request is not provenance
Ask Claude whether the source it provided is one it is confident about
questions.why: Asking for a source after the fact produces a plausible source, not necessarily the actual one. The retrieved citation needs the same verification as the statistic did.
questions.traps: Producing a source on demand is not provenance. A second generated source has the same status, and self-confidence adds nothing checkable.

questions.stem: An associate wants to know whether a Claude workflow is reliable enough to use unsupervised. It has produced correct output on the last twelve runs.
options: Conclude it is reliable, since twelve consecutive correct runs is a strong record
Run it twelve more times and use it unsupervised if the streak continues
Use it unsupervised and monitor for errors over the following month
Test against cases chosen to be difficult rather than the routine ones
questions.why: Reliability is determined by behaviour at the edges, and routine runs do not sample there. Deliberately hard cases are what reveal whether the failure modes are acceptable.
questions.traps: A longer streak of easy cases is more of the same evidence. Monitoring in production discovers failures by shipping them.

questions.stem: A team defines good output as output that needs no edits. Under this rule, an associate accepts a shorter, less useful summary because it required no changes.
options: Keep the rule but require summaries to meet a minimum length as well
Define quality by fitness for purpose, not by how little editing
Measure editing time instead of counting the number of edits made
Ask reviewers to note why they edited so the rule can be refined over time
questions.why: Edit count measures convenience, not value, and optimising it selects for output that is easy to accept rather than useful. Fitness for purpose is the standard that avoids that.
questions.traps: A length floor patches one symptom. Editing time is the same proxy in different units, and logging reasons improves a metric that is measuring the wrong thing.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to list the regulatory requirements for a process. The list is accurate and covers the requirements that apply in most jurisdictions.
options: Ask Claude which jurisdictions the requirements it listed apply to
Ask for additional requirements that may apply in less common jurisdictions
Check the list against an authoritative source for the specific jurisdiction that applies
Accept the list, since the requirements it contains have been confirmed as accurate
questions.why: A list that is right for the typical case can be dangerously incomplete for yours. Only the authoritative source for your jurisdiction settles which requirements apply.
questions.traps: Asking the model to scope its own answer produces another unverified claim. Requesting more items does not target your jurisdiction, and accuracy of the items present is not coverage.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to evaluate two vendors. The evaluation is balanced in structure but consistently describes the better-known vendor's weaknesses more gently.
options: Ask for a more critical evaluation of the better-known vendor specifically
Ask Claude to evaluate the vendors without being told which is better known
Ask for the evaluation twice with the vendor order reversed and compare
Apply the same specific criteria to both vendors, then compare results
questions.why: Asymmetric treatment is corrected by imposing symmetric criteria. Applying the same checklist to both makes any remaining difference attributable to the vendors rather than their reputations.
questions.traps: Asking for extra criticism of one side overcorrects. Withholding identity is impractical, and order reversal detects the asymmetry without fixing the evaluation.

questions.stem: An associate is asked where a claim in their report came from. The claim came from Claude, which produced it while working from three uploaded documents.
options: Trace the claim to a specific document and a specific passage
Say that the claim came from the analysis of the three uploaded documents
Ask Claude which of the three documents the claim came from
Remove the claim from the report, since its provenance cannot be established
questions.why: Provenance means pointing at a passage. Attributing a claim to a set of documents in aggregate is not traceability, and the claim may not be in any of them.
questions.traps: Naming the document set is the vague attribution being questioned. Asking the model to attribute after the fact is unverified, and removal is premature before checking.

questions.stem: A team routes all Claude output through the same reviewer regardless of what it is. The reviewer is a strong writer with no background in the technical subject matter.
options: Give the reviewer more time so they can research the technical claims themselves
Match the reviewer to what actually needs checking
Ask Claude to explain the technical claims so the reviewer can follow them
Reduce the technical content so the existing reviewer can assess all of it
questions.why: Review is only as good as the reviewer's ability to detect the relevant errors. Matching expertise to content is what makes the step a real control rather than a formality.
questions.traps: Research time does not create domain expertise. Model explanations of its own claims are not independent, and stripping technical content damages the work.

questions.stem: Claude reports that a metric grew by 40% and separately that it went from 250 to 340. The associate notices the two statements do not agree.
options: Use the percentage, since it is the figure that was requested in the prompt
Ask Claude which of the two figures is correct and use its answer
Recompute from the underlying figures, since the stated percentage and the values conflict
Use the raw values, since raw numbers are generally more reliable than derived ones
questions.why: An internal contradiction means at least one figure is wrong, and the arithmetic from the raw values settles which. It takes seconds and is conclusive.
questions.traps: Choosing either figure on principle is a guess. Asking the model to adjudicate its own contradiction is not independent verification.

questions.stem: An associate needs to verify ten claims but has time for three. The claims vary in how much rests on them.
options: Verify the claims that most affect the decision you are making
Verify the first three claims, since early claims often set up the later ones
Verify the three claims that seem least plausible on their face
Verify three claims chosen at random to get an unbiased sample
questions.why: Under a time constraint, verification is a risk-management activity. Checking what carries the decision protects the most, which random or positional sampling does not.
questions.traps: Position is unrelated to importance. Implausibility catches obvious errors but misses plausible ones, and randomness ignores stakes entirely.

questions.stem: A team finds that Claude describes a software feature that does not exist in the product. The description is detailed and matches how similar products behave.
options: Ask Claude whether the feature exists in the current version of the product
Ask for the feature's documentation link so its existence can be confirmed
Assume the feature exists in some form, since the description is specific
Verify the feature claims against the product's own documentation
questions.why: Plausibility is what makes this error hard to catch, because the description is drawn from how the category behaves. Only the product's documentation settles what this product does.
questions.traps: Asking the model to confirm or link invites more generated content. Assuming a specific description implies existence is exactly the inference that failed.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to grade its own answer from one to ten. It gives itself a seven and lists three weaknesses. All three are real, but the answer's main flaw is not among them.
options: Accept the three weaknesses as the complete list of issues with the answer
Use the self-assessment as a start and review independently
Ask Claude to find more weaknesses until the main flaw is eventually identified
Ask Claude to grade the answer again to see whether the score is stable
questions.why: Self-assessment surfaces the issues a model can see, which excludes its own blind spots by definition. It is a useful prompt for review, not a substitute for one.
questions.traps: Treating the list as complete is the error. Repeated prompting mines the same limited view, and score stability measures consistency rather than coverage.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to summarise the objections raised in a consultation. The summary covers the written responses well but omits the objections raised verbally at the public meeting.
options: Ask for a more thorough summary that includes all of the objections raised
Ask Claude whether it is aware of objections beyond those in the written responses
Check whether the sources given to Claude actually covered everything that was needed
Ask for the summary again with an instruction to include verbal objections
questions.why: Completeness of output depends on completeness of input. When something is missing, the first question is whether it was ever supplied, not whether the model overlooked it.
questions.traps: Instructions cannot recover content that was never provided. Asking the model about material outside its input invites invention.

questions.stem: An associate has to decide whether a drafted email is good enough to send. They keep rereading it and finding small improvements.
options: Keep refining until no further improvements can be identified in the draft
Ask Claude to assess whether the email is ready to be sent to the recipient
Ask a colleague to read it and send it once they have no further suggestions
Judge it against whether it achieves its purpose for its actual reader
questions.why: Every draft admits further tweaks, so a purpose-based stopping rule is what prevents refinement from running indefinitely. Fitness for purpose is a threshold rather than a maximum.
questions.traps: Refining to exhaustion has no endpoint. Model self-assessment is not independent, and a colleague without the standard faces the same open-ended question.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to summarise arguments for and against a proposal. The against section is shorter, and the team concludes the case for the proposal is stronger.
options: Recognise that section length reflects expression rather than strength
Accept the conclusion, since a balanced summary would have produced equal sections
Ask for the sections to be rewritten at equal length and compare them again
Ask Claude to state which side it considers stronger and why
questions.why: Length in a summary tracks the volume and articulacy of the source material, not the merit of a position. Reading it as evidence of strength imports an artefact of the writing.
questions.traps: Assuming balance means equal length inverts the relationship. Equalising length is cosmetic, and asking for a verdict substitutes the model's judgement for yours.

questions.stem: A team wants to catch errors in Claude's output but reviewing everything is not feasible. Volume has grown to two hundred items a week.
options: Review a fixed ten percent of items chosen at random each week
Review by risk rather than reviewing everything
Ask Claude to identify which items warrant human review each week
Review everything but more quickly so the whole volume is covered
questions.why: Risk-weighted review concentrates limited attention where errors would cost most, which is the only allocation that scales without leaving high-stakes output unchecked.
questions.traps: Uniform random sampling treats a contract like a social post. Model triage is not independent, and faster review of everything degrades the check across the board.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to calculate a compound growth figure over five years. The result is plausible but they cannot reproduce it with a calculator.
options: Trust the calculator, since arithmetic done as text generation is unreliable here
Ask Claude to recalculate and use the figure if the second attempt matches
Ask Claude to show the formula it used so the discrepancy can be located
Use the model's figure, since it accounted for factors the calculator did not
questions.why: A deterministic calculation has one right answer and a calculator produces it. Where the two disagree, the arithmetic tool wins without further investigation.
questions.traps: Repetition can reproduce the same error. The formula is worth seeing for learning but does not change which result is correct, and there are no hidden factors in compound growth.

questions.stem: A team's report cites a figure to Claude itself, on the grounds that Claude is where the figure came from.
options: Cite Claude, since transparency about how the figure was obtained is good practice
Remove the citation and present the figure without attribution
Cite the underlying source the figure came from, not the tool used
Cite Claude alongside a note about the date the figure was generated
questions.why: A model is not a source of fact and citing it tells a reader nothing they can check. Provenance means the origin, which has to be located and verified.
questions.traps: Citing the tool is transparent about process while leaving the claim unverifiable. Removing attribution is worse, and adding a date does not create provenance.

questions.stem: An associate verifies a claim by asking Claude to search for supporting evidence. It returns three sources that support the claim.
options: Accept the claim, since three independent sources were found to support it
Ask for sources that contradict the claim as well to balance the evidence
Ask Claude to assess the quality of the three sources it has found
Read the sources directly rather than the retrieved summaries
questions.why: Verification finishes at the source, not at a summary of it. Reading the material is what confirms it says what the summary claims it says.
questions.traps: Three summarised sources is one unverified step repeated. Contradicting sources improve balance but still need reading, and quality assessment is another summary.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to identify dependencies for a project plan. The list captures technical dependencies thoroughly and omits the approval that must be obtained before work starts.
options: Ask for a longer list so non-technical dependencies are more likely to appear
Ask about dependency types explicitly, including approvals
Ask Claude whether it has missed any dependencies in the plan
Review the list against the project charter to identify what is missing
questions.why: Enumerating the categories is what stops a generic request from returning the most commonly discussed type. Approvals are a dependency people forget to ask about.
questions.traps: Volume samples the same skew. Self-checking is unreliable, and charter review is a good practice that arrives after the omission.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude whether their proposed approach is sound. The response is broadly supportive and raises two minor caveats.
options: Accept the support, since the response did engage critically enough to raise caveats
Ask the same question again in a different conversation to check consistency
Ask what would have to be true for this approach to fail, rather than asking for approval
Ask Claude to be more critical of the approach that has been described
questions.why: Presenting your own approach frames the question as validation. Asking what would make it fail reframes the task so criticism is the requested output rather than an aside.
questions.traps: Two minor caveats is the shape agreement takes. Repetition reproduces the same framing, and asking for criticism without restructuring the question yields performative objections.

questions.stem: A team introduces a review step but reviewers approve nearly everything, because the drafts read well and reviewing carefully takes longer than they were given.
options: Give reviewers the time and the specific checks the review is meant to perform
Ask reviewers to reject a minimum proportion of drafts to keep standards up
Ask Claude to make the drafts less polished so reviewers scrutinise them harder
Remove the review step, since it is not currently catching anything
questions.why: A review with no defined checks and no time becomes a rubber stamp. Specifying what to look for and resourcing it is what turns the step into a control.
questions.traps: A rejection quota manufactures rejections. Degrading drafts is perverse, and removing the step abandons the control rather than repairing it.

questions.stem: An associate tests a prompt on the three examples they have available. All three work. They roll it out across the team.
options: Roll out and rely on colleagues to report problems as they encounter them
Gather harder and more varied cases before rolling the prompt out widely
Test the same three examples several times each to confirm the results are stable
Roll out to a small group first and expand if no problems are reported
questions.why: Three cases cannot represent the variety a team will encounter. Building a varied test set before rollout is what surfaces failures before other people meet them.
questions.traps: Relying on reports discovers failures through users. Repeating the same three tests measures stability rather than coverage, and a staged rollout still ships an undertested prompt.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude about a niche technical standard. The answer is detailed and confident, and the standard is obscure enough that nobody on the team can assess it.
options: Accept the answer, since the level of detail indicates familiarity with the standard
Ask Claude how well-documented the standard is before relying on the answer
Ask the question again and compare the two answers for consistency
Verify against the standard itself, not the model's confidence
questions.why: Fluency does not degrade gracefully on thin topics, so a confident detailed answer about something obscure is exactly where verification matters most.
questions.traps: Detail is generated, not evidence of familiarity. Self-assessment of coverage is unreliable, and consistency between two runs is not accuracy.

questions.stem: An associate is reviewing a Claude-drafted analysis and finds themselves checking whether they agree with its conclusions rather than whether the reasoning holds.
options: Evaluate whether the evidence supports the conclusion, separately from your agreement
Accept conclusions that match your expectations and scrutinise the ones that do not
Ask Claude to argue the opposite conclusion and compare the two arguments
Have someone who disagrees with the conclusion review the analysis instead
questions.why: Agreement is not a quality signal, and reviewing for it means a congenial error passes while a correct surprise gets challenged. Assessing the reasoning is the check that works either way.
questions.traps: Differential scrutiny by agreement is the bias itself. Counterarguments and dissenting reviewers help but do not replace assessing the reasoning on its own terms.

questions.stem: A team receives a forecast from Claude with figures given to two decimal places. The underlying inputs were rough estimates rounded to the nearest thousand.
options: Keep the decimals, since more precise figures are more useful for planning purposes
Ask Claude to recalculate using more precise input figures where available
Round the output to reflect the precision of the inputs that produced it
Present the figures with a note explaining that they are based on estimates
questions.why: Precision in an output cannot exceed the precision of its inputs. Reporting two decimals from rounded thousands communicates a confidence the numbers do not support.
questions.traps: Spurious precision misleads regardless of usefulness. Better inputs would change the analysis, and a caveat does not undo the visual claim the decimals make.

questions.stem: An associate needs to confirm a date mentioned in a Claude-generated timeline. The date is central to the argument the timeline supports.
options: Ask Claude to confirm the date is correct before relying on the timeline
Confirm the date against a primary record before building on it
Compare the date against the other dates in the timeline for consistency
Present the timeline with the date marked as approximate
questions.why: Dates are specific, checkable, and frequently wrong in generated content. A load-bearing date gets confirmed at the source before anything is built on it.
questions.traps: Model self-confirmation is not independent. Internal consistency can be maintained around a wrong date, and marking it approximate weakens the argument it supports.

questions.stem: A team asks for the pros and cons of a decision. The response lists five of each, and the team notes the symmetry approvingly.
options: Accept the balance as evidence that the decision is genuinely finely poised
Ask for more items on each side to test whether the balance holds
Ask Claude which of the ten points it considers most significant
Treat the symmetry as a stylistic artefact, not a finding
questions.why: Matched lists are a formatting habit rather than a measurement. Real decisions are rarely balanced, and reading symmetry as evidence imports a property of the presentation.
questions.traps: Treating symmetry as a finding is the error. More items extend the artefact, and ranking works within a list already shaped by it.

questions.stem: A team's process requires two reviewers for Claude-generated content. Both reviewers read the output only, and neither sees the prompt or the sources used.
options: Add a third reviewer so more perspectives are applied to the output
Give reviewers the prompt and the sources, not just the finished output text
Ask reviewers to reconstruct the likely prompt before reading the output
Ask Claude to summarise its sources at the top of each piece of output
questions.why: Review without inputs can only assess plausibility. Seeing the prompt and sources is what lets a reviewer check whether the output answers the question and reflects the material.
questions.traps: More reviewers without inputs repeats the same limited check. Reconstruction is guesswork, and a self-reported source summary is not the sources.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to analyse why a project failed. The analysis focuses on process and communication issues and does not raise that the project's goal was never achievable.
options: Ask for a deeper analysis so the underlying causes are eventually surfaced
Ask Claude to consider factors outside process and communication
Ask several colleagues for their views and compare them to the analysis
Ask whether the premise itself was sound before analysing that failure
questions.why: A question about why something failed presupposes it could have succeeded. Surfacing that assumption is what lets the most fundamental explanation enter the analysis.
questions.traps: Depth and breadth both operate inside the assumed frame. Colleague views may share the same premise.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to check whether its output followed all the instructions in the prompt. It reports full compliance, but one instruction was not followed.
options: Ask Claude to check again more carefully against each instruction in turn
Ask Claude to list the instructions it identified before checking compliance
Check compliance yourself against the original instruction list
