Accept the compliance report, since the model had the instructions available to it
questions.why: The same reading of the prompt that produced the omission produces the compliance check. An external comparison against the list is the only check that does not share the fault.
questions.traps: Repeating and restating both re-run the reading that failed. Having the instructions available is what makes the miss surprising, not what makes the check reliable.

questions.stem: An associate uses Claude to summarise a paywalled article they cannot access. The summary is detailed and specific about the article's argument.
options: Treat the summary as unverified rather than as access
Accept the summary, since it is specific enough to indicate genuine knowledge of the article
Ask Claude to quote a passage so the summary can be checked against it
Ask Claude whether it has access to the article's full text
questions.why: Content behind a paywall is likely absent from what the model can draw on, so a confident summary may describe the subject generally. Specificity is generated, not evidence of access.
questions.traps: Requested quotations from inaccessible text invite fabrication. Asking about access produces a claim you cannot check.

questions.stem: A team's standard for Claude output is that it must be at least as good as what a junior colleague would produce. Two reviewers apply this standard and disagree constantly.
options: Ask both reviewers to calibrate by reviewing the same junior colleague's work
Replace the comparison with concrete checks that the output has to actually pass
Lower the standard so borderline cases are more likely to be accepted
Have the junior colleague produce a version for direct comparison each time
questions.why: A comparative benchmark that lives in each reviewer's head is not a standard. Concrete checks are what make two reviewers reach the same verdict on the same artefact.
questions.traps: Calibration exercises help but leave the standard implicit. Lowering the bar dodges the disagreement, and parallel production defeats the point of drafting.

questions.stem: An associate finds no errors when checking a Claude output and concludes the model handles this task reliably.
options: Conclude the task is handled reliably and reduce checking on future outputs
Check one more output and reduce scrutiny if that one is also clean
Recognise that one clean output is weak evidence about the task in general
Ask Claude whether it finds this kind of task difficult to perform accurately
questions.why: A single clean result is consistent with a wide range of true error rates. Drawing a conclusion about the task from one observation is the inference error here.
questions.traps: Reducing scrutiny after one or two observations acts on the same thin evidence. Asking the model about its own difficulty is not measurement.

questions.stem: A team is deciding how much to verify a Claude-drafted internal memo that summarises a decision already made and recorded in the minutes.
options: Check it against the minutes, which settle what the memo actually asserts
Verify the memo thoroughly, since all generated content requires the same level of checking
Circulate the memo without checking, since it describes an internal decision
Ask Claude to confirm the memo matches the meeting minutes it was given
questions.why: Verification effort scales with what is at stake and how easily it can be settled. A memo with one authoritative reference is cheap to check completely.
questions.traps: Uniform heavy verification wastes effort where a reference exists. Skipping the check on an easy comparison is careless, and self-confirmation is not independent.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to evaluate a proposal they wrote themselves, mentioning in the prompt that it is their own work.
options: Accept the evaluation, since the model assesses content
Ask Claude to evaluate it as though it were written by someone else entirely
Ask for both a supportive and a critical evaluation and compare the two
Ask for the evaluation without signalling who wrote it
questions.why: Signalling authorship frames the request as feedback to a person rather than assessment of an artefact, which softens it. Removing the signal is the simplest way to get the sterner read.
questions.traps: Assuming authorship is ignored is the misconception here. A role instruction competes with a signal already given, and paired evaluations produce a performed critique alongside a performed endorsement.

questions.stem: A team receives a Claude-drafted briefing containing twelve factual claims. Nine are about their own company and three are about the wider market.
options: Verify all twelve claims to the same standard regardless of their subject matter
Verify the market claims most carefully, since internal facts can be checked by colleagues quickly
Verify the internal claims first, since errors about your own company are most embarrassing
Ask Claude which of the twelve claims it is least certain about and check those
questions.why: Verification effort follows both consequence and how hard something is to check. Internal facts have cheap authoritative checks; external market claims do not, which is where care concentrates.
questions.traps: Uniform effort ignores that some checks are trivial. Ordering by embarrassment misreads risk, and model-flagged uncertainty misses confident errors.

questions.stem: An associate reads a Claude-generated answer and finds one detail that is clearly wrong. Everything else in the answer seems correct.
options: Correct the wrong detail and accept the remainder of the answer as written
Ask Claude to correct the detail and regenerate the surrounding paragraph
Increase scrutiny of the rest, since a confirmed error means it was unreliable
Note the error and continue, since a single wrong detail is within normal tolerance
questions.why: A confirmed error is direct evidence about this specific output's reliability. It should raise your estimate of errors elsewhere in it rather than being treated as isolated.
questions.traps: Treating the error as contained assumes independence you have no reason to expect. Regeneration and tolerance framing both skip the update the evidence warrants.

questions.stem: A team compares two prompts by running each once on the same input. Prompt A's output is noticeably better, so they adopt it.
options: Run both several times, since one pair cannot separate prompts from variation
Adopt prompt A, since a clearly better output on the same input is convincing evidence
Run prompt A again to confirm the quality is reproducible before adopting it
Ask Claude to compare the two prompts and explain which should perform better
questions.why: Output varies run to run, so a single comparison can be decided entirely by that variation. Multiple runs are what distinguish a prompt difference from noise.
questions.traps: A clear single win is exactly what noise produces sometimes. Re-running only the winner tests stability of one arm, and model opinion is not output evidence.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to rewrite a paragraph, then asks whether the rewrite is better than the original. Claude says it is.
options: Accept the assessment, since the model compared both versions directly
Ask Claude to explain what specifically makes the rewrite better
Ask Claude to compare them again without knowing which version it wrote
Compare them yourself against what the paragraph must do
questions.why: A model asked whether its own edit improved something will say yes. The comparison inherits the same judgement that produced the rewrite.
questions.traps: Explanations justify the verdict already given. Blinding is not achievable within the same conversation where it produced the text.

questions.stem: A team asks for output that is "accurate, clear and comprehensive". A draft arrives that is accurate and clear but omits an area, and reviewers cannot agree whether it meets the bar.
options: Rank the three properties, so reviewers know what to do when any of them conflict
Ask for a draft that satisfies all three properties fully in the next attempt
Add more detail to the requirements so each property is defined more precisely
Ask Claude which of the three properties its draft satisfies best
questions.why: Multiple quality properties trade off, and a standard that does not rank them cannot resolve the case where one is sacrificed. Priority is what makes the bar decidable.
questions.traps: Demanding all three fully ignores the trade-off. More definition of each property does not order them, and self-assessment does not settle a policy question.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to summarise the findings of a study. The summary covers the significant findings and omits the null results the study also reported.
options: Ask for a longer summary so more of the study's content is represented
Ask Claude whether the study reported any findings that were not significant
Ask specifically for the null and the negative findings too
Read the results section directly rather than relying on the summary
questions.why: Absence of effect is a finding that summarisation systematically drops as uninformative. Asking for it explicitly is what brings it into scope.
questions.traps: Length does not restore a category treated as non-content. A yes-or-no follow-up may be answered from the same compressed view, and reading it yourself forfeits the summary.

questions.stem: A team receives a percentage change calculated by Claude. The base figure it used is not stated anywhere in the output.
options: Accept the percentage, since the calculation itself was requested and performed
Ask for the base figure that the percentage was taken from
Ask Claude to recalculate and include more detail in the output
Compare the percentage against last quarter's figure for plausibility
questions.why: A relative figure without its base is not a number you can act on, and stating the base also makes the calculation checkable. Both problems are solved by asking for it.
questions.traps: Accepting it leaves the figure uninterpretable. A vaguer request for detail may not surface the base, and plausibility comparison does not supply it.

questions.stem: An associate's report includes a claim Claude produced while working from a supplied document. When checked, the document supports a weaker version of the claim.
options: Keep the claim, since the document broadly supports the point being made
Add a citation to the document so readers can assess the claim themselves
Ask Claude to find additional support for the stronger version of the claim
Restate the claim at the strength the document actually supports
questions.why: Strengthening during summarisation is a common drift, and the fix is to match the claim to the evidence. Citation without correction points a reader at a document that does not say it.
questions.traps: Broad support is not support for the specific claim. Citing an unmatched source is worse than not citing it, and seeking new support starts from the overstated version.

questions.stem: A team wants to know whether their review step is working. They have no record of what reviewers have caught over the past six months.
options: Ask reviewers whether they feel the review step is catching enough errors
Start recording what review catches, since an unmeasured control cannot improve
Increase the number of reviewers to improve the chance of catching errors
Compare the current error rate against the rate before review was introduced
questions.why: A control with no record produces no evidence about its own effectiveness. Logging catches is what makes the question answerable at all.
questions.traps: Reviewer impressions are unreliable. Adding reviewers changes a process you cannot yet evaluate, and a before-and-after comparison needs the data that was never kept.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude "why is this approach better than the alternative?" and receives a well-argued case for the approach.
options: Ask which of the approaches is better and why, rather than assuming
Accept the argument, since it engaged with the comparison that was requested
Ask the same question about the alternative and compare the two arguments
Ask Claude to identify weaknesses in the argument it just produced
questions.why: A leading question gets a compliant answer. Rephrasing so the comparison is open is what lets the model reach either conclusion.
questions.traps: The argument answers the question asked, which was the wrong question. Arguing both sides produces two advocacy pieces, and self-critique operates on a case built to a brief.

questions.stem: A team has to decide whether to verify a claim that would take two hours to check and appears in an internal document read by four people.
options: Verify it, since any factual claim in a document should be confirmed
Skip verification, since an internal document with four readers is low stakes
Weigh the checking cost against what a wrong claim would cost
Ask Claude to assess how likely the claim is to be accurate
questions.why: Verification is a cost-benefit decision, and both sides of it are known here. Reasoning explicitly about the trade-off is what produces a defensible answer either way.
questions.traps: Blanket rules in either direction ignore the specific costs. Asking the model to estimate its own reliability is not evidence.

questions.stem: An associate notices Claude has attributed a policy position to a government agency. The position is one the agency plausibly holds but has not publicly stated.
options: Accept the attribution, since it is consistent with the agency's known direction
Soften the attribution to say the agency is understood to hold the position
Ask Claude for a link to where the agency stated the position
Verify against the agency's own published material first
questions.why: Attributing an unstated position to a named body is a factual claim about that body. Consistency with its direction is what makes the fabrication credible rather than what verifies it.
questions.traps: Softening publishes an unverified attribution in weaker words. A requested link may be generated rather than retrieved.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude for lessons learned from a project. The list is thoughtful and every item concerns things the team did wrong.
options: Ask for more lessons so the positive ones eventually appear in the list
Ask what went well too, since a lessons request is read as a request for problems
Ask Claude to balance the list between positive and negative lessons
Accept the list, since lessons learned conventionally focus on improvements
questions.why: The framing of "lessons learned" selects for failure. Asking about what worked is what surfaces practices worth repeating, which is half the value of the exercise.
questions.traps: Volume samples the same framing. A balance instruction manufactures symmetry, and accepting the convention keeps the gap.

questions.stem: An associate receives two Claude drafts. One is more thorough and one is more readable. The audience is a busy executive who will skim it.
options: Choose the thorough one, since completeness is the more objective measure of quality
Combine them into a version that is both thorough and highly readable
Choose the readable one, since fitness for the actual reader is the standard
Ask Claude which of the two drafts is objectively better written
questions.why: Quality is relative to purpose and audience. For a skimming executive, thoroughness that will not be read is not a quality advantage.
questions.traps: Treating thoroughness as objectively better ignores the reader. A combined version has to make the same trade-off, and there is no author-independent verdict to ask for.

questions.stem: A team includes an instruction telling Claude to say when it is unsure. Outputs rarely include such statements, and errors still occur.
options: Treat the absence of any uncertainty statement as uninformative
Conclude that outputs without uncertainty statements are reliable enough to use
Strengthen the instruction so uncertainty is flagged more consistently
Ask Claude after each output whether it was uncertain about anything
questions.why: A model does not reliably detect its own errors, so silence about uncertainty is not a signal of correctness. The instruction cannot make an unavailable signal available.
questions.traps: Treating silence as assurance is the trap. Stronger wording and follow-up questions both ask for a signal the model cannot generate reliably.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to compare two figures and it reports the difference as a percentage. The two figures are counts of different things measured over different periods.
options: Check the arithmetic, since that is the part most likely to contain an error
Ask Claude to normalise the two figures so the comparison becomes valid
Present the percentage with a note explaining what each figure measures
Question whether the comparison is meaningful at all
questions.why: A correctly computed comparison between incomparable quantities is still meaningless. Validity of the comparison is the prior question to its arithmetic.
questions.traps: Checking arithmetic validates the wrong thing. Normalisation may not be possible, and a caveat presents a meaningless figure with an explanation attached.

questions.stem: A team's reviewers see Claude's output only after it has been formatted into the final template. Errors are caught less often than when drafts were reviewed as plain text.
options: Review before formatting, since polished presentation reduces scrutiny of the content
Ask reviewers to read the formatted version more carefully than they currently do
Add a second review pass after formatting has been applied to the draft
Format the drafts more plainly so they look less finished during review
questions.why: Finished-looking artefacts attract less scrutiny, so the review is better placed before presentation is applied. This is a sequencing fix rather than an effort one.
questions.traps: Asking for more care fights a well-documented effect. A second pass costs more for the same bias, and deliberately degrading formatting is a workaround for the sequencing.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to summarise feedback from twenty customers. The summary emphasises the two most articulate complaints and treats them as representative.
options: Ask for a longer summary so the less articulate feedback is also represented
Ask Claude to weight all twenty responses equally in the summary
Read the individual responses rather than relying on a summary of them
Ask how many customers raised each theme, rather than how well
questions.why: Articulacy translates into salience during summarisation. Requesting counts is what grounds emphasis in how many people said something rather than how well they said it.
questions.traps: Length does not rebalance emphasis. An equal-weighting instruction states a goal without a mechanism, and reading everything forfeits the summary.

questions.stem: A team measures a prompt's accuracy at 92% on 25 test cases. They report this as the accuracy the team should expect in production.
options: Report 92% as the expected accuracy, since it was measured on real test cases
Note that 25 cases give a wide margin of error here
Round the figure to 90% to be conservative about what was measured
Test 25 more cases and report the average of the two measurements
questions.why: A small sample gives an imprecise estimate, and test cases are usually easier and less varied than production traffic. Both caveats matter to anyone acting on the number.
questions.traps: Reporting the point estimate hides both problems. Rounding down is arbitrary, and a second small sample narrows the interval slightly without addressing the distribution difference.

questions.stem: An associate needs to check a Claude claim about a competitor's pricing. The competitor's site shows a different price than the one Claude gave.
options: Ask Claude to explain the discrepancy between the two prices
Use Claude's figure, since it may reflect pricing not shown publicly
Use the price shown on the competitor's own site
Note both figures in the report and let readers decide which to use
questions.why: A live authoritative source settles a factual question about current pricing. There is no scenario in which the generated figure is the better evidence here.
questions.traps: Asking for an explanation invites a rationalisation. Speculating about hidden pricing and presenting both figures both preserve a number known to be wrong.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to identify stakeholders for a change programme. The list covers internal teams thoroughly and does not mention customers or regulators.
options: Ask for a longer list so external groups eventually appear in it
Ask about external stakeholders explicitly rather than in the general case
Ask Claude whether the list is complete before using it for planning
Review the list against a stakeholder framework to identify the gaps
questions.why: Naming the categories is what prevents a generic request from returning only the most commonly discussed group. External stakeholders are the systematic omission here.
questions.traps: Volume samples the same skew. A completeness self-check is unreliable, and framework review is good practice arriving after the omission.

questions.stem: An associate has been asked to define what "good enough" means for Claude-drafted customer emails. They are unsure where to start.
options: Describe what a bad email would cause, and set the bar just there
Set the bar at the quality a senior colleague would produce unaided
Define good enough as requiring no more than two edits before sending
Ask Claude to propose a quality standard for customer emails
questions.why: Working backwards from consequences produces a standard that is specific and defensible, because it is anchored in what actually goes wrong rather than in a comparison.
questions.traps: A senior-colleague benchmark is unshared and unmeasurable. Edit counts measure convenience, and a model-proposed standard is not grounded in your context.

questions.stem: A team catches an error in Claude's output after it has been sent to a client. They correct it and move on.
options: Add an extra reviewer to the process to reduce the chance of a repeat
Ask Claude to be more careful with this type of content in future
Examine why the review step actually missed it this time
Accept that some errors will get through and focus on responding well when they do
questions.why: An escaped error is information about the control. Diagnosing why review missed it is what turns a single incident into a process improvement.
questions.traps: Adding reviewers without knowing the failure mode may not address it. Instructing the model does not fix the control, and accepting escapes skips a free diagnosis.

questions.stem: An associate is reviewing Claude output in a subject they know well and one they do not. They find two errors in the familiar subject.
options: Conclude the unfamiliar section is probably fine, since no errors were visible in it
Ask Claude to check the unfamiliar section for errors of the same kind
Ask a colleague with the relevant expertise to review the unfamiliar section
Assume the unfamiliar section has a similar error rate
questions.why: Your detection rate depends on your knowledge, not on the output's quality. Errors found where you can see them imply errors where you cannot.
questions.traps: Absence of detected errors in an area you cannot assess is not evidence of quality. Self-checking is not independent, though expert review is a reasonable next step it does not follow from the reasoning being tested.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to rank five options by cost. The ranking is correct, but two options are described as having costs that differ by an amount the source does not support.
options: Accept the ranking, since the order is what the analysis was needed for
Ask Claude to recheck the figures used to produce the ranking
Verify the underlying figures separately from the ranking that they produced
Present the ranking without the underlying cost figures attached
questions.why: Ordering and magnitude are different claims and can fail independently. A correct ranking is not evidence that the values behind it are right.
questions.traps: Accepting the ranking ignores that the figures will be quoted. Self-rechecking is not independent, and hiding the figures conceals rather than corrects.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude a question and it gives an answer that combines information from an uploaded report with general industry knowledge, without distinguishing the two.
options: Ask for the answer again with an instruction to use only the uploaded report
Accept the answer, since both the report and industry knowledge are relevant here
Ask Claude to cite the report wherever the report supports a claim
Ask it to separate what came from the report from what did not come from it
questions.why: Blended answers need unblending before use, because the two parts have different verification requirements. Asking for the split preserves the answer you already have.
questions.traps: A rerun discards the broader answer. Assuming both are fine ignores that one part is unverified, and retrofitted citations may be misattached.

questions.stem: A team's process asks Claude to rate each output's quality from one to five and routes anything below four to human review. Errors still reach customers in outputs rated five.
options: Route by the consequence of the content, not the model's rating
Lower the threshold so outputs rated four also go to human review
Ask Claude to be stricter when rating the quality of its own output
Add a second rating pass and route anything either pass rates low
questions.why: Self-rating cannot detect the errors the model is blind to, so no threshold on that scale catches them. Routing on stakes is a criterion that does not depend on the model's self-knowledge.
questions.traps: Every threshold-based fix assumes the rating carries signal about the errors that matter. A second pass shares the blind spot.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to assess a risk and mentions in the prompt that the team has already decided to proceed.
options: Accept the assessment, since the risk analysis is separable from the decision context
Ask for the assessment without mentioning the decision
Ask Claude to assess the risk as though the decision had not yet been made
Ask for the assessment and then ask what would change if the decision were reversed
questions.why: Mentioning a settled decision reframes the task from evaluation to support. Removing that context is the cleanest way to get an assessment that could still say no.
questions.traps: Assuming separability is the misconception. A counterfactual instruction competes with context already supplied, and a follow-up works within the framed answer.

questions.stem: A team receives a Claude analysis of why sales fell. Every explanation offered concerns the company's own actions.
options: Ask about external market factors explicitly rather than internal ones
Ask for more explanations so external factors eventually appear
Ask Claude whether external factors could also explain the decline
Compare the analysis against market data to see what it missed
questions.why: Causal analyses gravitate toward the actor's own behaviour. Naming external categories is what brings market, competitor and seasonal factors into consideration.
questions.traps: Volume samples the same bias. A yes-or-no follow-up produces agreement without analysis, and market comparison is a check after the fact.

questions.stem: An associate checks a Claude-generated figure against a second Claude conversation, which produces the same figure.
options: Accept the figure, since it was confirmed by an independent check
Run a third conversation and accept the figure if all three agree
Recognise that two runs of the same model are not independent sources
Ask Claude in the second conversation to be especially careful about accuracy
questions.why: Independence is the property that makes corroboration meaningful, and two runs of the same model share the same tendencies. Agreement between them is close to no evidence.
questions.traps: Treating a second run as independent is the core error. A third run compounds it, and instructions about care do not create independence.

questions.stem: A team wants to reduce review burden as their confidence in Claude's output grows. They are unsure how to do it safely.
options: Reduce review uniformly across all categories as overall confidence increases
Keep review constant, since reducing it will eventually let errors through
Reduce review and rely on customer reports to identify any problems that arise
Reduce review only on categories where measurement shows low risk
questions.why: Confidence is category-specific, so relaxation should be too. Measured low-risk categories are where the burden can safely come off while high-stakes content stays covered.
questions.traps: Uniform reduction lowers the control where it matters most. Never relaxing ignores real evidence, and relying on customers to find errors externalises the check.

questions.stem: An associate finds that Claude's output meets every requirement they specified but is not what they actually wanted.
options: Accept the output, since it satisfies the requirements that were agreed
Treat the gap as a sign the requirements were wrong
Ask Claude to produce something better while keeping the same requirements
Add more requirements until the output matches what was wanted
questions.why: A requirements-satisfying output that misses the need means the specification is wrong. Revising it is what fixes the problem for this attempt and future ones.
questions.traps: Accepting it delivers the wrong thing. Asking for better against the same spec is undirected, and stacking requirements patches without diagnosing.

questions.stem: A team notices Claude performs worse on Fridays. They have four weeks of observations and roughly ten outputs per week.
options: Treat the pattern as unsupported, and look for a difference in the inputs instead
Investigate what changes on Fridays that might affect the model's performance
Collect more data over the next several months to confirm the pattern
Adjust the workflow to avoid running important tasks on Fridays
questions.why: Forty observations spread over five weekdays cannot support a day-of-week effect. The likelier explanation is a difference in what gets submitted, which is checkable now.
questions.traps: Investigating the day itself assumes the pattern is real. More data may eventually help but the input difference is the cheaper hypothesis, and changing the workflow acts on an unverified pattern.

questions.stem: An associate receives a Claude-generated budget breakdown. The categories sum correctly to the total, but one category is labelled with a name that does not match its contents.
options: Accept the breakdown, since the figures reconcile with the stated total
Ask Claude to relabel the category to match its contents
Ask Claude to explain what it included in each of the categories
Check the labels as well as the arithmetic in the breakdown
questions.why: Arithmetic consistency and semantic correctness are separate properties. A breakdown can add up perfectly while assigning items to the wrong buckets.
questions.traps: Treating reconciliation as validation is the error. Relabelling assumes the contents are right, and an explanation is a useful diagnostic rather than a check.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude about their own internal process. The answer is confident, detailed and describes a process the company does not follow.
options: Ask Claude where it obtained its information about the internal process
Recognise the model has no access to the internal processes
Correct the answer and ask Claude to remember the actual process
Assume the answer describes an earlier version of the process
questions.why: Questions about private internal facts have no source in what the model can draw on, so the answer is a plausible generic construction. Recognising that class of question is the durable lesson.
questions.traps: Asking for a source invites invention. Assuming it describes an old version rationalises a fabrication, and correction addresses one instance.

questions.stem: An associate needs to show where each claim in a Claude-drafted section came from. The section was produced from four uploaded documents in one request.
options: Ask Claude to add source labels to the section it has already produced
Cite all four documents at the end of the section as its collective sources
Regenerate the section with each claim naming its source
Read the four documents and attach sources to the claims manually
questions.why: Provenance is far more reliable when required during generation than reconstructed afterwards. Regenerating with the requirement in place produces traceable output.
questions.traps: Retrofitted labels are guesses about the model's own earlier process. A collective citation is not traceability, and manual attribution is expensive and still uncertain.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to write a case study about a project. The case study is accurate but reads as uniformly successful, when the project had significant setbacks.
options: Ask for a more balanced case study in a follow-up request
Ask for the setbacks and how they were handled to be included as part of the account
Ask Claude to add a challenges section to the case study it produced
Accept it, since case studies conventionally emphasise successful outcomes
questions.why: Case study is a genre with a promotional default. Naming setbacks and their resolution as required content is what changes what gets written rather than what gets appended.
questions.traps: A balance instruction is vague. A bolted-on challenges section sits apart from the narrative, and accepting the convention keeps the distortion.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to check a document against a compliance checklist. It reports on every item in the checklist and does not mention a compliance issue outside it.
options: Ask Claude to check for compliance issues generally in addition to the checklist
Expand the checklist to cover the issue that was missed this time
Recognise that a checklist review is bounded by the checklist itself
Ask Claude whether it noticed anything concerning beyond the checklist items
questions.why: A checklist defines scope, and anything outside it is out of scope by construction. Knowing that limitation is what tells you a second, open-ended pass is needed.
questions.traps: A general instruction bolted onto a checklist review muddles both. Expanding the checklist fixes one gap, and a follow-up question is weaker than a dedicated pass.

questions.stem: A team's reviewers approve Claude output faster than they approved human drafts of the same kind, and are catching fewer issues.
options: Ask reviewers to be aware that generated content needs more scrutiny
Route generated content to more experienced reviewers than human drafts
Add an automated check before generated content reaches reviewers
Give reviewers the same time and criteria for each of the drafts
questions.why: The speed difference reflects an expectation attached to the source rather than to the artefact. Equalising time and criteria removes the source from the review decision.
questions.traps: Awareness alone rarely changes behaviour under time pressure. Reallocating reviewers and adding automation both leave the differential in place.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to identify the weakest part of its own analysis. It names a section that is genuinely weak, and the team fixes it.
options: Use the answer as one input and review the rest independently
Fix the identified section and treat the analysis as strengthened overall
Ask Claude to identify the next weakest part and continue until it stops
Ask Claude to confirm the analysis is sound after the fix has been applied
questions.why: Naming a real weakness does not establish it was the most serious one. The model's view of its own output is partial, so the answer is a lead rather than a verdict.
questions.traps: Treating it as the weakest point is the unsupported step. Iterating mines the same partial view, and a self-confirmation adds nothing.

questions.stem: A team is checking a Claude-generated document and finds the sources it cites are real and say roughly what is claimed, but each claim is slightly stronger than its source.
options: Accept the document, since the sources support the general direction of each claim
Ask Claude to soften the claims that overstate their sources
Adjust each claim to match its source, since consistent overstatement is a systematic drift
Add a caveat noting that claims are summarised from the cited sources
questions.why: A consistent pattern of strengthening is a systematic issue affecting every claim, so it is corrected claim by claim against the sources rather than treated as acceptable rounding.
questions.traps: Directional support is not support for the stated strength. A softening pass repeats the summarisation that drifted, and a caveat does not correct the claims.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude for a figure and receives one that matches their expectation exactly. The figure is unusually round.
options: Verify it, since matching your expectations is a reason for scrutiny
Accept it, since it agrees with what the associate already believed to be true
Ask Claude whether the figure is exact or approximate
Use the figure and note that it is approximate in the document
questions.why: Agreement with expectation removes the friction that would normally prompt a check, and roundness suggests a plausible construction. Both are reasons to verify rather than to relax.
questions.traps: Confirmation is the weakest reason to accept a figure. Asking about precision and labelling it approximate both publish an unverified number.

questions.stem: A team asks whether Claude's output is good. Different stakeholders answer differently because each is judging against their own unstated purpose.
options: Collect all the stakeholder views and average them into an overall verdict
Ask the most senior stakeholder to make the final quality decision
Ask Claude to assess the output against each stakeholder's likely concerns
Establish the purpose the output serves before judging its quality
questions.why: Quality is meaningless without a purpose, and unstated purposes are why the judgements diverge. Fixing the purpose is what makes the assessments comparable.
questions.traps: Averaging incommensurable judgements produces a number with no meaning. Seniority settles it by authority rather than by standard, and modelling stakeholder concerns does not agree the purpose.

questions.stem: An associate wants to show that using Claude improved their team's output quality. They compare this quarter's work against last quarter's.
options: Present the comparison, since it covers a substantial period of real work
Note that many things changed between the two quarters
Compare against the same quarter last year to control for seasonal effects
Ask the team whether they believe quality has improved this quarter
questions.why: A before-and-after comparison across a quarter confounds the tool with everything else that changed. Stating that limitation is what keeps the claim honest.
questions.traps: Presenting it as evidence overclaims. Year-on-year comparison controls for one confounder among many, and team perception is a different and weaker measure.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to summarise a policy document. The summary is accurate and omits the exceptions section, which is where most of the practical complexity sits.
options: Ask for the exceptions and the edge cases specifically, not just the main rules
Ask for a longer summary so the exceptions section is more likely to survive
Ask Claude to summarise each section of the document separately
Ask Claude whether the policy has exceptions that were not summarised
questions.why: Exceptions read as detail during compression and are dropped early. Requesting them explicitly is what preserves the part that determines how a policy actually operates.
questions.traps: Length helps marginally without targeting the category. Section-by-section summarisation is heavier than needed, and a follow-up may be answered from the compressed view.

questions.stem: An associate finds Claude has described a meeting that did not happen, in an otherwise accurate summary of a project history.
options: Remove the meeting and accept the rest of the project history as accurate
Ask Claude to confirm which meetings in the summary actually took place
Verify the events as well as the facts in the generated narrative
Assume the meeting happened but was not recorded in the documents provided
questions.why: Narrative generation fills gaps with plausible connecting events. A described meeting is a factual claim about the world and needs the same verification as a figure.
questions.traps: Assuming an unrecorded meeting rationalises the fabrication. Removing it in isolation ignores what else may be constructed, and self-confirmation is not independent.

questions.stem: A team has one reviewer who catches far more issues than the others. They are becoming a bottleneck.
options: Route all high-stakes content to that reviewer and accept the bottleneck
Find out what that reviewer checks and turn it into shared criteria
Ask the other reviewers to spend more time on each item they review
Reduce the volume of content so the strong reviewer can review all of it
questions.why: An effective reviewer is following criteria the others are not. Making those criteria explicit distributes the capability instead of concentrating dependence on one person.
questions.traps: Routing everything to them entrenches the bottleneck. More time without better criteria does not close the gap, and cutting volume constrains the work to fit one person.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to summarise a debate. The summary presents both positions fairly but treats a fringe position and a mainstream one as equally weighted.
options: Accept the summary, since presenting both positions fairly is what balance requires
Ask Claude to indicate which position it considers more likely to be correct
Ask for a longer summary so the mainstream position receives more coverage
Ask what level of support each position actually has
questions.why: Balanced presentation of unbalanced positions distorts by implying parity. Asking about the level of support restores the proportion without suppressing the minority view.
questions.traps: Equating fairness with equal treatment is the false-balance error. A model verdict substitutes opinion, and more length does not encode standing.

questions.stem: A team needs to check twenty claims and has a subject expert available for one hour.
options: Have the expert check as many claims as possible in the hour available
Have the expert check the claims that appear first in the document
Have the expert check the claims that only an expert is able to evaluate
Ask Claude to identify which claims require expert judgement to verify
questions.why: Scarce expertise goes where it is the only thing that works. Claims checkable against documents do not need the expert, so routing by what the check requires maximises what the hour buys.
questions.traps: Working through in order wastes expert time on checkable claims. Position is arbitrary, and asking the model to triage is not independent.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to list what it does not know about a topic. The list is thoughtful and does not include the specific gap that later causes a problem.
options: Accept the list as a reasonable map of the model's limitations on the topic
Treat such a list as partial by construction rather than as complete
Ask Claude to extend the list until the relevant gap is eventually included
Ask Claude to rate its overall coverage of the topic as a percentage
questions.why: A model can only report gaps it can represent, which excludes the ones that matter most. The list is useful as a prompt for your own thinking, not as a boundary.
questions.traps: Treating it as a map is the error. Iterating mines the same representable set, and a coverage percentage is an unfounded self-estimate.

questions.stem: A team's quality bar for Claude output is that a reviewer would not be embarrassed to have written it. Outputs that clear this bar still contain factual errors.
options: Add an explicit accuracy check alongside the presentation bar
Raise the bar so reviewers apply a stricter standard when assessing outputs
Ask reviewers to imagine the output being published externally
Ask Claude to check its output against the same standard before submitting it
questions.why: An authorship-embarrassment test measures how the writing reads. Factual correctness is a separate property needing its own check against sources.
questions.traps: Raising or reframing the same presentational bar does not add a source comparison. Model self-checking is not independent.

questions.stem: A team publishes a Claude-drafted article that draws on three sources. A reader asks which claim came from which source and nobody on the team can answer.
options: Ask Claude to reconstruct which source supported each claim in the article
List the three sources at the end of the article as its bibliography
Remove the specific claims that cannot be attributed to a particular source
Require per-claim sourcing at generation time
questions.why: Traceability has to be built during generation, because reconstructing it later is guesswork about a process that left no record. Requiring it up front is the only reliable point of intervention.
questions.traps: Reconstruction produces plausible attributions rather than real ones. A bibliography does not map claims to sources, and stripping claims discards content that may be perfectly well supported.

questions.stem: An associate is under deadline and a Claude-drafted section contains six claims. They have time to check two of them properly or skim all six.
options: Skim all six so every claim receives at least some level of attention
Check the two claims the argument depends on properly, since a skim confirms nothing
Check the two claims that would be easiest to verify in the time available
Ask a colleague to skim the section while the associate checks two claims
questions.why: A skim tests plausibility, which is the property a wrong claim already has. Two real checks on load-bearing claims produce actual knowledge; six skims produce none.
questions.traps: Coverage without depth is the illusion of verification. Choosing by ease optimises for speed rather than risk, and a colleague's skim has the same limitation.

questions.stem: A team notices that Claude's errors cluster in the parts of its output that are most specific: names, dates, figures and citations.
options: Focus verification on the general claims, since those carry the argument
Verify specific details and general claims at the same level of effort
Ask Claude to reduce the specificity of its output to lower the error rate
Focus verification on the specific details, where fabrication concentrates
questions.why: Specificity is where generation has the least support and the most room to construct. Concentrating checks there matches effort to where errors actually live.
questions.traps: General claims are more robust and less checkable. Uniform effort ignores the observed pattern, and reducing specificity removes the useful detail.

questions.stem: An associate wants to compare two approaches. Approach A was used on the ten easiest cases and approach B on the ten hardest, and A performed better.
options: Conclude approach A performs better and adopt it for future work
Adjust the results to account for the difficulty difference between the case sets
Note the comparison is confounded by the difference in case difficulty
Run approach B on the ten easy cases as well and compare those results
questions.why: Non-random assignment of cases makes the outcome difference attributable to difficulty rather than approach. Naming the confound is what stops a spurious conclusion.
questions.traps: Adopting A acts on the confound. Adjusting requires a difficulty measure nobody has, and testing B on easy cases is a reasonable next step but does not repair this comparison.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to check whether its output contains hallucinations. It reports none. Two fabricated details are later found.
options: Recognise a model cannot detect fabrications it produced
Ask Claude to check more carefully using a stricter definition of hallucination
Ask Claude to check its output in a separate conversation
Accept that self-checking catches most cases and add spot checks for the rest
questions.why: A fabrication is generated as a confident claim, so nothing distinguishes it internally from a true one. Self-checking is structurally unable to find them.
questions.traps: Stricter definitions do not create the missing signal. A fresh conversation lacks the output's context, and assuming most are caught is unsupported.

questions.stem: An associate has to sign off on Claude-drafted content but is unsure what signing off commits them to.
options: Sign off, since review has already been performed by another team member
Establish what the sign-off actually asserts before you agree to take it on here
Sign off with a note that the content was drafted with Claude's assistance
Ask Claude what a reviewer should check before signing off on content
questions.why: Sign-off is an accountability act and its meaning has to be defined. Knowing what you are asserting determines what you have to check first.
questions.traps: Relying on prior review without knowing its scope is unfounded. A tool disclosure does not limit accountability, and asking the model does not settle a governance question.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to review a contract for risks. It identifies risks in the clauses present and does not note that a limitation of liability clause is missing.
options: Ask for a more thorough review of the contract's clauses and terms
Ask Claude whether the contract is missing any standard clauses
Compare the contract against a template to identify structural omissions
Ask what should be present and is not, since text review misses absence
questions.why: Reviewing what is written cannot find what was never written. Framing the question around expected content is what makes absence detectable.
questions.traps: Thoroughness applies to present text. A yes-or-no follow-up is weaker than the reframed question, and template comparison is sound practice but not the framing lesson here.

questions.stem: An associate receives a table from Claude where every row is correct but the rows do not cover the period the analysis claims to address.
options: Verify the individual figures more carefully across all of the rows
Ask Claude to extend the table to cover the full period claimed
Check the scope of the data against the claim being made here
Adjust the claim to match the period the table actually covers
questions.why: Correct values within the wrong scope still support a false claim. Checking that the data covers what the analysis asserts is a separate and prior check.
questions.traps: More value checking validates the wrong thing. Extending or restating are fixes that follow the diagnosis rather than replacing it.

questions.stem: A team wants to review Claude output but each item takes ten minutes to check properly and they produce forty items a day.
options: Narrow the task, or sample against a defined level of risk
Ask reviewers to work faster so all forty items can be checked each day
Review the first twenty items each day and leave the rest unchecked
Ask Claude to produce fewer, higher-quality items each day
questions.why: When the check cannot scale, either the work or the risk posture has to change. Making that an explicit decision is better than letting throughput silently degrade the control.
questions.traps: Speeding up degrades the check. Reviewing by arrival order is arbitrary sampling, and asking for fewer items does not address the ratio.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to evaluate three options and lists them in order of their own preference.
options: Accept the evaluation, since the model assesses each option on its merits
Ask Claude to evaluate the options in reverse order and compare results
Present the options in a neutral order rather than in your own preference order
Tell Claude to ignore the order in which the options were presented
questions.why: Presentation order carries information the model uses. Neutralising it is the simple prevention rather than a correction applied afterwards.
questions.traps: Assuming order is ignored is the misconception. Reverse-order comparison detects the effect, and an instruction to ignore a signal already given is unreliable.

questions.stem: A team receives a Claude summary of a webpage. The summary is plausible but the page has changed since the model would have seen it.
options: Open the page and check its current content against the summary
Accept the summary, since the general content of such pages changes slowly
Ask Claude when it last had information about the page's contents
Ask Claude to summarise the page again to get more current information
questions.why: Web content changes and generated summaries reflect training data of unknown vintage. Reading the live page is the only way to know what it says now.
questions.traps: Assuming slow change is a guess. Asking about recency produces an unreliable self-report, and a second summary draws on the same stale information.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to list the steps in a process. The list is complete for the normal path and does not mention what happens when a step fails.
options: Ask for more steps so the failure handling eventually appears in the list
Ask Claude whether the process has any exception handling built into it
Ask for the process to be described as a flowchart instead of a list
Ask about the failure paths explicitly, not only the normal one
questions.why: The happy path is the default reading of "the steps". Naming exception handling is what brings the branches into scope, and those branches carry most of the operational risk.
questions.traps: Volume extends the normal path. A follow-up question is weaker than the reframe, and changing format does not change what is described.

questions.stem: A team's Claude output cites a document by name. The document exists, but the specific page cited discusses a different topic.
options: Accept the citation, since the document itself is real and relevant to the topic
Check citations at the page level, not only the document
Ask Claude to correct the page number in the citation it provided
Cite the document without the page number to avoid the specificity problem
questions.why: Document, page and content are separately checkable, and a correct document with a wrong locator is a common pattern. Verification has to reach the level of the claim.
questions.traps: A real document is not evidence about the page. Self-correction is not independent, and removing the locator hides the problem rather than resolving it.

questions.stem: An associate asks whether a draft is ready. The draft has one unverified claim, three minor wording issues, and achieves its purpose otherwise.
options: Fix the unverified claim first, and treat the wording issues as optional
Fix all four issues before releasing the draft to its audience
Release the draft and fix the issues in a subsequent revision
Ask Claude to assess whether the remaining issues are significant
questions.why: Issue severity is not uniform, and an unverified claim is a different category from wording. Triaging by consequence is what makes a release decision defensible.
questions.traps: Treating all issues equally wastes effort or delays release. Shipping the unverified claim carries the real risk, and model triage is not independent.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to compute a metric and it produces a figure using a definition of the metric that differs from the company's own.
options: Accept the figure, since the computation was performed correctly as described
Ask Claude which definition of the metric it used in the calculation
Recompute the figure yourself using the company's own definition
Specify the definition, since a single metric name means different things
questions.why: Metric names are ambiguous across organisations, and the model applies the common definition. Supplying yours is what makes the output comparable to your other numbers.
questions.traps: Correct computation of the wrong metric is still wrong. Asking afterwards diagnoses it, and manual recomputation forfeits the task.

questions.stem: An associate reviews Claude output by reading it once from start to finish and noting anything that seems wrong.
options: Read the output twice so more issues are noticed on the second pass
Review against a defined list of checks rather than reading it through
Read the output slowly so that subtle problems are more likely to be noticed
Ask a second person to read it as well so two perspectives are applied
questions.why: Unstructured reading finds what stands out, which systematically misses omissions and unverified specifics. A defined checklist is what makes review reproducible.
questions.traps: Repetition and slowness both scale the same unstructured attention. A second unstructured reader adds a correlated pass.

questions.stem: A team tracks Claude's accuracy and finds it has fallen from 94% to 89% over two weeks. Each measurement is based on about thirty items.
options: Investigate what changed in the workflow over the past two weeks
Adjust the prompt to compensate for the drop in measured accuracy
Continue measuring before acting on a two-sample change
Report the decline so the team is aware performance has degraded
questions.why: The difference between two small samples is well within ordinary variation. Accumulating more data is what distinguishes a real trend from noise before anyone acts on it.
questions.traps: Investigating and adjusting both treat noise as signal. Reporting a decline that may not exist creates unwarranted concern.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude for examples of companies that have implemented a practice. Three of the five examples are real and correctly described; two companies exist but never did this.
options: Accept the examples, since all five companies are real organisations
Ask Claude for sources for each of the five examples it provided
Use only the three examples the associate already recognises as accurate
Verify every one of the examples against the company's own published account
questions.why: Attributing a real practice to a real company is a factual claim about that company. The components being real is what makes the composite claim persuasive rather than verified.
questions.traps: Existence of the company is not evidence about its actions. Requested sources may be generated, and recognition is a weak filter.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to explain its reasoning, hoping this will make errors visible. The explanations are coherent and the errors persist.
options: Ask for more detailed reasoning so the error becomes visible in the steps
Treat the explanation as a description, not a record of the reasoning
Ask Claude to check each reasoning step for correctness individually
Accept that coherent reasoning indicates the answer is probably correct
questions.why: An explanation is generated alongside the answer and can be coherent while the answer is wrong. It is useful for review but is not a trace you can audit for the actual fault.
questions.traps: More detail produces more coherent narrative. Self-checking steps shares the same reasoning, and treating coherence as correctness is the trap.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude what the risks of a course of action are, having described it in positive terms throughout the prompt.
options: Describe the action neutrally rather than in positive language
Accept the risk list, since the request explicitly asked for risks
Ask for the risks again with a request to be more critical
Ask what the risks would be if the action were described negatively
questions.why: A positively framed description produces risks phrased as manageable. Neutral description is what lets the risk analysis reflect the action rather than the framing.
questions.traps: Asking for risks does not neutralise the frame. A criticality instruction operates within it, and a negatively framed rerun swaps one bias for another.

questions.stem: A team needs to verify a claim about a change in law. Claude's answer describes the law as it stood before an amendment that has since taken effect.
options: Ask Claude whether the law has been amended since its information was current
Ask Claude for the date of the version it is describing
Check the current consolidated text of the law
Use the answer and note that the law may have been amended
questions.why: Legal content changes and a model's account reflects an unknown vintage. The current authoritative text is the only thing that settles what the law says now.
questions.traps: Self-reports about recency are unreliable. A caveat publishes an answer known to be potentially superseded.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to identify costs for a proposal. The list covers direct costs and omits the internal time the change will consume.
options: Ask about the cost categories explicitly, including internal time and effort
Ask for more cost items so internal time eventually appears in the list
Ask Claude whether there are any indirect costs it did not include
Estimate the internal time separately and add it to Claude's list
questions.why: Cost lists default to the categories that appear on invoices. Naming the less visible categories is what brings internal effort into the analysis where it belongs.
questions.traps: Volume samples the same default. A follow-up question is weaker than the reframe, and separate estimation solves this instance only.

questions.stem: A team judges Claude output as acceptable if nobody objects to it. Over time, output quality drifts downward without anyone noticing.
options: Ask reviewers to object more readily when they notice quality problems
Sample outputs periodically and compare them against earlier examples
Ask Claude to maintain a consistent quality standard across outputs
Define what acceptable actually means in concrete terms here
questions.why: A negative standard ratchets downward because each individual step is small enough not to trigger an objection. A stated positive standard is what anchors the bar.
questions.traps: Encouraging objections still leaves the standard implicit. Periodic comparison detects drift after it happens, and instructing the model does not define the bar.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to sum a column of figures they pasted in. The total is wrong because one figure was misread from the paste.
options: Ask Claude to recalculate the total from the same pasted figures
Check the model read the inputs correctly before checking arithmetic
Check the arithmetic of the sum rather than the values that were used
Use a spreadsheet to compute the total instead of asking the model
questions.why: Input fidelity is the first thing to check when a computed result is wrong, because correct arithmetic over misread inputs produces a wrong answer that survives an arithmetic check.
questions.traps: Recalculation repeats over the same misreading. Checking only the arithmetic misses the actual fault, and switching tools avoids the diagnosis being tested.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to summarise research on a topic. The summary describes a consensus, but the sources it draws on are not identified and may not be recent.
options: Accept the summary, since consensus positions change slowly in most fields
Ask Claude to focus on the most recent research in a follow-up request
Ask which sources and what period the summary reflects
Search for recent papers and compare them against the summary
questions.why: A consensus claim without sources or a period is unanchored. Establishing what it is based on is what determines whether it can be used at all.
questions.traps: Assuming slow change is a guess. A recency instruction produces another unanchored summary, and independent search is useful but starts by ignoring the diagnosis.

questions.stem: An associate is asked to review Claude output produced from a prompt they did not write, for a purpose they were not told.
options: Establish the purpose and read the prompt before you review any of the output text
Review the output for accuracy and clarity, which apply regardless of purpose
Ask Claude what the output was intended to achieve before reviewing it
Review the output and note that the purpose was not communicated
questions.why: Review requires a standard, and the standard comes from purpose. Without it a reviewer can only assess general properties and will miss fitness failures.
questions.traps: General properties miss the fitness question entirely. Asking the model to infer intent is guesswork, and noting the gap defers rather than resolves it.

questions.stem: A team finds Claude reliably correct on a topic over dozens of uses, then encounters a confident and completely fabricated answer on an adjacent question.
options: Conclude the model has become less reliable and reduce their use of it
Treat reliability as topic-specific rather than as a general property
Assume the fabricated answer was caused by an unusually worded question
Continue as before, since one failure among dozens is an acceptable rate
questions.why: Support varies sharply across a topic's edges, so a record of accuracy in the centre says little about the periphery. Adjacency is not coverage.
questions.traps: A single failure is not evidence of general degradation. Blaming the wording rationalises, and treating it as an acceptable rate ignores that the failure mode is silent.

questions.stem: An associate tests a workflow on cases from the past month. It performs well. The past month happened to contain no cases of the type that usually cause problems.
options: Test on a longer period so more case types are naturally included
Conclude the workflow performs well, since the test used real cases
Ask colleagues whether they have encountered problems with similar workflows
Test deliberately on the difficult case types rather than these
questions.why: Convenience samples miss the cases that matter. Deliberately constructing tests around known difficulty is what makes a test informative about failure.
questions.traps: A longer period improves the odds without guaranteeing coverage. Real cases are not automatically representative, and colleague experience is anecdote.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to identify problems with a competitor's product. The list is detailed and one-sided, and the team uses it in a sales conversation.
options: Use the list, since the team asked specifically about problems with the product
Ask Claude for the competitor's strengths as well to balance the picture
Recognise the list answers the question asked, then check it
Ask Claude to verify each claim on the list before the sales conversation
questions.why: A prompt asking for problems produces problems, generated to satisfy the request. Anything said externally about a competitor is a factual claim carrying real exposure.
questions.traps: Using it unchecked is the risk. Adding strengths balances internally without verifying the claims, and model self-verification is not independent.

questions.stem: An associate has verified that a Claude-generated document is accurate. Two months later they reuse it without rechecking.
options: Recheck the time-sensitive claims before reusing the document two months on
Reuse it, since the document was thoroughly verified when it was created
Ask Claude whether anything in the document is likely to have changed
Add a note stating when the document was originally verified
questions.why: Verification has a shelf life determined by how fast the underlying facts move. Rechecking the time-sensitive parts is proportionate to what actually goes stale.
questions.traps: Past verification says nothing about current accuracy. Asking the model about change is unreliable, and a date stamp informs readers without correcting anything.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to summarise what a report recommends. The summary lists the recommendations but omits the conditions the report attached to them.
options: Ask for a longer summary so the conditions are more likely to be retained
Ask for the conditions attached to each of the recommendations
Ask Claude to list the recommendations with their supporting evidence
Read the recommendations section directly rather than summarising it
questions.why: Conditions are the qualifying material that compression removes first, and they often determine whether a recommendation applies at all. Requiring them explicitly is the fix.
questions.traps: Length helps without targeting. Supporting evidence is a different attachment, and reading it yourself forfeits the summary.

questions.stem: An associate produces Claude output that is technically correct but that their audience will find condescending in tone.
options: Release it, since the content is accurate and tone is a matter of taste
Ask Claude to rewrite it in a warmer tone before releasing it
Ask a colleague whether the tone reads as condescending to them
Treat audience reception as part of quality, not just taste
questions.why: Fitness for purpose includes how the audience receives it. Recognising tone as a quality dimension rather than a preference is what makes the rewrite necessary rather than optional.
questions.traps: Dismissing tone as taste is the error being tested. The rewrite is the right action but follows from the judgement, and a colleague check confirms rather than decides.

questions.stem: A team receives Claude's estimate of a project's cost. The estimate is presented as a single figure with no indication of uncertainty.
options: Accept the figure, since a single number is easier to plan against
Ask Claude how confident it is in the estimate it produced
Ask for a range with the assumptions behind it
Add a contingency percentage to the figure for planning purposes
questions.why: A point estimate conceals both the uncertainty and the assumptions that drive it. A range with stated assumptions is what makes an estimate reviewable.
questions.traps: Ease of planning is not accuracy. Self-reported confidence is unreliable, and a blanket contingency is applied without knowing what drives the variance.

questions.stem: An associate finds that reviewing Claude output takes longer than writing the content themselves would have.
options: Reconsider whether the task is a good fit, since review cost is part of the total cost
Continue, since reviewing is less mentally demanding than writing from scratch
Reduce the depth of review so the total time becomes competitive
Ask Claude to produce output that is easier to review
questions.why: If verification costs more than production, the tool is not saving anything on that task. Counting review as part of the cost is what makes the comparison honest.
questions.traps: Comparative ease is not the measure. Cutting review depth manufactures a saving by weakening the control, and easier-to-review output does not change the arithmetic much.

questions.stem: A team notices Claude sometimes says it is unsure. They start treating outputs without such statements as verified.
options: Treat outputs without uncertainty statements as more reliable than those with them
Ask Claude to always state its confidence so the signal is consistently available
Verify only the outputs where uncertainty was expressed by the model
Continue verifying regardless, since the absence of a hedge means nothing at all
questions.why: Expressed uncertainty is informative when present and uninformative when absent, because the model cannot detect what it does not know. Asymmetric signals need asymmetric treatment.
questions.traps: Reading silence as assurance is the error. Mandating a confidence statement does not create knowledge, and verifying only flagged outputs misses the confident failures.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to summarise a meeting and mentions that one participant is the project sponsor.
options: Accept the summary, since knowing roles helps the model understand the discussion
Ask for the summary without identifying any of the roles
Ask Claude to weight all participants' contributions equally in the summary
Ask for two summaries, one with roles identified and one without
questions.why: Status information supplied in the prompt becomes emphasis in the summary. Withholding it is what keeps the record about what was said rather than who said it.
questions.traps: Role context helps interpretation but skews the record. An equal-weighting instruction competes with information already given, and paired summaries double work.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude what could go wrong with a plan. The answer covers plausible failures and omits the scenario where the plan succeeds but is no longer needed.
options: Ask for more failure scenarios so unusual ones eventually appear
Ask Claude to consider low-probability high-impact scenarios as well
Ask about changes in the plan's premises too
Run a structured risk workshop instead of asking the model
questions.why: Failure framing produces execution failures. Premise failure is a different category that only enters the analysis when the question is broadened to include it.
questions.traps: Volume extends the same category. Probability framing is a different axis, and abandoning the tool avoids rather than answers.

questions.stem: An associate finds Claude's answer matches a source they found through a search engine. The source turns out to be a blog summarising another article.
options: Accept the corroboration, since an independent source agrees with the answer
Follow the chain back to the original source rather than stopping at a summary page
Look for a second blog that agrees with the first to strengthen the corroboration
Cite the blog, since it is a locatable source for the claim
questions.why: Corroboration is only as good as the source's own basis. A derivative source can repeat an error, so verification follows the chain to the original.
questions.traps: Treating a derivative as independent is the error. A second derivative may share the same origin, and citing a blog for a checkable fact is weak.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to describe a product feature and the description is correct except that it names a menu path that does not exist.
options: Accept the description, since the feature and its behaviour were described correctly
Ask Claude to confirm the menu path is correct in the current version
Check the interface details against the product, not against memory
Describe the feature without naming a specific path in the interface
questions.why: Correct concept with wrong specifics is the characteristic shape here, and interface details change frequently. Checking them against the product is what catches it.
questions.traps: Correct behaviour is not evidence about the path. Self-confirmation is not independent, and removing specifics avoids the error without verifying anything.

questions.stem: An associate is asked how reliable Claude is for their team's work. They have used it extensively and formed a strong impression.
options: Point to measured results on defined tasks, not impressions
Report their impression, since extensive use is a reasonable basis for judgement
Ask other team members for their impressions and report the consensus
Ask Claude to describe its own reliability for the tasks in question
questions.why: Impressions from use are shaped by memorable successes and failures rather than by rates. Measured results on defined tasks is what answers a reliability question.
questions.traps: Extensive use produces vivid recall, not statistics. Aggregating impressions aggregates the same bias, and self-description is not evidence.

questions.stem: A team is deciding whether Claude output needs to be as good as a human expert's or merely good enough for the task.
options: Set the standard at expert parity, since that is the highest available benchmark
Set the standard slightly below expert parity to allow for practical constraints
Ask an expert to define the standard the output should meet
Set the standard from what the task actually requires
questions.why: Standards follow requirements. Anchoring on expert parity imports a benchmark that may exceed the need and makes otherwise useful work look like a failure.
questions.traps: Expert parity and a discount off it both anchor on the wrong reference. An expert can inform the standard but the task determines it.

questions.stem: An associate reviews Claude output thoroughly on Monday and gradually less thoroughly through the week as confidence builds and workload rises.
options: Accept the drift, since confidence built through the week is based on real experience
Review more thoroughly later in the week to counteract the tendency
Fix the review depth by content type rather than letting it drift with confidence and workload
Rotate reviewers through the week so nobody's confidence accumulates
questions.why: Review depth should be a property of the content's risk, not of the reviewer's mood or schedule. Fixing it by type is what makes the control consistent.
questions.traps: Accepting the drift lets the control weaken exactly as volume rises. A counter-drift instruction fights a tendency without a rule, and rotation adds cost.

questions.stem: A team receives figures from Claude that are consistent with each other and with the team's expectations, but the underlying data was never supplied to the model.
options: Accept the figures, since they are consistent and match the team's expectations
Recognise that figures generated without any data are constructed
Ask Claude which data it used to produce the figures
Use the figures as estimates and refine them when real data is available
questions.why: Consistency is a property of construction, not of derivation. Without data as input, the figures cannot be measurements of anything.
questions.traps: Consistency plus expectation is exactly what makes this dangerous. Asking about data invites invention, and treating fabrications as provisional estimates embeds them.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to review a plan and it identifies six issues. The associate is unsure whether six is thorough or whether more exist.
options: Review against a structured framework so the coverage is defined
Ask Claude whether there are more issues beyond the six it identified
Ask for the review again and compare the two lists for additional items
Accept six as a reasonable number of issues for a plan of this size
questions.why: Open-ended output has no defined coverage, so completeness cannot be assessed from the output alone. A framework supplies the reference the count needs.
