questions.traps: Asking for more mines the same view. Comparing two runs measures variability, and treating a count as a coverage signal is unfounded.

questions.stem: A team's Claude output includes a statistic attributed to a survey. The survey exists but measured a different population than the output implies.
options: Accept the attribution, since the survey is real and the statistic appears in it
Ask Claude to clarify which population the survey covered
Cite the survey with a note about its methodology
Check what the source actually measured
questions.why: Real source, real figure, wrong application is a distinct failure from fabrication and is only caught by reading what the source measured. Applicability is part of verification.
questions.traps: Existence of the figure is not evidence of relevance. Self-clarification is unreliable, and a methodology note does not fix a misapplied statistic.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to write a business case. The case is persuasive and does not mention the option of doing nothing.
options: Ask for a more balanced business case in a follow-up request
Add a section on the do-nothing option to the case that was produced
Ask for the do-nothing option to be evaluated alongside the actual proposal
Accept it, since a business case is meant to argue for a course of action
questions.why: A business case is a persuasive genre and the status quo is the option it omits by default. Requiring its evaluation is what makes the comparison honest.
questions.traps: A balance instruction is vague. A bolted-on section sits outside the argument, and accepting the genre keeps the omission.

questions.stem: A team is asked to state how confident they are in a Claude-drafted analysis. They verified the figures but not the reasoning connecting them.
options: State that the figures were verified and that the reasoning was not
State high confidence, since the figures underlying the analysis were checked
State low confidence, since not everything in the analysis was verified
Ask Claude to assess the strength of the reasoning in its analysis
questions.why: Confidence should be reported at the granularity it was established. Separating verified inputs from unverified reasoning is more useful than a single blended figure.
questions.traps: A blended high or low figure discards the distinction. Model self-assessment of its own reasoning is not independent.

questions.stem: An associate notices Claude gives different answers to the same question depending on how it is phrased, and asks Claude which phrasing gives the more accurate answer.
options: Use the answer Claude identifies as more accurate when asked to compare them
Verify both of the answers against a source outside the model
Use the answer from the phrasing that seems more natural to the associate
Average the two answers to arrive at a more balanced result
questions.why: A model cannot rank its own outputs by accuracy because it has no access to the truth they diverge from. An external source is what settles which is right.
questions.traps: Self-adjudication is the trap. Naturalness of phrasing is unrelated to accuracy, and averaging is meaningless for factual claims.

questions.stem: A team's review process is documented but nobody follows it, because the documented process takes longer than the time available.
options: Ask the team to follow the documented process as it is written
Remove the documentation so the process is not misrepresented
Allocate more time so the documented process becomes feasible
Redesign the process to fit the time actually available
questions.why: A control nobody follows provides no assurance while creating the impression of one. Aligning the documented process with reality is what restores the assurance.
questions.traps: Instructing compliance without resourcing repeats the failure. Deleting documentation removes the record, and more time may not be available.

questions.stem: An associate must decide whether Claude output is fit to send to a regulator. It is accurate and clear but uses informal phrasing throughout.
options: Judge it against the regulator's own expectations, including the register it uses
Send it, since accuracy is what matters most in regulatory correspondence
Ask Claude to make the phrasing more formal and send it without further review
Ask a colleague whether the informal phrasing is likely to cause a problem
questions.why: Fitness is context-specific and a regulator's expectations include register. Naming the relevant standard is what makes the judgement rather than a stylistic preference.
questions.traps: Accuracy alone is not fitness here. The rewrite is the likely action but follows the judgement, and a colleague's view is input rather than standard.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to identify a trend in six data points. It describes a clear upward trend, and two of the six points are substantially below the others.
options: Accept the trend, since the overall direction across the six points is upward
Question whether six such points support a trend claim at all
Ask Claude to recalculate the trend excluding the two low points
Ask Claude how strong the trend is on the data provided
questions.why: Six noisy points rarely support a confident trend statement. Questioning whether the claim is warranted is prior to refining how it is calculated.
questions.traps: Accepting the direction ignores the variation. Excluding inconvenient points is worse, and asking the model to rate its own trend is not evidence.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to summarise a document and the summary includes a conclusion the document builds toward but never actually states.
options: Accept the summary, since the conclusion follows from the document's argument
Ask Claude whether the conclusion appears explicitly in the document
Check the summarised conclusions against the text itself
Present the conclusion as an inference rather than as the document's position
questions.why: Summarisation completes arguments, and a completed conclusion reads identically to a quoted one. Checking whether it was stated is what preserves the distinction that matters.
questions.traps: Following from the argument is not the same as being asserted. Self-checking is not independent, and relabelling requires already knowing which it is.

questions.stem: A team wants to know whether a new prompt is better than the old one. They run each on the same fifty cases and the new one wins on 27 of them.
options: Adopt the new prompt, since it won on more cases than the old one did
Adopt the new prompt provisionally and monitor its performance over time
Run the comparison again on fifty different cases and adopt whichever wins twice
Recognise that 27 out of 50 is close to a coin flip
questions.why: A 27-23 split is well within what chance produces when two options perform identically. Treating a narrow margin as a result is the inference error the scenario targets.
questions.traps: Adopting on a coin-flip margin acts on noise. Provisional adoption embeds the same unsupported choice, and a best-of-two rule compounds the problem rather than increasing the sample.

questions.stem: An associate has a Claude-drafted document with claims about their own industry. They know the industry well and nothing looks wrong.
options: Verify the specific figures and the named entities, since familiarity alone does not catch them
Accept the document, since an experienced practitioner reviewed it against their knowledge
Ask a more experienced colleague to read the document as a second opinion
Ask Claude to identify which claims in the document are most specific
questions.why: Domain knowledge catches implausible claims and misses plausible specifics, which is where fabrication lives. Detail-level checks are the complement to expert reading.
questions.traps: Expert plausibility review has a known blind spot for specifics. A second expert shares it, and asking the model to flag specificity is a step toward the right answer without taking it.

questions.stem: A team's Claude output is consistently accurate but takes longer to produce than expected because prompts need several rounds each time.
options: Accept the process, since accuracy is the property that matters most here
Reduce the number of rounds by accepting slightly lower quality output
Ask Claude to produce better output on the first attempt each time
Count the prompting rounds in the assessment as part of the overall cost
questions.why: Value is accuracy relative to total cost, and prompting rounds are part of that cost. Including them is what makes the assessment complete rather than flattering.
questions.traps: Accuracy alone is not value. Trading quality for speed decides before measuring, and instructing the model to be right first time is not a lever.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude for the arguments against a proposal. The list is thorough and every argument concerns implementation rather than the proposal's premise.
options: Ask for more arguments so premise-level objections eventually appear
Ask Claude to consider objections at every level of the proposal
Ask about the premise separately from the implementation concerns
Accept the list, since implementation objections are the most actionable ones
questions.why: Objection lists gravitate to implementation because the premise is treated as given by the question. Separating the levels is what surfaces the more fundamental challenge.
questions.traps: Volume extends the same level. A vague instruction about levels does not name them, and treating actionability as sufficient keeps the gap.

questions.stem: A team wants a single reviewer to check accuracy, tone, compliance and formatting on every Claude output.
options: Provide a combined checklist covering all four areas for the single reviewer
Split the checks so each reviewer applies criteria they can actually judge
Ask the reviewer to prioritise accuracy and treat the other three as secondary
Ask Claude to check tone, compliance and formatting so the reviewer covers accuracy
questions.why: Different checks need different expertise and different attention. Combining four into one pass produces shallow coverage of all of them.
questions.traps: A combined checklist does not supply missing expertise. Prioritising abandons three checks, and model self-checking is not independent for compliance.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to evaluate a decision they made six months ago, describing what happened afterwards.
options: Accept the evaluation, since the outcome is relevant evidence about the decision
Ask Claude to evaluate the decision without being told the outcome
Ask for both an outcome-aware and an outcome-blind evaluation
Ask for the evaluation based on what was known at the time, not on how it turned out
questions.why: Decision quality is judged on the information available when it was made. Supplying the outcome guarantees the evaluation reads it backwards into the reasoning.
questions.traps: Outcome is evidence about luck as well as judgement. A blinding instruction competes with information already given, and paired evaluations double the work.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to calculate a figure and receives one. They ask again in a new conversation and receive a slightly different figure.
options: Compute it yourself, since a deterministic result should not vary at all
Use the first figure, since it was produced before any anchoring could occur
Use the average of the two figures as the best available estimate
Ask a third time and use whichever figure appears twice
questions.why: Variation on a deterministic calculation means at least one run is wrong and possibly both. The calculation has a single correct answer that is cheap to obtain directly.
questions.traps: Every option that selects among generated figures treats variation as sampling error rather than as evidence of unreliable arithmetic.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to check a document for compliance with a policy they uploaded. It reports compliance and cites the relevant policy sections.
options: Accept the report, since it engaged with specific sections of the policy
Check that the cited sections really say what the compliance report claims
Ask Claude to explain its reasoning for each compliance determination
Ask Claude to check again focusing on the sections most likely to be breached
questions.why: A compliance determination involves locating the right section and reading it correctly. Both steps need checking, and citations make that verification possible rather than unnecessary.
questions.traps: Citations enable checking; they are not the check. Explanations and repeat passes share the interpretation that may be wrong.

questions.stem: A team's Claude workflow has produced correct output on every case they have checked. They have checked the cases where output looked unusual.
options: Conclude the workflow is reliable, since every checked case was correct
Continue checking unusual cases, since that is where errors are most likely
Recognise the sample was biased toward cases that already looked wrong
Check the same number of cases chosen at random as a comparison
questions.why: Checking only what looked suspicious and finding it fine says nothing about the outputs that looked fine and were not checked. The sample cannot support a general claim.
questions.traps: Concluding reliability from a biased sample is the error. Continuing the same selection compounds it, and random checking is the fix rather than a comparison.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude a question and receives an answer beginning with a hedge, followed by a confident and specific account.
options: Verify the specific account that follows, since an opening hedge does not qualify any of it
Treat the whole answer as uncertain because of the hedge at the beginning
Ask Claude to remove the hedge and restate the answer more directly
Accept the specifics, since the hedge shows the model is being appropriately careful
questions.why: A general hedge does not attach to particular claims, and the specifics carry the same fabrication risk as they would unhedged. They still need checking.
questions.traps: Treating the hedge as covering everything is too coarse. Removing it changes presentation, and reading it as carefulness inverts what it signals.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to summarise three documents and note where they disagree. It reports no disagreements, and the documents do conflict on one point.
options: Ask Claude to look again specifically for disagreements between the documents
Extract each document's position separately and compare them yourself
Ask for a longer summary so the disagreement has room to appear
Accept the summary, since the model had all three documents available
questions.why: Synthesis smooths conflict by construction. Separate extraction preserves each position so the comparison happens on evidence rather than inside a generation pass.
questions.traps: A second synthesis pass has the same tendency. Length does not counteract smoothing, and availability of documents is not the constraint.

questions.stem: An associate is the only person who reviews their own Claude output before it goes to customers.
options: Continue, since the associate understands the content better than anyone else
Review the output twice with a gap between the two readings
Ask Claude to review the output as a second check before it is sent
Arrange an independent reviewer for the output before it goes
questions.why: Independence is what makes review a control, and reviewing output you prompted for shares your assumptions about what it should say. Another person is what supplies it.
questions.traps: Familiarity is not independence. Spaced re-reading helps with typos rather than assumptions, and model self-review adds no independence at all.

questions.stem: A team defines a quality threshold and finds that 80% of Claude outputs meet it. They are unsure whether that is good.
options: Conclude it is good, since a substantial majority of outputs meet the standard
Conclude it is poor, since one in five outputs fails the quality threshold
Compare it against the prior process and against what the task needs
Ask Claude what a typical pass rate is for tasks of this kind
questions.why: A rate is meaningless without a reference. The relevant references are the prior process and the requirement, which together say whether 80% is an improvement and whether it is enough.
questions.traps: Judging the number in isolation in either direction has no basis. Asking the model for a benchmark produces an unfounded figure.

questions.stem: An associate needs to check a Claude claim and finds a source that agrees. The source was published after the claim's subject matter changed.
options: Check the source's date against the events it describes before treating it as proof
Accept the confirmation, since the source agrees with the claim being checked
Look for a second source that also agrees with the claim
Note that the claim is confirmed by a source of unknown currency
questions.why: Agreement from a source that predates or postdates the relevant change may confirm a superseded state. Date-checking is part of assessing whether a source is on point.
questions.traps: Agreement alone is not confirmation. A second undated source repeats the problem, and noting uncertainty publishes an unresolved check.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to identify who needs to approve a change. The list covers the obvious approvers and omits a body whose approval is required only in certain circumstances.
options: Ask for more approvers so conditional ones eventually appear in the list
Ask about the conditional approvals as well as the standard ones too
Ask Claude whether any additional approvals might be required
Check the list against the organisation's approval matrix
questions.why: Conditional requirements sit outside the default answer to "who approves this". Asking about the conditional path is what brings them into scope.
questions.traps: Volume samples the same default. A follow-up question is weaker than the reframe, and matrix comparison is a good check that arrives after the omission.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to help write a response defending a decision. The response is well-argued and treats every counterargument as something to rebut.
options: Accept the response, since the associate asked for a defence of the decision
Ask Claude to steelman the counterarguments within the response
Ask what the strongest counterargument is, and whether it succeeds
Ask for the response and a separate assessment of the decision's merits
questions.why: A defence brief produces advocacy, which is fine if the decision is settled and dangerous if it is not. Testing the counterargument first is what establishes which situation you are in.
questions.traps: Advocacy delivered as requested may defend an indefensible position. Steelmanning within a defence still serves the brief, and a separate assessment written afterwards is anchored by it.

questions.stem: A team receives a Claude analysis using figures from a spreadsheet they uploaded. The figures match, but the spreadsheet contained a filtered view rather than the full dataset.
options: Verify the figures again against the spreadsheet that was uploaded
Ask Claude whether the data appeared to be complete
Note the filter in the analysis and present the results as partial
Check the data supplied represents what the analysis covers
questions.why: Correct arithmetic over a partial dataset produces a confidently wrong conclusion. Checking what the input represents is a prior step to checking the numbers within it.
questions.traps: Re-verifying against the same partial source repeats the error. The model cannot know what was filtered out, and a footnote does not correct the conclusion.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to list the requirements of a standard. The list is plausible and the associate cannot find the standard online to check it.
options: Use the list, since it is detailed and consistent with related standards
Ask Claude to confirm the requirements it listed are current
Treat the list as unverified and find an authoritative copy before relying on it
Use the list with a note that it could not be independently verified
questions.why: Inability to verify is a reason to hold, not to proceed. Plausibility on an unverifiable topic is exactly the condition under which fabrication is undetectable.
questions.traps: Consistency with related standards is what a construction would have. Self-confirmation is not independent, and a caveat still relies on unverified requirements.

questions.stem: A team measures Claude's performance on a task and gets 88%. They repeat the measurement a month later on the same test set and get 91%.
options: Note that the test set is now familiar and the comparison may mislead
Conclude performance has improved by three percentage points over the month
Repeat the measurement a third time to see whether the trend continues
Ask what changed in the workflow that could explain the improvement
questions.why: Re-measuring on a set that has informed intervening changes contaminates the comparison. Naming that is what keeps the improvement claim honest.
questions.traps: Treating it as improvement ignores the contamination. A third measurement on the same set repeats it, and hunting for causes assumes the effect is real.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude whether its answer would change if given more information. It says yes and lists what would help.
options: Accept the list as a complete account of what the answer depends on
Treat the list as a useful prompt rather than as a complete account
Supply everything on the list and treat the resulting answer as complete
Ask Claude to extend the list until it has nothing further to add
questions.why: A model can name dependencies it can represent, which excludes the ones it does not know it is missing. The list is a helpful starting point rather than a specification.
questions.traps: Treating it as complete is the error. Supplying the list and iterating both work within the same representable set.

questions.stem: A team's reviewers each catch different kinds of issues, and which reviewer sees an item is effectively random.
options: Have every item reviewed by all reviewers so no issue type is missed
Train all reviewers so their strengths converge over time
Accept the variation, since across many items every issue type gets covered
Route each item to a reviewer whose strengths match the content
questions.why: Matching reviewer strengths to content risk is what makes each review effective. Random assignment means a compliance-heavy item may get a reviewer who checks style.
questions.traps: Reviewing everything by everyone does not scale. Training is slow and may not remove specialisation, and the averaging argument fails for individual high-stakes items.

questions.stem: An associate has to explain to a client why Claude-drafted work is acceptable. The client is uneasy about the tool being used at all.
options: Explain that the model is highly capable and widely used in the industry
Offer to have the work redone without the tool if the client prefers
Explain what was checked and by whom, since assurance comes from the process
Explain that the output was reviewed by a qualified person before delivery
questions.why: Client assurance rests on the verification process, and describing what was checked and who checked it is what makes it concrete rather than a claim about the tool.
questions.traps: Capability claims about the tool do not address the concern. Offering to redo it concedes the point, and "reviewed by a qualified person" is the right direction stated too vaguely to reassure.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to summarise a long email thread. The summary captures the decisions and omits an unresolved question that was raised twice and never answered.
options: Ask for a longer summary so the open question appears in it
Ask for open questions as well as decisions in the summary
Ask Claude whether anything in the thread remained unresolved
Read the thread directly rather than relying on the summary
questions.why: Summaries resolve toward conclusions and drop loose ends. Asking for open items explicitly is what preserves the part that still needs action.
questions.traps: Length does not target the category. A follow-up question is weaker than the reframe, and reading it yourself forfeits the summary.

questions.stem: An associate has to verify a claim and finds two authoritative sources that disagree with each other.
options: Report the disagreement rather than choosing between the two
Choose the more recent source and treat the claim as settled
Choose the source that agrees with Claude's original claim
Ask Claude which of the two sources is more likely to be correct
questions.why: When authoritative sources conflict, that is the state of the evidence. Reporting it lets the reader account for it rather than inheriting a hidden choice.
questions.traps: Recency is a reasonable tiebreak but presents a contested claim as settled. Choosing by agreement with the model is backwards, and model adjudication is not evidence.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to identify why a competitor is succeeding. The analysis attributes the success entirely to the competitor's strategy.
options: Ask for a deeper analysis of the competitor's strategic decisions
Ask Claude to consider whether luck played a role in the outcome
Compare the analysis against the competitor's own public statements
Ask about the factors outside the competitor's own control too
questions.why: Success narratives attribute outcomes to decisions and understate circumstance. Naming external factors is what balances the account into something you can learn from.
questions.traps: Depth stays inside the strategic frame. Asking about luck is a narrower version of the right idea, and public statements share the same attribution bias.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to work out how many staff are needed. The answer uses an assumption about productivity that is stated but never questioned.
options: Accept the answer, since the assumption was stated transparently in the output
Ask Claude to justify the productivity assumption it used
Test the answer's sensitivity to that assumption, since the whole result depends on it
Replace the assumption with the organisation's own figure and accept the result
questions.why: A stated assumption is transparent but not validated, and a headcount answer is a direct function of it. Sensitivity testing shows how much the conclusion actually depends on getting it right.
questions.traps: Transparency is not validation. Justification rationalises the chosen figure, and substituting your own number without testing sensitivity leaves the same fragility.

questions.stem: A team introduces spot-check sampling of Claude output. Reviewers pick which items to check themselves and tend to choose ones that look interesting.
options: Ask reviewers to pick a wider variety of items to check each week
Increase the sample size so reviewer preference matters less
Accept the approach, since interesting items are often the riskiest ones
Select the sample systematically rather than leaving it to reviewers
questions.why: Self-selected samples cannot support conclusions about the population. Systematic selection is what makes a spot check informative about the whole.
questions.traps: Asking for variety does not remove the selection effect. A larger biased sample is still biased, and interestingness is not a risk measure.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude the same factual question three times and receives the same specific answer each time. The answer is wrong.
options: Recognise that consistency reflects a stable pattern rather than accuracy
Accept the answer, since it was reproduced consistently across three attempts
Ask the question a fourth time with different wording to test the answer
Ask Claude to explain why it is confident in the repeated answer
questions.why: Repeated generation draws on the same underlying pattern, so a wrong answer can be perfectly consistent. Consistency and correctness are unrelated properties here.
questions.traps: Treating repetition as corroboration is the error. Rewording may vary the answer without establishing truth, and confidence explanations rationalise.

questions.stem: A team needs to show a regulator where each factual claim in a submission came from. The submission was drafted with Claude from internal documents.
options: Explain to the regulator that the submission was drafted from internal documents
Map every claim to a specific internal document and a specific passage
Ask Claude to identify the source of each claim in the submission
List the internal documents used as an appendix to the submission
questions.why: Regulatory traceability means claim-level provenance verified by a person. Building the map is work that has to be done rather than asserted.
questions.traps: A general explanation is not traceability. Model attribution after the fact is unverified, and a document list does not map claims.

questions.stem: An associate is comparing Claude output against what they would have written themselves. The output is different but not obviously worse.
options: Prefer their own version, since they understand the requirement best
Prefer Claude's version, since it was produced faster and reads well
Combine the strongest elements of both versions into a single document
Compare both against what the task requires rather than against each other
questions.why: Comparing two artefacts to each other has no anchor. Judging both against the requirement is what makes the comparison decidable rather than a matter of preference.
questions.traps: Preferring either by default substitutes authorship or speed for fitness. Combining without a standard produces a third unassessed version.

questions.stem: A team asks whether Claude handles a task well. They recall three cases where it worked and one where it did not.
options: Recognise that recalled cases are not a sample and set up a measurement
Conclude it works about three quarters of the time based on recollection
Ask more team members for their recollections to build a larger sample
Assume the failure was unusual and that the success rate is higher
questions.why: Recall is shaped by memorability rather than frequency, so the ratio is not an estimate of anything. A defined measurement is what answers the question.
questions.traps: Computing a rate from recall gives it false precision. Aggregating recollections aggregates the same bias, and discounting the failure is arbitrary.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to check a plan for gaps. It identifies gaps within the activities described and does not note that no budget is mentioned anywhere.
options: Ask Claude to check the plan for gaps a second time
Ask for a longer analysis so structural gaps are more likely to appear
Ask what a complete plan should contain, then check it
Ask Claude whether the plan is missing any major components
questions.why: Checking a document against itself finds internal gaps, not missing sections. An external reference for what should be present is what makes absence detectable.
questions.traps: A second internal pass repeats the frame. Length does not change the reference, and a general completeness question is weaker than a defined expectation.

questions.stem: A team has verified a Claude-generated document and found it accurate. They want to know how much this tells them about the next document.
options: Conclude that documents of this type are generally accurate
Treat it as weak evidence rather than as an established error rate
Reduce verification on the next document since this one was accurate
Ask Claude whether it expects similar accuracy on the next document
questions.why: A single verified document supports a very wide range of true error rates. Recognising the limit of the inference is what keeps verification calibrated to evidence.
questions.traps: Generalising from one observation is the error. Reducing verification acts on it, and asking the model to predict its own accuracy is not evidence.

questions.stem: An associate reviews Claude output and finds it acceptable, but cannot say what would have made them reject it.
options: Continue reviewing and note rejection reasons as cases arise
Ask a colleague to define rejection criteria for the associate to apply
Define the rejection criteria before reviewing, since otherwise nothing fails
Accept that some review judgements are necessarily subjective
questions.why: A review with no articulable failure condition is not a control. Defining what would fail is what makes acceptance meaningful.
questions.traps: Learning criteria from cases leaves early reviews ungrounded. Delegating the definition avoids the work, and subjectivity is a reason to define criteria rather than not to.

questions.stem: A team receives a Claude analysis where a key figure is described as approximately 2 million. The decision they face depends on whether it is above or below 1.8 million.
options: Use 2 million, since it is clearly above the 1.8 million threshold
Ask Claude for a more precise version of the same figure
Proceed on the assumption that the figure is above the threshold
Obtain a precise figure, since the approximation cannot resolve it
questions.why: An approximation is only useful if its precision resolves the decision. Here it does not, because "approximately 2 million" is consistent with values below the threshold.
questions.traps: Treating a round approximation as clearly above ignores its error range. Asking the model to sharpen an estimate produces false precision, and assuming resolves nothing.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to review a document and mentions that it was written by a senior executive.
options: Accept the review, since the model evaluates the document
Ask for the review without identifying the document's own author
Ask Claude to review it as though the author were unknown
Ask for a review and then ask separately what its weakest points are
questions.why: Author status supplied in the prompt shapes how directly problems are raised. Withholding it is the simplest way to get an unsoftened review.
questions.traps: Assuming authorship is ignored is the misconception. A blinding instruction competes with information already given, and a follow-up works within the softened frame.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to flag anything in its output that a reviewer should check. The flags are useful, and a serious error appears in an unflagged section.
options: Use the flags to prioritise while still reviewing the rest of it
Review only the flagged sections, since the model identified where risk concentrates
Ask Claude to flag more sections so coverage of the output improves
Ask Claude why it did not flag the section containing the error
questions.why: Self-flagging surfaces risks the model can see, which excludes its blind spots. Flags are a priority signal layered on top of review, not a substitute for it.
questions.traps: Reviewing only flagged sections is the error. More flags dilute the signal, and asking for a post-hoc explanation produces a rationalisation.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude about a topic and receives an answer that contradicts something they read last week but cannot immediately locate.
options: Accept Claude's answer, since the associate cannot produce the conflicting source
Ask Claude whether there are alternative views on the topic
Note both positions and present the topic as contested
Find the source they remember and compare, since a remembered conflict is worth resolving
questions.why: A remembered conflict is a real signal that something is wrong somewhere. Locating the source is what resolves which account is right rather than leaving both in play.
questions.traps: Deferring to the model because the source is not to hand inverts the evidence. Asking about alternative views and presenting it as contested both avoid resolving a resolvable question.

questions.stem: A team wants a single number to represent Claude output quality so they can track it over time.
options: Track a small set of measures rather than collapsing them to one
Track accuracy alone, since it is the most important quality property
Track a weighted average of accuracy, clarity and completeness
Ask reviewers for an overall quality score on each output
questions.why: Quality is multidimensional and collapsing it loses the information needed to act. A small set of measures preserves the trade-offs a single number conceals.
questions.traps: Accuracy alone ignores fitness. A weighted average buries the components, and reviewer scores are the single number in a different form.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude for the implications of a change. The response covers immediate effects thoroughly and does not address what happens after the first quarter.
options: Ask for more implications so longer-term effects eventually appear
Ask about the implications over the specified time horizons
Ask Claude to consider the long-term implications as well
Accept the response, since immediate implications are the most actionable
questions.why: Open requests return near-term effects because they are the most concrete. Naming the horizons is what makes the model reason across each of them.
questions.traps: Volume extends the near term. A vague long-term instruction does not specify a horizon, and treating actionability as sufficient keeps the gap.

questions.stem: A team is asked to justify continued use of Claude. They have qualitative feedback from users and no quantitative measurement.
options: Present the qualitative feedback as sufficient evidence of value
Estimate the quantitative benefit from the qualitative feedback received
Set up a measurement now while presenting the qualitative evidence
Delay the justification until quantitative measurement is available
questions.why: Qualitative evidence is real and limited, and saying so while starting measurement is the honest position that also improves the next answer.
questions.traps: Presenting it as sufficient overclaims. Deriving numbers from impressions manufactures precision, and delaying leaves the question unanswered.

questions.stem: An associate notices they approve Claude output more readily when they are the one who wrote the prompt.
options: Continue, since the prompt author best understands what the output should contain
Have someone else review the output from any prompt you wrote, since you are invested
Wait a day before reviewing output from your own prompts
Ask Claude to review the output alongside the associate's own review
questions.why: Investment in the prompt creates investment in its output. Separating prompt authorship from review is what restores the independence the check needs.
questions.traps: Understanding intent is not independence. A delay helps marginally, and model review adds no independence.

questions.stem: A team receives a Claude answer that is correct in substance but uses a term the company defines differently, which changes what the answer implies.
options: Accept the answer, since its substance is correct as stated
Ask Claude to define the terms it used in the answer
Add a glossary to the document explaining the terms as Claude used them
Check the terminology against the organisation's own definitions
questions.why: Shared vocabulary is what makes an answer transferable. A term used in its general sense inside an organisation with a specific definition produces a real misunderstanding.
questions.traps: Substance and interpretation are not separable here. Definitions and glossaries document the mismatch rather than resolving it for readers who will not read them.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to summarise a report and mentions that the team hopes it supports a particular conclusion.
options: Ask for the summary without stating the conclusion you hope to see
Accept the summary, since the model summarises the report's actual content
Ask Claude to summarise the report objectively despite the stated hope
Ask for two summaries, one framed by the hope and one without it
questions.why: Stating a desired conclusion biases what gets emphasised in a summary. Removing the statement is the direct prevention.
questions.traps: Assuming the hope is ignored is the misconception. An objectivity instruction competes with context already given, and paired summaries double work for a preventable problem.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to allocate a budget across five areas. The allocation sums correctly and gives one area an amount that is not feasible to spend.
options: Accept the allocation, since it distributes the budget correctly across the areas
Ask Claude to reallocate the budget more evenly across the five areas
Check each allocation against the real-world spending constraints that apply
Ask Claude whether any of the allocations would be difficult to spend
questions.why: Arithmetic validity says nothing about operational feasibility. Checking allocations against what each area can absorb is a separate and necessary step.
questions.traps: Correct summation is not the check. Even distribution is arbitrary, and asking the model about feasibility relies on knowledge it does not have.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to identify what could delay a project. The answer covers internal delays thoroughly and does not mention supplier lead times.
options: Ask for more delay factors so external ones eventually appear
Ask about dependencies on external parties as a named category of delay
Ask Claude whether external factors could also cause delays
Review the answer against the project's dependency list
questions.why: Delay analysis defaults to what the team controls. Naming external dependencies is what brings supplier and third-party timing into the assessment.
questions.traps: Volume samples the same default. A yes-or-no follow-up produces agreement without analysis, and dependency-list review arrives after the omission.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to rate how difficult it found a task. It reports the task was straightforward, and the output contains a significant error.
options: Accept the output, since the model found the task within its capability
Ask Claude to attempt the task again more carefully given the error found
Ask Claude to rate difficulty before each task and review the hard ones
Treat difficulty self-reports as uninformative about accuracy on that task
questions.why: Reported difficulty does not track where errors occur, because the errors the model makes are the ones it does not experience as difficult.
questions.traps: Reading ease as reliability is the trap. Retrying and difficulty-based routing both depend on a signal that does not correlate with accuracy.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude for a summary of recent developments in a fast-moving area. The summary is coherent and describes developments the associate has not heard of.
options: Accept the summary, since the associate is not close enough to the area to judge it
Ask Claude for dates and sources for each development mentioned
Verify each of the developments individually before repeating them
Treat the summary as a starting point and read around the topic generally
questions.why: Unfamiliar specifics in a fast-moving area are exactly where fabrication is undetectable by the reader. Each development is a checkable factual claim.
questions.traps: Deferring to the model because you cannot judge inverts the caution. Requested dates and sources may be generated, and general reading does not confirm the specific claims.

questions.stem: A team's Claude output meets its quality bar but users have stopped reading it because it is longer than what it replaced.
options: Treat actual readership as part of quality, since unread output fails
Keep the current standard, since the output meets the defined quality bar
Ask users to read the output more carefully than they currently do
Reduce the length and accept a lower score against the quality bar
questions.why: An artefact that is not read has failed regardless of its internal quality. Incorporating actual use into the standard is what corrects a bar measuring the wrong thing.
questions.traps: Meeting a bar nobody benefits from is the failure. Asking users to change is not a fix, and cutting length without revising the bar treats a good change as a compromise.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude a question and it gives an answer while noting it is drawing on general knowledge rather than the uploaded documents.
options: Accept the answer, since the model was transparent about where it came from
Treat that as a useful signal and verify the answer against an appropriate source
Ask Claude to answer again using only the uploaded documents
Ask Claude to indicate how confident it is in the general knowledge answer
questions.why: Transparency about the basis is genuinely helpful and tells you which verification applies. It identifies the answer as unsourced rather than establishing it as correct.
questions.traps: Transparency is not verification. Re-asking within the documents may produce nothing, and confidence adds an unreliable second signal.

questions.stem: A team's Claude output goes through three review steps. Each reviewer assumes the others are checking accuracy, and none of them is.
options: Assign each of the checks to a single named step in the process
Ask all three reviewers to check accuracy as well as their own area
Add a fourth review step dedicated specifically to accuracy
Ask reviewers to confirm what they checked after each review
questions.why: Diffusion of responsibility across multiple reviewers is a recognised failure of layered controls. Explicit assignment is what closes it without adding steps.
questions.traps: Asking everyone to check everything recreates the diffusion. A fourth step adds cost, and after-the-fact confirmation records the gap rather than preventing it.

questions.stem: A team asks Claude to assess whether a project should continue, mentioning that significant money has already been spent on it.
options: Accept the assessment, since past spending is relevant context for the decision
Ask Claude to weigh the sunk investment against the cost of stopping now
Ask for the assessment both with and without the spending mentioned
Ask whether the remaining investment is justified by the future benefit
questions.why: Money already spent is unrecoverable and should not affect a forward-looking decision. Framing the question around remaining cost and benefit is what keeps the sunk cost out of the reasoning.
questions.traps: Supplying prior spend invites it to be weighed, which is the fallacy. Explicitly weighing it is worse, and paired assessments leave you choosing between a biased and an unbiased answer.

questions.stem: An associate is verifying a Claude claim and finds a source that appears authoritative. The source is a page that aggregates content from elsewhere without attribution.
options: Accept the source, since the page presents the information authoritatively
Look for a second aggregator page that carries the same claim
Trace the claim back to an attributable original before using it
Cite the aggregator, since it is a stable and locatable web source
questions.why: An unattributed aggregator has no accountable origin and may itself be reproducing an error or generated content. Verification requires a source that can be held to the claim.
questions.traps: Authoritative presentation is a design choice, not provenance. A second aggregator may draw on the first, and citing one passes the problem to your reader.

questions.stem: A support team must classify roughly 50,000 tickets a day into twelve well-documented categories. Cost per ticket and response latency are both hard limits.
options: Opus, because classification accuracy is the highest-stakes property of this workflow
Sonnet, as a mid-tier model is the safe default whenever the requirements are not yet clear
Haiku, since the task is narrow and high-volume with cost and latency binding
Opus at first, downgrading once the routing rules have stabilised in production
questions.why: High volume, a simple taxonomy, and binding cost and latency constraints is the textbook case for the fastest tier. Accuracy on twelve documented categories is not the scarce resource here.
questions.traps: Opus optimises a variable that is not binding. Sonnet-as-default is a habit rather than a rationale, and starting at the top tier inverts the sensible order of piloting cheap then escalating.

questions.stem: An analyst needs help reasoning through a novel legal structuring question with several interacting constraints and no established precedent to follow.
options: Haiku, since legal questions are well represented in training data and need only retrieval
Opus, since open-ended reasoning over interacting constraints is where it earns its cost
Sonnet, because it balances capability and cost for most professional work
A cheaper tier with a longer, more carefully written prompt to compensate
questions.why: Novel reasoning across interacting constraints with no precedent is precisely the work that separates tiers. This is the case where paying for capability changes the answer's quality.
questions.traps: Treating a novel structuring problem as retrieval misreads it. Sonnet is a reasonable default that is not the best fit here, and prompt effort does not substitute for reasoning capability.

questions.stem: A team's internal tool calls Claude on every keystroke to suggest completions. Users complain the suggestions arrive after they have already finished typing.
options: Increase the capability tier so the suggestions are good enough to wait for
Add a loading indicator so users understand a suggestion is on its way
Cache the most common completions and serve those instead of calling at all
Move to the fastest tier and debounce the calls so fewer requests are made
questions.why: Interactive suggestion is a latency-bound problem, so the fix is a faster model plus fewer calls. Both levers pull in the same direction here.
questions.traps: A higher tier makes latency worse. An indicator manages perception without fixing the delay, and caching helps common cases while leaving the general path slow.

questions.stem: A finance team runs a monthly batch that summarises 4,000 documents overnight. It finishes in four hours and nobody sees the output until morning.
options: Optimise for cost and quality rather than for latency
Optimise for latency so the batch finishes sooner and leaves more headroom
Split the batch across several parallel runs to reduce the total elapsed time
Move the batch to the fastest available tier to reduce the overall spend
questions.why: When no one is waiting, elapsed time has no value and the budget should buy quality or savings instead. Recognising which constraint is slack is the selection skill being tested.
questions.traps: Latency optimisation spends effort on a dimension nobody experiences. Parallelism and the fastest tier both chase speed that the schedule already provides for free.

questions.stem: A marketing associate wants to draft copy, iterate on it conversationally, and keep the campaign brief and brand guidelines to hand across several sessions.
options: A single long conversation, kept open and returned to whenever work resumes
The API, so the brief can be passed programmatically with each request
A Project, which holds the brief and guidelines as persistent context across sessions
A new conversation each session with the brief pasted in at the start
questions.why: Persistent knowledge reused across many sessions is exactly what Projects exist for. The alternative is re-supplying the same context by hand every time.
questions.traps: A long conversation degrades and cannot be organised. The API is developer surface for a non-developer task, and re-pasting is the manual work Projects remove.

questions.stem: A developer needs Claude to read a repository, make changes across several files, run the tests, and iterate until they pass.
options: The web interface, pasting each file in and copying the changes back out
Claude Code, which works against the filesystem and can run the tests
A Project containing the repository files uploaded as project knowledge
The API, sending each file's contents as a separate request in sequence
questions.why: Multi-file editing with a test loop needs a surface that can read, write and execute. That is the agentic coding surface rather than a chat window.
questions.traps: Pasting files back and forth is unworkable at repository scale. Uploaded knowledge is read-only context, and raw API calls provide no filesystem or execution.

questions.stem: An associate asks the same kind of question about the same three reference documents several times a week, re-uploading the documents each time.
options: Keep one conversation open permanently and scroll back to the documents
Summarise the three documents once and paste the summary each time
Upload the documents once and rely on Claude remembering them afterwards
Create a Project with the three documents as knowledge, so they persist
questions.why: Repeated use of a stable document set is the signal for a Project. The documents become persistent context rather than something re-supplied per conversation.
questions.traps: A permanent conversation grows unwieldy. A summary loses detail the questions may need, and conversations do not retain uploads across sessions.

questions.stem: A team member has a one-off question about a document they will never look at again.
options: A single conversation with the document attached
A Project created for the document so it is available if needed later
A Project shared with the team in case a colleague has the same question
A saved prompt template so the question can be repeated efficiently
questions.why: One-off work does not justify the setup and maintenance a Project carries. Matching the container to the lifespan of the work is the judgement being tested.
questions.traps: Creating a Project for a document you will not revisit is overhead without payoff. Sharing and templating both assume repetition that the scenario rules out.

questions.stem: An associate needs Claude to produce a self-contained interactive calculator their colleague can open and use without any installation.
options: Ask for the code in the chat and have the colleague run it themselves
Describe the calculation steps so the colleague can build it in a spreadsheet
Ask for an Artifact, which renders as a working, shareable output they can open
Ask for a document explaining how the calculator should be constructed
questions.why: A runnable, shareable interactive output is what Artifacts produce. The alternatives all hand the colleague work rather than a working tool.
questions.traps: Code in chat needs someone able to run it. A spreadsheet description and a build document both stop short of the deliverable that was asked for.

questions.stem: A researcher wants Claude to work through a difficult multi-step derivation where intermediate reasoning errors would be easy to miss.
options: Enable extended thinking so reasoning is worked through before answering
Ask for the answer and then ask Claude to explain how it got there
Break the derivation into separate prompts and check each step yourself
Ask for the answer several times and compare the results for consistency
questions.why: Extended thinking allocates reasoning effort before the response, which is what a hard derivation needs. A post-hoc explanation is generated after the answer already exists.
questions.traps: Explaining afterwards rationalises rather than reasons. Manual stepping works but is slower, and consistency across runs is not correctness.

questions.stem: A team is choosing a tier for extracting five fixed fields from structured invoices. The layout is consistent and the fields are unambiguous.
options: The most capable tier, since extraction errors are costly to correct downstream
The cheapest tier that passes their accuracy test on a varied sample
A mid-tier model, since extraction sits between simple and complex work
The tier their vendor recommends for document processing workloads
questions.why: Selection is an empirical question: define the accuracy bar, test from the cheapest tier upward, and stop when it is met. Consistent structured extraction usually clears it early.
questions.traps: Reaching for the top tier without testing overpays. Positioning a task on an intuitive scale is not measurement, and vendor guidance does not know your accuracy bar.

questions.stem: A workflow currently uses a top-tier model. A team member proposes moving to a cheaper tier to cut costs by roughly 70%.
options: Switch, since a 70% saving outweighs the modest quality difference between tiers
Keep the current tier, since the workflow is already working reliably
Switch for low-stakes items and keep the top tier for the rest
Test the cheaper tier on the same cases before switching
questions.why: The decision needs evidence about whether quality holds on this workload. Testing the same cases on both is what converts an assumption into a measurement.
questions.traps: Switching on the saving alone assumes a quality difference nobody has measured. Refusing outright ignores real money, and splitting by stakes is sensible only after the test.

questions.stem: An associate notices their team's Claude spend has tripled. The volume of work has not changed, but prompts now include a large reference document every time.
options: Shorten the reference document so fewer tokens are sent on each request
Move the reference document into a Project so it is not resent with every prompt
Reduce how often the team uses Claude until the spend comes back down
Switch to a cheaper tier so the same volume costs proportionally less
questions.why: Repeatedly resending stable context is the cost driver, and persistent project knowledge is the structural fix. It removes the duplication rather than shrinking it.
questions.traps: Trimming the document loses content and only reduces the waste. Cutting usage sacrifices the work, and a cheaper tier pays less for the same avoidable duplication.

questions.stem: A team runs a first-pass screen over incoming applications, flagging anything that needs a human to look at it closely.
options: A fast tier for the screen, with flagged items escalated to a stronger one
The strongest tier for everything, since screening decisions affect people
A fast tier for everything, since a human reviews the flagged items anyway
A mid tier for the screen, with no escalation path for flagged items
questions.why: Tiered triage puts cheap capacity on the high-volume pass and reserves capability for the cases that need it. That is the pattern this workload is shaped for.
questions.traps: Top tier everywhere overpays for the routine majority. No escalation wastes the triage, and a single mid tier splits the difference without matching either need.

questions.stem: An operations manager wants a repeatable weekly report generated from a spreadsheet, with no coding involved and consistent formatting each week.
options: A fresh conversation each week describing the format from scratch
A developer-built integration calling the API on a weekly schedule
A saved document containing the instructions to copy and paste each week
A Project holding the format and instructions, with the sheet added
questions.why: A Project carries the standing instructions and format so only the data changes week to week. That is repeatability without any code.
questions.traps: Describing the format each week invites drift. An API integration is disproportionate for a non-technical weekly task, and copy-paste is the manual step a Project removes.

questions.stem: A team needs Claude to answer questions using information that changes daily and lives on public websites.
options: A Project with the relevant pages uploaded as knowledge documents
A prompt that describes the information as accurately as possible
A surface with web search, since training data cannot keep pace
The most capable tier, since stronger models have more current knowledge
questions.why: Information that changes daily has to be fetched at question time. No model's training data and no static upload keeps pace with it.
questions.traps: Uploaded pages go stale immediately. Describing the data does not retrieve it, and capability does not make training data more recent.

questions.stem: A pilot using Claude on 50 documents a week works well. The team now wants to run 5,000 a week.
options: Scale directly, since the workflow has already been proven on real documents
Re-test at the new volume and at the new cost, since a pilot establishes neither
Scale gradually and watch for problems as the volume increases
Move to a cheaper tier to keep the cost proportionate at the new volume
questions.why: A hundredfold increase changes both the cost picture and the variety of inputs encountered. Re-testing at scale is what turns a pilot into a decision.
questions.traps: A 50-document pilot proves little about 5,000. Gradual scaling discovers problems in production, and switching tiers pre-empts a measurement not yet made.

questions.stem: Several people on a team each keep their own conversation with the same set of policy documents, and their answers to the same questions differ.
options: A standard prompt everyone copies into their own separate conversations
A weekly meeting to reconcile the differences between their answers
Nominating one person to ask all the questions on the team's behalf
A shared Project so everyone works from the same knowledge and rules
questions.why: Divergent answers from separately assembled context is what shared Projects solve. One knowledge base and one set of instructions produces consistency by construction.
questions.traps: A shared prompt does not share the documents. Reconciliation treats the symptom, and funnelling through one person creates a bottleneck.

questions.stem: An associate asks which model to use for drafting routine internal emails that a person will read and lightly edit before sending.
options: The most capable tier, since written communication represents the company
A mid tier, since email drafting is neither trivial nor especially demanding
A fast, inexpensive tier, since routine drafting gets reviewed anyway
Whichever tier the associate finds produces the most pleasing prose
questions.why: Routine drafting with a human editing step is exactly where the cheap tier is sufficient. The review step absorbs the quality difference that would otherwise matter.
questions.traps: The top tier overpays for work that gets edited anyway. A mid tier is defensible but unnecessary, and personal preference is not a selection criterion.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude to analyse a 200-row spreadsheet of sales figures and identify which regions are underperforming.
options: Attach the file so the actual values are available
Paste the first 20 rows and ask Claude to infer the pattern from those
Describe the data in words and ask what would typically be underperforming
Ask for an analysis method the team can apply to the spreadsheet themselves
questions.why: Analysis needs the data. Attaching the file makes the real values available rather than a sample or a description of them.
questions.traps: A 20-row sample cannot identify which regions underperform. A verbal description invites generic answers, and a method hands the work back.

questions.stem: A customer-facing chatbot has a two-second response budget. The current setup takes four seconds, most of which is model generation time.
options: Add a typing indicator so the four seconds feel shorter to the customer
Increase the tier so the answer is good enough to justify the wait
Cache responses for the twenty most common customer questions
Move to a faster tier and also shorten the length of the responses requested
questions.why: Generation time scales with tier and output length, so both levers attack the actual bottleneck. That is what a hard latency budget requires.
questions.traps: A typing indicator manages perception, not the budget. A higher tier is slower, and caching helps the common cases while the rest stay over budget.

questions.stem: A team's task involves summarising documents that are mostly routine, but roughly one in twenty contains unusual legal language that changes the meaning.
options: Route the unusual documents to a stronger tier and handle the rest cheaply
Use the stronger tier for everything, since the unusual cases cannot be predicted
Use the cheaper tier for everything and accept occasional summary errors
Ask the cheaper tier to flag documents it finds difficult and review those
questions.why: Mixed difficulty with an identifiable hard subset is the case for routing. The economics work because the hard cases are the minority.
questions.traps: Top tier everywhere overpays for nineteen in twenty. Accepting errors on the cases that matter most inverts the risk, and self-flagged difficulty is an unreliable signal.

questions.stem: An associate with no coding background wants to automate a task that involves reading emails, extracting details, and updating a tracker.
options: Use the API, since automation across systems is what it exists for
Scope what the interface can do and involve a developer for the rest
Do the extraction in Claude manually and update the tracker by hand each time
Ask Claude to write the automation code and run it without further help
questions.why: Automation across email and a tracker crosses systems, which needs development work. Knowing where the non-technical surface ends is the judgement being tested.
questions.traps: The API is the right mechanism but not something a non-developer implements alone. Manual work is not automation, and running unreviewed generated code is not a safe path.

questions.stem: A team's Claude workflow costs $200 a month and saves roughly eight hours of work. They are considering an upgrade that would cost $600 and save eleven hours.
options: Upgrade, since eleven hours saved is better than eight hours saved
Stay, since the current setup already delivers a positive return
Compare the extra three hours against the extra $400
Upgrade for a trial month and decide based on how it feels
questions.why: Upgrade decisions turn on the marginal change, not the totals. Three extra hours for $400 is the comparison that actually decides it.
questions.traps: Comparing totals ignores what the increment costs. Staying because the current return is positive skips the same arithmetic, and a feel-based trial substitutes impression for the numbers already available.

questions.stem: An associate has been using the top tier for everything and wants to know where they could safely move down.
options: Move everything down a tier and move back whatever produces poor results
Identify the tasks that are routine and well-specified, and test those first
Keep the top tier, since the cost difference is small relative to the value
Move down only the tasks that are least important to the business
questions.why: Routine, well-specified work is where cheaper tiers most often hold quality. Testing there first finds the savings with the least risk.
questions.traps: Blanket downgrading degrades the tasks that needed capability. Keeping everything at the top forgoes real savings, and importance is a poor proxy for task difficulty.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude's answers to a customer question to always follow the company's approved wording for that topic.
options: Paste the approved wording into each conversation before asking
Ask Claude to use approved wording and trust it to recall the phrasing
Review each answer against the approved wording before it is sent
Put the approved wording into the project's standing instructions
questions.why: Standing requirements that apply to every response belong in project configuration. That is what makes them automatic rather than remembered.
questions.traps: Pasting each time is the manual work configuration removes. Trusting recall of unsupplied wording invites invention, and review catches drift without preventing it.

questions.stem: An associate is choosing between one request that processes ten documents together and ten requests processing one document each.
options: Always batch, since fewer requests means lower cost and less overhead
Always separate, since each document gets the model's full attention
Judge by whether the documents need to be compared against one another
Batch when the documents are short and separate them when they are long
questions.why: The right unit depends on whether the task is comparative. If the answer requires relating documents to each other, they belong in one request; if not, separate passes give each a full pass.
questions.traps: Blanket batching and blanket separation both ignore what the task needs. Document length is a secondary consideration to whether comparison is required.

questions.stem: A consultant works with eight clients and keeps confusing which brand guidelines apply to which piece of work.
options: A separate Project per client, carrying only its guidelines
One Project containing all eight sets of guidelines clearly labelled
A note at the top of each conversation naming which client it concerns
A single conversation per client, returned to whenever that client comes up
questions.why: Isolation by client is what prevents cross-contamination of context. Each Project carries only what applies, which removes the confusion structurally.
questions.traps: One combined Project keeps all eight sets in scope at once. A naming note relies on the model selecting correctly, and long-running conversations degrade.

questions.stem: A team needs a model to follow a fifteen-step procedure exactly, where skipping a step produces a silently wrong result.
options: Use the strongest tier, since complex instruction-following favours capability
Test the tiers against the whole procedure and pick the cheapest one that holds up
Break the procedure into fifteen separate single-step requests
Use any tier and add a checklist review after the output is produced
questions.why: Long-procedure adherence varies by tier, so the answer is empirical. Testing against the actual procedure is what identifies the cheapest tier that holds.
questions.traps: Assuming the top tier is required skips the test. Fifteen separate requests is a workaround, and review after the fact catches failures rather than preventing them.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude available inside the tool their staff already use all day, rather than asking them to switch to a separate window.
options: Training so staff become comfortable switching to a separate window
A browser shortcut making the separate window faster to reach
An integration into that tool, so Claude appears where the work happens
A weekly digest of Claude-generated content delivered into the tool
questions.why: Adoption follows the path of least friction, and meeting people inside their existing tool removes the switch entirely.
questions.traps: Training people to tolerate friction rarely works. A shortcut shortens the switch without removing it, and a digest is not interactive use.

questions.stem: A successful pilot ran with two enthusiastic volunteers. The team now wants to roll out to forty people, most of whom are indifferent.
options: Expect different results, since volunteers were not typical
Roll out directly, since the pilot demonstrated the workflow works
Roll out to twenty first and then to the remaining twenty
Ask the two volunteers to train the other thirty-eight people
questions.why: Self-selected enthusiasts are the least representative possible sample. Anticipating that the wider group behaves differently is what makes the rollout plan realistic.
questions.traps: Treating the pilot as predictive ignores the selection effect. Staging the rollout and peer training both help without addressing the sampling problem.

questions.stem: An associate needs to compare two long contracts clause by clause and keep track of which differences matter.
options: Paste the contracts into the conversation one after the other
Summarise each contract separately and compare the two summaries
Ask which clauses usually differ between contracts of this type
Attach both documents and compare them clause by clause
questions.why: Both documents need to be present and addressable for a clause-level comparison. Attaching them keeps the full text available rather than a compressed version.
questions.traps: Pasting long contracts is unwieldy and lossy. Comparing summaries loses the clause detail, and asking about typical differences never touches these contracts.

questions.stem: A team asks whether a stronger model would fix the errors they are seeing, which turn out to be caused by an ambiguous prompt.
options: Upgrade the tier, since stronger models handle ambiguity more gracefully
Upgrade and fix the prompt at the same time to resolve it faster
Fix the prompt first, since a stronger model would inherit the same ambiguity
Add examples to the prompt and keep the current tier unchanged
questions.why: An ambiguous instruction is under-specification, and capability does not resolve what was never specified. Diagnosing before spending is the discipline being tested.
questions.traps: Upgrading to absorb ambiguity pays to paper over a fixable defect. Doing both at once obscures which change helped, and examples help without addressing the ambiguity directly.

questions.stem: An associate's task produces long outputs, most of which the reader skims. The cost per request has become the team's largest line item.
options: Move to a cheaper tier and keep the output length unchanged
Run the task less often so fewer requests are made each month
Ask readers to read the full output so the length is not wasted
Request shorter outputs, since output length drives most cost
questions.why: When output dominates the token count, shortening it attacks the cost directly and also matches how the output is actually consumed.
questions.traps: A cheaper tier reduces the rate while leaving the waste. Reducing frequency sacrifices the work, and asking readers to change behaviour does not reduce spend.

questions.stem: A team's Project has accumulated forty documents over a year. Answers have become less precise and sometimes cite superseded material.
options: Remove the superseded documents, since project knowledge needs upkeep
Add a note to the project instructions saying which documents are current
Create a second Project containing only the current documents
Ask more specific questions so the superseded documents are not consulted
questions.why: Project knowledge is a curated set, and stale material actively degrades answers. Removing it is maintenance the container requires.
questions.traps: An instruction competes with the documents themselves. A parallel Project leaves the stale one in use, and more specific questions work around a fixable problem.

questions.stem: A team is unsure whether their task needs a capable model or a well-designed prompt, having tried neither systematically.
options: Start with the strongest tier so capability is not the limiting factor
Establish a baseline, then vary one factor at a time
Start with the cheapest tier so the cost floor is established first
Try several combinations at once and pick whichever performs best
questions.why: Varying one factor at a time from a sensible baseline is what makes the result interpretable. Otherwise you cannot tell which change mattered.
questions.traps: Starting at either extreme anchors the investigation. Changing several things at once produces a winner you cannot explain or generalise.

questions.stem: An associate wants a colleague to be able to use a carefully built prompt without needing to understand or modify it.
options: Send the prompt text and ask the colleague to paste it each time
Explain how the prompt works so the colleague can rebuild it themselves
Share it as a Project the colleague can use without editing the instructions
Run the prompt for the colleague whenever they need it
questions.why: Sharing a configured Project gives the colleague the capability without the maintenance. The prompt becomes infrastructure rather than a snippet to manage.
questions.traps: Pasted text drifts as it is copied. Teaching reconstruction is unnecessary overhead, and running it for them creates a dependency.

questions.stem: A team wants to know whether to build a custom integration or keep using the standard interface for a workflow used twice a week.
options: Build the integration, since automation is more reliable than manual use
Build a partial integration covering the most repetitive parts
Decide based on whether the team enjoys using the standard interface
Keep the interface, since twice-weekly use rarely repays integration effort
questions.why: Integration cost is amortised over usage frequency, and twice a week is thin. Matching the investment to the volume is the judgement being tested.
questions.traps: Reliability arguments ignore the build and maintenance cost. A partial build carries much of the cost, and preference is not an investment criterion.

questions.stem: A team needs Claude's output to be checked against a fixed list of rules every time, and the checking currently happens inconsistently by hand.
options: Encode the rules in project instructions so they always apply
Circulate the rules so each person applies them consistently themselves
Ask Claude to remember the rules at the start of each conversation
Check a sample of outputs against the rules rather than all of them
questions.why: Rules that must apply every time belong in the configuration rather than in each person's memory. That is what makes consistency structural.
questions.traps: Circulating rules relies on human consistency that has already failed. Per-conversation reminders are manual, and sampling accepts inconsistency by design.

questions.stem: A team measures three tiers on their task and finds accuracies of 91%, 93% and 94%, at costs of one, four and twelve units respectively.
options: Choose the 94% option, since accuracy is the most important property
Compare the extra accuracy against the cost multiple
Choose the 91% option, since the accuracy difference is small
Choose the middle option, since it balances the two considerations
questions.why: Three points on a cost-accuracy curve is a trade-off question, and the answer depends on what an accuracy point is worth in this workload. That valuation is the missing input.
questions.traps: Picking any option on general principle skips the valuation. The middle option is a compromise rather than a reasoned choice, and "small difference" depends entirely on the stakes.

questions.stem: A team needs Claude to draft responses to routine policy questions where the answers are already documented and rarely change.
options: A capable tier, because policy questions carry compliance risk and a wrong answer could expose the organisation to real regulatory consequences
Whichever tier the team already pays for on other workloads
A mid tier, since policy work sits between routine drafting and genuine analysis
A fast tier, since the answers are documented and the task is retrieval and rephrasing
