questions.why: Documented, stable answers make this a retrieval and rephrasing task, which the fast tier handles. Compliance risk is managed by the review step, not by the model tier.
questions.traps: Compliance framing argues for review rather than capability. Convenience is not a criterion, and placing the task intuitively on a scale is not measurement.

questions.stem: An associate discovers their prompt sends the same 12-page style guide with every one of 400 daily requests.
options: Move the style guide into persistent project configuration so it is not resent
Shorten the style guide to its most important pages so fewer tokens go each time
Accept the cost, since the style guide is genuinely needed for every single request and removing it would degrade the consistency of the output
Batch the requests together so fewer copies of the guide are sent
questions.why: Stable context reused across every request belongs in configuration rather than in each prompt. That removes the duplication instead of merely shrinking it.
questions.traps: Trimming loses guidance and only reduces the waste. Accepting it pays repeatedly for the same tokens, and batching changes the request shape without removing the repetition.

questions.stem: A non-technical team lead wants a colleague to be able to ask questions of a policy library that is updated monthly.
options: An API integration that fetches the current documents on each question asked
A monthly email containing the updated documents for people to attach themselves
A Project holding the library, with the documents refreshed when they change
A single long conversation that people return to each time
questions.why: A Project gives non-technical users persistent access to a curated document set, and monthly refresh is ordinary maintenance rather than engineering.
questions.traps: An integration is disproportionate for a non-technical monthly cadence. Emailing documents pushes the work back to users, and a long conversation is not a library.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude to produce a one-page visual summary that stakeholders can view in a browser without any software being installed.
options: Ask for a description of the visual so a designer can build it afterwards
Ask for an Artifact so the summary renders directly and can be shared as-is
Ask for the summary as formatted text that stakeholders read in the conversation
Ask for slides that stakeholders can open in their usual software
questions.why: A browser-viewable, shareable rendered output is exactly what Artifacts produce, and the requirement rules out anything needing installation.
questions.traps: A description defers the deliverable to someone else. Text in a conversation is not a visual summary, and slides require software to open.

questions.stem: A workflow performs well on the 200 cases the team has tried. Extending it to a new department would add case types nobody has tested.
options: Test the new department's case types before extending, since they are unlike the current ones
Extend, since 200 successful cases is a substantial track record for this workflow
Extend to the new department and monitor closely for problems during the first month
Extend to the new department but keep the current model tier
questions.why: Two hundred cases of one kind say nothing about a different kind. Testing the new case types is what makes the extension a decision rather than a hope.
questions.traps: Track record on unlike cases is not evidence. Monitoring finds failures by shipping them, and holding the tier addresses a variable that is not the risk.

questions.stem: An associate wants to know whether the difference between tiers matters for summarising short meeting notes into three bullet points.
options: Assume it matters, since a stronger model produces better writing on any task
Test it, since the difference is likely small on a task this constrained
Assume it does not matter, since summarisation is a basic capability for every tier
Use the strongest tier available so capability is never the limit
questions.why: Short, tightly constrained tasks are where tiers converge, so the question is empirical and cheap to settle. Testing beats assuming in either direction.
questions.traps: Both assumptions substitute intuition for a measurement that takes minutes. Defaulting to the top tier pays for a difference nobody has demonstrated.

questions.stem: A team's Project instructions have grown to two pages as people added rules over six months. Recent additions seem to have little effect.
options: Add the newest rules again at the end so they carry more weight in the ordering
Split the instructions across two Projects so each carries a shorter set of rules
Consolidate the instructions around the rules that matter, since accretion dilutes them
Delete the oldest rules on the basis that they are least relevant
questions.why: Instructions compete for attention, and an accreted two-page set dilutes every rule in it. Consolidating around what matters restores the leverage each one has.
questions.traps: Repetition and reordering redistribute a bloated set. Splitting fragments the workflow, and deleting by age discards rules that may still matter.

questions.stem: A task involves reading a contract and answering questions that require holding several clauses in mind at once and reasoning about how they interact.
options: A fast tier, since contract text is well represented in training data
A fast tier with the relevant clauses extracted and supplied separately
Any tier at all, provided every output is carefully reviewed
A capable tier, since reasoning across interacting clauses is where tiers genuinely differ
questions.why: Multi-clause interaction is the reasoning-heavy end of document work, and that is where capability differences show up most clearly.
questions.traps: Familiarity with contract language is not the same as reasoning over a specific one. Pre-extraction does the hard part for the model, and review catches errors rather than preventing them.

questions.stem: An associate needs to make the same twenty-step edit to sixty files in a code repository and verify nothing broke.
options: A Project containing all sixty files uploaded as knowledge for reference
Claude Code, since it can act on the repository and run the verification itself
Sixty separate conversations, one per file, with the edit described each time
A single conversation with all sixty files pasted into it at once
questions.why: Bulk edits with verification need filesystem access and the ability to run checks. That is the agentic coding surface rather than a chat context.
questions.traps: Uploaded knowledge is read-only. Sixty conversations is unmanageable, and pasting sixty files exceeds what a conversation can usefully hold.

questions.stem: A team is deciding whether to enable extended thinking on a high-volume classification task that is currently accurate and fast.
options: Enable it, since more reasoning improves accuracy on any classification problem
Enable it only for the items the model is least confident about classifying
Leave it off, since extended thinking adds cost and latency without helping a settled task
Enable it during business hours when response quality matters most
questions.why: Extended reasoning earns its cost on hard, open-ended problems. Applying it to a task that is already accurate spends latency and money for no gain.
questions.traps: Assuming reasoning always helps ignores the cost side. Confidence-based routing relies on an unreliable signal, and time-of-day has no bearing on task difficulty.

questions.stem: A researcher needs Claude to work from twelve academic papers and produce a synthesis with traceable claims.
options: Attach the papers and require each claim to name the paper it came from
Ask for a synthesis and add citations afterwards once the text is written
Summarise each paper separately and ask for a synthesis of the summaries
Ask about the field generally rather than about these twelve papers
questions.why: Traceability is far more reliable when required during generation than reconstructed later, and the papers themselves have to be present for it to mean anything.
questions.traps: Retrofitted citations are guesses about a process that left no record. Synthesising summaries loses the detail citations would point at, and a general question never touches the papers.

questions.stem: A team's Claude usage is growing and finance has asked what it will cost next year. The team has monthly totals but no breakdown.
options: Extrapolate the monthly totals forward using the growth rate observed so far
Ask finance to set a budget cap and keep the usage within whatever is allocated
Estimate next year's spend from the expected growth in headcount
Break the spend down by workflow, since a single total cannot be projected sensibly
questions.why: Different workflows scale with different drivers, so a single total hides what will actually grow. Breaking it down is what makes a projection defensible.
questions.traps: Extrapolating an aggregate assumes uniform growth. A cap manages spend without forecasting it, and headcount is not the driver for most workloads.

questions.stem: An associate has a task where the cheapest tier gets it right 78% of the time and a human must check every output regardless.
options: Keep the cheapest tier, since every output is checked by a person anyway
Keep the cheapest tier and reduce the checking to a sample of outputs
Consider a stronger tier, since checking cost is driven by how often it is wrong
Alternate between the two tiers from one request to the next
questions.why: When every output is reviewed, the real cost is the correction work, and a 22% error rate drives a lot of it. Model cost and review cost have to be weighed together.
questions.traps: Treating review as absorbing all errors ignores what correction costs. Sampling weakens the control, and alternating produces inconsistency without addressing the rate.

questions.stem: A team wants new joiners to get consistent answers about internal processes without each of them having to assemble context first.
options: A shared Project with the process documents and standing instructions in place
A written guide telling new joiners which documents to upload themselves
A nominated expert who answers process questions for the whole team
A conversation template that new joiners copy for each question
questions.why: A configured shared Project makes correct context the default rather than something each person assembles. That is what produces consistency across people.
questions.traps: A guide relies on each person following it. A nominated expert becomes a bottleneck, and a template does not carry the documents.

questions.stem: An associate wants to try an idea quickly and does not yet know whether it will become a repeated workflow.
options: A Project, so the work is organised properly from the very beginning
A single conversation, since setting up a Project before knowing is premature
A shared Project so colleagues can see the experiment as it develops
An API prototype built to test the idea properly from the start
questions.why: Exploratory work does not justify setup that may be discarded. Matching the container to what you know so far is the judgement here.
questions.traps: Building structure before knowing whether it is needed is premature. Sharing an unformed experiment adds noise, and a prototype is heavier still.

questions.stem: A team measures that a cheaper tier matches the expensive one on 94% of their cases, and the 6% where it differs are all high-value transactions.
options: Use the cheaper tier, since it matches on the overwhelming majority of cases
Use the expensive tier for everything, since the difference cannot be predicted
Use the cheaper tier and increase how much output gets reviewed
Route by value, since the difference concentrates exactly where the stakes are highest
questions.why: The pattern in the disagreements is the finding: they are not randomly distributed but concentrated in high-value cases, which makes value a usable routing key.
questions.traps: A 94% match rate is misleading when the misses are the expensive ones. Top tier everywhere ignores a usable signal, and more review absorbs errors rather than avoiding them.

questions.stem: A team needs the same analysis run on a new dataset every Monday, with output in an identical format each week.
options: A Project holding the format and method, with only the dataset changing weekly
A saved prompt that each person pastes into a fresh conversation on Monday
A conversation reopened each week and continued from the previous analysis
A written procedure document describing the weekly analysis steps
questions.why: Standing method and format belong in configuration so only the variable input changes. That is what makes weekly output identical in shape.
questions.traps: A pasted prompt drifts between people. A reopened conversation accumulates and degrades, and a procedure document leaves the work manual.

questions.stem: An associate finds their requests are slow because each one includes the full conversation history, which has grown to forty exchanges.
options: Continue the conversation, since the history contains useful earlier context
Ask Claude to summarise the history and continue in the same conversation
Move to a faster tier so the accumulated history processes quicker
Start a fresh conversation carrying only the context that is still relevant
questions.why: Long histories are resent with each request, which costs both time and money. Restarting with only what still matters removes the accumulated weight.
questions.traps: Continuing keeps the growth. A summary inside the same thread does not shed the history, and a faster tier still processes the same volume.

questions.stem: A pilot showed a 30% time saving. Rolling out more widely, the team observes closer to a 10% saving and wants to know why.
options: Conclude the pilot measurement was wrong and disregard its result entirely
Look at how the wider group differs from the pilot group in skill and task mix
Provide more training so the wider group reaches the pilot group's saving
Accept the 10% figure as the workflow's true level of benefit
questions.why: A gap between pilot and rollout is usually explained by who was in each group and what they were doing. Investigating the difference is what tells you which figure to believe.
questions.traps: Discarding the pilot throws away information. Training assumes skill is the cause without checking, and accepting the number explains nothing.

questions.stem: A team wants to reduce cost but is worried that a cheaper tier would produce subtly worse output nobody notices until it causes a problem.
options: Stay on the current tier, since undetectable quality loss is too risky to accept
Switch and ask users to report anything that seems worse than before
Define what subtly worse would look like and test for it specifically before switching
Switch to the cheaper tier for a month and review what happened
questions.why: A vague worry becomes testable once you name the failure it describes. Defining the degradation is what lets you measure whether it happens.
questions.traps: Refusing to test forgoes savings on an untested fear. User reports and a trial month both discover subtle problems only after they have had effects.

questions.stem: An associate needs Claude to reference a document that changes several times a day and must always reflect the current version.
options: A surface that reads the live document rather than a stored copy of it
A Project with the document uploaded and refreshed whenever it changes
A conversation with the current version pasted in at the start of each session
A daily scheduled export of the document into the Project
questions.why: Content that changes several times a day cannot be served from a stored copy without going stale between updates. It has to be read live.
questions.traps: Refreshing an upload several times daily is unsustainable manual work. Pasting per session captures one point in time, and a daily export is already behind.

questions.stem: A team notices that answers from their Project are shaped by an instruction someone added months ago for a project that has since ended.
options: Add a newer instruction that overrides the obsolete one where they conflict
Remove the obsolete instruction, since standing configuration applies to everything
Tell people to mention when the old instruction should not apply to their question
Create a new Project and leave the obsolete instruction behind
questions.why: Standing instructions apply to every response until removed. Deleting what no longer applies is basic configuration hygiene.
questions.traps: Layering an override leaves two competing rules. Asking users to work around it puts the burden in the wrong place, and a new Project abandons the existing knowledge.

questions.stem: A team's task is simple but the consequences of a rare error are severe, and errors would not be visible until much later.
options: Choose by task difficulty, since a simple task does not need a capable model
Choose the cheapest tier and add a verification step to catch any errors
Choose the strongest tier so the rare error becomes rarer still
Weigh tier choice against the cost of a late-discovered error, not just task difficulty
questions.why: Selection weighs difficulty against consequence. A simple task with severe, late-surfacing failures justifies more capability than difficulty alone would suggest.
questions.traps: Difficulty alone ignores the consequence side. Verification is valuable but the scenario says errors surface late, and reaching for the top tier skips the reasoning.

questions.stem: An associate wants Claude to check a spreadsheet's figures against a PDF report and flag any that disagree.
options: Paste the key figures from each and ask Claude to compare those
Ask Claude what figures typically appear in reports of this kind
Attach both files so the comparison happens against the actual documents
Ask for a checking procedure the team can carry out themselves
questions.why: Cross-document verification needs both documents present. Attaching them is what makes the comparison about these files rather than about a sample or a generality.
questions.traps: A pasted subset checks only what you already selected. A question about typical figures never touches either document, and a procedure hands the work back.

questions.stem: A team's workflow makes three sequential calls where the second and third each depend on the previous result.
options: Check whether the steps genuinely need to be sequential before optimising further
Combine all three into one call so only a single request is made
Run all three in parallel to reduce the total elapsed time
Move to the fastest tier so the three calls complete sooner
questions.why: Sequential dependency is what forces the latency, so the first question is whether the dependency is real. That determines which optimisations are even available.
questions.traps: Combining removes the checkpoints between steps. Parallelism is impossible if each genuinely depends on the last, and a faster tier optimises within an unexamined structure.

questions.stem: An associate built a workflow that only they know how to maintain. They are going on leave for two months.
options: Pause the workflow until the associate returns from their leave
Document it and hand it over, since a workflow with one owner is fragile
Ask a colleague to run it without documentation and escalate if it breaks
Automate the remaining steps so less of it depends on one person
questions.why: Single-owner dependence is an operational risk that leave makes concrete. Documenting and transferring is what turns personal capability into team capability.
questions.traps: Pausing forfeits the value for two months. Running it blind invites failures nobody can diagnose, and further automation deepens the dependency.

questions.stem: A team's prompt works reliably on the strongest tier and produces inconsistent structure on a cheaper one.
options: Stay on the strongest tier, since the cheaper one cannot handle the task
Accept the inconsistency and add a cleanup step after the cheaper tier
Alternate tiers from one request to the next to average it out
Tighten the prompt's format specification and retest the cheaper tier
questions.why: Format inconsistency is often under-specification that a capable model absorbs. Tightening the spec is what tests whether the cheaper tier can hold once the ambiguity is removed.
questions.traps: Concluding incapability before improving the prompt is premature. A cleanup step pays for the ambiguity forever, and alternating produces two different behaviours.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude to draft replies inside their support tool so agents never leave the ticket they are working on.
options: A second window agents switch to whenever they want a draft
A daily batch of pre-written replies for the most common ticket types
An integration into the support tool, so drafting happens where the ticket is
A shared Project that agents open alongside the support tool
questions.why: Removing the context switch is the whole point when someone is working inside a ticket queue. The integration puts the capability where the work already is.
questions.traps: A second window is the friction being removed. Pre-written batches cannot address specific tickets, and a shared Project still requires leaving the tool.

questions.stem: An associate is unsure whether to put a document in project knowledge or attach it to a single conversation.
options: Always use project knowledge, since it keeps everything organised in one place
Ask whether it will be needed again, since that is what project knowledge is for
Always attach to the conversation, since that keeps each Project small
Put the document in both the Project and each individual request
questions.why: Reuse is the criterion. Persistent knowledge earns its place when the document will be needed repeatedly; a one-off attachment is right when it will not.
questions.traps: Blanket rules in either direction ignore the reuse question. Duplicating the document creates two copies to keep in step.

questions.stem: A team wants to know whether their task is limited by the model or by the quality of the information they are supplying it.
options: Upgrade the tier and observe whether the results get noticeably better
Improve the inputs and observe whether the results get noticeably better
Give a capable tier ideal inputs and see whether the output improves
Change both the tier and the input quality at the same time
questions.why: Testing with a strong model and clean inputs establishes the ceiling. If output still disappoints, the limit is elsewhere, and that isolates the question cleanly.
questions.traps: Changing one variable is informative but slower than establishing the ceiling first. Changing both at once leaves you unable to attribute the difference.

questions.stem: A team needs a document that several people will edit over time, with Claude helping draft sections as they go.
options: Draft in Claude and maintain the document in the tool the team already edits in
Keep the document inside conversations and copy the current version out when needed
Give each person their own conversation and merge the versions periodically
Ask for a completely new full draft each time it is edited
questions.why: Collaborative editing belongs in a collaboration tool, with the model used for drafting. Conflating the two puts version control somewhere it does not exist.
questions.traps: Conversations do not provide shared editing or version history. Parallel conversations create merge work, and regenerating discards accumulated edits.

questions.stem: An associate notices that asking Claude to explain its reasoning roughly doubles the length of every response and the cost with it.
options: Always ask for reasoning, since it makes the output easier to trust
Never ask for reasoning, since the cost increase is not justified
Ask for shorter reasoning so the cost increase is smaller
Ask for reasoning only where it will actually be read and used
questions.why: Reasoning has real value when someone reviews it and none when nobody reads it. Matching the request to actual use is what makes the spend purposeful.
questions.traps: Always and never both ignore whether it gets used. Shortening the reasoning degrades it without asking whether it was needed.

questions.stem: A team is asked to expand a successful workflow to a region with different regulations and a different language.
options: Expand directly, since the workflow logic is the same in both regions
Expand and adjust whatever turns out not to work in the new region
Treat it as a new workflow to validate rather than an expansion of the existing one
Expand only the parts of the workflow that operate in English
questions.why: Different regulation and different language change both the correctness criteria and the model's performance. That makes it a new thing to validate, not a rollout.
questions.traps: Assuming the logic transfers ignores both changes. Adjusting after launch discovers regulatory problems in production, and a partial expansion still faces the regulatory difference.

questions.stem: A team asks whether they should standardise on one tier across all their workflows for simplicity.
options: Standardise on the strongest tier so no workflow is ever under-served
Match the tier to each workload, since simplicity is worth less than fit here
Standardise on the cheapest tier and escalate only when problems appear
Standardise on a mid tier as a compromise across the workloads
questions.why: Workloads differ enough in volume, difficulty and stakes that a single tier either overpays or under-serves. The administrative simplicity does not repay that.
questions.traps: Standardising high overpays across the board. Standardising low discovers under-service through failures, and a mid tier splits the difference for everyone.

questions.stem: An associate needs an answer once, urgently, about a topic requiring no special context or documents.
options: A single conversation, which is the fastest path to a one-off answer
A Project set up for the topic in case it comes up again in future
A shared Project so colleagues benefit from the same answer
A saved template kept in case the same question arises again
questions.why: Urgent one-off work wants the least setup. Recognising when no infrastructure is warranted is as much a selection skill as knowing when it is.
questions.traps: Every alternative adds setup that the urgency and the one-off nature make unnecessary.

questions.stem: A team's Project produces good answers but a member complains it is slow compared to a plain conversation.
options: Accept the slowness, since project knowledge is what makes the answers good
Move to a faster tier so the added context is processed more quickly
Remove the project knowledge so responses process more quickly
Check whether the project knowledge is larger than the questions actually need
questions.why: More context costs time to process, so the question is whether all of it is earning its place. Curating to what questions actually need addresses the cause.
questions.traps: Accepting it forgoes an easy improvement. A faster tier pays to process context that may be unnecessary, and removing knowledge entirely discards what makes the answers good.

questions.stem: A workflow's errors turn out to be caused by inconsistent input formatting rather than by the model's reasoning.
options: Fix the input formatting, since a stronger tier applies the same reasoning to bad inputs
Upgrade the tier so the model copes better with inconsistent input formats
Add a prompt instruction telling the model to handle inconsistent formats
Add a cleanup step and upgrade the tier at the same time
questions.why: Input quality is upstream of model choice, and capability spent absorbing avoidable inconsistency is capability wasted. Fixing the source is the leverage point.
questions.traps: Upgrading pays to tolerate a fixable defect. An instruction asks the model to compensate, and doing both obscures which change mattered.

questions.stem: An associate wants Claude to remember a preference about tone across every future conversation they have.
options: Mention the preference at the start of each new conversation
Ask Claude to remember it and rely on that in later conversations
Put the preference in configuration so it applies without being restated
Write the preference in a document the team can refer to
questions.why: Preferences that should always apply belong in configuration. That is what makes them persistent rather than dependent on being restated.
questions.traps: Restating each time is the manual work configuration removes. Conversations do not carry preferences forward, and a document is not applied automatically.

questions.stem: A team's monthly bill is dominated by one workflow that produces long analytical reports nobody has read in three months.
options: Move it to a cheaper tier so the unread reports cost less to produce
Stop running it, since the cheapest workflow is the one that is not needed
Shorten the reports so the unused output is smaller
Run the reporting workflow quarterly rather than monthly
questions.why: Output nobody consumes has no value at any price. Removing the workflow is the optimisation, and noticing that is the point of the scenario.
questions.traps: Every alternative optimises the cost of producing something unread, which treats the wrong quantity as the variable.

questions.stem: A team wants to add Claude to a process where the current bottleneck is waiting for a legal signature, not drafting.
options: Add Claude to drafting anyway, since faster drafts are an improvement in themselves
Add Claude and measure whether overall throughput improves afterwards
Automate the request for signature so it is sent sooner
Address the signature bottleneck, since speeding up drafting will not help throughput
questions.why: Improving a step that is not the constraint does not improve the outcome. Identifying the real bottleneck first is what makes the effort worth spending.
questions.traps: Faster drafting queues work at the same signature. Measuring after the fact wastes the effort, and automating the request is not the same as removing the wait.

questions.stem: A team is choosing a tier for a nightly job that rewrites 20,000 product descriptions, where quality matters but nothing is time-critical.
options: Choose the strongest tier available, because product descriptions are customer-facing content and the cost difference across a single nightly batch is unlikely to be material to the business
Test from the cheapest tier upward and stop at the first that meets the quality bar
Choose the fastest tier, since the job runs overnight and has plenty of time
Choose whichever tier the team already uses elsewhere in the business
questions.why: With no latency pressure and a defined quality bar, the cheapest tier that clears the bar is the right answer, and testing upward is how you find it.
questions.traps: Customer-facing framing argues for a quality bar rather than a tier. Speed is irrelevant overnight, and reusing an existing choice is convenience rather than fit.

questions.stem: An associate's team is billed by usage and their largest cost is a workflow that sends an entire 90-page manual with each of 600 daily questions.
options: Move the manual into persistent knowledge so it is not resent with every question
Continue as it is, because every question genuinely could touch any part of the manual and removing it would risk answers that miss relevant sections entirely
Split the manual into chapters and send only the relevant chapter
Reduce the number of questions the team is allowed to ask each day
questions.why: Resending stable reference material 600 times a day is pure duplication, and persistent knowledge removes it without losing coverage.
questions.traps: Keeping it accepts the duplication. Chapter routing needs a router that may itself misfire, and rationing questions sacrifices the work.

questions.stem: A team of analysts wants Claude embedded in the spreadsheet tool where they spend most of their day.
options: A separate browser tab that analysts switch to whenever they want Claude's help, with the relevant spreadsheet data pasted across each time they need something
A weekly training session on switching between tools efficiently
An integration into that tool so the capability sits where the analysis happens
A shared Project holding exported copies of the main spreadsheets
questions.why: Adoption follows friction, and putting the capability inside the tool people already use removes the switch entirely rather than making it faster.
questions.traps: Tab-switching with manual pasting is the friction being removed. Training people to tolerate it rarely works, and exported copies go stale.

questions.stem: A consultant keeps one Project containing guidelines for all six of their clients, and answers occasionally apply the wrong client's brand rules.
options: Keep the single Project but label each document clearly with the client name so the model can tell which set of guidelines applies to the question being asked
Mention the client's name at the start of every question asked
Keep the single Project and review each answer for cross-contamination
Split into one Project per client so only the relevant guidelines are ever in scope
questions.why: Isolation is structural: if only one client's guidelines are present, the wrong ones cannot be applied. Labelling relies on correct selection every time.
questions.traps: Labels and per-question naming both depend on the model choosing correctly. Review catches contamination after it happens rather than preventing it.

questions.stem: A team needs Claude to answer questions about pricing that changes weekly, and last week's answer was quoted to a customer incorrectly.
options: Upload the current price list to a Project and remember to replace the file every week when the new prices are published by the commercial team
Include the current prices in the prompt each time a question is asked
Connect Claude to the live pricing source rather than a copy that goes stale
Add a disclaimer that prices should be confirmed before quoting
questions.why: Weekly-changing data quoted to customers has to come from the live source. Anything copied is stale between updates, and this failure already happened.
questions.traps: Manual weekly refresh is exactly the step that gets missed. Per-prompt pasting is the same problem distributed, and a disclaimer shifts risk to the reader.

questions.stem: A team's task requires following a strict twelve-step checklist where omitting any step produces output that looks complete but is wrong.
options: Use the strongest tier, since long procedural instructions are exactly the kind of work where model capability makes the largest and most visible difference to reliability
Test tiers against the full checklist and choose the cheapest one that follows it reliably
Split the checklist into twelve separate requests
Use any tier and verify the twelve steps afterwards
questions.why: Procedure adherence varies by tier, so the answer is empirical. Testing against the real checklist identifies the cheapest tier that holds.
questions.traps: Assuming the top tier is needed skips a cheap test. Twelve requests is a workaround, and after-the-fact verification catches failures instead of avoiding them.

questions.stem: A team's pilot saved 12 hours a week across four people. Scaling to forty people, the saving per person has fallen to roughly two hours a week.
options: Investigate what differs between the two groups before projecting any further growth
Accept the lower figure and report the total saving, since eighty hours a week across forty people is still a substantial and worthwhile return for the organisation
Provide more training so the wider group reaches the pilot's per-person saving
Conclude the pilot's measurement was unreliable and disregard it
questions.why: A large per-person drop signals a real difference between the groups, and understanding it is what makes any further projection trustworthy.
questions.traps: Reporting the total without explaining the drop hides the trend. Training assumes a cause, and discarding the pilot throws away the comparison.

questions.stem: An associate reports that a cheaper tier produces answers that are correct but noticeably blunter in tone than the tier they were using.
options: Return to the more expensive tier, since tone is part of quality and customer-facing communication should not read as blunt or abrupt to the people receiving it
Accept the blunter tone as the cost of the saving
Edit each output by hand to soften the tone before it is sent
Address tone through the prompt and configuration before concluding the tier is unsuitable
questions.why: Tone is highly responsive to instruction, so it is worth exhausting the cheap lever before paying for the expensive one. Correctness is already established.
questions.traps: Upgrading to buy tone pays a lot for something a prompt often supplies. Accepting bluntness ignores the reader, and hand-editing repeats forever.

questions.stem: An associate needs to run the same analysis over a folder of 300 files and write the results back into that folder.
options: The web interface, uploading the files in batches and downloading each result to place back into the folder manually
A Project containing all 300 files as uploaded knowledge
Claude Code, which can read the folder, process each file and write results back
Three hundred separate conversations, one for each file
questions.why: Reading a directory, processing its contents and writing results back is filesystem work, which is what the agentic coding surface provides.
questions.traps: Batch upload and manual placement does not scale to 300. Project knowledge is read-only, and 300 conversations is unmanageable.

questions.stem: A team wants a shareable interactive dashboard summarising quarterly numbers, viewable by executives who will not install anything.
options: Ask for the dashboard code and have a developer host it somewhere the executives can reach
Ask for an Artifact, which renders as an interactive page they can open and share
Ask for a static document containing the same numbers
Ask for a description of what the dashboard should contain
questions.why: An interactive, shareable, install-free rendered output is what Artifacts provide, which is exactly the stated constraint.
questions.traps: A hosted build is heavier than needed. A static document is not interactive, and a description is not a deliverable.

questions.stem: A team's chatbot must answer within three seconds. Testing shows the model responds in 1.2 seconds but retrieval of context takes a further 2.5 seconds.
options: Optimise the retrieval step, since that is where most of the elapsed time is spent
Move to a faster model tier so the generation portion of the response completes more quickly and leaves additional headroom within the three-second budget for retrieval
Shorten the responses so generation finishes sooner
Increase the response time budget from three seconds to six
questions.why: The bottleneck is retrieval at 2.5 of 3.7 seconds. Optimising the smaller component cannot bring the total inside budget.
questions.traps: Faster generation saves at most 1.2 seconds and the budget is already exceeded. Shorter output has the same ceiling, and moving the budget abandons the requirement.

questions.stem: A team member leaves and their Projects contained the only copy of several carefully written instruction sets.
options: Recreate the instruction sets from scratch, since the departing colleague's approach may not have been the best one and the team can improve on it
Ask the departing colleague to write documentation before they leave
Copy the Projects into a shared location as they leave
Treat Project configuration as shared infrastructure with an owner and a backup
questions.why: Single-owner configuration is an operational risk, and treating it as shared infrastructure with defined ownership is the durable fix rather than a one-time rescue.
questions.traps: Rebuilding discards working configuration. Exit documentation and a one-time copy both address this departure without changing the pattern.

questions.stem: A team wants to know whether their disappointing results come from the model or from the fact that half their input documents are poor-quality scans.
options: Test on clean documents first, since input quality is upstream of model choice
Upgrade to a stronger tier, since better models are more robust to noisy or degraded input and this would resolve the problem
Add an instruction telling the model to handle poor scans carefully
Accept the current results and add a human review step afterwards
questions.why: Establishing whether clean inputs produce good output isolates the cause. Paying for capability to absorb avoidable input noise is spending in the wrong place.
questions.traps: Upgrading treats a fixable input problem with money. An instruction cannot recover illegible text, and review absorbs errors rather than diagnosing them.

questions.stem: An associate is asked to justify why a workflow uses an expensive tier. They chose it at the start and have not revisited the choice.
options: Justify it on the grounds that the workflow is important and has been working reliably since it was set up
Move to a cheaper tier since the cost is being questioned
Test the cheaper tiers now and let the result justify whichever tier is kept
Ask the vendor which tier they recommend for this workload
questions.why: An unrevisited default is not a justification. Testing produces evidence that supports whichever tier turns out to be right.
questions.traps: Reliability under one tier says nothing about the others. Downgrading under budget pressure without testing is as unfounded as the original choice, and vendor guidance does not know your bar.

questions.stem: A workflow that works well for one team is being proposed for company-wide rollout. The originating team has unusually clean data.
options: Roll out company-wide, since the workflow has been demonstrated to work on real business data and other teams will benefit from the same efficiency the pilot team found
Check whether other teams' data is comparable before committing to the rollout
Roll out and let each team adapt the workflow to their own data
Roll out to the three teams with the largest headcount first
questions.why: Clean data is the pilot team's unusual property, and the workflow's success may depend on it. Checking comparability is what makes the rollout decision informed.
questions.traps: Assuming transferability ignores the stated difference. Per-team adaptation pushes an unsolved problem outward, and sizing the rollout does not address data quality.

questions.stem: A team needs Claude to compare figures across eleven monthly spreadsheets and identify the months where a metric moved unusually.
options: Paste the headline figure from each month and ask which of those eleven numbers looks unusual relative to the others in the series that has been provided
Describe the general trend and ask what would count as unusual
Ask for a comparison method the team can apply to the files themselves
Attach the spreadsheets so the comparison runs against the actual monthly values
questions.why: Cross-file numerical comparison needs the files. Attaching them makes the analysis about the real data rather than a summary of it.
questions.traps: A pasted headline figure discards the detail that defines "unusual". A verbal trend invites generic answers, and a method hands the work back.

questions.stem: An associate wants to test whether Claude can help with a task at all, before committing any time to setting anything up.
options: A Project configured with the relevant documents and instructions so the test reflects how the workflow would actually run
A single conversation, since exploration should not require configuration first
A developer-built prototype using the API to test the idea properly
A shared Project so colleagues can watch the test
questions.why: Exploration wants the shortest path to an answer. Building configuration before knowing whether the task is viable is investment ahead of evidence.
questions.traps: A configured Project, a prototype and a shared space all front-load setup that the exploration may show to be unnecessary.

questions.stem: A team could halve their spend by moving to a cheaper tier, at the cost of roughly ten extra minutes of human correction per day.
options: Compare the saving against the cost of ten minutes a day of skilled correction time
Move to the cheaper tier, since halving a recurring bill is a substantial saving and ten minutes a day is a small amount of time for any individual to absorb
Stay on the current tier, since human time is more valuable than model cost
Move to the cheaper tier and reduce the correction to a sample
questions.why: The comparison is between two quantified costs, and both are known. Working out which is larger is the whole decision.
questions.traps: Both blanket answers assert a conclusion without the arithmetic. Sampling the correction weakens the control to make the numbers work.

questions.stem: A workflow needs the model to say when it cannot answer rather than guessing. Cheaper tiers guess more often on this task.
options: Move to the strongest tier, since knowing the limits of one's own knowledge is a capability that improves with model strength and cannot be reliably prompted for
Accept the guessing and verify every answer the workflow produces
Test whether prompting for abstention closes the gap before paying for a stronger tier
Add a confidence threshold below which answers are discarded
questions.why: Abstention behaviour responds well to explicit instruction and examples, so that lever is worth testing before spending on capability.
questions.traps: Treating abstention as unpromptable skips a cheap test. Verifying everything absorbs the cost, and confidence thresholds rest on an unreliable signal.

questions.stem: An associate's Project answers well on the topics its documents cover and confidently wrong on adjacent topics they also ask about.
options: Add documents covering the adjacent topics so the Project's knowledge extends to the questions people are actually asking it
Tell colleagues to only ask about the covered topics
Move the adjacent questions to a plain conversation
Instruct the Project to answer from its documents and say when they do not cover a question
questions.why: The failure is that the boundary is invisible, so making the Project declare when it is outside its knowledge is what stops confident answers from unsupported territory.
questions.traps: Adding documents extends the boundary without making it visible. Telling people the scope relies on them knowing it, and routing elsewhere does not fix the Project.

questions.stem: A team's task produces occasional badly wrong answers on all tiers they have tested, at roughly the same rate.
options: Investigate the task itself, since a rate that does not vary with tier is not a capability limit
Move to the strongest tier, since even a small reduction in the rate of badly wrong answers is worth paying for when those answers reach customers directly
Accept the error rate as something inherent to this kind of task
Add a review step and keep using the cheapest available tier
questions.why: A failure rate that is flat across tiers points at the prompt, the inputs or the task definition rather than at model capability. That is where the fix is.
questions.traps: Upgrading spends on a variable shown not to matter. Accepting the rate skips diagnosis, and review manages a symptom whose cause is still unknown.

questions.stem: A team plans to move from 500 to 50,000 monthly requests and asks whether anything changes besides the bill.
options: Expect only the cost to change, since the workflow logic and the model behaviour are identical
Expect the cost per request to fall at higher volume
Expect input variety, error handling and review capacity to change, not just cost
Expect nothing to change until the volume is reached
questions.why: A hundredfold increase surfaces input variety the pilot never saw and outstrips any review process built for 500. Cost is the most visible change, not the only one.
questions.traps: Assuming only cost scales is the misconception. Unit pricing is a separate question, and waiting to find out defers the planning that matters.

questions.stem: An associate needs the same five checks applied to every document the team produces, and people currently remember them inconsistently.
options: Circulate a checklist so each person applies the five checks themselves before submitting their work
Encode the checks in project instructions so they are applied to every response
Ask Claude to recall the checks at the start of each conversation
Audit a sample of finished documents against the five checks
questions.why: Standing checks belong in configuration, which is what makes them automatic rather than dependent on individual memory that has already proven inconsistent.
questions.traps: A circulated checklist relies on the consistency that is already failing. Per-conversation recall is manual, and sampling accepts inconsistency by design.

questions.stem: A team discovers that most of their cost comes from a small number of very long documents rather than from request volume.
options: Reduce the overall number of requests across the whole team so the total cost falls proportionally
Move every request to a cheaper tier so the total spend falls
Ask people to submit shorter documents so each one costs less
Handle the long documents differently, since they are where the cost concentrates
questions.why: Cost concentrated in a few large inputs is addressed by treating those inputs differently, not by uniform reductions that mostly affect the cheap majority.
questions.traps: Cutting overall volume mostly reduces inexpensive requests. A cheaper tier pays less for the same skew, and shorter submissions may not be possible.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude to act on a schedule without anyone triggering it, producing a report every Monday at 6am.
options: A scheduled automation, since unattended execution needs something that runs on its own
A Project with instructions saying the report should be produced every Monday morning at six, so the schedule is recorded alongside the rest of the configuration
A calendar reminder for someone to run it manually
A conversation left open over the weekend so it is ready Monday
questions.why: Unattended scheduled execution requires a scheduler. Configuration describing a schedule does not cause anything to run.
questions.traps: Instructions describe intent without triggering execution. A reminder makes it manual, and an open conversation does nothing on its own.

questions.stem: A team is choosing between spending on a stronger tier and spending the same amount on better source documents.
options: Spend on the stronger tier, since model capability affects every task the team runs
Spend on better documents, since inputs constrain everything downstream
Split the available budget evenly between the two options
Test which change moves the result more, since both are plausible and only one is measured
questions.why: Two competing hypotheses with a fixed budget is an empirical question. Testing which lever moves the outcome is what makes the spend defensible.
questions.traps: Both assertions are plausible and untested. Splitting the budget buys half of each without learning which mattered.

questions.stem: An associate wants their Project to behave differently for two distinct kinds of question, but a single instruction set applies to both.
options: Write conditional instructions describing which behaviour applies to which kind of question, so a single Project can serve both purposes
Ask people to specify which mode they want in each question
Use two Projects, since standing instructions apply to everything in one of them
Alternate the instructions from one week to the next
questions.why: Standing instructions apply to every response in a Project. When two behaviours are genuinely different, separate Projects is the structural answer.
questions.traps: Conditional instructions ask the model to classify correctly every time. Per-question mode selection puts the burden on users, and alternating serves neither well.

questions.stem: A team notices their cheapest-tier workflow fails specifically on inputs longer than about ten pages.
options: Move everything to a stronger tier, since the team cannot always predict in advance which inputs will exceed the length where the cheaper tier begins to fail
Route long inputs to a stronger tier and keep the cheap one for the rest
Truncate inputs to ten pages before processing them
Accept that long inputs will sometimes fail and move on
questions.why: A clean, observable predictor of failure is exactly what makes routing work. Input length is known before the request, so the split is reliable.
questions.traps: Upgrading everything ignores a usable signal that is trivially available. Truncation discards content, and accepting failures on long inputs abandons those cases.

questions.stem: A team's manual review process handles 50 items a day comfortably. The workflow they are scaling will produce 800 a day.
options: Redesign the review approach, since a process built for 50 will not stretch to 800
Hire additional reviewers so the existing review process can be applied to the full volume at the same depth it is currently applied to the fifty daily items
Keep the same review process and let the backlog grow
Ask reviewers to work faster so the whole volume is covered
questions.why: A sixteenfold increase breaks a process designed for the smaller volume. Redesigning around risk-weighted review is what makes the control survive the scale.
questions.traps: Linear hiring is expensive and may not be available. A growing backlog is a failing control, and asking for speed degrades the check.

questions.stem: An associate wants Claude to work from a document but is not allowed to upload it because of a data classification rule.
options: Upload the document anyway, since the analysis is internal and the resulting output will not be shared outside the organisation or retained beyond the current task
Paste the document's text rather than uploading the file
Summarise the document by hand and work from the summary
Confirm what the classification permits before choosing any technical approach
questions.why: A classification rule is a governance constraint, and the permitted approaches follow from what it actually says. Establishing that comes before any technical choice.
questions.traps: Uploading against the rule is a policy breach regardless of intent. Pasting is the same disclosure by another route, and hand-summarising may also be prohibited.

questions.stem: A team's workflow runs a second verification call on every output, doubling the cost. Verification catches an error roughly once in eighty runs.
options: Remove the verification step, since catching one error in eighty runs does not justify doubling the cost of every single request the workflow makes
Keep the verification, since any error caught is worth the cost
Weigh the doubled cost against what one error in eighty would cost if it escaped
Run the verification call on a random tenth of outputs
questions.why: The decision needs both numbers: the doubled cost and the cost of an escaped error. One in eighty may be cheap or catastrophic depending on what the error does.
questions.traps: Both blanket answers decide without the consequence figure. Random sampling reduces cost and catch rate together without reasoning about either.

questions.stem: A team's task involves both simple extraction and difficult judgement, currently handled in a single request on an expensive tier.
options: Keep the single request, since splitting introduces a handoff between steps where information can be lost and adds complexity to a workflow that currently works reliably
Split the task so the simple part runs cheaply and only the judgement uses the strong tier
Move the whole combined task to a cheaper model tier
Run the task twice on different tiers and compare
questions.why: Mixed-difficulty work in one request pays the top rate for the easy portion. Splitting lets each part run on the tier it needs.
questions.traps: Keeping it whole overpays for the extraction. Downgrading everything under-serves the judgement, and duplicate runs double the cost.

questions.stem: A team's shared Project is used by twelve people, and one of them keeps changing the instructions to suit their own workflow.
options: Ask that person to stop making changes to the shared instructions
Give that person a separate Project of their own to configure
Revert the shared instructions whenever they are changed
Establish who owns the configuration and how changes are agreed
questions.why: Shared configuration needs an ownership model, otherwise every user is an editor and the behaviour drifts. That is a governance fix rather than an interpersonal one.
questions.traps: A request without a rule relies on goodwill. A separate Project addresses one person, and reverting is an ongoing conflict rather than a resolution.

questions.stem: An associate wants to know if the newest model is automatically the right choice for their existing, well-tuned workflow.
options: Test it against the current setup, since a newer model is not automatically better for a tuned workflow
Adopt it, since newer models are generally more capable and the workflow will benefit from the improvement
Stay on the current model indefinitely to avoid any disruption
Adopt the newer model for new workflows only, not existing ones
questions.why: A prompt tuned against one model may not transfer cleanly. Testing is what establishes whether the change helps this particular workflow.
questions.traps: Assuming newer is better for a tuned setup skips the test. Never changing forgoes real improvements, and a new-work-only rule avoids the question.

questions.stem: A team wants non-technical staff to run a workflow that currently requires someone to assemble three documents and write a careful prompt each time.
options: Write a detailed instruction document explaining how to assemble the three documents and construct the prompt, so any staff member can follow the same procedure reliably
Have the technical person run the workflow whenever it is needed
Package it as a Project so the documents and prompt are already in place
Train all the staff to assemble and write the prompt themselves
questions.why: Packaging the assembly into configuration removes the expertise requirement entirely. Staff supply only what actually varies.
questions.traps: A procedure document leaves the assembly manual and error-prone. A single operator is a bottleneck, and training everyone is disproportionate.

questions.stem: An associate needs Claude to explain a decision it made three weeks ago in a conversation that has since been deleted.
options: Ask Claude to recall the conversation and explain the reasoning it used at the time
Recognise the reasoning is not recoverable and rebuild the analysis from the inputs
Ask Claude to reconstruct what it probably said three weeks ago
Check whether a colleague remembers the explanation
questions.why: A deleted conversation is gone, and asking for a reconstruction produces a plausible account rather than a record. Rebuilding from the inputs is honest.
questions.traps: Both recall options invite fabrication presented as memory. A colleague's recollection is weak evidence about a specific analysis.

questions.stem: A team's costs spiked in one week with no change in usage volume. They have per-request logs available.
options: Move to a cheaper tier to bring the cost back down to its previous level before investigating what caused the increase, so the budget impact is contained immediately
Assume it was a pricing change and query the invoice
Examine the logs to find which requests changed in size or shape that week
Average the cost over the quarter so the spike is less visible
questions.why: Per-request logs make the cause directly findable. Diagnosing before acting is what prevents an unnecessary change to a workflow that may be fine.
questions.traps: Downgrading treats a symptom of an unknown cause. Assuming a pricing change skips available evidence, and averaging conceals the signal.

questions.stem: A team's workflow works on the strongest tier and fails on every cheaper one, and they have not examined why it fails.
options: Accept that the task requires the strongest tier and budget accordingly
Retest the cheaper tiers using a longer and fuller prompt
Use the strongest tier and revisit the question next year
Look at how the cheaper tiers fail, since the pattern may point at a fixable prompt issue
questions.why: The failure mode carries diagnostic information. A consistent structural failure often reflects under-specification that a capable model absorbs and a cheaper one does not.
questions.traps: Accepting the result without examining it forgoes a likely saving. A longer prompt is an untargeted change, and deferring keeps paying meanwhile.

questions.stem: An associate is asked whether a workflow should be rolled out to a team that works in a language the pilot never tested.
options: Roll out, since the workflow logic is language-independent and the model handles many languages capably enough for the same process to produce comparable results
Test in that language before rolling out, since performance varies across languages
Roll out with an instruction to work in the new language
Roll out and have the outputs translated after they are produced
questions.why: Model performance varies by language, so an untested language is an untested workload. Testing is what turns the assumption into knowledge.
questions.traps: Assuming language independence is the misconception. An instruction does not establish quality, and translating afterwards adds a step and a new error source.

questions.stem: A team wants to preserve a particularly good conversation so its approach can be reused, but conversations are not a durable store.
options: Extract what made it work into reusable configuration rather than keeping the thread
Keep the conversation open and return to it whenever similar work comes up, continuing from the point where the good result was originally produced by the team
Export the conversation as a text file for reference
Ask Claude to summarise what made the conversation effective
questions.why: The reusable asset is the prompt and context that produced the result, not the transcript. Extracting it into configuration is what makes it repeatable.
questions.traps: A long-running thread degrades and cannot be shared cleanly. An export is a record rather than a working setup, and a summary is commentary rather than configuration.

questions.stem: A finance team automates monthly reporting: pull figures from a spreadsheet, have Claude draft the commentary, send to stakeholders.
options: After the commentary is drafted and immediately before anything is sent out to stakeholders
Before the spreadsheet figures reach Claude
At both the data-input stage and the pre-send stage, since each fails differently
At quarter end, reviewing the three monthly outputs together in one batch
questions.why: Stale inputs and inaccurate commentary are separate failure modes. A pre-send check catches the second while good reasoning over wrong data still reads plausibly.
questions.traps: A single pre-send checkpoint misses bad inputs. An input-only check misses bad commentary, and quarterly review arrives after three months of sending.

questions.stem: A team places a human approval step on every Claude output. Approvers now rubber-stamp because the volume makes real review impossible.
options: Reduce what requires approval so the remaining approvals are genuine
Keep approval on everything and ask approvers to be more thorough in how they read each item
Remove the approval step from the process entirely
Add a second approver to share the load
questions.why: A control applied to everything at a volume nobody can handle provides no assurance while appearing to. Narrowing scope is what restores real review.
questions.traps: Asking for thoroughness without reducing volume repeats the failure. Removing the control abandons it, and a second rubber-stamper doubles the cost of nothing.

questions.stem: A team wants to automate a step where the correct answer depends on a judgement two senior staff currently disagree about.
options: Automate it using whichever interpretation is more commonly applied across the team
Settle the disagreement first, since an unspecified rule cannot be automated correctly
Automate it and have Claude explain its reasoning
Leave the step manual on a permanent basis
questions.why: An unresolved judgement has no specification, and automating one produces confidently wrong output. The disagreement is a prerequisite, not an obstacle to work around.
questions.traps: Picking the common interpretation encodes a position nobody agreed. Explanations do not make an undefined rule correct, and permanent manual handling assumes the disagreement is unresolvable.

questions.stem: An associate is asked where Claude could help in a twelve-step process. They pick the step that looks most tedious.
options: Pick the most tedious step, since removing unpleasant work improves morale and the people doing it will be most receptive to the change being introduced
Automate the first step so the benefit flows downstream
Automate every one of the steps that involves writing text
Find the step that constrains the whole process, since that is where a gain compounds
questions.why: Improving a step that is not the constraint does not improve throughput. Finding the bottleneck is what makes the effort produce a visible result.
questions.traps: Tedium is about experience rather than throughput. Position in the sequence is arbitrary, and automating by activity type ignores where the process actually binds.

questions.stem: A workflow has Claude draft, a person edit, then Claude polish. The polish step routinely reverses the person's edits.
options: Ask the polish step to make only minimal changes to whatever document it receives, so the human's work is less likely to be overwritten during the final pass
Mark the human edits as deliberate so the polish step preserves them
Move the human edit to after the polish step has already been applied
Remove the polish step from the workflow so edits survive intact
questions.why: A later step cannot distinguish a deliberate edit from a rough patch in the draft. Marking them is what makes them survive.
questions.traps: Minimal-change instructions are a degree without a target. Reordering leaves the human's work unpolished, and removing the step discards its value.

questions.stem: A team designs a workflow assuming Claude's output will be correct, with no provision for what happens when it is not.
options: Design the handling of wrong output as part of the workflow, not as an exception
Add a review step at the end so incorrect output is caught before it goes anywhere
Choose a stronger model so errors are rarer
Monitor for errors and respond to them as they occur
questions.why: Workflows that assume correctness break in undefined ways when it fails. Designing the wrong-output path is what makes the failure survivable rather than surprising.
questions.traps: A review step is part of that design but not the whole of it. A stronger model reduces frequency without defining behaviour, and reactive monitoring is not a design.

questions.stem: A team must decide where to place one reviewer in a four-step chain where errors get progressively more expensive to correct.
options: At the final step, since that is where the output leaves the team and where the consequences of any remaining error would actually be felt by the recipients
At the step that produces the most output for the reviewer to see
At the earliest step where an error is both detectable and cheap to fix
At whichever step the reviewer finds most interesting
questions.why: Placing the check where errors are detectable and still cheap minimises the cost of the ones it catches. A late check finds expensive problems.
questions.traps: A final check catches errors after three steps of compounding. Volume and reviewer preference are unrelated to where errors originate.

questions.stem: An associate wants Claude's output to land in the team's tracker automatically, but the output format varies between runs.
options: Build the integration with error handling that copes with the variation, so the tracker receives whatever the model produces and flags anything it cannot parse properly
Ask people to paste the output into the tracker by hand each time
Integrate and fix the format problems as they surface
Fix the output format before integrating, since an integration needs a stable contract
questions.why: Integration depends on a predictable contract at the boundary. Stabilising the format first is what stops the integration from being a permanent source of failures.
questions.traps: Tolerant parsing normalises the instability. Manual pasting abandons the integration, and fixing problems as they surface debugs in production.

questions.stem: A team's Claude workflow produces good results when one particular person runs it and mediocre results when anyone else does.
options: Have that person run the workflow for everyone, since they clearly have a feel for it that the others have not developed through the same amount of practice
Train the other team members up to that same standard over a period
Capture what that person does differently and build it into the shared setup
Accept the variation in results between different people running it
questions.why: Person-dependent quality means the expertise lives in someone's head rather than in the workflow. Extracting it into shared configuration is what makes results consistent.
questions.traps: Routing through one person creates a bottleneck. Training is slow and may not transfer tacit judgement, and accepting variation gives up on repeatability.

questions.stem: A team claims their Claude workflow saves twenty hours a week. The figure comes from asking people how much time they think they save.
options: Accept the figure, since the people doing the work are best placed to judge how long it used to take them and how long the same work takes them now
Measure the actual time before and after, since estimates of one's own saving are unreliable
Halve the reported figure in order to be conservative about it
Ask a manager to estimate the time saving instead of the team
questions.why: Self-estimated time savings are systematically unreliable. Measuring the actual work is what turns a claim into evidence that will survive scrutiny.
questions.traps: Practitioner confidence does not make recall accurate. Halving is arbitrary, and a manager's estimate is further from the work.

questions.stem: A team maps their process and finds Claude could help at seven of eleven steps. They have capacity to change two.
options: Choose the two earliest steps so the benefit propagates through the rest of the process before anyone has to make further decisions about the remaining steps
Choose the two steps that would be easiest for the team to change
Choose the two steps people complain about most
Choose the two where the gain is largest relative to the effort and risk
questions.why: With limited capacity, the selection criterion is return against cost and risk. That is what makes the two changes worth the capacity they consume.
questions.traps: Sequence position does not predict value. Ease ignores return, and complaints reflect experience rather than impact.

questions.stem: A team is considering automating a decision that affects whether individual customers receive a refund.
options: Keep a person accountable for the decision and use Claude to prepare the case
Automate it fully, since the refund rules are documented and applying documented rules consistently is exactly the kind of work that benefits from removing human variation
Automate the decision and audit a sample of those outcomes monthly
Automate the approvals and route refusals to a person
questions.why: Decisions affecting individuals need an accountable person. Using the model to prepare rather than decide keeps the benefit without moving accountability onto a system.
questions.traps: Full automation moves accountability. Sampling audits after the fact, and asymmetric routing still auto-decides in the customer's favour without oversight.

questions.stem: A two-step workflow passes Claude's classification into a drafting step. Misclassifications produce confident drafts in the wrong register.
options: Ask the drafting step to check whether the classification looks right for the request it has received
Combine the two steps into a single request
Add a confidence score to the classification
Surface the classification so a person can catch a wrong one before drafting
questions.why: Making the intermediate decision visible turns a silent pipeline error into a catchable one. The classification determines everything downstream.
questions.traps: Downstream self-checking uses the same signal that produced the class. Merging hides the decision, and confidence scores catch only cases the model already doubts.

questions.stem: A workflow silently produces an empty result when its input file is missing, and downstream steps treat the empty result as valid.
options: Make the missing-input case fail loudly rather than producing an empty result
Add a check at the end of the workflow that looks for empty results and raises an alert so the team knows when something has gone wrong during the process
Ask people to confirm the input file exists before running
Add a default value to be used whenever the input file is missing
questions.why: Silent failure that looks like success is the worst failure mode. Making it loud at the point of failure is what stops it propagating as valid data.
questions.traps: An end-of-workflow check catches it after downstream steps have consumed it. Manual confirmation is unreliable, and a default value manufactures fake data.

questions.stem: A team rolls out a Claude workflow. Three months later two people use it daily and six have quietly gone back to the old way.
options: Mandate use of the new workflow so the benefit is realised across the whole team
Provide more training on the new workflow
Find out what the six ran into, since quiet abandonment usually signals a real obstacle
Accept that adoption varies between individuals
questions.why: Quiet reversion is evidence about the workflow rather than about the people. Understanding the obstacle is what makes the next iteration work.
questions.traps: Mandating use without knowing the obstacle forces people through it. Training assumes a skill gap, and accepting the split forfeits most of the value.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude to read from a system that holds personal data, and nobody has checked what the system's access rules permit.
options: Design the integration with strong access controls so that only the necessary fields are read
Establish what the access rules permit before designing the integration
Read only anonymised data from the system
Ask the system owner after the integration is built
questions.why: Permitted access is a governance question that constrains the design. Establishing it first is what stops effort going into something that cannot be approved.
questions.traps: Controls chosen without knowing the rules may not satisfy them. Anonymisation may not be sufficient or possible, and asking afterwards risks rework.

questions.stem: A team's workflow depends on a prompt one person keeps in a personal note. Nobody else can find it when they are away.
options: Ask that person to share the note with the team so colleagues have a copy available
Ask them to document how the prompt works
Move the prompt into shared configuration where the workflow itself lives
Rebuild the prompt when it is needed
questions.why: A workflow's working parts belong with the workflow. Personal storage is a single point of failure that sharing a copy only partially addresses.
questions.traps: A shared copy drifts from the original. Documentation describes rather than provides, and rebuilding rediscovers work already done.

questions.stem: A team wants to show their workflow is worth continuing. They have output volume but no measure of whether the output is used.
options: Measure whether the output is acted on, since volume alone does not demonstrate value
Report the output volume alongside the cost, which shows what the workflow produces relative to what it consumes and lets leadership draw their own conclusion
Survey the team about whether they find the workflow valuable
Compare the volume against what the team produced before
questions.why: Volume measures activity, not value. Whether anyone acts on the output is what distinguishes a useful workflow from an expensive one.
questions.traps: Volume against cost is still activity. Perception surveys are weak evidence, and a before-and-after volume comparison measures the same wrong quantity.

questions.stem: A team's reviewer sees only Claude's final output, not the source documents it worked from or the prompt that produced it.
options: Ask the reviewer to focus on accuracy and internal consistency
Add a summary of the sources to the output
Have a second reviewer check the sources separately
Give the reviewer the prompt and sources, since output alone can only be judged for plausibility
questions.why: Review without inputs can only assess whether something reads well. Access to the prompt and sources is what makes the check substantive.
questions.traps: Internal consistency is preserved by confident errors. A self-reported source summary is not the sources, and splitting the check across two people fragments it.

questions.stem: An associate maps a process and discovers three of the eight steps exist only to correct errors introduced by step two.
options: Automate the three correction steps with Claude, since they are repetitive and well-defined and removing that manual effort would deliver an immediate and measurable saving
Fix step two, since three downstream steps exist to compensate for it
Combine the three correction steps into a single consolidated step
Automate step two so it introduces errors more consistently
questions.why: Correction steps that exist because of an upstream defect are waste. Fixing the source removes all three rather than making them cheaper to perform.
questions.traps: Automating the corrections entrenches the defect. Combining them is the same waste reorganised, and making errors consistent misses the point entirely.

questions.stem: A team is deciding whether to let Claude send emails directly or draft them for a person to send.
options: Send directly, since the drafts have been consistently good and the review step adds delay
Send directly for internal recipients only
Send directly and recall anything that turns out to be wrong
Draft for review, since sending is irreversible and the review cost is small
