questions.why: Irreversibility is the deciding property. When the downside cannot be undone and the check is cheap, the check stays.
questions.traps: Consistent past quality does not bound future errors on an irreversible action. Internal recipients still receive it, and recall is unreliable.

questions.stem: A team's workflow works well until an input arrives in an unexpected format, at which point it produces plausible nonsense.
options: Add an instruction telling Claude to handle unexpected formats gracefully and to do its best with whatever input it receives during the course of the workflow
Choose a stronger model that copes better with format variation
Validate the input format and reject what does not match before processing
Review the output on any occasion where it happens to look unusual
questions.why: Plausible nonsense from bad input is caught at the boundary, not after. Validating the contract is what makes the failure explicit and local.
questions.traps: Graceful handling masks bad input as acceptable. A stronger model produces more convincing nonsense, and reviewing what looks unusual misses what looks fine.

questions.stem: A team introduces a workflow that requires people to change how they name their files. Compliance is around 40%.
options: Change the workflow to work with how people already name files
Send reminders about the naming convention until compliance improves to an acceptable level across the team and the workflow can operate as it was designed to
Reject files that do not follow the convention
Have one nominated person rename the files on behalf of the others
questions.why: Workflows that require behaviour change get partial compliance. Designing around existing behaviour is what makes adoption automatic rather than enforced.
questions.traps: Reminders fight a habit indefinitely. Rejection blocks work, and centralised renaming creates a bottleneck to serve a design choice.

questions.stem: Two teams share a workflow. The first team's output format changed and the second team's step broke without either noticing for a week.
options: Ask the first team to notify the second whenever they change anything about their output, so the second team can adjust their step before it stops working
Define and check the contract at the boundary between the two teams
Have a single team take ownership of both of the steps involved
Add a weekly check that the workflow is still working
questions.why: A shared boundary needs an explicit contract with a check, otherwise changes on one side break the other silently. That is what makes the dependency visible.
questions.traps: Notification relies on remembering. Single ownership is a reorganisation, and a weekly check still allows a week of silent failure.

questions.stem: A team's workflow saves time but the saved time is spread thinly across twelve people, none of whom has a reduced workload.
options: Report the aggregate saving, since twelve people each saving a small amount adds up to a substantial total that is worth recording as a benefit of the workflow
Concentrate the workflow on fewer people so the saving is visible
Stop measuring time and measure output quality instead
Measure whether the saved time is being reallocated to anything of value
questions.why: Thinly distributed time savings often evaporate rather than converting into value. Checking where the time goes is what determines whether the saving is real.
questions.traps: Aggregating unreallocated minutes reports a benefit nobody received. Concentrating usage changes the workflow, and switching measures avoids the question.

questions.stem: A team wants to add Claude to a process but cannot describe the current process consistently between them.
options: Document the current process first, since you cannot improve what is not agreed
Add Claude to the steps everyone does agree on, and leave the disputed steps unchanged until the team has had a chance to work out how those parts actually run
Have each person automate their own version of the process they run
Ask Claude to infer the process from examples
questions.why: Disagreement about the current state means there is no baseline to design against. Establishing it is the prerequisite rather than a delay.
questions.traps: Partial automation embeds one interpretation. Parallel versions multiply the inconsistency, and inferring a process from examples produces a plausible fiction.

questions.stem: A team wants to reduce review effort. They currently review every output at the same depth regardless of what it is.
options: Reduce the depth of review uniformly across all outputs so the total effort falls
Review a random sample at full depth
Vary the depth by what the output is and what a mistake would cost
Review only the outputs the model flags
questions.why: Risk-weighted review concentrates limited attention where errors cost most. Uniform depth spends the same effort on a contract and a social post.
questions.traps: Uniform reduction weakens the check where it matters most. Random sampling ignores stakes, and model flags miss confident errors.

questions.stem: An associate builds an integration that works, then discovers the source system rate-limits requests during business hours.
options: Request that the rate limit be raised for this integration so the workflow can run at the volume it needs during the hours when people are actually working
Design around the limit, since it is a property of the system rather than a bug
Run the integration only outside business hours
Retry the requests repeatedly until each of them finally succeeds
questions.why: A published constraint is part of the design space. Building within it produces something that works reliably rather than something that fights the system.
questions.traps: A limit increase may not be granted. Off-hours running may not suit the workflow, and aggressive retries make rate-limiting worse.

questions.stem: A team can automate a step that is currently done well by an experienced person who will retire in two years, taking undocumented judgement with them.
options: Capture the judgement now, whether or not the step ends up being automated
Automate the step before they retire so the knowledge is embedded in the workflow
Leave the step manual and recruit a replacement to train
Document the step after they retire using their outputs
questions.why: Undocumented expertise is the real risk, and it needs capturing regardless of the automation decision. That is the action that holds under either outcome.
questions.traps: Automating to capture knowledge assumes it can be specified, which is the open question. Recruitment still needs the knowledge, and post-retirement reconstruction is too late.

questions.stem: A team's workflow produces different results depending on the order in which documents are attached, and nobody knew this until now.
options: Ask people to attach documents in a consistent order so the results stop varying between different runs of the same workflow by different members of the team
Accept the variation as something inherent in how the tool works
Attach all documents in a single combined file
Fix the order dependence or make the required order explicit in the workflow
questions.why: Hidden order dependence is a defect. Either removing it or making it explicit turns an invisible source of variation into a known property.
questions.traps: A convention people must remember is the weakest form of the fix. Accepting it leaves the variation, and combining files changes the input in ways that may have their own effects.

questions.stem: A team's workflow has run without incident for six months. They have no plan for what to do if it produces a serious error tomorrow.
options: Continue as they are, since six months without incident suggests the workflow is reliable and planning for an unlikely event would consume effort better spent elsewhere
Add further review steps to reduce the chance of an error occurring
Decide now who is accountable and what happens, before it is needed
Plan a response once an error has actually occurred
questions.why: Incident response designed under pressure is worse than one designed calmly. Six incident-free months does not mean the next output is safe.
questions.traps: Treating a clean record as proof of safety is the trap. More review lowers probability without defining a response, and planning after the fact is too late.

questions.stem: An associate finds colleagues use Claude for tasks it handles poorly and avoid it for tasks it handles well.
options: Provide general training on prompting so colleagues become better at getting good results from the tasks they are already choosing to bring to the tool
Give the team concrete guidance on which tasks it suits and which it does not
Restrict access so it can only be used for tasks it handles well
Let people work it out through their own experience
questions.why: Misdirected use is a knowledge gap about fit rather than about technique. Concrete task-level guidance is what redirects effort to where it pays.
questions.traps: Prompting training improves execution on badly chosen tasks. Restriction is heavy-handed, and learning by trial is slow and discouraging.

questions.stem: A workflow passes a summary from Claude to a person who then makes a decision. The summary omits information the decision depends on.
options: Define what the summary must contain based on what the decision requires
Ask for longer summaries so more of the source material survives into the version the decision-maker actually reads before making their choice
Have the decision-maker read the source documents instead
Ask Claude to make the decision as well as writing the summary
questions.why: A summary feeding a decision has a specification: it must carry what the decision needs. Deriving that from the decision is what makes the handoff work.
questions.traps: Length does not target the specific omission. Reading everything defeats the summary, and moving the decision to the model changes the workflow rather than fixing the handoff.

questions.stem: A team is asked whether their workflow is working. They have three months of output but never defined what success would look like.
options: Present the three months of output and let the people asking form their own view about whether the workflow has been delivering the value that was expected
Ask the team members whether they think the workflow is working
Compare the current output against the first month's output
Define success now and measure against it, even though it is late to do so
questions.why: Without a definition of success, no evidence answers the question. Defining it late is better than continuing to produce evidence nobody can interpret.
questions.traps: Presenting output without a standard pushes the judgement onto others. Team opinion is not measurement, and comparing output to itself measures consistency rather than success.

questions.stem: A team's process has a step where work waits an average of two days for someone to be available.
options: Use Claude to speed up the steps either side of the wait so the total elapsed time falls
Run the surrounding steps in parallel
Address the waiting step, since it is where the elapsed time actually goes
Accept the wait as a constraint of the organisation
questions.why: Elapsed time is dominated by the wait. Speeding up work around a queue does not reduce the queue.
questions.traps: Optimising around the constraint leaves the constraint. Parallelism does not remove the wait, and accepting it forgoes the largest available gain.

questions.stem: An associate is asked to automate a task that takes ten minutes and is performed twice a year.
options: Automate it, since automated steps are more consistent and the effort will pay back over the lifetime of the process
Leave it manual, since twenty minutes a year does not repay building anything
Automate the step as a useful learning exercise for the team
Automate it if it can be done in under an hour
questions.why: Automation cost is amortised over frequency. Twenty minutes a year cannot repay design, testing and maintenance.
questions.traps: Consistency arguments ignore the arithmetic. Learning is a separate goal, and an hour still exceeds three years of the manual task.

questions.stem: A team's integration works but breaks whenever the upstream system is briefly unavailable, requiring someone to restart it manually.
options: Add retry and recovery so brief outages are handled without human intervention
Ask the upstream team to improve their system's availability so the outages that cause the integration to fail stop happening as frequently as they currently do
Have someone check that the integration is still running each morning
Run the integration less often so outages are less likely to coincide
questions.why: Transient upstream unavailability is expected, and handling it is the integration's responsibility. Retry and recovery is what makes it robust.
questions.traps: Upstream availability is outside the team's control. Daily checks are manual recovery, and reducing frequency does not remove the exposure.

questions.stem: A team wants a workflow to produce identical formatting every time, but it varies slightly between runs.
options: Ask for consistent formatting in the prompt and accept that small variations are an inherent property of generated text that cannot be entirely eliminated
Have a person reformat the output by hand on each separate occasion
Use the first run's output as a template for later runs
Specify the format precisely and validate the output against it
questions.why: A precise specification reduces variation and validation catches what remains. Together they produce reliable formatting.
questions.traps: A general consistency request has already failed. Manual reformatting repeats forever, and a template does not constrain generation.

questions.stem: A team's approval step is performed by someone who lacks the expertise to evaluate the content they are approving.
options: Give the approver a checklist covering the main things to look for so they can apply a consistent standard even
Match the approver to what the approval is meant to assure
Add a second approver with the same background
Remove the approval step since it adds no assurance
questions.why: An approval is only as good as the approver's ability to detect the relevant problems. Matching expertise to content is what makes it a real control.
questions.traps: A checklist helps a capable reviewer but cannot supply missing expertise. A second unqualified approver adds cost, and removing the control abandons rather than repairs it.

questions.stem: A workflow has run correctly on every input so far. The team has never tested what happens with an input that should be rejected.
options: Continue, since the workflow has handled every real input correctly and the rejection path will be exercised naturally when such an input eventually arrives
Add an instruction about rejecting bad inputs
Test the rejection path deliberately, since it has never been exercised
Assume that the rejection path works exactly as it was designed to
questions.why: An untested path is an unknown path, and the first time it runs will be with real work depending on it. Exercising it deliberately is cheap now and expensive later.
questions.traps: Waiting for a real bad input tests in production. An instruction is not a test, and assuming correctness of untested code is how silent failures happen.

questions.stem: A team lead announces that everyone should start using Claude. Three weeks later most people have not tried it.
options: Send a follow-up message restating the importance of adopting the new tool and explaining the benefits the organisation expects to see from it across the coming quarter
Arrange a training session covering the tool's main features and how to write effective prompts for the kinds of work the team does
Wait longer, since adoption of new tools takes time to build
Give people a specific task to try it on
questions.why: A general instruction gives people nothing to act on. A specific first task removes the blank-page problem that stalls adoption.
questions.traps: Restating importance adds pressure without direction. Feature training answers a question nobody has asked yet, and waiting assumes the obstacle resolves itself.

questions.stem: A team reports that Claude reduced their document turnaround from five days to two. The five-day figure came from memory.
options: Report the improvement as stated, since the team who did the work are best placed to know how long it used to take them before the new workflow was introduced
Check the five-day figure against records
Present the figure with a caveat noting that the baseline was estimated
Round the improvement down to be conservative
questions.why: A before-and-after claim rests entirely on the baseline. If that number is recalled rather than measured, the improvement is unverified.
questions.traps: Practitioner recall is systematically unreliable. A caveat publishes an unverified figure, and rounding does not make an unmeasured baseline sound.

questions.stem: An associate wants Claude to update records in a system where a wrong update cannot be undone.
options: Have Claude propose the update for a person to apply
Build the integration with a confirmation dialogue so the person applying the change sees what will happen before the update is written to the irreversible system
Write updates to a staging area first and copy them across after a nightly review of everything that has been queued
Log every update so wrong ones can be identified afterwards
questions.why: Irreversibility means the human decision must come before the write. Proposing rather than acting keeps the accountable decision with a person.
questions.traps: A confirmation dialogue is close but still frames the model as the actor. Staging adds delay without changing who decides, and logging identifies damage after it is done.

questions.stem: A team's workflow depends on a single prompt that has not been changed in eight months and is not stored anywhere except the Project.
options: Document what the prompt does so it could be rebuilt if it were ever lost
Keep a copy in the personal notes of the person who wrote it, so there is at least one additional copy available if something goes wrong
Back up the configuration somewhere outside the tool
Accept the risk since the Project is unlikely to be deleted
questions.why: A working prompt is an asset with a single point of failure. Backing it up outside the tool is the direct fix.
questions.traps: Documentation describes rather than restores. A personal copy recreates the single-owner problem, and dismissing the risk ignores accidental deletion.

questions.stem: A team maps their process and finds that two of nine steps consume 70% of the elapsed time.
options: Focus the effort on those two steps
Apply Claude across all nine steps so the whole process benefits from the improvement
Reduce the number of steps by combining the ones that are quick
Start with the step the team finds most frustrating
questions.why: Effort spent where the time is produces proportionate returns. Two steps holding 70% of elapsed time is where the leverage sits.
questions.traps: Spreading effort across nine steps dilutes it. Combining fast steps changes the diagram without changing the duration, and frustration is unrelated to elapsed time.

questions.stem: A team's review step catches formatting problems reliably and has never caught a factual error.
options: Add a factual accuracy criterion to the review checklist so reviewers know they are expected to check claims as well as presentation when they look at each document
Accept that formatting is what this review is for and add a separate factual check later in the process when there is capacity to resource it
Check whether reviewers have access to the sources
Ask reviewers to spend rather longer on each item they look at
questions.why: A review that only catches presentation usually lacks what it needs to check substance. Whether reviewers can even reach the sources is the first question.
questions.traps: Adding a criterion without the sources asks for an impossible check. Deferring accepts the gap, and more time does not supply missing inputs.

questions.stem: An associate proposes automating a step where the input is a free-text complaint that sometimes contains safeguarding concerns.
options: Automate it with an instruction telling Claude to flag anything that appears to raise a safeguarding concern so those cases can be escalated to a person for review
Automate the routine complaints and route only the ones the model is uncertain about to a human reviewer for a closer look
Automate it and audit a monthly sample of the decisions
Keep a person in the path for this step
questions.why: Safeguarding content carries consequences that a missed detection cannot be recovered from. That places it outside what should run unattended.
questions.traps: Model flagging misses what it does not recognise. Uncertainty routing relies on the same limitation, and monthly audits find missed cases far too late.

questions.stem: A workflow passes Claude's output to a second Claude step. When the first step returns an unexpected shape the second fails confusingly.
options: Add an instruction to the second step telling it to handle whatever input it receives as gracefully as it can and to continue processing where possible
Validate the shape at the boundary between steps
Combine the two steps into a single request so there is no boundary between them where a shape mismatch could occur in the first place
Rerun the whole workflow whenever the second step fails
questions.why: Chains need contracts at their boundaries. Checking shape converts a confusing downstream failure into a clear, local one.
questions.traps: Graceful handling masks bad input. Merging removes the checkpoint, and blind reruns treat a deterministic problem as noise.

questions.stem: A team runs the same analysis monthly. Each month someone rewrites the prompt slightly and the outputs are not comparable across months.
options: Fix the prompt and change only the data
Ask people to note what they changed each month so the differences between outputs can be understood when the months are compared against one another later
Compare only the most recent two months, since those are most likely to have been produced using similar prompts and are therefore roughly comparable
Accept that month-to-month comparison is not possible
questions.why: Comparability across periods requires holding the method constant. Fixing the prompt is what makes the data the only variable.
questions.traps: Change logs explain incomparability without removing it. Limiting the comparison window accepts the defect, and abandoning comparison forfeits the analysis.

questions.stem: A team's workflow is popular with staff but has produced no measurable change in any business outcome.
options: Continue the workflow, since staff satisfaction is itself a valuable outcome and the people using it clearly find that it makes their working day better
Discontinue it, since a workflow that does not move a business outcome is not delivering value
Measure more outcomes until one shows a change
Establish which outcome it was meant to move
questions.why: Popularity without an outcome usually means the intended outcome was never named. Establishing it is what makes the value question answerable.
questions.traps: Treating satisfaction as the outcome may be right but should be a stated goal. Discontinuing acts before diagnosing, and measuring until something moves invites a spurious finding.

questions.stem: An associate builds a workflow that requires colleagues to learn a new set of concepts before they can use it.
options: Run training sessions so colleagues understand the concepts well enough to use the workflow confidently and can troubleshoot it themselves when something goes wrong
Hide the complexity behind a simpler interface
Write comprehensive documentation covering the concepts so people can refer to it
Accept that only some of the colleagues will end up adopting it
questions.why: Adoption is inversely related to what users must learn first. Packaging the complexity so it never surfaces is what makes the workflow usable.
questions.traps: Training and documentation both accept the learning requirement rather than removing it. Accepting partial adoption forfeits most of the value.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude to read from three systems, and each system's data uses a different identifier for the same customer.
options: Ask Claude to work out which records refer to the same customer based on the other fields available in each of the three systems being brought together
Process each system separately and combine the results afterwards
Resolve the identifiers before Claude sees the data
Use whichever identifier appears in the most systems
questions.why: Identity resolution is a data problem that belongs upstream. Asking the model to infer identity across systems introduces errors that are hard to detect.
questions.traps: Inferred matching produces confident wrong joins. Separate processing avoids the join that the task requires, and picking the most common identifier does not resolve the others.

questions.stem: A workflow produces output that is wrong in a way nobody notices for three weeks because the output looks entirely normal.
options: Increase the frequency of review so problems are noticed sooner than three weeks after they first begin appearing in the output the workflow produces
Choose a stronger model so that this category of error becomes less likely to occur in the first place during normal operation of the workflow
Ask reviewers to be more alert to the subtler kinds of problem
Add a check that would detect this specific failure
questions.why: Failures that look normal are only caught by a check designed for them. Generic vigilance does not detect what appears correct.
questions.traps: More frequent generic review still passes normal-looking output. A stronger model lowers frequency without adding detection, and alertness is not a control.

questions.stem: A team wants to redesign a process around Claude but the process crosses four departments with different priorities.
options: Design the process around what works best technically and present it to the four departments for their agreement
Agree the shared objective before redesigning anything
Redesign the parts within a single department first and expand later
Ask each department to redesign their own portion
questions.why: Cross-departmental redesign without an agreed objective produces a design each department evaluates against different criteria. Agreement comes first.
questions.traps: A technically optimal design presented for approval invites rejection on grounds nobody stated. Incremental and devolved approaches both defer the alignment problem.

questions.stem: A team places their only review checkpoint immediately after the most expensive step in the workflow.
options: Move the check before the expensive step
Keep the check where it is, since reviewing after the expensive step means the reviewer sees the most complete version of the work that the process produces
Add a second checkpoint before the expensive step while keeping the existing one in place
Move the check to the end of the workflow
questions.why: Checking before an expensive step avoids spending on work that will be rejected. That is where a single checkpoint buys the most.
questions.traps: Reviewing complete work after paying for it wastes the expense. A second checkpoint is better but costs more than moving one, and a final check is later still.

questions.stem: A team can automate a step, but doing so would remove the only point where a person currently notices when upstream data is wrong.
options: Automate the step and add a data quality check upstream
Automate the step and accept that upstream data problems will be caught later in the process when their effects become visible in the final output
Preserve the detection before automating the step
Leave the step as a manual one on a permanent basis
questions.why: Manual steps often provide incidental detection nobody designed. Recognising and preserving that function is what stops automation from removing a control silently.
questions.traps: An upstream check is a reasonable replacement but must exist before the removal. Accepting later detection loses the control, and permanent manual work is more than the situation requires.

questions.stem: A workflow's first step produces a summary and its second step makes a decision, but the two steps were designed by different people.
options: Ask the second step to request more information whenever the summary it receives does not contain enough to reach a decision on the case in front of it
Check that the summary carries what the decision needs
Combine both steps into one request so the same context is available throughout and no information is lost at the boundary between them
Have the same person redesign both of the two steps involved
questions.why: Independently designed steps rarely agree on what crosses the boundary. Verifying that the summary meets the decision's requirements is the direct check.
questions.traps: A step cannot request what is not in its input. Merging removes a useful checkpoint, and reassigning ownership does not itself verify the contract.

questions.stem: A team's workflow gives different results when run in the morning and the afternoon, and nobody can explain why.
options: Look for what differs in the inputs, not the time
Investigate whether system load at different times of day affects the results the workflow produces during busier periods of the working day
Standardise on running the workflow at one time of day so the variation stops affecting the comparability of the results produced
Accept the variation as inherent to generated output
questions.why: Time of day is not a causal mechanism, so the likely explanation is a difference in what gets submitted at each time. That is checkable immediately.
questions.traps: Investigating load treats the correlation as causal. Standardising the time hides the variation, and accepting it abandons a diagnosable problem.

questions.stem: An associate wants to compare their team's performance before and after introducing Claude, but the team also gained two members in the same period.
options: Present the before-and-after comparison, since the improvement is real
Adjust the figures for headcount so the comparison reflects output per person
Compare against a different team that did not change
Note that the comparison cannot separate the two changes
questions.why: Two simultaneous changes cannot be separated by a before-and-after comparison. Stating that limitation is what keeps the claim honest.
questions.traps: Presenting it as a Claude effect overclaims. Per-person adjustment handles one confounder crudely, and another team differs in many other ways.

questions.stem: A team's most experienced member refuses to use the workflow, saying it produces worse results than their own approach.
options: Ask them to use it anyway so the team has consistency in how the work is done across all of its members
Exempt them from using it, since their own approach clearly produces acceptable results and forcing the change would create unnecessary friction
Compare the two approaches on the same cases
Ask them to explain their objection in detail
questions.why: An experienced person's claim is testable, and testing it either improves the workflow or resolves the objection with evidence.
questions.traps: Mandating use ignores a possibly correct objection. Exempting them loses the information, and an explanation without a comparison remains an assertion.

questions.stem: An associate's integration sends data to Claude that includes fields the task does not need, including some personal details.
options: Add an instruction telling Claude to ignore the personal fields and to base its analysis only on the fields that are actually relevant to the task at hand
Send only the fields the task requires
Anonymise the personal fields before sending them so that the data cannot be traced back to specific individuals if it were ever exposed
Document which fields are sent so the practice is transparent
questions.why: Minimising what is sent is the structural control. Fields that are never transmitted cannot be misused, which no instruction can guarantee.
questions.traps: An instruction to ignore data does not prevent its transmission. Anonymisation is weaker than omission, and documentation records the practice without changing it.

questions.stem: A team's workflow has two failure modes: one produces obviously broken output and one produces subtly wrong output.
options: Prioritise fixing the obvious failure, since it occurs more visibly and disrupts the workflow
Treat both failure modes as equally important and address them in whatever order is most convenient for the team's current workload
Prioritise detection for the subtle failure
Add a general review step covering both of the failure modes
questions.why: Obvious failures announce themselves and get handled. Subtle ones propagate undetected, which makes detection for them the higher-value investment.
questions.traps: Prioritising the visible failure addresses the one already being caught. Equal treatment ignores the asymmetry, and a general review misses what looks normal.

questions.stem: A team is asked to identify where Claude fits in a process nobody has written down.
options: Write the process down first
Ask each person to describe the parts of the process they are involved in and identify opportunities within their own portion of the overall workflow
Start with the steps that involve producing written material
Ask Claude to suggest where it could help
questions.why: An undocumented process cannot be analysed. Writing it down is the prerequisite, and often reveals the answer by itself.
questions.traps: Per-person descriptions produce fragments without a whole. Filtering by activity type presumes the answer, and asking the model about an undescribed process invites invention.

questions.stem: A team wants to know how much review is enough. They currently review everything and it is unsustainable.
options: Review a fixed proportion of outputs each week so that the total effort is predictable and the team can plan their capacity around a known and stable commitment
Review whatever the team has capacity for each week and accept that the proportion will vary
Ask reviewers how much they think is enough
Base the level on what an error would cost
questions.why: Review depth follows consequence. Tying it to what errors cost is what makes the level defensible rather than arbitrary.
questions.traps: A fixed proportion ignores that items differ in stakes. Capacity-driven review lets workload set the control, and reviewer opinion is not a risk assessment.

questions.stem: An associate wants to automate a step where the rules are clear but the exceptions are numerous and poorly documented.
options: Automate the clear rules and route exceptions to a person
Automate everything including the exceptions, since the model can be given the documented rules and asked to use judgement where the rules do not clearly apply
Document all the exceptions first and then automate the whole step
Leave the whole step manual until the exceptions are fully understood
questions.why: Splitting on what is specifiable captures the value from the clear majority while keeping judgement with a person where the rules run out.
questions.traps: Asking for judgement where rules are undocumented produces confident guesses. Full documentation may take a long time, and leaving everything manual forgoes the clear cases.

questions.stem: A workflow hands output from Claude to a person who reformats it before passing it on, taking about fifteen minutes each time.
options: Ask the person to reformat more efficiently or to build a template that speeds up the manual step they perform on each item that passes through
Specify the required format so reformatting is unnecessary
Accept the fifteen minutes as the cost of getting the output into the shape that the downstream recipient requires for their own process
Have a second Claude step carry out the reformatting instead
questions.why: A recurring manual reformat means the format was never specified. Stating it upstream removes the step entirely.
questions.traps: Faster manual work keeps the step. Accepting it normalises avoidable effort, and a second model call pays to fix a specification gap.

questions.stem: A team's workflow works reliably but only when the person running it remembers to attach a particular reference document.
options: Add a reminder to the workflow documentation so the person running it knows to attach the reference document before they begin the analysis
Ask the person to build the habit of checking for the reference document each time they start a run of this particular workflow
Put the reference into persistent configuration
Make the workflow fail loudly when the document is missing
questions.why: Something needed every time belongs in configuration rather than in someone's memory. That removes the failure mode instead of warning about it.
questions.traps: Reminders and habits both rely on the memory that already fails. Failing loudly is better than silent failure but still stops the work.

questions.stem: A team's workflow has clear benefits and clear costs, and leadership wants a single number to decide whether to continue.
options: Give the single number requested, since leadership have asked for a simple answer and adding qualifications will make the decision harder
Decline to give a single number, since the benefits and costs are not directly comparable in a way that reduces sensibly to one figure
Give a range of figures instead of a single point estimate
Give the number with the assumptions it rests on
questions.why: A single figure is usable when its assumptions are visible, because those are what a reader needs to challenge or accept it.
questions.traps: An unqualified number hides what drives it. Refusing does not serve the decision, and a range without assumptions has the same problem as a point estimate.

questions.stem: A team introduces a workflow and usage is high for two weeks, then falls sharply.
options: Reintroduce the workflow with additional training so people are reminded of its benefits and feel more confident using it in their day-to-day work
Accept the drop as normal, since initial enthusiasm for any new tool tends to fade
Ask the people who stopped what happened
Add usage targets so people continue using it
questions.why: A sharp drop after initial use means people tried it and stopped, which is specific information available by asking.
questions.traps: Retraining assumes a skill gap. Attributing it to novelty explains it away, and usage targets force behaviour without addressing the cause.

questions.stem: A team's integration works in testing but the production system returns data in a slightly different shape.
options: Test against production-shaped data before deploying
Deploy the integration and handle the shape differences as they surface during the first weeks of real operation with actual production data flowing through
Ask the production system's owners to change their output so it matches the shape used in the testing environment the team built against
Build the integration so that it accepts either of the shapes
questions.why: Testing against representative data is what makes a test predictive. A test environment that differs from production tests the wrong thing.
questions.traps: Deploying to discover differences debugs in production. Changing production to match a test is backwards, and accepting both shapes tolerates a mismatch rather than resolving it.

questions.stem: A workflow's error handling logs failures to a file nobody has opened in four months.
options: Improve the log format so that failures are easier to identify and understand when someone does eventually come to look at the file that has been accumulating
Route failures somewhere a person will actually see
Add a summary of the log to the team's weekly meeting agenda
Accept that the failures are evidently not important
questions.why: A log nobody reads is not error handling. Routing failures into a channel with attention is what makes the handling real.
questions.traps: A better format helps a reader who does not exist. A weekly agenda item is better but slow, and inferring unimportance from inattention is unfounded.

questions.stem: An associate finds that a process step exists only because of a system limitation that was removed two years ago.
options: Automate the step with Claude so it takes less effort to perform
Document why the step exists so that future team members understand its history and can decide whether it should be kept in the process
Keep the step in case the limitation returns
Remove the step
questions.why: A step serving a constraint that no longer exists is pure waste. Removing it is simpler and better than making it cheaper to perform.
questions.traps: Automating obsolete work entrenches it. Documenting preserves it, and keeping it against a hypothetical reversion pays a permanent cost.

questions.stem: A team's reviewers approve faster when the output looks polished, and errors in polished output reach customers more often.
options: Ask reviewers to be aware that polished output can still contain errors and to apply the same level of scrutiny
Review before formatting is applied
Add a second review specifically for polished output so that the additional scrutiny compensates for the tendency to approve it more readily
Reduce the polish applied before review
questions.why: Finished-looking artefacts attract less scrutiny, so reviewing before presentation is applied is a sequencing fix rather than an effort one.
questions.traps: Awareness rarely overcomes the effect under time pressure. A second review costs more for the same bias, and deliberately degrading output is a workaround.

questions.stem: A team is deciding whether Claude should decide or recommend on a step with moderate consequences and a clear rule.
options: Have it decide, since the rule is clear and consistent application is exactly what automation is good at delivering across a high volume of cases
Have it decide for the straightforward cases and recommend only where the rule does not clearly apply to the situation in front of it
Have it decide and log every one of the decisions for later review
Have it recommend, since accountability is cheap to keep here
questions.why: With a clear rule and moderate stakes, keeping a person accountable costs little and preserves the ability to intervene.
questions.traps: Full automation moves accountability for a small efficiency gain. Split handling is defensible but more complex, and logging enables review after the consequence.

questions.stem: A workflow passes work between two people and Claude sits in the middle, but neither person knows what the other expects.
options: Ask Claude to produce output that is as complete as possible
Have the two people meet to discuss their expectations informally and reach an understanding about what each of them needs from the other
Define what each handoff must contain
Combine the two separate roles into a single person's job
questions.why: Handoffs need explicit contracts. Defining what crosses each boundary is what makes the workflow work regardless of who is in the roles.
questions.traps: Maximal output shifts the filtering burden downstream. An informal understanding is not durable, and merging roles is a reorganisation rather than a design fix.

questions.stem: A team wants their workflow to survive the departure of the person who built it.
options: Write down the decisions and why they were made
Ask the person to record a walkthrough video explaining how the workflow operates so colleagues can watch it
Have a colleague shadow them for a week so the knowledge is transferred through observation before the person leaves the organisation
Rebuild the workflow with a second person involved
questions.why: The fragile knowledge is why things are the way they are, since that is what a successor needs to change anything safely.
questions.traps: A walkthrough shows what without why. Shadowing transfers some knowledge informally, and rebuilding duplicates work already done.

questions.stem: A team measures their workflow's accuracy but not how long it takes people to use it.
options: Continue measuring accuracy, since that is the property that determines whether the workflow produces output the team can rely on for their work
Measure time instead of accuracy, since the accuracy has been stable for several months and the time cost is the variable that is currently unknown
Measure both, since a slow accurate workflow may still not be worth it
Ask people whether the workflow feels fast enough to them
questions.why: Value depends on accuracy and cost together. Measuring only one leaves the trade-off invisible.
questions.traps: Accuracy alone cannot show whether the workflow is worth using. Swapping the measure loses the other half, and perception is not measurement.

questions.stem: A workflow requires people to trust output they cannot easily verify, and several colleagues are uncomfortable doing so.
options: Explain how the model works so colleagues understand why the output can be relied upon in the kinds of cases this workflow is designed to handle
Give them a way to check, even a partial one
Point to the accuracy measurements the team has collected so far
Accept that some of the people will simply not adopt it
questions.why: Discomfort with unverifiable output is reasonable. Providing a means to check addresses the actual concern rather than arguing against it.
questions.traps: Explaining the mechanism does not let anyone check a specific output. Aggregate accuracy says nothing about the item in front of them, and accepting non-adoption forfeits the value.

questions.stem: An associate's integration calls Claude once per row of a spreadsheet, and the spreadsheet has grown from 50 rows to 5,000.
options: Move to a faster tier so the five thousand individual calls complete more quickly than they currently do under the existing configuration
Run the integration overnight so that the time it takes does not affect anyone during the working day when they need the results
Split the spreadsheet and run several copies in parallel
Reconsider the per-row design at this volume
questions.why: A design that suited 50 rows may be wrong at 5,000. Revisiting the unit of work is the question the volume change raises.
questions.traps: A faster tier optimises within an unexamined design. Overnight running and parallelism both scale the same per-row pattern.

questions.stem: A team's workflow fails safely but produces no indication that anything went wrong, so people assume it ran.
options: Make success and failure both visible
Add an alert that fires when the workflow fails so that the team is notified promptly
Ask people to check whether the output was produced before they rely on it in their own work downstream of this particular process
Run the workflow more frequently so a failure is less consequential
questions.why: Silent success and silent failure are indistinguishable. Making both visible is what lets people tell the difference without checking.
questions.traps: A failure alert helps but leaves silence ambiguous when alerting itself fails. Manual checking is the burden being removed, and frequency does not address visibility.

questions.stem: A team wants to introduce Claude into a process where three of the seven steps are waiting for approvals from other departments.
options: Apply Claude to the four steps the team controls, since those are the parts where improvement can be delivered
Address the approval waits first, since they dominate elapsed time and no drafting gain reaches them
Ask the other departments to approve rather faster
Run the drafting steps in parallel with the approval waits so the total elapsed time is compressed
questions.why: Elapsed time sits in the approval queues, so improving the drafting steps produces work that waits in the same place. The constraint has to move first.
questions.traps: Improving the controllable steps feels productive but does not change throughput. Asking for speed is not a design change, and parallelism does not shorten the waits themselves.

questions.stem: A team's workflow has a review step that catches roughly one error a month, and reviewers spend four hours a week on it.
options: Remove the review step, since catching one error a month does not justify four hours of skilled reviewer time each and every week that the workflow operates
Reduce the review down to a sample of the total output
Weigh what those errors would have cost against sixteen hours of reviewer time a month
Keep the review, since any error reaching a customer is more costly than the reviewer time spent preventing it from happening in the first place
questions.why: Both quantities are known, so the decision is an explicit comparison. What the caught errors would have cost is the missing half of it.
questions.traps: Removing or keeping the step on principle decides without the consequence figure. Sampling reduces both cost and catch rate without reasoning about either.

questions.stem: An associate is asked to automate a step whose output is used as evidence in regulatory filings.
options: Automate it fully with a comprehensive audit trail so that every step of the process is recorded and can be reconstructed later if a regulator asks how a particular figure was produced
Automate it and have a person sign off on the filings monthly
Automate the routine filings and keep a person involved only for the ones that involve unusual circumstances or figures that fall outside the normal expected ranges
Keep a person accountable for what is filed, using Claude to prepare rather than to submit
questions.why: Regulatory filings carry personal accountability, which cannot sit with a system. Preparing rather than submitting keeps the benefit and the accountability in the right places.
questions.traps: An audit trail records what happened without making anyone accountable. Monthly sign-off follows the filing, and exception-only involvement still auto-files the majority.

questions.stem: A team's workflow depends on an external service that has been reliable for a year. There is no fallback if it becomes unavailable.
options: Decide in advance what the workflow does when the service is unavailable
Add monitoring so the team is alerted quickly if the external service becomes unavailable and can respond to the situation before it affects too much work
Choose a more reliable external service to depend upon
Accept the risk, since a year of reliable operation is reasonable evidence that the service is dependable enough for the workflow's purposes going forward
questions.why: A dependency with no defined behaviour on failure fails in an undefined way. Deciding the fallback in advance is what makes the outage survivable.
questions.traps: Monitoring tells you it broke without saying what to do. Switching services moves the dependency, and past uptime does not bound future outages.

questions.stem: A team's monthly workflow produced a different answer this month, and nobody kept a record of the prompt or data used last month.
options: Rerun last month's analysis using the current prompt to see whether the difference comes from the prompt or from the data that was used in each of the two months
Accept that some variation between the months is to be expected
Start recording the inputs and configuration for each run so differences become explainable
Ask the person who ran it last month whether they remember doing anything differently on that occasion than they have done this time around
questions.why: Without a record of what was run, a difference cannot be attributed to anything. Recording inputs is what makes future differences diagnosable.
questions.traps: Rerunning cannot recover last month's prompt. Accepting variation abandons comparability, and recollection is unreliable for exactly this kind of detail.

questions.stem: A team's workflow writes results into a shared document that several people edit at the same time.
options: Add a note at the top of the shared document asking people not to edit it
Write into a location the workflow owns, and let people copy from it
Run the workflow overnight when nobody is editing
Have the workflow check whether the document has been modified and skip writing if it has
questions.why: Automated writes and concurrent human editing conflict by design. Giving the workflow its own output location removes the contention entirely.
questions.traps: A request not to edit relies on compliance. Overnight running narrows the window without closing it, and skip-on-modification silently drops results.

questions.stem: A team is asked whether Claude has improved quality. They have no measure of quality from before it was introduced.
options: Compare the current quality against what the team believes the previous quality was
Use output volume as a proxy for quality since it is the measure that is actually available for both periods and shows a clear and substantial increase
Ask customers whether they have noticed an improvement in quality over the past few months since the new workflow was introduced
Say plainly that the before figure does not exist, and start measuring quality now
questions.why: An honest answer names the missing baseline and starts the measurement. That serves the question better than a reconstructed figure.
questions.traps: Recalled quality is unreliable. Volume is not quality, and customer recall over months is weak and confounded by everything else that changed.

questions.stem: A team's workflow is used enthusiastically by the people who helped design it and ignored by everyone else.
options: Involve the non-users in the next iteration rather than explaining the current one to them
Run a demonstration session showing the non-users how the workflow operates and what benefits the designers have seen from using it in their own daily work
Ask the designers to encourage their colleagues to take it up
Accept the split, since the people who designed it are the ones whose work it was designed around and others may have genuinely different needs
questions.why: Participation in design is what produces ownership, and that is the difference between the two groups. Involving non-users addresses the cause.
questions.traps: A demonstration explains a design made without them. Peer encouragement does not change the artefact, and accepting the split forfeits most of the value.

questions.stem: A workflow passes a document from Claude to a person, who often has to go back to the source to understand a claim in it.
options: Ask for a shorter document so the person has less material to work through when they are checking the claims that the workflow has produced for them
Require each claim to name where it came from, so the source is reachable from the document
Attach the source documents alongside the output that is produced
Ask the person to check only the claims that seem most important
questions.why: Repeated returns to the source mean the document lacks provenance. Naming the source per claim removes the lookup entirely.
questions.traps: Shortening reduces the material without adding traceability. Attaching sources still requires searching them, and checking selectively accepts unverified claims.

questions.stem: A team maps a process and finds that the same information is entered by hand three times in different systems.
options: Use Claude to speed up each of the three data entry steps
Combine the three systems into one single system
Address the duplicate entry, since it is waste that also creates three chances to introduce an error
Add a validation step that checks the three entries match
questions.why: Triple entry is waste and a triple error surface. Removing the duplication addresses both, which speeding it up does not.
questions.traps: Faster duplication is still duplication. System consolidation is a large project, and validation detects the errors the waste creates rather than preventing them.

questions.stem: A team wants to automate a step where the correct behaviour differs between two jurisdictions and nobody has confirmed which rules apply where.
options: Establish the jurisdictional rules before automating anything
Automate using the stricter of the two jurisdictions' rules everywhere
Automate and add a jurisdiction field so the behaviour can be adjusted
Leave the step manual until the position is clear
questions.why: An unconfirmed rule cannot be automated correctly. Establishing the requirement is the prerequisite rather than something to work around.
questions.traps: The stricter rule may be wrong or costly in the other jurisdiction. A placeholder field automates before the rule exists, and leaving it manual defers rather than resolves.

questions.stem: A team wants a checkpoint but every candidate reviewer is already fully committed to other work.
options: Add the review to someone's workload anyway, since the control is necessary and the team will need to find a way to absorb the additional time it requires
Automate the review by adding a second Claude step to do it
Skip the review for now and add it later once capacity becomes available somewhere in the team for someone to take on the additional responsibility
Reduce what needs reviewing so the remaining volume fits the capacity that exists
questions.why: When review capacity is fixed, the scope of what is reviewed has to shrink to fit. Narrowing to the high-consequence subset is what makes the control real.
questions.traps: Adding unfunded work produces the rubber stamp. A second model step is not independent, and deferring leaves the control absent indefinitely.

questions.stem: An associate's workflow depends on a file arriving in a shared folder each morning, and occasionally it arrives late or not at all.
options: Make the workflow wait and report when the file has not arrived, rather than proceeding without it
Run the workflow later in the day so that the file has had more time to arrive before the process attempts to read it from the shared folder
Ask the team that produces the file to deliver it earlier and more reliably than they currently manage to do on most mornings
Use the previous day's file when the current one has not arrived
questions.why: A missing input should stop the workflow visibly rather than producing output from nothing or from stale data. Reporting is what makes the dependency's failure explicit.
questions.traps: A later run narrows the window without handling absence. Upstream reliability is outside the team's control, and falling back to yesterday's file produces confidently wrong output.

questions.stem: A team's workflow catches errors reliably but the person notified about them has no authority to fix the underlying cause.
options: Ask the notified person to escalate the errors they receive to the team that owns the underlying system
Log the errors to a file for later analysis by the team
Route the notification to whoever can actually address the cause
Ask the notified person to correct each error manually as it arises
questions.why: A control that notifies someone powerless produces a queue rather than a fix. Routing to the person who can act is what closes the loop.
questions.traps: Manual escalation adds a hop and depends on persistence. Logging defers, and manual correction treats symptoms indefinitely.

questions.stem: A team's workflow behaves differently for two people because each has different personal settings configured in their account.
options: Ask both people to align their personal settings so that the workflow behaves the same way
Move the workflow into shared configuration so personal settings do not affect it
Document the settings that the workflow requires to run
Have one person run the workflow for the whole team so that the settings in use are consistent across every run that the team relies on for its work
questions.why: Account-level settings are invisible inputs to every request. Moving the workflow into shared configuration removes the dependency on individual accounts.
questions.traps: Aligning settings by hand relies on both people maintaining them. Documentation records the requirement without enforcing it, and single-operator running creates a bottleneck.

questions.stem: A team's workflow demonstrably saves time, and the team has used the saved time to take on more of the same work.
options: Report the saving as realised, since the time was genuinely freed and the team has been able to use it productively on further work of the same kind
Report the saving as unrealised since headcount did not change
Measure the additional output produced and report that as the benefit instead of reporting the time saving that made the additional output possible in the first place
Check that the additional work is worth doing before counting the saving as a benefit
questions.why: A saving reinvested in more of the same work is only a benefit if that work has value. Checking that is what distinguishes real value from busier people.
questions.traps: Counting it as realised assumes the extra work is worthwhile. Calling it unrealised ignores real output, and measuring volume repeats the same assumption.

questions.stem: An associate's colleagues find the workflow useful but say they forget it exists when they are busy.
options: Put it where the work already happens so remembering is not required
Send periodic reminders about the workflow so that it stays in people's minds during the busy periods when they are most likely to forget that it is available
Add it to the team's written process documentation instead
Ask the team lead to mention it in team meetings so that colleagues are regularly reminded that the workflow exists and is available for them to use
questions.why: Forgetting under pressure is a placement problem. Putting the capability in the path of the work removes the need to remember it at all.
questions.traps: Reminders, documentation and meeting mentions all rely on recall at the moment of need, which is exactly what fails when people are busy.

questions.stem: A workflow has Claude produce a draft that a person finishes, but the person rewrites most of it because the draft is aimed at the wrong reader.
options: Ask the person to give feedback after each draft so that the prompt can be improved over time and future drafts require less rewriting than the current ones do
Ask for a shorter draft so that there is less of it to rewrite
Accept the rewriting as the normal division of labour between the model producing raw material and the person shaping it into something that suits the audience
Supply the reader and purpose as inputs so the draft starts in the right place
questions.why: A draft aimed at the wrong reader is missing an input rather than needing more polish. Supplying audience and purpose fixes it at the source.
questions.traps: Iterative feedback eventually converges but repeats the waste meanwhile. A shorter draft is less wasted work rather than better work, and accepting the rewriting normalises a fixable gap.

questions.stem: A team is asked to reduce a process from ten days to five and has identified Claude as the way to do it.
options: Apply Claude to every step that involves producing written material
Apply Claude to the single longest step in the process
Find where the ten days actually go before assuming drafting is the constraint
Set the five-day target as a goal and let each step's owner work out how to contribute to reaching it within their own part of the overall process
questions.why: A target without a breakdown of where the time goes cannot be planned against. Locating the ten days is the prerequisite to any intervention.
questions.traps: Filtering by activity type presumes the answer. The longest step may not be reducible, and devolving the target does not reveal where the time sits.

questions.stem: A team can automate a step, but the manual version currently produces a written record that an auditor relies on.
options: Automate the step and generate the record separately afterwards
Ensure the automated version produces an equivalent record before the manual one is removed
Ask the auditor whether the record is still needed
Automate the step and keep the manual version running in parallel for a period
questions.why: A manual step often produces artefacts other people depend on. Preserving the record as part of the automated design is what avoids breaking an obligation.
questions.traps: A separately generated record is a version of the right answer but sequenced after the removal. Asking the auditor is reasonable but does not itself preserve anything, and parallel running defers the problem.

questions.stem: A team's checkpoint is placed correctly but the person staffing it changes weekly, so standards vary noticeably.
options: Assign the checkpoint permanently to one person so that the standard applied to each item is consistent from one week to the next across the whole workflow
Rotate the reviewers rather less frequently than at present
Have two people staff the checkpoint together each week
Write down what the check must cover so the standard travels with the role
questions.why: Variation between reviewers means the standard lives in individuals rather than in the process. Documenting it is what makes the check reproducible regardless of who performs it.
questions.traps: A permanent assignment removes variation by removing rotation, at the cost of a single point of failure. Slower rotation and pairing both dilute the variation without defining the standard.

questions.stem: An associate wants to connect Claude to a system, and the only available access method returns far more data than the task needs.
options: Send the full response and rely on Claude to use only the parts of it that are relevant to the task it has been asked to perform on each occasion
Filter the data down to what the task needs before it is sent
Request a narrower access method from the system's owners
Accept the additional data since it costs little and may occasionally contain something useful that the task turns out to need at some point in the future
questions.why: Sending only what is needed limits both cost and exposure. Filtering at the boundary is the control that does not depend on the model ignoring what it receives.
questions.traps: Relying on the model to ignore data still transmits it. A narrower method may not exist, and accepting excess data ignores both the cost and the exposure.

questions.stem: A team's workflow has never failed, and the team has concluded that error handling would be unnecessary complexity.
options: Recognise that an untested failure path is a risk rather than an absent one
Add error handling only for the failure modes that have actually occurred
Accept the current design since it has proven reliable in practice over an extended period of real use and adding complexity would introduce its own risks
Add a general catch-all that stops the workflow on any unexpected condition
questions.why: Absence of observed failure is not absence of failure modes. Treating the untested path as a real risk is what makes the design honest.
questions.traps: Handling only past failures waits for each one to happen once. Inferring safety from an incident-free record is the trap, and a blanket stop is a reasonable tactic rather than the reasoning being tested.

questions.stem: A team's workflow produces good output but the quality depends on how carefully the person phrases their request each time.
options: Train the team to write better requests so that everyone reaches the standard the most careful person currently achieves when they use the workflow
Ask Claude to clarify any request that seems vague to it
Standardise the request so the variable input is data rather than phrasing
Accept that output quality will vary with the effort each person puts into their request
questions.why: Phrasing-dependent quality means the prompt is doing work that should be fixed in configuration. Standardising it removes the variable.
questions.traps: Training raises the floor without removing the dependency. Clarification adds a round trip, and accepting the variation forfeits repeatability.

questions.stem: A team wants to compare two versions of a workflow but can only run one at a time on real work.
options: Alternate between them over a period so both meet a comparable mix of work
Run the first version for a month and the second for the following month, then compare the results from the two months to see which performed better overall
Run both of the versions on historical cases instead
Ask the team which version they prefer after they have had a chance to use each of them for a reasonable period of time in their normal work
questions.why: Alternating within the same period balances the mix of work each version encounters, which sequential months do not.
questions.traps: Consecutive months confound the version with whatever else differed between them. Historical cases may not reflect current work, and preference is not measurement.

questions.stem: A team's workflow requires a change that makes one person's job noticeably harder while making four people's jobs easier.
options: Proceed, since the workflow produces a net benefit across the team
Address the cost falling on that person rather than treating it as an acceptable trade
Ask that person to accept the change for the good of the team as a whole
Compensate that person with recognition for absorbing the additional difficulty that the change has created within their own part of the process
questions.why: Concentrated costs and diffuse benefits is the classic pattern that stalls adoption. Addressing the concentrated cost is what makes the change stick.
questions.traps: Net-benefit reasoning ignores who bears the cost. Appeals to team spirit and recognition both ask one person to absorb a fixable design problem.

questions.stem: A workflow's output is consumed by a downstream team who have never been asked what they need from it.
options: Send them the current output and ask for feedback so that improvements can be made
Design the output to include everything that might be useful
Ask them what they need before designing the output format any further
Ask the upstream team what they think the downstream team probably needs
questions.why: The consumer's requirements are the specification for the output. Asking is faster and more accurate than inferring or iterating toward it.
questions.traps: Feedback on a design made without them is slower. Including everything shifts filtering downstream, and second-hand assumptions are guesses.

questions.stem: A team's process includes a step that everyone agrees is unnecessary, but nobody knows why it was introduced.
options: Remove the step, since everyone involved in the process agrees that it serves no useful purpose in the work as it is currently carried out by the team
Keep the step, since it was presumably introduced for a reason and removing it might cause a problem that nobody currently anticipates happening
Automate the step so it costs less while remaining in place in case it turns out to serve some purpose that is not currently understood
Find out why it exists before removing it
questions.why: Steps usually exist for a reason that outlived its explanation. Finding the reason is what distinguishes safe removal from removing a control.
questions.traps: Removing on consensus risks deleting something load-bearing. Keeping it forever pays a permanent cost, and automating preserves the waste.

questions.stem: An associate proposes automating a step where the model would need to interpret tone in customer messages to decide how to route them.
options: Automate it, since tone is a well-understood property of text and language models are generally capable of assessing it accurately across a range of contexts
Route the tickets on keywords rather than on tone
Test how well tone interpretation performs before designing anything around it
Automate it and have a person review the routing decisions for the first month
questions.why: Whether tone routing works on this team's messages is an empirical question. Testing it is what determines whether the design is viable at all.
questions.traps: Assuming capability skips the test. Keyword routing is a different design chosen without evidence, and a review month tests in production.

questions.stem: A team's reviewers are asked to check accuracy but are given the output only in a format that makes checking slow and awkward.
options: Give reviewers the output in a form that makes the check practical
Ask reviewers to allow more time for each item so that the awkward format does not prevent them from completing the checks they are supposed to perform
Reduce the number of items that are reviewed each week
Ask Claude to produce a summary of the key claims alongside the output
questions.why: A check that is awkward to perform gets performed badly. Making it practical is the direct fix and costs less than the alternatives.
questions.traps: More time absorbs the friction rather than removing it. Reviewing fewer items weakens the control, and a model-generated claim list is not independent of the output.

questions.stem: A team's integration passes data to Claude and stores the response, but nothing records which version of the prompt produced each response.
options: Store the responses with a timestamp so that the approximate period each one was produced in can be identified later if questions arise about a particular result
Record the prompt version with each stored response so results stay interpretable
Keep a separate change log recording every prompt edit
Ask the person who maintains the prompt to note when they make significant changes so the team has some record of when the behaviour may have shifted
questions.why: Stored results are only interpretable against the configuration that produced them. Recording the version with the response is what preserves that link.
questions.traps: A timestamp requires correlating against a separate history. A change log and manual notes both leave the association to be reconstructed.

questions.stem: A workflow produces one wrong output in every two hundred, and the team has decided that rate is acceptable.
options: Continue, since a failure rate of one in two hundred is low by most standards and the effort to reduce it further would be substantial relative to the benefit
Reduce the failure rate further before doing anything else
Measure the rate more precisely so the team has a more accurate figure to base their acceptance decision on than the current approximate estimate
Check that the consequences of the wrong ones are also acceptable, not just the rate
questions.why: An acceptable rate depends entirely on what a failure does. The rate alone cannot support the judgement without the consequence.
questions.traps: Accepting on the rate skips the consequence. Reducing it further acts without knowing whether it matters, and a more precise rate is still only half the picture.

questions.stem: A team's workflow works when run against clean data and fails unpredictably when the data has small inconsistencies.
options: Validate and normalise the data before it enters the workflow
Add instructions telling Claude how to handle each of the inconsistencies the team has encountered so far in the data they have been working with
Ask the upstream team to send data that is already clean
Add a review step that checks the output whenever the input data contained inconsistencies
questions.why: Input variability handled at the boundary makes downstream behaviour predictable. Normalising is what turns unpredictable failure into a controlled path.
questions.traps: Per-case instructions grow indefinitely and miss new cases. Upstream cleanliness is outside the team's control, and reviewing afterwards catches rather than prevents.

questions.stem: A team's workflow has been running for a year and nobody has checked whether the problem it solves still exists.
options: Continue the workflow, since it has been running successfully for a year and there is no indication that anything has changed about the situation it addresses
Expand the workflow so that it covers more cases than now
Confirm the problem is still there before continuing to invest in solving it
Measure the workflow's performance more thoroughly so that the team has better evidence about how well it has been operating over the past twelve months
questions.why: Workflows outlive the problems that justified them. Confirming the problem still exists is the question that determines whether any of the other measurement matters.
questions.traps: Continuing on momentum is the pattern being tested. Expanding scales a possibly obsolete solution, and better performance data does not establish continued relevance.

questions.stem: An associate's workflow is adopted quickly but people use it for a different purpose than it was designed for.
options: Correct the misuse by explaining what the workflow was designed for and asking people to use it for that purpose
Redesign the workflow around the original purpose
Restrict the workflow so that it can only be used for the purpose it was originally designed to serve
Find out what problem they are actually solving with it
questions.why: Unprompted repurposing is strong evidence about where the real need is. Understanding it is more valuable than correcting it.
questions.traps: Correcting the usage discards the signal. Redesigning around the original purpose doubles down on it, and restricting removes value people are evidently getting.

questions.stem: A workflow requires the person receiving Claude's output to know context that was available upstream but is not passed along.
options: Ask the receiving person to request the context from the upstream team
Pass the context forward as part of the handoff
Have the receiving person sit with the upstream team
Ask Claude to include any context it used in its output so the receiving person has visibility of what informed the result they are being asked to work with
questions.why: Context a downstream step needs is part of what the handoff must carry. Passing it forward is the design fix.
questions.traps: Requesting it on demand adds delay and depends on knowing what is missing. Co-location is a heavy fix, and a model-reported context summary is not the upstream context.

questions.stem: A team is deciding whether to improve an existing process or redesign it, and the existing process was built around constraints that no longer apply.
options: Improve the existing process incrementally, since that is less disruptive to the people who work within it and delivers benefits sooner than a full redesign would
Redesign only those steps that are most affected by the change
Keep the existing process and add Claude to the steps where it fits most naturally
Redesign, since the current shape reflects constraints that have since disappeared
questions.why: A process built around removed constraints is optimised for a world that no longer exists. Incremental improvement preserves that shape.
