questions.traps: Incremental improvement and partial redesign both keep the obsolete structure. Adding a tool to an obsolete process improves the wrong thing.

questions.stem: A team wants to automate a step and has established that the model performs it correctly 96% of the time.
options: Automate it, since 96% accuracy exceeds the rate that the manual process was achieving before the automation was proposed by the team
Ask what happens in the other 4% and whether that is detectable and recoverable
Automate the step and review a sample of the decisions
Improve the prompt until the accuracy is higher than 96% before automating the step
questions.why: The decision turns on what the 4% does and whether anyone will notice. An accuracy figure alone cannot support an automation decision.
questions.traps: Comparing to the manual rate ignores the failure's consequence. Sampling catches some, and chasing a higher rate defers the same unanswered question.

questions.stem: A team's workflow is designed so that a failure in one step stops everything downstream, including steps that do not depend on it.
options: Decouple the independent steps so an unrelated failure does not block them
Add error handling to the failing step so that it recovers automatically and the downstream steps are not blocked when a problem occurs during its execution
Run the independent steps first, before the one that fails
Accept the coupling since it is simpler to reason about a workflow where a failure anywhere stops the whole process
questions.why: Unnecessary coupling turns a local failure into a total one. Decoupling genuinely independent steps limits the blast radius.
questions.traps: Recovery in the failing step does not address the coupling. Reordering helps by accident, and accepting the coupling keeps the amplification.

questions.stem: An associate's workflow depends on a colleague manually triggering it each morning, and it is skipped whenever that colleague is away.
options: Ask the colleague to arrange cover with someone else whenever they are going to be away
Document the trigger procedure so that anyone on the team is able to run the workflow if the usual person happens to be unavailable on a given day
Schedule the trigger so the workflow does not depend on one person being present
Run the workflow twice as often on the days it does run
questions.why: A workflow that needs a specific person present each morning has an availability dependency that scheduling removes entirely.
questions.traps: Arranged cover and documentation both keep a human trigger that can be missed. Running more often on available days does not fill the gaps.

questions.stem: A team is designing a workflow and must decide whether the human checkpoint reviews every item or only the ones that meet certain conditions
options: Review everything, since conditions may not capture every case where an error would matter and full coverage is the only way to be certain nothing important is missed
Review a fixed proportion of the items that come through
Review whatever the reviewer has time for on any given day, adjusting the proportion up or down
Define conditions tied to what an error would cost, and review those items fully
questions.why: Conditional review tied to consequence concentrates the available attention where errors cost most, which is what makes limited review capacity effective.
questions.traps: Reviewing everything is the unsustainable pattern this question is about. A fixed proportion ignores stakes, and capacity-driven review lets workload set the control.

questions.stem: A team's process has one step that fails often and one step that fails rarely but catastrophically
options: Address the frequently failing step first, since it disrupts the process regularly and fixing it will produce the most visible improvement to how the process runs day to day
Weigh frequency against consequence rather than addressing whichever fails more often
Address the catastrophic step first because of its severity
Address both steps at the same time so that neither of the two problems is left outstanding
questions.why: Risk is frequency times consequence, and neither dimension alone determines priority. Weighing both is what produces a defensible ordering.
questions.traps: Prioritising by frequency ignores severity. Prioritising by severity ignores exposure, and doing both at once avoids the prioritisation the question is testing.

questions.stem: An associate is asked whether a step should be automated, and the step currently takes forty minutes a day across the team
options: Ask what the step's errors would cost before deciding on the time saving alone
Automate it, since forty minutes a day across a team is over three working weeks a year and that is a substantial saving to leave on the table indefinitely
Automate it if the automation can be built quickly enough
Leave it manual, since forty minutes spread across a team is a small amount per person and does not justify the effort of building and maintaining an automation
questions.why: Automation decisions weigh the saving against what automated errors would cost. The time figure is only half of the input.
questions.traps: Deciding on the time saving alone in either direction omits the risk side. Build speed is a cost consideration rather than a decision criterion.

questions.stem: A workflow's most likely failure is that the model produces plausible output from an input it did not fully receive
options: Add a review step that reads the output carefully to identify anything that looks as though it might have been produced from incomplete information during the run
Choose a stronger model so the problem occurs less often
Check that the input arrived complete before the output is produced or used
Ask Claude to state whether it received the complete input
questions.why: Truncated input producing plausible output is only caught by verifying the input, since the output gives no signal. That check has to be upstream.
questions.traps: Reviewing output cannot detect what was never there. A stronger model produces more plausible output from partial input, and self-reported completeness is unreliable.

questions.stem: A team wants their workflow to produce the same result if it is run again in six months with the same inputs
options: Pin the configuration and record it, since defaults and models change over time
Document the workflow thoroughly so that it can be reconstructed in six months if anyone needs to reproduce the result that was originally obtained from it
Save the output somewhere so it can be consulted later
Run the workflow again now and confirm that it produces the same result
questions.why: Reproducibility over time requires pinning what varies and recording it. Models and defaults change, so an unpinned workflow drifts.
questions.traps: Documentation describes without pinning. Saving output preserves a result rather than the ability to reproduce it, and a repeat run today says nothing about six months out.

questions.stem: A team's workflow reads from a system whose owners are planning a change to its data format next quarter
options: Wait until the change happens and fix the workflow at that point
Build the workflow so that it accepts both of the formats
Ask the system owners to delay their change until the team has had time to prepare the workflow for the new format they intend to introduce
Agree the change with them and adapt before it lands, rather than after
questions.why: A known upcoming change is something to coordinate around. Adapting before it lands avoids an outage that is entirely predictable.
questions.traps: Waiting guarantees a break. Accepting both formats adds permanent complexity for a transition, and asking others to delay is not within the team's control.

questions.stem: A team wants to demonstrate their workflow's value but the benefit is that a rare expensive mistake no longer happens
options: Report that the mistake has not occurred since the workflow was introduced
Express the value as the expected cost avoided, with the frequency and cost stated
Report the time saved by the workflow instead of the value
Wait until enough time has passed to show a statistically meaningful reduction in the rate at which the expensive mistake occurs across the organisation
questions.why: Prevention value is expressed as expected cost avoided, which makes both the frequency and the consequence explicit and lets a reader judge the estimate.
questions.traps: Absence over a short period is weak evidence for a rare event. Time saved measures something else, and waiting for statistical significance on a rare event takes years.

questions.stem: A team's workflow requires people to trust it with work they consider high-stakes, and adoption has stalled at the low-stakes cases
options: Encourage people to try it on higher-stakes work so that they can see for themselves that it performs just as well there as it does on the simpler cases
Mandate its use on the high-stakes work as well as the rest
Treat the low-stakes adoption as the evidence base for extending upward
Accept the current split, since using it on low-stakes work
questions.why: Accumulated low-stakes performance is exactly the evidence that justifies extending scope. Using it deliberately turns caution into a staged rollout.
questions.traps: Encouragement without evidence asks for trust. Mandating removes the judgement, and accepting the split forgoes the value where it is largest.

questions.stem: A workflow's two steps are owned by different people who each optimise their own step, and the overall result has got worse
options: Measure and optimise the end-to-end result rather than each step separately
Ask both owners to coordinate their changes so that improvements to one step do not create problems for the other step in the sequence
Combine both of the steps under a single named owner
Add a third step that corrects whatever problems arise from the interaction between the first two steps in the workflow
questions.why: Local optimisation against local measures degrades the whole. Measuring end to end is what aligns the incentives with the outcome.
questions.traps: Coordination without a shared measure leaves both optimising locally. Single ownership is a reorganisation, and a corrective step treats the symptom.

questions.stem: An associate discovers that the process they are mapping is performed differently by each of the five people who do it
options: Standardise on the approach used by the most experienced person
Establish which variations are deliberate before standardising anything
Standardise on whichever of the variations is the fastest
Let each person keep their own variation and design the workflow to accommodate all five of the different approaches that are currently in use across the team
questions.why: Variation often encodes real differences in the cases each person handles. Distinguishing deliberate adaptation from drift is what makes standardisation safe.
questions.traps: Standardising on seniority or speed may discard necessary adaptations. Accommodating all five builds complexity around variation nobody has understood.

questions.stem: A team's workflow asks a person to approve output they did not request and have no context for
options: Ask the approver to request context from the person who initiated the work
Add a summary of the context to each item under review
Ask the approver to approve on the basis of whether the output looks internally consistent and well-formed
Give the approver the context, or move the approval to someone who has it
questions.why: An approval without context is a formality. Supplying context or relocating the approval is what makes it a real decision.
questions.traps: On-demand context requests add delay and depend on knowing what is missing. A generated summary is not independent, and approving on form alone concedes the point.

questions.stem: A team wants to automate a step, and doing so would mean nobody in the team understands how that part of the work is done any more
options: Automate it, since the point of automation is that people no longer need to concern themselves with the details of how the work is performed on a routine basis
Document the step in detail before automating any of it
Keep enough understanding in the team to supervise and change the step later
Rotate people through the manual version occasionally so that the knowledge does not disappear entirely from the team over the longer term
questions.why: Automating away all understanding leaves a step nobody can supervise, debug or modify. Retaining working knowledge is what keeps the team in control of it.
questions.traps: Treating opacity as the goal is the misconception. Documentation and rotation are both mechanisms for retaining understanding rather than alternatives to it.

questions.stem: A workflow retries automatically when a step fails, and a persistent failure now produces thousands of retries
options: Increase the interval between retries so that the volume of attempts is lower
Remove the retry logic so the workflow stops after one attempt
Ask someone to monitor the workflow so that persistent failures are noticed and the process can be stopped manually when this situation arises again
Cap the retries and escalate when the cap is reached
questions.why: Retries handle transient failures and must not run unbounded against a persistent one. A cap plus escalation distinguishes the two cases.
questions.traps: Longer intervals reduce the rate of a still-unbounded loop. Removing retries loses transient recovery, and manual monitoring is a person doing what a cap does automatically.

questions.stem: A team's workflow relies on a document that a colleague updates informally whenever they think of it
options: Ask the colleague to notify the team whenever they update the document
Establish a defined update cadence and owner for the document
Take a copy of the document for reference
Add a note to the workflow saying that the document may not be current
questions.why: An input that changes informally makes the workflow's behaviour unpredictable. Defining ownership and cadence is what makes the dependency reliable.
questions.traps: Notification depends on remembering. A copy goes stale immediately, and a caveat documents the problem without fixing it.

questions.stem: An associate's integration works but sends credentials in a way the security team has not reviewed
options: Have the security team review it before the integration goes into use
Proceed, since the integration is internal and the credentials do not leave the organisation's own systems at any point during its normal operation
Ask the security team to review it after launch
Use a different credential with fewer permissions so that the risk is lower even
questions.why: Credential handling is a security review matter and the review belongs before use. That is a governance boundary rather than a technical preference.
questions.traps: Internal scope does not exempt credential handling from review. Post-launch review accepts the exposure, and reducing permissions without review still bypasses the control.

questions.stem: A team's workflow shows a clear benefit in the pilot metrics but the people using it say it makes their work harder
options: Trust the metrics, since they measure the outcome objectively
Trust the user reports rather than the measured pilot figures
Investigate the discrepancy rather than choosing which signal to believe
Continue the workflow and monitor whether the user reports change over the coming months as people become more familiar with how it operates
questions.why: A gap between measured benefit and experienced burden usually means the metric misses a real cost. Investigating is what reconciles them.
questions.traps: Choosing either signal discards information. Waiting for familiarity assumes the complaint is an adjustment problem rather than a finding.

questions.stem: A team's workflow was designed by someone who has since left, and the current team does not know why it works the way it does
options: Reconstruct the reasoning before changing anything
Change whatever seems suboptimal, since the current team are the ones who use it and are best placed to judge what would work better for them now
Leave the workflow unchanged rather than risking a regression
Rebuild the workflow from scratch so that the current team fully understands every decision that has gone into the version they are working with
questions.why: Undocumented design decisions often encode constraints. Reconstructing the reasoning is what makes change safe rather than a gamble.
questions.traps: Changing what looks suboptimal risks removing something load-bearing. Freezing it forever is a permanent cost, and rebuilding discards a working system.

questions.stem: A workflow passes output to a system that silently truncates anything over a certain length
options: Ask Claude to produce shorter output so that the material it generates stays within the limit that the receiving system is able to accept
Increase the receiving system's length limit so nothing is cut
Enforce the length limit at the handoff so truncation cannot happen silently
Check the receiving system periodically to identify records that appear to have been truncated so they can be corrected when the problem is found
questions.why: Silent truncation at a boundary is a contract violation that must be caught where it occurs. Enforcing the limit makes the failure explicit.
questions.traps: Shorter output reduces the incidence without preventing it. Raising the limit may not be possible, and periodic checks find truncation after the data is already wrong.

questions.stem: A team wants to measure a process before changing it, but measuring would itself take three weeks of effort
options: Measure the process thoroughly, since a change made without a baseline cannot be evaluated afterwards and the three weeks is an investment in knowing whether it worked
Measure the one or two things the decision actually depends on
Skip the measurement and change the process
Measure after the change instead, since that will show how the new process performs and the old one is being replaced anyway so its performance matters less
questions.why: Measurement should be scoped to what the decision needs rather than to the process as a whole. That is what makes a baseline affordable.
questions.traps: Full measurement over-invests. Skipping it loses the baseline entirely, and measuring only afterwards leaves nothing to compare against.

questions.stem: A team is considering automating a step where the input occasionally contains something the model should refuse to process
options: Automate it and rely on the model to decline when it encounters material it should not process
Keep the step manual so that the incidental knowledge is retained
Automate it and add a review step that identifies any cases where the model processed something it should have declined to handle in the first place
Design the refusal path deliberately rather than leaving it to the model's judgement
questions.why: A refusal path that matters should be designed and tested rather than assumed. Defining what the workflow does with such input is part of the design.
questions.traps: Relying on default behaviour leaves the boundary undefined and untested. Manual handling forgoes the automation, and after-the-fact review catches failures rather than preventing them.

questions.stem: A team's workflow was designed around one failure mode and a different one has now occurred twice
options: Revisit the failure analysis, since the assumptions behind it have been shown incomplete
Add handling for the new failure mode alongside the existing handling
Increase the level of monitoring applied
Treat the two occurrences as unusual and continue with the current design
questions.why: Two occurrences of an unanticipated mode is evidence that the original analysis was incomplete. Revisiting it is what surfaces what else was missed.
questions.traps: Patching the new mode addresses this one and leaves the analysis unrevised. More monitoring watches without understanding, and dismissing two occurrences ignores the evidence.

questions.stem: A team's workflow gives consistent results within a single session and different results across sessions
options: Accept the variation, since some difference between sessions is a normal property of working with a model and the results within any single session remain consistent
Run everything within a single session to avoid the variation entirely
Identify what differs between sessions, since something is varying that should not be
Average the results across several sessions so that the variation between them is smoothed out in the figure the team actually reports and uses
questions.why: Consistency within sessions and variation across them points at a session-scoped input such as accumulated context or configuration. That is findable.
questions.traps: Accepting it abandons a diagnosable problem. Forcing single sessions is a workaround, and averaging conceals rather than explains the variation.

questions.stem: An associate wants to integrate Claude into a process, and the integration would be the only automated part of an otherwise manual workflow
options: Build the integration, since automating any part of a manual process delivers a saving and the surrounding manual steps do not prevent that part from being faster
Check whether the manual steps around it would absorb the benefit
Automate the whole of the process rather than only this single step
Automate the step and measure whether the overall process time falls
questions.why: A single automated step inside a manual process often produces work that then waits. Checking whether the surrounding steps absorb the gain is the prior question.
questions.traps: Assuming the local saving reaches the outcome is the error. Full automation may not be feasible, and measuring afterwards spends the effort before asking.

questions.stem: A team's workflow reduces errors but the errors it prevents were previously caught by a downstream check that still runs
options: Report the error reduction, since fewer errors being produced is a genuine improvement
Remove the downstream check entirely now that errors are prevented upstream
Continue running both, since redundant checks provide additional assurance and the cost of the downstream check was already being incurred before the workflow was introduced
Check whether the downstream check can now be reduced, since otherwise the saving is not realised
questions.why: If a downstream check still absorbs the same cost, preventing errors upstream has not yet produced a saving. Whether the check can be reduced is what realises it.
questions.traps: Reporting the reduction claims a benefit that has not landed. Removing the check outright is premature, and keeping both indefinitely means the workflow pays for itself twice.

questions.stem: A team introduces a workflow and the people who use it most are the ones who were already most productive
options: Consider the rollout a success, since the workflow is being adopted and the people using it are getting value from it in their day-to-day work
Target the least productive users in the next phase of the rollout
Check whether the workflow is widening rather than closing the gap
Accept the pattern, since more capable users adopting new tools more readily is a common and expected outcome that does not require any particular intervention
questions.why: If a tool amplifies existing capability, the aggregate improves while the spread widens. Noticing that is what tells you whether the rollout met its goal.
questions.traps: Adoption by the already-productive is not the same as the intended outcome. Targeting others assumes the cause, and accepting the pattern skips the check.

questions.stem: A workflow's output includes a confidence indicator that the receiving person has learned to ignore because it is rarely informative
options: Explain to the receiving person what the confidence indicator means
Replace it with a numeric score
Keep it, since it costs nothing to produce and may occasionally be useful
Remove it or make it meaningful, since an ignored signal is worse than none
questions.why: A signal people have learned to ignore trains them to ignore signals generally. Either making it informative or removing it is the honest response.
questions.traps: Explaining an uninformative signal does not make it informative. A numeric version of the same weak signal is no better, and keeping it normalises ignoring indicators.

questions.stem: A team is asked to make a process faster, and the process is already faster than the downstream team can consume its output
options: Look downstream, since speeding up production ahead of consumption creates a queue
Speed up the process as requested, since that is what has been asked for and the downstream team's capacity is not within this team's control or responsibility
Slow the process down so it matches what the downstream team can take
Speed up the process and store the additional output until the downstream team is ready to consume it
questions.why: Producing faster than the next stage can absorb builds inventory rather than delivering value. The constraint is downstream.
questions.traps: Delivering the request as stated produces a growing queue. Slowing down is not the ask, and buffering output is inventory rather than throughput.

questions.stem: An associate is asked to automate a decision that is currently made by consensus between three people
options: Automate it using the position the three people usually converge on, since that represents the collective judgement they would have reached anyway in most cases
Establish whether the consensus encodes a rule or genuine disagreement
Keep the decision manual rather than automating any part of the step
Automate it and route to the three people only in the cases where the model is uncertain about which way the decision should go on the evidence available
questions.why: Consensus may be an agreed rule applied by three people or a genuine negotiation. Which it is determines whether the decision can be specified at all.
questions.traps: Encoding the usual outcome assumes a rule exists. Keeping it manual forgoes the analysis, and uncertainty routing presumes specifiability.

questions.stem: A workflow has good error handling for the failures the team anticipated and no handling for anything else
options: Add a defined behaviour for unanticipated failures rather than leaving them undefined
Extend the error handling to cover additional failure modes as the team identifies them through experience of running the workflow over time
Choose a stronger model so that the truncation problem happens less
Accept the current coverage, since the anticipated failures are the ones most likely to occur and handling every conceivable failure is not a realistic goal
questions.why: Unanticipated failures need a defined default such as stopping safely and escalating. That is what stops an unknown failure from becoming an undefined one.
questions.traps: Extending coverage case by case leaves each new mode undefined until it happens. A stronger model does not define behaviour, and accepting the gap leaves the workflow open-ended.

questions.stem: A team's workflow is run by four people and produces four noticeably different levels of quality
options: Train all four people to the standard achieved by whoever currently produces the best results
Have the best performing person run everything for the team
Standardise the parts that vary rather than training four people toward one standard
Accept the variation as the normal range of quality that different people produce when performing the same task in their own individual ways
questions.why: Person-dependent quality means the workflow leaves too much to the operator. Moving the variable parts into fixed configuration is what makes quality independent of who runs it.
questions.traps: Training toward a standard leaves the dependency in place. Single-operator running is a bottleneck, and accepting variation forfeits repeatability.

questions.stem: A team's integration works reliably but nobody has recorded what it does, and the person who built it has moved teams
options: Leave it alone, since it works reliably and there is no immediate need to spend time documenting something that is not currently causing any problems for anyone
Rebuild it so the current team understands it
Contact the person who built it whenever a question arises about how the integration works or what it is doing in a particular situation
Document what it does and who owns it now, before anything needs changing
questions.why: An undocumented, unowned integration is a problem the moment it needs changing or breaks. Documenting and assigning ownership now is cheap.
questions.traps: Leaving it works until it does not. Rebuilding discards a working system, and depending on someone in another team is a fragile arrangement.

questions.stem: A team's workflow is measured on how many items it processes, and the team has started routing easy items to it to improve the number
options: Ask the team to stop selecting easy items so that the throughput figure reflects the workflow's performance across a representative mix of the work
Change the measure, since it is driving behaviour that does not serve the goal
Keep the measure and add a quality measure alongside it
Accept the selection, since processing easy items through the workflow is still productive work
questions.why: A measure that can be gamed will be. Changing it so it aligns with the goal is what removes the incentive rather than policing it.
questions.traps: Asking people not to respond to an incentive rarely works. A second measure alongside a gameable one leaves the incentive, and accepting the selection accepts a meaningless figure.

questions.stem: A team's workflow requires a small amount of setup per user, and half the team have not completed it
options: Do the setup for them, since a small barrier is stopping half the benefit
Send instructions explaining how to complete the setup so that the remaining team members can get themselves up and running when they have a moment
Remind people weekly until the setup is complete
Accept the partial adoption, since the people who completed the setup are presumably the ones who found the workflow most useful for their own work
questions.why: Small barriers stop adoption disproportionately. Removing the barrier entirely is cheaper than repeatedly asking people to cross it.
questions.traps: Instructions and reminders both leave the barrier in place. Inferring preference from an uncrossed barrier confuses friction with disinterest.

questions.stem: A workflow's steps are each fast, but work waits between them because each step runs on a different schedule
options: Speed up the individual steps so that the total processing time falls
Combine all of the steps together into one single larger step
Align the schedules or make the steps trigger each other
Run each step more frequently so that work waits a shorter time between the completion of one step and the start of the next one in the sequence
questions.why: Elapsed time is dominated by waiting between steps rather than by the steps themselves. Triggering removes the wait rather than shortening it.
questions.traps: Faster steps do not touch the waits. Combining steps is a larger change than needed, and more frequent runs reduce the wait without eliminating it.

questions.stem: A team maps their process and finds that half the steps produce output nobody downstream actually uses
options: Automate the production of the unused output with Claude
Ask downstream teams whether they might use it
Keep producing it, since somebody may have needed it at some point and stopping could cause a problem that is not currently visible to the team
Stop producing the unused output
questions.why: Work producing unused output is waste. Stopping it is a larger and simpler gain than making it cheaper to produce.
questions.traps: Automating waste entrenches it. Canvassing for hypothetical users looks for a reason to continue, and preserving it against an unknown need pays permanently.

questions.stem: A team can automate a step, and the person who currently performs it uses the time to notice patterns that inform other decisions
options: Automate the step, since noticing patterns is not the purpose of the step and the person will find other opportunities to observe the same information elsewhere
Identify what that noticing produces and preserve it deliberately
Leave the step manual and recruit a replacement person to be trained
Automate the step and ask the person to review the automated output periodically
questions.why: Manual work often produces incidental value nobody designed. Identifying it before automating is what stops a hidden benefit from disappearing silently.
questions.traps: Assuming the noticing will happen elsewhere is unfounded. Leaving it manual is more than needed, and periodic review of output is not the same as working through the material.

questions.stem: A workflow fails in a way that is obvious to the team but invisible to the customers who receive its output
options: Ask the team to check the output more carefully so that the failures they can recognise are caught before anything reaches the customers who would not notice them
Notify the customers whenever one of these failures actually occurs
Accept the situation, since the team notices the failures and can correct them when they are identified during the course of their normal work
Add detection at the point the customer would experience the problem
questions.why: A failure invisible to the person affected needs detection oriented to their experience rather than to the team's. That is where the control belongs.
questions.traps: More careful team checking still catches only what the team recognises. Notification follows detection, and relying on incidental team awareness leaves customers exposed.

questions.stem: A team wants their workflow to be usable by a different team with different data but the same underlying task
options: Separate the parts that are specific to this team's data from the general method
Give the other team a copy of the workflow and let them adjust whatever does not fit their own data and processes
Rebuild the workflow from scratch for the other team involved
Document the workflow in detail so the other team can understand how it works and decide for themselves what they need to change about it
questions.why: Reusability comes from separating the general method from the local specifics. That is what makes a second deployment a configuration exercise rather than a rebuild.
questions.traps: Handing over a copy to adapt distributes the same untangling work. Rebuilding duplicates effort, and documentation describes without separating.

questions.stem: A team is asked for the return on their workflow and the largest benefit is that a task can now be done at all
options: Estimate what the task would have cost to do manually and report that figure as the saving the workflow has delivered to the organisation
Report the cost figure without any benefit figure alongside
Describe the new capability rather than forcing it into a time-saved figure
Report the time saved on the other smaller tasks the workflow also performs
questions.why: A capability that did not previously exist is not a saving, and describing it as one distorts it. Naming it as new capability is the honest account.
questions.traps: A hypothetical manual cost invents a baseline that never existed. Reporting cost alone omits the benefit, and substituting a minor measurable benefit understates the main one.

questions.stem: A team's workflow works well and a colleague in another team wants to copy it for a task that is superficially similar
options: Share the workflow, since it works well and the colleague can adapt whatever does not fit their own situation
Check whether the underlying task is actually the same before copying it across
Advise the colleague to build their own version from scratch instead
Share the workflow and offer to help them set it up so that the transfer goes smoothly and they get the benefit as quickly as possible in their own team
questions.why: Superficial similarity often hides different requirements. Checking whether the tasks match is what determines whether copying will work at all.
questions.traps: Sharing on surface similarity risks a poor fit discovered later. Advising a rebuild forgoes reuse, and helping with setup accelerates a transfer that may be wrong.

questions.stem: An associate is setting up a Project for a recurring analysis and is unsure what belongs in the instructions versus what belongs in each request.
options: Put everything in the instructions so that each request can be as short as possible and users do not need to remember what to include when they come to use it
Put what stays constant in the instructions and what changes in the request
Put everything into each individual request rather than the instructions
Put the instructions in both places so that they are reinforced and the model is more likely to follow them consistently across the different requests it receives
questions.why: Configuration holds the invariant part and the request carries the variable part. That division is what makes a Project reusable without re-explaining the task.
questions.traps: Loading everything into instructions leaves no room for the variable input. Putting everything in the request abandons the Project, and duplication creates two places to maintain.

questions.stem: A team uploads twelve documents to a Project. Four are current policies and eight are drafts that were never adopted.
options: Label the drafts clearly so the model can tell which documents represent adopted policy and which were superseded before they were ever put into effect
Keep all twelve of the documents there for the sake of completeness
Add an instruction telling the model to prefer the current policies over the drafts
Remove the drafts, since knowledge that was never adopted will still be treated as authoritative
questions.why: Everything in project knowledge is treated as available context. Unadopted drafts will be drawn on as readily as policy, so removal is the reliable fix.
questions.traps: Labels and preference instructions both rely on correct selection every time. Completeness is not a virtue when the extra content is wrong.

questions.stem: A team's project instructions run to three pages and people have noticed that recently added rules seem to have less effect than older ones.
options: Move the newer rules to the top of the instructions so that they are encountered first and carry more weight in how the model interprets the whole set
Split the instructions across two Projects
Consolidate around the rules that matter, since a long instruction set dilutes each rule
Repeat the newer rules at both the beginning and the end of the instructions
questions.why: Instructions compete for attention, and a three-page set dilutes everything in it. Consolidating restores the leverage each remaining rule has.
questions.traps: Reordering and repetition redistribute attention within a bloated set. Splitting fragments the workflow rather than simplifying the instructions.

questions.stem: A Project has accumulated documents over eighteen months and nobody has ever removed one.
options: Establish a review cadence so knowledge is curated rather than only added to
Remove the documents that are obviously out of date now
Add newer documents so the current material outweighs the older material in the overall body of knowledge the Project holds
Ask people to be more selective about what they upload in future
questions.why: Project knowledge is a curated set that degrades without maintenance. A review cadence is what turns curation into a process rather than a one-off cleanup.
questions.traps: A one-time cleanup fixes today and leaves the pattern. Adding more material dilutes rather than curates, and asking for selectivity does not address what is already there.

questions.stem: An associate notices their Project's answers have become less precise since they added a large reference manual to its knowledge.
options: Move to a model with a larger context window so that the manual can be included
Check whether the manual is needed for the questions actually being asked
Ask more specific questions of the Project when using it
Split the manual into sections and upload only the section that relates to whatever question is being asked at the time it is needed
questions.why: More context is not automatically better, and irrelevant material competes with what matters. Checking whether it earns its place is the first question.
questions.traps: A larger window accommodates the problem rather than solving it. More specific questions work around it, and manual section selection is a workaround for an unexamined inclusion.

questions.stem: A team shares a Project and one member keeps changing the instructions to suit their own preferences.
options: Ask that person to consult the team before making further changes to the shared instructions that everyone else depends on for their own work
Give that person a separate Project of their own
Agree who owns the configuration and how changes get made
Revert the instructions each time they are changed so that the configuration returns to the version the team originally agreed on together
questions.why: Shared configuration without an ownership model means every user is an editor. Establishing ownership is the governance fix rather than an interpersonal one.
questions.traps: A request relies on goodwill. A separate Project addresses one person, and reverting is an ongoing conflict rather than a resolution.

questions.stem: An associate has fourteen Projects and cannot remember which one holds the documents they need.
options: Search across all fourteen Projects whenever they need to find something
Consolidate everything into one Project
Keep a separate note listing what each of the fourteen Projects contains
Adopt a naming and scoping convention so the right Project is identifiable
questions.why: Findability comes from consistent naming and clear scope. That scales, whereas memory and external indexes do not.
questions.traps: Searching everywhere is the symptom. Consolidation destroys the isolation Projects provide, and an external index is another thing to maintain.

questions.stem: A team's Project answers questions well but occasionally cites a document that was uploaded for a different purpose entirely.
options: Scope the Project to one purpose so unrelated documents are not in play
Add an instruction telling the model which documents are relevant to which kinds of question
Ask questions that specify which document should be used
Remove the document that is being cited inappropriately
questions.why: Everything in a Project is in scope for every question. Matching the Project's scope to a single purpose is what prevents cross-contamination structurally.
questions.traps: Routing instructions and per-question specification both rely on correct selection. Removing one document leaves the pattern for the next one.

questions.stem: A team wants their Project to behave one way for drafting and another way for reviewing, and the instructions currently describe both.
options: Write conditional instructions describing when each behaviour applies
Ask users to state which of the two modes they want
Alternate the instructions depending on which kind of work the team is doing during any particular week of the month
Use two Projects, since standing instructions apply to every response in one
questions.why: Standing instructions apply to everything. Two genuinely different behaviours belong in two Projects rather than in a conditional that must be resolved correctly each time.
questions.traps: Conditional instructions ask the model to classify every request. Per-request mode selection puts the burden on users, and alternating serves neither purpose well.

questions.stem: A Project contains a document that is correct but describes a process the team stopped following six months ago.
options: Keep it as a historical record so the team can refer back to how the process used to work if they ever need to understand a decision made under the old approach
Add a note to the document saying the process is no longer followed
Remove it, since a correct description of an abandoned process is still misleading
Keep it and add an instruction telling the model that the process described in that document is no longer current and should not be recommended to users
questions.why: Accuracy about the past is not relevance to the present. A document describing an abandoned process will be drawn on as guidance unless removed.
questions.traps: Historical records belong somewhere other than active knowledge. Notes and instructions both rely on the qualification being applied every time.

questions.stem: An associate wants to add a 400-page manual to a Project where questions only ever concern two of its chapters.
options: Add the whole manual so that any question can be answered, including ones that fall outside the two chapters people have happened to ask about so far
Add only the chapters the questions concern
Add the manual and rely on the model to find the relevant chapters within it
Summarise the manual and add the summary instead of the full document
questions.why: Curating to what is actually used keeps answers precise and costs less. The two chapters are the evidence of what the Project needs.
questions.traps: Adding everything for hypothetical questions dilutes the material that matters. Relying on retrieval within noise is weaker, and a summary loses the detail questions need.

questions.stem: A team is creating a Project and debating whether to include instructions about tone.
options: Include it if tone matters for every response the Project produces
Leave tone out of the instructions, since it varies between different pieces of work and is better specified in each individual request when it matters
Include a detailed style guide within the project instructions
Include tone instructions but keep them brief so that they do not take up too much room within the overall set of instructions the Project carries
questions.why: Configuration is for what applies universally. If tone is constant across the Project's outputs, it belongs there; if it varies, it belongs in the request.
questions.traps: Excluding it by default ignores the case where it is constant. A detailed style guide may be more than needed, and brevity is a formatting concern rather than the criterion.

questions.stem: A team wants everyone to get the same answers, and each member currently maintains their own copy of the same Project.
options: Ask everyone to keep their copies synchronised so that the configurations stay the same and the answers people receive remain consistent with one another
Nominate one person's copy as authoritative
Compare the copies periodically to identify where they have diverged
Consolidate into one shared Project so there is a single configuration
questions.why: Parallel copies diverge. A single shared configuration is what makes consistency structural rather than something to maintain.
questions.traps: Manual synchronisation across copies is exactly what fails. A nominated authoritative copy still leaves others in use, and periodic reconciliation is ongoing work.

questions.stem: An associate keeps one Project per client and one per internal workstream, and some pieces of work involve both.
options: Decide which dimension the Project boundary follows and handle the overlap explicitly
Create a third Project for the work that involves both a client and an internal workstream
Put the overlapping work in whichever Project seems more relevant at the time the work is being carried out by whoever happens to be doing it
Merge the client and workstream Projects so that everything is available in one place and the question of where something belongs does not arise
questions.why: Two organising dimensions that cross produce ambiguity at the intersection. Choosing the primary boundary and defining how overlap is handled resolves it.
questions.traps: A third Project multiplies the problem. Ad-hoc placement makes things unfindable, and merging destroys the isolation.

questions.stem: A team's Project gives good answers about the documents it holds and confident wrong answers about topics those documents do not cover.
options: Add documents covering the additional topics so that the Project's knowledge extends to the questions people are actually bringing to it in practice
Tell colleagues to only ask about covered topics
Instruct it to answer from its documents and to say when they do not cover a question
Ask more specific questions so that the model is more likely to find relevant material
questions.why: The problem is that the knowledge boundary is invisible. Making the Project declare when it is outside its documents is what stops confident answers from unsupported ground.
questions.traps: Adding documents moves the boundary without making it visible. Telling people the scope relies on them knowing it, and specificity does not prevent the fallback.

questions.stem: An associate's project instruction says to be concise, and answers have become too brief to be useful.
options: Remove the conciseness instruction so that answers return to the length they were before the instruction was added to the Project's configuration
Say what conciseness applies to and what must be included regardless
Ask for longer answers within each individual request instead
Add a second instruction saying that answers should also be complete
questions.why: A global brevity instruction applies to everything including what carries the value. Scoping it and protecting the essentials keeps both properties.
questions.traps: Removing it abandons a real goal. Per-request overrides fight the standing instruction, and stacking a competing adjective leaves the trade-off unresolved.

questions.stem: A team discovers two documents in their Project that contradict each other on an important point.
options: Add an instruction telling the model which of the two documents takes precedence
Keep both so the model can present both positions
Add a note to each document explaining that there is a conflicting version and that users should check which one applies to their particular situation
Resolve which is correct and remove the other
questions.why: Contradictory knowledge produces inconsistent answers. Resolving the conflict at source is the only fix that makes the Project's output reliable.
questions.traps: Precedence rules rely on correct application. Presenting both positions passes the unresolved conflict to users, and notes document the problem without fixing it.

questions.stem: A Project's answers are good but noticeably slower than a plain conversation on the same topic.
options: Accept the slower responses, since the additional context is what makes the answers better than they would be
Move to a faster model tier so responses come back sooner
Check whether all the loaded knowledge is needed for the questions being asked
Ask shorter questions so that the total amount of material being processed on each request is smaller than it currently is for the Project
questions.why: Loaded context costs time to process on every request. Whether all of it earns its place is the question that addresses the cause.
questions.traps: Accepting it forgoes an easy improvement. A faster tier pays to process possibly unnecessary material, and shorter questions do not reduce the loaded knowledge.

questions.stem: A team is deciding whether a piece of standing guidance belongs in project instructions or in an uploaded document.
options: Put everything in documents so that the instructions stay short and everything the Project knows is held consistently in one type of place
Put short standing rules in instructions and reference material in documents
Put everything into the instructions rather than into documents
Put it in whichever place has more room available, since the distinction between the two does not make a practical difference to how the Project behaves
questions.why: Instructions shape behaviour and documents supply reference material. Matching content to that distinction is what makes both work as intended.
questions.traps: Collapsing everything into one type loses the distinction. Choosing by available space treats a design question as a capacity one.

questions.stem: An associate shares a Project with a colleague who then asks questions it was never configured to answer.
options: Clarify the Project's scope so its purpose travels with the share
Add documents covering the colleague's questions so that the Project becomes useful for their work as well as for the original purpose
Ask the colleague to use a different Project
Ask the colleague to check with the associate before asking questions
questions.why: A shared Project needs its scope communicated, otherwise recipients discover the boundary by getting bad answers. Stating it is the fix.
questions.traps: Expanding scope for one colleague changes the Project. Redirecting them and requiring pre-checks both work around the missing scope statement.

questions.stem: A team's Projects are named after the person who created them rather than what they contain.
options: Keep a directory mapping each person's name to the contents of the Projects they created
Ask people to create rather fewer Projects overall
Ask each person to explain what their Projects contain when a colleague needs something from one of them
Rename them after their purpose so they can be found by what they do
questions.why: Names are the primary means of finding things. Purpose-based naming makes Projects discoverable without external lookup or asking someone.
questions.traps: A directory is another artefact to maintain. Fewer Projects does not make them findable, and asking people is a bottleneck.

questions.stem: A team uploads a spreadsheet to a Project and finds the model answers from the column headers rather than the data.
options: Convert the spreadsheet to a document format before uploading it
Reduce the number of columns held in the uploaded spreadsheet
Ask questions that require the values and state that answers must come from the rows
Upload the spreadsheet again in case the original upload did not process the data correctly when it was first added to the Project's knowledge
questions.why: Headers are salient and self-describing, so a loosely framed question can be answered from them alone. Requiring the answer to rest on the rows forces the model into the data.
questions.traps: Reformatting and trimming columns change presentation without changing what the question demands. Re-uploading addresses a failure that did not occur.

questions.stem: An associate adds an instruction to their Project and it works, so they add four more the same week.
options: Continue adding instructions as needs arise, since each one addresses a real requirement and the set will naturally converge on the behaviour the team wants
Test the effect of each addition, since instructions interact rather than accumulate cleanly
Add all five of the instructions and review them on a monthly basis
Order the five instructions by importance so that the most important ones are encountered first and are more likely to be followed by the model
questions.why: Instructions compete rather than stack, so an addition that helps alone may weaken others. Testing the combined effect is what catches that.
questions.traps: Unchecked accumulation is how instruction sets become diluted. Monthly review is slow feedback, and ordering does not reveal interaction effects.

questions.stem: A team's Project knowledge includes a document that has been updated externally three times since it was uploaded.
options: Establish who refreshes uploaded copies and when
Upload the current version now so that the Project reflects the latest state of the document as it exists in the external system today
Add a note saying the document may not be current
Link to the external document instead of uploading a copy
questions.why: Uploaded copies are snapshots that drift. Assigning refresh ownership is what keeps them current rather than relying on someone noticing.
questions.traps: A one-time refresh fixes today and leaves the pattern. A staleness note documents the problem, and linking may not be supported as a knowledge source.

questions.stem: A team wants to add every document their department produces to one Project so nothing is ever missing.
options: Add everything, since a question could concern any of the documents and having them available means nothing is ever unavailable when it is needed
Add everything and rely on retrieval to find what is relevant
Curate to what questions actually need, since irrelevant material degrades answers
Add everything but organise it into clearly named sections
questions.why: Precision falls as irrelevant material competes with what matters. Curation is what makes a knowledge base useful rather than merely complete.
questions.traps: Comprehensiveness for hypothetical questions is the misconception. Relying on retrieval within noise is weaker, and organisation does not remove the competition.

questions.stem: An associate is setting up a Project and wants to know how much detail the instructions need.
options: As much as possible, since more detailed instructions leave less room for the model to make choices that do not match what the team is looking for
Include as little detail as possible in the project instructions
Enough to describe the task fully, including background about why the work matters and how it fits into the wider process the team is responsible for
Enough to remove the decisions you would otherwise repeat in every request
questions.why: Instructions exist to remove repeated decisions. That criterion tells you what to include and what to leave out.
questions.traps: Maximal detail produces the dilution problem. Minimal instructions leave the repetition, and background context is usually not what shapes behaviour.

questions.stem: A team member leaves and their Projects held configuration nobody else has a copy of.
options: Ask departing team members to hand over their Projects as part of the standard leaving process
Treat Project configuration as shared infrastructure with an owner and a backup
Recreate the configuration from scratch
Copy the Projects into a shared location when someone announces they are leaving
questions.why: Single-owner configuration is an ongoing risk that a departure makes visible. Treating it as shared infrastructure is the durable fix.
questions.traps: A handover step addresses planned departures only. Recreation discards working configuration, and a copy at notice time is the same one-off rescue.

questions.stem: An associate cannot decide whether to organise Projects by client, by task type, or by team.
options: Choose the dimension along which context is least shared
Organise by whichever dimension has the most Projects so that each one contains a manageable amount of material within it
Organise by client, since that is the most common approach
Organise by all three dimensions using a naming convention that captures each of them
questions.why: Project boundaries exist to isolate context. Splitting along the dimension where context is least shared is what makes each Project coherent.
questions.traps: Counting Projects is not a design criterion. Convention for its own sake ignores the specific situation, and encoding three dimensions in names does not create isolation.

questions.stem: A team's Project contains a document with information that is correct but that the team is not permitted to share externally.
options: Add an instruction telling the model not to include information from that document in any output that is intended for an external audience
Remove the document from the Project's knowledge altogether
Check whether the Project's sharing scope matches the document's restrictions
Mark the document as confidential so that anyone using the Project is aware of the restriction that applies to the material it contains
questions.why: Restricted material in a Project shared beyond its permitted audience is a disclosure risk regardless of instructions. Matching scope to restriction is the control.
questions.traps: Output instructions rely on correct application every time. Removing it may lose needed content, and a marking informs users without restricting access.

questions.stem: A team's project instructions describe the output format, and the format has changed but the instructions have not.
options: Ask people to specify the new format in their requests until the instructions can be updated at some point when someone has time to do it
Add the new format alongside the old one in the instructions
Ask the model to use the most recent format it has seen
Update the instructions, since they are the authority for every response
questions.why: Standing instructions govern every response until changed. Updating them is the direct fix and takes less effort than working around them.
questions.traps: Per-request overrides fight the configuration. Keeping both formats creates ambiguity, and asking the model to infer recency is unreliable.

questions.stem: An associate wants to know whether their Project's knowledge is still serving its purpose.
options: Ask people whether they are satisfied with the answers so that any problems with the Project's knowledge can be identified from user feedback
Check whether recent questions were answered from the documents or from general knowledge
Count up how many documents the Project currently holds in total
Compare the current documents against the list of documents that were originally uploaded to see what has been added or changed since the Project was created
questions.why: Whether answers actually draw on the loaded knowledge is the direct test of whether that knowledge is doing its job.
questions.traps: Satisfaction surveys measure perception. Document counts measure volume, and comparing against the original list tracks changes rather than usefulness.

questions.stem: A team notices their Project performs worse on questions that require combining information from two documents than on questions about a single document.
options: Ask questions that name both documents and the relationship being examined
Move to a model with a larger context window so that both documents can be held in mind more effectively during the course of a single question
Merge the two documents together into a single combined document
Upload the two documents again so that they are positioned next to each other in the Project's knowledge and are more likely to be considered together
questions.why: Cross-document questions benefit from being framed explicitly, because naming both sources and the relationship directs attention to the comparison rather than to either document alone.
questions.traps: A larger window addresses capacity rather than framing. Merging changes the source material, and upload order is not a meaningful lever.

questions.stem: A team is setting up a Project for work that will be done by people with very different levels of expertise.
options: Configure for the most expert user so that the Project's full capability is available and less experienced people can ask for simpler explanations when needed
Create two separate Projects for the two different levels of expertise
Configure for the average level of expertise across the team
Configure for the least expert user, since experts can add detail in their requests
questions.why: Configuring for the least expert user makes the Project usable by everyone, and expertise adds detail through the request rather than requiring different configuration.
questions.traps: Configuring for experts leaves novices stranded. Two Projects doubles maintenance, and an average configuration suits nobody precisely.

questions.stem: An associate shares a Project and colleagues start adding documents to it without telling anyone.
options: Establish who may add knowledge and how additions are agreed
Ask colleagues to notify the team whenever they add a document
Remove the documents that colleagues have added without asking
Review the Project's contents periodically to identify documents that have been added and decide whether each of them should remain in place
questions.why: Shared knowledge needs a contribution model. Establishing who may add and how is the governance fix rather than a cleanup.
questions.traps: Notification relies on remembering. Removing additions is a conflict, and periodic review is ongoing cleanup rather than prevention.

questions.stem: A team's Project works well but is named in a way that means nothing to anyone outside the two people who set it up.
options: Add a description to the Project explaining what it is for, so that the name can stay as it is
Rename it so its purpose is clear to someone encountering it for the first time
Explain the name to colleagues when they need to use it
Keep the name, since the two people who set it up are the main users and renaming would disrupt their own familiarity with the Project
questions.why: Names are what people navigate by. A name that only makes sense to its creators is a barrier to everyone else.
questions.traps: A description helps but the name is what appears in lists. Explaining it is a bottleneck, and preserving creator familiarity prioritises two people over everyone else.

questions.stem: A team's Project holds a policy document, and the questions people ask are mostly about exceptions to that policy.
options: Ask the model to reason about likely exceptions based on the policy document that has been uploaded to the Project's knowledge already
Tell people to ask about the policy instead
Add the material covering exceptions, since that is what the questions are actually about
Add an instruction saying that exceptions exist and should be considered when answering questions about how the policy applies to particular situations
questions.why: Project knowledge should match the questions being asked. When exceptions dominate the questions, exception material is what the Project needs.
questions.traps: Asking the model to infer exceptions invites invention. Redirecting the questions ignores the real need, and an instruction about exceptions without the content adds nothing.

questions.stem: An associate writes a project instruction that works well and wants to know whether to apply it to their other Projects.
options: Test it in each Project, since instructions interact with the material there
Apply it everywhere, since an instruction that improves output in one Project will produce the same improvement in the others as well
Apply the instruction only to the Projects that are similar
Keep it in the one Project, since instructions are specific to the context they were written for and are unlikely to transfer usefully elsewhere
questions.why: Instructions interact with a Project's knowledge and purpose, so transfer is an empirical question rather than an assumption in either direction.
questions.traps: Blanket application assumes transfer. Similarity is a weak proxy, and assuming no transfer forgoes a possible improvement without testing.

questions.stem: A team's Project produces good answers, and nobody knows which of its twenty documents are actually being used.
options: Keep all twenty, since the answers are good and removing documents risks degrading the quality that the Project currently delivers to its users
Check which documents answers draw on so unused material can be removed
Remove whichever of the documents happen to be the oldest ones
Ask users which documents they think are most useful so that the Project's knowledge can be trimmed based on the feedback they provide
questions.why: Identifying which documents contribute is what makes curation evidence-based rather than a guess about what might matter.
questions.traps: Keeping everything because it works avoids the question. Age is not usage, and users cannot see which documents answers drew on.

questions.stem: A team is deciding whether to put a large body of reference material in a Project or to attach the relevant part to each request.
options: Put it in the Project, since persistent knowledge is more convenient than attaching material to every individual request that people make
Attach the relevant material to each separate request instead
Base it on whether the same part is needed each time or a different part each time
Put it in the Project and also attach the relevant part to each request
questions.why: If the same material is needed every time, it belongs in the Project; if a different part is needed each time, attaching is more precise. Usage pattern is the criterion.
questions.traps: Convenience and precision arguments both ignore the usage pattern. Doing both duplicates the material and costs twice.

questions.stem: An associate is asked to set up a Project for a process that is about to change substantially.
options: Set it up now based on the current process so that people can start using it and adjust the configuration
Set it up based on the expected future process
Set up two Projects, one for the current process and one for the future one
Wait until the process settles, or configure only the parts that will not change
questions.why: Configuring against a process that is about to change produces rework. Building only the stable parts is what avoids wasted effort.
questions.traps: Configuring the current process guarantees rework. Configuring an unfinalised future process guesses, and two Projects doubles the work.

questions.stem: A team's Project holds meeting minutes going back two years, and questions are almost always about the last quarter.
options: Keep everything, since an older meeting could occasionally be relevant and having the full history available means those questions can still be answered when they arise
Add an instruction to prefer recent minutes
Keep the recent minutes and archive the rest elsewhere
Reorganise the minutes by topic rather than by date so that the relevant material is easier to locate
questions.why: Curating to the material questions actually use keeps answers precise. Two years of unused minutes compete with the quarter that matters.
questions.traps: Keeping everything for rare cases dilutes the common ones. A preference instruction relies on correct application, and reorganising does not reduce the volume.

questions.stem: An associate's project instruction tells the model to always ask a clarifying question before answering, and colleagues find it slow.
options: Remove the instruction so that answers come back immediately
Keep the instruction exactly as it is
Ask colleagues to provide more detail in their initial requests
Scope the clarifying question to cases where the request is genuinely ambiguous
questions.why: An unconditional clarification rule fires on requests that need no clarification. Scoping it to ambiguity keeps the benefit without the friction.
questions.traps: Removing it loses the benefit on genuinely ambiguous requests. Keeping it ignores the complaint, and asking users to pre-empt it shifts the burden.

questions.stem: A team wants to know whether a document should stay in their Project, and it has not been referenced in any answer for four months.
options: Remove it, and restore it if a question later shows it was needed
Keep it, since four months without a reference does not mean it will never be relevant to a question somebody asks at some point in the future
Keep it in place but mark it as being low priority
Ask the team whether anyone expects to need it, and keep it if any of them says that they might do so at some stage in their work
questions.why: Unused knowledge costs precision on every question. Removing with the option to restore makes curation reversible and low-risk.
questions.traps: Keeping against hypothetical need is how knowledge bases bloat. Priority marking does not reduce the material, and canvassing for maybes finds a reason to keep everything.

questions.stem: A team shares a Project with a partner organisation and wants to be sure nothing confidential is exposed.
options: Add an instruction telling the model not to disclose confidential information to external users who are accessing the Project through the sharing arrangement
Review what the Project holds against what the partner may see, before sharing
Share it and monitor the questions that get asked
Ask the partner to agree not to ask questions that would require confidential information to be included in the answers they receive from the Project
questions.why: Sharing exposes the Project's contents to its audience. Auditing what it holds against what the audience may see is the control that does not depend on runtime behaviour.
questions.traps: Output instructions rely on correct classification every time. Monitoring detects after disclosure, and a partner agreement does not restrict what the system can produce.

questions.stem: An associate has Projects that are each used by one person and Projects used by the whole team, with no way to tell them apart.
options: Ask people to check with the team before changing any Project in case it turns out to be one that other people are also relying on for their work
Make every one of the Projects a shared Project
Keep a list recording which Projects are shared and which are personal
Adopt a convention that distinguishes shared Projects from personal ones
questions.why: The distinction matters for how changes are made, so it needs to be visible at the point of use. A naming convention carries it.
questions.traps: Pre-change checks depend on remembering. Making everything shared removes personal space, and an external list is another artefact to maintain.

questions.stem: A team is configuring a Project and wants the model to refuse questions outside its scope.
options: Assume the model will recognise when a question falls outside the Project's purpose based on the documents that have been uploaded to it
List out the topics that it should refuse to answer
State the scope and instruct it to decline and say why when asked outside it
Add an instruction telling the model to be cautious about answering questions that seem to fall outside what the Project was designed to handle
questions.why: Refusal behaviour needs the boundary stated and the response defined. Saying why the question is out of scope is what makes the refusal useful.
questions.traps: Assuming recognition leaves the boundary implicit. An exclusion list cannot be exhaustive, and vague caution produces hedged answers rather than clear refusals.

questions.stem: A team's Project answers have degraded since they doubled the number of documents, and all the documents are relevant.
options: Check whether the questions need all of them, or split into focused Projects
Accept the degradation as the cost of having comprehensive knowledge available within a single Project that covers the whole of the team's subject area
Move to a model with a larger context window
Ask users to be more specific in their questions so that the relevant documents are easier to identify within the larger body of material
questions.why: Relevance to the subject is not the same as relevance to each question. Splitting into focused Projects restores precision where broad coverage was diluting it.
questions.traps: Accepting degradation forgoes a fixable problem. A larger window accommodates rather than resolves, and user specificity works around the structure.

questions.stem: An associate uploads a document to a Project and answers do not appear to reflect it at all.
options: Rewrite the questions so that they refer more directly to the material contained in the document that has recently been added to the Project
Check the document uploaded and processed correctly before changing anything else
Upload the document again in case it failed
Add an instruction telling the model to consult the newly uploaded document when answering questions that relate to the topics it covers
questions.why: When new knowledge has no effect, the first question is whether it is actually present and readable. That is checkable before any other change.
questions.traps: Rewording, re-uploading and instructing all assume the document is there and usable, which is the assumption to test first.

questions.stem: A team's project instructions include a rule that was added to fix a problem that no longer occurs.
options: Keep it in case the problem recurs, since removing it would mean the issue could come back
Keep it but note that it may be obsolete
Move it to the end of the instructions so that it has less influence
Remove it, since standing instructions apply to everything and cost attention
questions.why: Every instruction consumes attention that other instructions need. A rule addressing a resolved problem is a permanent cost for no benefit.
questions.traps: Retaining against recurrence pays indefinitely. A note does not reduce the cost, and repositioning keeps it in effect.

questions.stem: A team's Project knowledge is accurate but written for an audience with more expertise than the people now asking questions.
options: Keep the material as it is, since it is accurate and the model can be relied upon to explain technical content in accessible terms when it is asked to do so
Ask users to look up terms they do not understand
Add material pitched at the current audience, or instruct the model to translate
Replace the material with simpler versions so that everything in the Project is pitched at the level of the people who are currently using it
questions.why: A mismatch between source register and audience is addressed by adding accessible material or instructing translation, both of which preserve the accurate source.
questions.traps: Assuming automatic translation without instruction is unreliable. Asking users to look things up shifts the burden, and replacing accurate material risks losing precision.

questions.stem: An associate wants colleagues to use their Project but not to change how it is configured.
options: Ask colleagues not to change the instructions, since they should have no reason to modify a configuration that has been set up for the purpose they are using it for
Share it in a way that grants use without configuration rights
Keep the Project private and run requests for them
Take a copy of the configuration so that it can be restored if a colleague changes something that affects how the Project behaves for other users
questions.why: Access levels are what enforce the distinction between using and editing. Sharing at the right level makes the constraint structural.
questions.traps: A request relies on compliance. Running requests for people is a bottleneck, and a restorable copy is recovery rather than prevention.

questions.stem: A team has one Project that has grown to serve four unrelated purposes because it was the first one anyone created.
options: Split it along the purposes so each has its own scope and knowledge
Keep it as a single Project and use clear instructions describing which behaviour applies to each of the four different purposes it currently serves
Keep the single Project and simply rename it
