Add documents covering all four purposes more thoroughly
questions.why: Four unrelated purposes in one Project means every question sees all four sets of context. Splitting restores the isolation each purpose needs.
questions.traps: Conditional instructions must be resolved correctly every time. Renaming changes the label, and adding material makes the dilution worse.

questions.stem: A team's Project includes a document that is mostly irrelevant but contains one crucial paragraph.
options: Include the whole document, since the crucial paragraph needs its surrounding context in order to be interpreted correctly by anyone reading it
Include the document and highlight the paragraph
Summarise the document so that the crucial paragraph is retained alongside a condensed version of everything else it happens to contain
Extract the paragraph and include that rather than the whole document
questions.why: Curating to what matters keeps the signal strong. One crucial paragraph does not justify carrying a document of irrelevant material on every question.
questions.traps: Including everything for context dilutes it. Highlighting relies on the emphasis being honoured, and summarising still carries the irrelevant material in compressed form.

questions.stem: An associate is setting up a Project and cannot decide whether to make it broad or narrow in scope.
options: Make it broad so that it can handle a wide range of questions
Make it narrow, since narrow scope produces precise answers and Projects are cheap to create
Make it broad initially and narrow it later
Make its scope match the department's remit so that the boundary is meaningful to the organisation and easy for people to reason about when they use it
questions.why: Narrow scope keeps context relevant to every question, and creating another Project is cheap. That trade favours precision.
questions.traps: Broad scope dilutes every answer. Narrowing later means untangling accumulated material, and organisational remit is not the same as question coherence.

questions.stem: A team's Project answers cite a document accurately but the document itself contains an error nobody has noticed.
options: Recognise that knowledge quality bounds answer quality, and verify the sources
Improve the instructions so the model checks claims before including them in the answers it produces for the team's questions
Add a second document that contradicts the first one
Ask the model to indicate when it is uncertain about a claim
questions.why: A Project cannot be more accurate than what it holds. Verifying the source material is the only thing that addresses an error in the knowledge itself.
questions.traps: Instructions cannot check facts against a source the model does not have. A contradicting document creates conflict, and uncertainty flags do not detect a confidently wrong source.

questions.stem: A team wants their Project to produce output in a fixed structure, and roughly one response in ten deviates.
options: Strengthen the wording of the instruction until the deviations stop occurring in the responses that the Project produces for the team
Ask users to reformat the responses that deviate
State the structure precisely and validate responses before they are used
Add an instruction telling the model to check its own output against the required structure before returning it to the person who asked the question
questions.why: Instruction plus validation is the durable pattern. The instruction lowers the rate and the check handles what gets through, which no wording alone eliminates.
questions.traps: Stronger wording chases an asymptote. Manual reformatting repeats forever, and self-checking inside the same response is not independent.

questions.stem: An associate finds their Project contains three versions of the same document uploaded at different times.
options: Keep all three so that the history of how the document has changed over time remains available to anyone who needs to understand its evolution
Rename the three versions by their upload date
Add an instruction telling the model to use the most recent of the three versions
Keep the current version and remove the others
questions.why: Multiple versions of the same document produce inconsistent answers. Keeping only the current one is what makes the Project's knowledge unambiguous.
questions.traps: Version history belongs elsewhere. Date naming relies on correct selection, and a recency instruction has the same dependency.

questions.stem: A team's shared Project is used by people in two departments who need slightly different things from it.
options: Add instructions covering both departments' needs so that the single Project serves each of them appropriately
Check whether the difference is large enough to warrant separate Projects
Ask each department to specify their department in their questions
Configure it for the larger department, since that covers the majority of the usage and the other department can adapt their questions accordingly
questions.why: Whether one Project can serve both depends on how far the requirements diverge. Assessing that is the question before choosing a mechanism.
questions.traps: Conditional instructions and per-question department flags both presume one Project is right. Configuring for the majority ignores the other department's needs.

questions.stem: An associate wants to find a Project they set up eight months ago and remembers only roughly what it was for.
options: Search each Project's contents until the right one is found
Recreate the Project from scratch instead
Improve the naming going forward so this does not recur
Ask colleagues whether they remember the Project being set up and what it might have been called at the time it was originally created
questions.why: The immediate search is unavoidable, but the durable answer is a naming convention that makes Projects findable by what they do.
questions.traps: Searching solves today and leaves the pattern. Recreating duplicates work, and asking colleagues about a personal Project is unlikely to help.

questions.stem: A team wants to know why their Project sometimes misses information that is definitely in one of its documents.
options: Ask questions that name the topic more specifically so retrieval has more to work with
Upload the document again so that it is processed freshly and the information becomes available to the model when it answers future questions
Reduce the total number of documents held
Add an instruction telling the model to search all documents thoroughly before concluding that information is not available in the Project's knowledge
questions.why: Retrieval over a body of documents depends on how well the question matches the material. Naming the topic specifically is the lever you control.
questions.traps: Re-uploading addresses a processing failure that is not indicated. Reducing documents is a blunt fix, and thoroughness instructions do not change how matching works.

questions.stem: A team is configuring a Project and wants to prevent people from using it for work it is not suitable for.
options: Restrict access to the people who understand what the Project is suitable for so that inappropriate use does not arise in the first place
State what it is for and what it is not for, in the instructions and the name
Rely on people's own judgement about scope
Monitor how the Project is being used and intervene when someone uses it for something it was not designed to handle appropriately
questions.why: Making the scope visible in the name and the instructions is what lets people self-select correctly without gatekeeping or monitoring.
questions.traps: Access restriction limits legitimate use. Relying on judgement without stating scope leaves people guessing, and monitoring intervenes after misuse.

questions.stem: An associate's Project holds documents in three languages and answers are inconsistent in quality between them.
options: Translate all the documents into one language so that the Project's knowledge is consistent and the answers do not vary
Ask questions in the language of the relevant document
Test performance per language and curate accordingly
Accept the variation, since handling several languages within one body of knowledge is inherently more difficult than working in a single language
questions.why: Performance varies by language, so measuring it per language is what tells you whether the material needs translating, splitting or leaving alone.
questions.traps: Translating everything is expensive and may be unnecessary. Matching question language is a workaround, and accepting variation skips the measurement.

questions.stem: A team's project instruction produces good results for most questions and unhelpful results for one common question type.
options: Rewrite the general instruction so that it produces good results for the problematic question type as well as for everything else it currently handles
Tell people to avoid that type of question
Create a second Project specifically for the question type that the current instructions do not handle well enough for the team's purposes
Add a scoped rule for that question type rather than changing the general instruction
questions.why: A scoped addition preserves what already works while handling the exception. Rewriting the general rule risks the majority case.
questions.traps: A general rewrite trades working behaviour for the exception. Avoiding the question type ignores a real need, and a second Project is heavier than a scoped rule.

questions.stem: A team's Project contains a document nobody can identify the source or date of.
options: Establish its provenance or remove it, since unattributable knowledge cannot be trusted
Keep it, since the content appears accurate and removing material that is producing useful answers would reduce the Project's usefulness to the team
Keep it and add a note about the uncertainty
Ask the team whether anyone recognises the document and keep it if nobody objects to it remaining in the Project's knowledge base
questions.why: Knowledge whose origin cannot be established cannot be verified or maintained. Resolving provenance or removing it is what keeps the Project trustworthy.
questions.traps: Apparent accuracy is not verification. A note documents the problem, and absence of objection is not provenance.

questions.stem: An associate wants to share a Project's configuration with another team without sharing its documents.
options: Share the whole Project and ask the other team not to look at the documents that are not relevant to the work they are doing with it
Describe the configuration to them verbally
Share the instructions as a template the other team populates with their own material
Give the other team read access so they can see how it is set up and build their own version based on what they observe about the configuration
questions.why: Separating the reusable method from the local material is what makes configuration shareable without exposing content.
questions.traps: Sharing everything with a request not to look is not a control. A verbal description is lossy, and read access still exposes the documents.

questions.stem: A team's Projects each work well individually but there is no record of which ones exist or who uses them.
options: Ask people to name their Projects clearly so that the purpose of each one is evident from its name
Maintain a register with owner and purpose for each Project
Consolidate the four purposes into fewer Projects
Review the Projects annually so that the team has an up-to-date picture of what exists and who is responsible for each one at that point in time
questions.why: An inventory with ownership is what makes a growing set of Projects governable, particularly when people leave or Projects fall out of use.
questions.traps: Good naming helps discovery but records neither ownership nor usage. Consolidation destroys isolation, and an annual review is a register maintained slowly.

questions.stem: A team's Project performs well on questions about recent documents and poorly on older ones, and all are equally relevant.
options: Upload the older documents again so that they are processed in the same way as the more recent ones that appear to be working correctly
Reduce the total number of documents held
Ask questions about older material more specifically so that the model is more likely to locate the relevant sections within those documents
Check whether the older documents are formatted differently from the recent ones
questions.why: A systematic difference between two groups of documents usually reflects a difference in the documents themselves, such as format or structure, which is checkable.
questions.traps: Re-uploading assumes a processing failure without evidence. Reducing documents is blunt, and question specificity works around an unexplained pattern.

questions.stem: An associate is setting up a Project and wants to know whether to include examples of good output.
options: Include them if the output has a shape that is hard to describe but easy to show
Include them always, since examples are the most reliable way to communicate what is wanted and will improve output
Leave the examples out of the configuration
Include a large number of examples so that the model has as much material as possible to learn the expected pattern from within the configuration
questions.why: Examples earn their place when the target is easier to demonstrate than to describe. That criterion is what decides whether to include them.
questions.traps: Always including examples spends configuration space regardless of need. Excluding them loses a strong technique, and a large number dilutes other instructions.

questions.stem: A team's Project holds a long document and questions concern only its tables, which the answers often get wrong.
options: Ask questions that refer specifically to the tables so that the model knows to look at them
Upload the document a second time to be sure
Add an instruction telling the model that the tables are the most important part of the document and should be consulted before the prose sections
Extract the tables into their own document so they are not buried in prose
questions.why: Structured data buried in a long prose document is harder to use. Extracting it into its own document is what makes it directly available.
questions.traps: Question specificity and instructions both work around the structure. Re-uploading does not change how the content is organised.

questions.stem: A team's project instructions have never been reviewed and were written by someone who has since changed roles.
options: Leave them, since the Project is producing good answers and changing the instructions risks degrading behaviour that currently works well for everyone
Rewrite the instructions from scratch entirely
Review them against what the Project is currently used for
Ask the original author whether the instructions are still appropriate for how the Project is being used by the team at the moment
questions.why: Configuration written for an earlier purpose may not match current use. Reviewing against actual usage is what establishes whether it still fits.
questions.traps: Leaving them unexamined assumes continued fit. Rewriting discards working configuration, and the original author no longer knows current usage.

questions.stem: An associate wants to add a document to a Project but is not sure whether it duplicates material already there.
options: Add it, since additional material can only improve the Project's coverage of the topics the team asks questions about in their work
Check what is already there before adding, since duplication produces inconsistency
Add it now and remove any duplicates later on
Add it and rely on the model to reconcile any differences between the new document and the material that is already in the Project
questions.why: Duplicated or near-duplicated material produces inconsistent answers depending on which copy is drawn on. Checking first prevents that.
questions.traps: Assuming more is better ignores the inconsistency. Deferring cleanup lets the problem operate, and expecting reconciliation asks the model to resolve a conflict it cannot verify.

questions.stem: A team's shared Project is producing answers that suit the person who configured it and not the rest of the team.
options: Gather what the others need and reconfigure against the whole team's use
Ask the other team members to adjust their questions so that they get the answers they need from the current configuration of the Project
Let each person keep their own separate Project
Ask the person who configured it to explain their reasoning
questions.why: Shared configuration should be built from shared requirements. Gathering what the team needs is what makes it serve the team rather than its author.
questions.traps: Asking users to adapt puts the burden in the wrong place. Individual Projects lose the sharing benefit, and an explanation does not change the configuration.

questions.stem: A team is deciding whether to keep one Project per document set or one per workflow.
options: Follow the document sets, since that keeps each Project's knowledge coherent and makes it obvious which documents belong in which Project
Follow the workflow, since that is what determines which material is needed together
Follow whichever of them produces fewer Projects
Follow the document sets initially and reorganise around workflows later
questions.why: Projects exist to serve work, and a workflow determines which material must be available together. That is the boundary that makes each Project coherent in use.
questions.traps: Document-set boundaries organise the material rather than the work. Minimising Project count is not a design criterion, and planned reorganisation defers the decision.

questions.stem: An associate's Project gives shorter answers than it used to, and the only change was adding more documents.
options: Check whether the added material is competing with what the questions need
Ask for longer answers in the instructions so that the responses return to the length they were before the additional documents were added
Remove whichever documents were most recently added
Accept the change, since answer length is not by itself an indication that the quality of the answers has declined in any meaningful way
questions.why: A change in behaviour following a change in knowledge points at the added material competing for attention. Checking that is the direct diagnosis.
questions.traps: A length instruction treats the symptom. Removing recent additions may be right but skips the diagnosis, and dismissing the change ignores a signal.

questions.stem: A team wants their Project to be usable by someone who has never used one before.
options: Write a guide explaining how Projects work so that new users understand the concept before they attempt to use the one the team has set up
Have an experienced user run the Project for them
Configure it so a first-time user needs to supply only the variable input
Add instructions to the Project explaining to the user what they should do
questions.why: Usability comes from removing what the user must know. If only the variable input is required, prior familiarity stops mattering.
questions.traps: A guide teaches a concept rather than removing the need for it. A proxy user is a bottleneck, and in-Project guidance still requires the user to act on it.

questions.stem: A team's Project contains documents that are correct individually but describe processes that changed at different times.
options: Keep them all and add an instruction explaining the order in which the processes changed
Keep only the most recent of the three documents
Add dates to each document so that the model can determine which of them describes the most current version of the process being asked about
Establish which describes current practice and remove the rest
questions.why: Overlapping descriptions of a changing process produce inconsistent answers. Identifying current practice and removing the rest is what resolves it.
questions.traps: Chronology instructions and dates both rely on correct inference. Keeping the most recent is close but assumes recency equals currency without checking.

questions.stem: An associate wants their Project to behave differently depending on who is asking, and everyone shares one configuration.
options: Write instructions describing the different behaviours and ask users to identify themselves at the start of each question they put to the Project
Configure it for the most common kind of user
Recognise that one configuration serves everyone, and split if the needs truly differ
Add all the different behaviours to the instructions so that the model can choose whichever one seems most appropriate for the question it receives
questions.why: Standing configuration applies uniformly. If per-user behaviour is genuinely needed, separate Projects is the structural answer rather than a runtime conditional.
questions.traps: Self-identification and model-selected behaviour both depend on correct resolution each time. Configuring for the common user ignores the others.

questions.stem: A team's Project knowledge is well curated but nobody has checked whether the documents are still accurate.
options: Verify the content, since curation and accuracy are different properties
Assume the documents are accurate, since they were selected deliberately and the team has been using the Project
Ask the model to check the documents itself
Re-upload the documents from their original sources so that the Project holds whatever the current version of each of them happens to be
questions.why: Selecting the right documents does not establish that they are correct. Verification is a separate check from curation.
questions.traps: Absence of noticed problems is weak evidence. Model self-checking has no external reference, and re-uploading refreshes without verifying.

questions.stem: A team wants to give a contractor access to a Project for a three-month engagement.
options: Grant access and remove it when the engagement ends, which the team will remember to do because the end date is known in advance to everyone involved
Grant the contractor permanent access instead
Give the contractor a copy of the Project so that they have what they need
Plan the access removal at the same time as granting it
questions.why: Time-bounded access should have its removal planned when it is granted, because that is when the end date is known and the intent is clear.
questions.traps: Relying on remembering at the end is how access persists. Permanent access outlives the engagement, and a copy distributes the material without any control at all.

questions.stem: An associate's Projects work well but they cannot explain to a new team member how the set is organised.
options: Explain the Projects individually so the new team member learns what each of them is for as they encounter them during the course of their work
Take the inability to explain it as the signal that the organisation needs work
Give them access to everything and let them look
Ask the new team member to work it out over time, since familiarity with how the Projects are organised will develop naturally as they use them
questions.why: If the scheme cannot be explained, it is not a scheme. That difficulty is the diagnostic rather than a communication problem.
questions.traps: Explaining case by case transfers a list rather than a structure. Broad access and learning by exposure both leave the disorganisation intact.

questions.stem: A team is creating a Project for work that involves both confidential client material and general reference documents.
options: Keep them together and restrict who can access it
Keep them together and label the confidential documents
Add an instruction about confidentiality
Separate them, since the confidential material constrains who the Project can be shared with and general reference does not
questions.why: The sharing scope of a Project is set by its most restricted content. Separating them lets the general material be shared freely while the confidential Project stays closed.
questions.traps: Restricting access to the combined Project applies the strictest rule to everything. Labels and instructions govern output rather than access.

questions.stem: An associate's Project answers questions about a document accurately but cannot answer questions that require combining it with a second document.
options: Upload the two documents as one combined file
Frame the question so it names both documents and the relationship between them that is actually being asked about
Ask about each document separately and combine the answers
Add an instruction about cross-referencing
questions.why: Cross-document reasoning improves markedly when the question names both sources and the relationship, because that directs attention to the comparison rather than to either document alone.
questions.traps: Combining files changes the source material. Separate questions leave the synthesis to you, and a general instruction does not shape a particular question.

questions.stem: A team's project instruction asks for citations, and the model cites the right documents but not the right passages within them.
options: Accept citations at the document level
Ask for direct quotations instead of citations
Ask for the specific passage or section, since a document-level citation is not precise enough to check
Add an instruction saying citations must be accurate
questions.why: A citation is only useful if it takes a reader to the claim. Specifying the granularity is what makes it checkable rather than merely present.
questions.traps: Document-level citations leave the reader searching. Quotations are heavier than needed, and an accuracy instruction does not specify precision.

questions.stem: A team's Project has grown steadily and answers are still good, so nobody sees a reason to review the knowledge.
options: Review anyway, since degradation is gradual and there is no point at which it announces itself
Wait until the answers get noticeably worse
Review only when documents are added
Ask users to report when answers seem to have declined in quality
questions.why: Knowledge degradation is gradual and invisible against a moving baseline. A scheduled review is what catches it before anyone notices a problem.
questions.traps: Waiting for visible decline means operating on degraded answers meanwhile. Add-triggered review misses staleness, and user reports are late and unreliable.

questions.stem: An associate wants to include a document that is mostly relevant but contains a long appendix that never matters.
options: Upload the whole of the document anyway
Upload it and instruct the model to ignore the appendix
Summarise the appendix rather than removing it
Remove the appendix before uploading, since it competes for attention on every question asked
questions.why: Every question pays the cost of irrelevant material. Removing what never matters is the simplest way to keep the remaining content prominent.
questions.traps: Uploading everything carries the cost permanently. An ignore instruction relies on correct application, and a summary still occupies space for no benefit.

questions.stem: A team wants a Project's answers to be consistent whether asked by a junior or senior colleague.
options: Ask each person to state their own level
Configure it once for the shared purpose, since standing configuration applies the same way to everyone
Create separate Projects by seniority
Add instructions describing how to adjust for different levels of experience
questions.why: A single configuration already produces the same behaviour for everyone. Consistency is the default here, and adding per-person variation is what would break it.
questions.traps: Self-identification introduces the variation the team wants to avoid. Seniority-based Projects fragment, and adjustment instructions create inconsistency deliberately.

questions.stem: A team's Project names are clear but the set has grown to thirty and finding the right one still takes time.
options: Rename them more descriptively
Reduce the overall number of Projects
Group them by the work they serve so the set has structure rather than only good names
Keep a list of the thirty Projects and what each one is used for
questions.why: Clear names solve identification but not navigation at scale. Grouping adds the structure that makes a large set traversable.
questions.traps: More descriptive names do not organise thirty items. Reducing the count discards useful isolation, and an external list is another artefact to maintain.

questions.stem: A team's Project holds a document that people frequently ask about, and the answers are consistently too general.
options: Check whether the document itself is general, since the answers cannot be more specific than the source
Ask more specific questions of it
Add an instruction requesting more detailed answers
Upload additional documents on the same topic
questions.why: Answer specificity is bounded by source specificity. Checking the document is what distinguishes a knowledge problem from a prompting one.
questions.traps: Question and instruction changes both assume the detail exists in the source. Adding documents may help but skips the diagnosis.

questions.stem: An associate's Project produces good answers but always in a formal register that does not suit the internal audience.
options: Ask for a less formal tone in each request
Rewrite the answers before sharing them
Set the register in the instructions, since it applies to every response the Project produces
Add examples of the desired tone to the Project's knowledge documents
questions.why: Register that should apply to every response belongs in standing configuration rather than being restated per request.
questions.traps: Per-request tone requests are the manual work configuration removes. Rewriting repeats forever, and tone examples in knowledge documents are weaker than an instruction.

questions.stem: A team wants to reduce their Project's knowledge but is worried about removing something that turns out to be needed.
options: Remove nothing at all from it
Remove in stages and watch for questions that stop being answerable
Remove everything not referenced in the last month
Ask the team to vote on which documents to keep
questions.why: Staged removal with observation makes curation reversible and evidence-based, which is what addresses the worry directly.
questions.traps: Removing nothing accepts the bloat. A one-month reference window may miss quarterly needs, and voting substitutes opinion for evidence.

questions.stem: A team notices that their Project handles the first question in a session well and later questions less well.
options: Check whether the conversation history is accumulating and competing with the project knowledge
Start a new session for each question
Move to a larger context window
Ask shorter questions later in the session
questions.why: Growing conversation history competes with loaded knowledge for attention. Identifying that as the cause is what points at the right remedy.
questions.traps: Restarting per question is a workaround. A larger window accommodates rather than diagnoses, and shorter questions do not reduce accumulated history.

questions.stem: An associate is asked to set up a Project and is given a folder of forty documents to include.
options: Include all forty of the documents
Include the twenty most recent documents
Include the documents and let usage show which ones matter
Ask what questions the Project must answer, and include what those questions need
questions.why: The Project's purpose determines its knowledge. Starting from the questions is what produces a curated set rather than a copied folder.
questions.traps: Including everything imports whatever the folder happened to hold. Recency and observed usage are proxies chosen without knowing the purpose.

questions.stem: A team's Project is shared widely and someone has asked whether its answers can be relied on for a regulatory submission.
options: Say yes, since the Project's answers have been reliable
Say no, since generated answers should not be used in regulatory work
Establish what the Project's knowledge covers and whether it has been verified for that purpose
Add a disclaimer to the Project's instructions
questions.why: Fitness for a regulatory purpose depends on what the knowledge covers and whether it has been verified to that standard. That is establishable rather than a matter of general policy.
questions.traps: A blanket yes rests on informal experience. A blanket no forecloses a legitimate use, and a disclaimer shifts risk without answering the question.

questions.stem: A team has Projects for active work and Projects for work that finished months ago, all appearing in the same list.
options: Delete the finished Projects outright
Archive the finished ones so the active set stays legible
Rename the finished ones with a prefix
Leave them, since they cost nothing to keep and may be useful for reference at some point in the future
questions.why: Separating active from finished keeps the working set navigable while preserving the finished work. That is what archiving is for.
questions.traps: Deletion loses material that may still be needed. Prefixes leave everything in one list, and leaving them mixed is the problem being described.

questions.stem: An associate's Project contains a document written in a heavily abbreviated internal style that the model interprets inconsistently.
options: Supply a key to the abbreviations, since the model has no way to resolve internal shorthand
Rewrite the whole document in full prose
Ask the model to infer the abbreviations from context
Accept the inconsistency as a limitation of the material
questions.why: Internal shorthand is not resolvable from general knowledge. Supplying the key is the smallest change that makes the document usable.
questions.traps: A full rewrite is expensive. Inference from context is exactly what is producing the inconsistency, and accepting it forgoes a cheap fix.

questions.stem: A team's project instructions and one of its knowledge documents give conflicting guidance on the same point.
options: Add an instruction saying the instructions take precedence
Remove the conflicting document
Ask users to specify which guidance they want applied
Resolve the conflict at source, since leaving it makes behaviour depend on which one wins
questions.why: A conflict between configuration and knowledge produces unpredictable behaviour. Resolving it is what makes the Project's output consistent.
questions.traps: A precedence rule leaves the contradiction in place. Removing the document may lose needed content, and per-user resolution pushes the conflict outward.

questions.stem: A team's Project has an owner on paper, but that person has not looked at it in a year and does not know what it contains.
options: Ask the current owner to review it
Reassign ownership to someone who will actually maintain it
Remove the owner designation
Distribute ownership across the team so that responsibility is shared
questions.why: Nominal ownership provides no maintenance. Assigning it to someone who will do the work is what makes the designation real.
questions.traps: A one-off review does not establish ongoing maintenance. Removing the owner leaves it unowned, and shared ownership diffuses responsibility.

questions.stem: An associate wants to know whether adding a document will slow their Project down noticeably.
options: Assume it will, since more context always costs time
Assume it will not, since documents are processed efficiently
Test with and without it, since the effect depends on the document and the questions
Add it and monitor the response times over the following weeks
questions.why: The effect depends on size and on how questions interact with it, which makes this a quick empirical question rather than a matter of assumption.
questions.traps: Both assumptions substitute a general belief for a cheap measurement. Monitoring after the fact is slower than testing before.

questions.stem: A team shares a Project and a colleague reports getting different answers than the person who configured it.
options: Check whether the colleague's own account settings are altering the responses
Assume it is just normal variation
Ask the colleague to rephrase their questions
Have the configuring person ask the same questions and compare the two sets of answers
questions.why: Account-level settings apply to every request and are invisible in the Project. They are the systematic explanation for a difference between two people using the same configuration.
questions.traps: Attributing it to variation skips a systematic cause. Rephrasing tests a different hypothesis, and comparing answers confirms the difference without explaining it.

questions.stem: A team's Projects are organised well but new team members keep creating duplicates because they cannot tell what already exists.
options: Delete the duplicate Projects as they appear
Delete the duplicates as they appear
Accept the duplication, since it is easier than policing how people organise their own work within the tool
Make the existing set discoverable before people start creating their own
questions.why: Duplication happens because discovery failed. Making the existing set visible is what removes the reason to create a new one.
questions.traps: Pre-creation checks depend on remembering and on knowing whom to ask. Deleting duplicates is ongoing cleanup, and accepting it lets the set fragment.

questions.stem: An associate is configuring a Project and wants to know whether to specify the output length.
options: Specify it if the length matters for how the output is used
Always specify it
Never specify the output length
Specify a maximum but not a minimum so the model has room to be brief when brevity is appropriate for the question being asked
questions.why: Configuration should encode what actually matters for the use. If length is load-bearing, it belongs in the instructions; if not, it is a constraint for no reason.
questions.traps: Always and never both ignore whether length matters. A maximum-only rule is a reasonable default rather than the criterion being tested.

questions.stem: A team's Project holds thorough documentation and users still ask questions the documentation covers, because they cannot find the answer themselves.
options: Direct users to the documentation instead
Remove the documentation from the Project
Add an instruction telling the model to point users to the relevant section
Recognise that this is the Project working as intended
questions.why: Making documented information accessible through questions is precisely what project knowledge is for. The described situation is the intended outcome.
questions.traps: Redirecting users to the documents removes the value. Removing the documentation removes the knowledge, and pointing rather than answering adds a step for no gain.

questions.stem: A team wants their Project to stop producing a particular unwanted behaviour and has added three instructions about it without effect.
options: Add a fourth instruction more forcefully worded
Remove all three of the instructions
Look at whether something else in the configuration is causing it
Ask users to correct the behaviour manually when it appears in the output they receive from the Project
questions.why: Three failed instructions suggests the cause is elsewhere, such as a knowledge document or a conflicting rule. Looking for it is what breaks the loop.
questions.traps: A fourth instruction repeats a failed approach. Removing them without diagnosis loses whatever partial effect they had, and manual correction accepts the behaviour.

questions.stem: A team's Project knowledge was curated carefully at setup and has had documents added ad hoc ever since.
options: Recurate the whole Project from scratch
Apply the same curation standard to additions as was applied at setup
Remove everything added since setup
Ask people to be more careful about what they add in future
questions.why: The setup standard exists and simply is not being applied to additions. Extending it to the ongoing process is what stops the drift.
questions.traps: A full recuration repeats work the setup already did. Removing all additions discards useful material, and asking for care without a standard changes nothing.

questions.stem: An associate finds their Project works well for short questions and poorly for long detailed ones.
options: Check whether the long questions are competing with the loaded knowledge for attention
Ask people to shorten their questions
Move to a larger context window
Split long questions into several shorter ones and combine the answers afterwards
questions.why: A long question adds to everything else being held at once. Recognising that the question itself consumes attention is the diagnosis.
questions.traps: Shortening questions loses detail. A larger window accommodates rather than explains, and splitting is a workaround for an undiagnosed cause.

questions.stem: A team wants two people to be able to change a Project's configuration but wants changes to be visible to everyone.
options: Give both people edit rights and ask them to tell the team about changes
Establish a change record alongside the edit rights
Give edit rights to one person only
Ask both people to keep their own notes about the changes they make to the Project
questions.why: Visibility of changes requires a record, and pairing it with the edit rights is what makes the arrangement work rather than depending on people announcing changes.
questions.traps: Verbal notification depends on remembering. Single editorship removes the second editor rather than solving visibility, and private notes are not visible to everyone.

questions.stem: A team's naming convention works but people keep abbreviating names differently when they refer to Projects in conversation.
options: Ask people to use the full Project names
Rename the Projects with shorter names
Publish a list of approved abbreviations so that everyone refers to each Project in the same way when they discuss them
Recognise this as a conversational habit rather than a problem with the organisation
questions.why: Informal abbreviation in speech does not affect how Projects are stored or found. Distinguishing a real organisational problem from a conversational one is the judgement here.
questions.traps: Policing speech is disproportionate. Renaming changes the system to suit informal usage, and an abbreviation list adds a rule for a non-problem.

questions.stem: An associate sets up a Project and the first few answers are poor, so they consider abandoning the approach.
options: Abandon it and use plain conversations
Add more documents to the Project
Check whether the configuration matches the questions before concluding the approach is wrong
Try a stronger model tier so the Project's answers improve
questions.why: Early poor results usually reflect a mismatch between configuration and questions. Diagnosing that is what distinguishes a fixable setup from an unsuitable approach.
questions.traps: Abandoning discards the approach on one attempt. More documents and a stronger tier both change inputs without identifying the mismatch.

questions.stem: A team's Project produces answers that mix the organisation's own policy with general industry practice, without distinguishing them.
options: Remove the general knowledge
Instruct it to answer from the documents and to mark anything drawn from general knowledge
Add more policy documents to it
Ask users to check whether each answer reflects internal policy or general practice before they rely on it in their own work
questions.why: The blend is invisible in the output. Requiring the distinction is what makes the two sources separable by the reader.
questions.traps: General knowledge cannot be removed from the model. More documents does not mark the boundary, and asking users to detect it puts an impossible check on them.

questions.stem: A team wants to know whether their project instructions are actually affecting the output.
options: Assume that they are working
Ask the model whether it is following the instructions
Review the output to see whether it looks like the instructions have been applied to it
Test with and without them, since assumption is not evidence about effect
questions.why: Removing the instructions and comparing is the direct test of whether they change anything, and it takes one comparison.
questions.traps: Assumption is what the question is testing. Self-reported compliance is unreliable, and inspecting output alone cannot separate instruction effects from default behaviour.

questions.stem: An associate's Project contains a document that is essential but changes weekly, and they keep forgetting to update it.
options: Assign the update to whoever produces the document, or connect to it live
Set a weekly reminder to update it
Add a note saying the document may be out of date
Update it whenever they happen to notice it has changed in the source system they take it from
questions.why: A manual weekly refresh that keeps being missed is a process problem. Moving the update to the producer or removing the copy entirely is the structural fix.
questions.traps: Reminders rely on the person who is already forgetting. A staleness note documents the problem, and opportunistic updates are what already fail.

questions.stem: A team's Project has a modest amount of knowledge and answers are still imprecise on one particular topic.
options: Add more documents on every topic
Move to a stronger model tier
Check whether the knowledge actually covers that topic in enough detail
Ask questions about that topic more specifically so the model has more to work with when it searches the loaded material
questions.why: Imprecision concentrated on one topic points at a coverage gap for that topic rather than at a general problem. Checking is the direct diagnosis.
questions.traps: Broad additions dilute without targeting. A stronger tier does not supply missing material, and specificity cannot retrieve what is not there.

questions.stem: A team's Project was built for one team and another team now wants to use it for similar work.
options: Share it, since the work is similar
Rebuild the Project for the other team
Share a copy so the other team can modify it freely without affecting the original team's configuration or the answers they receive from it
Check whether their work is actually the same before sharing the configuration
questions.why: Superficially similar work often has different requirements. Establishing that is what determines whether sharing will serve them.
questions.traps: Sharing on assumed similarity risks a poor fit. Rebuilding forgoes reuse, and a modifiable copy distributes the same untested assumption.

questions.stem: An associate is asked how many Projects is too many and does not know how to answer.
options: Set a limit of ten
Judge by whether people can find the right one, not by the count
Set no limit on the number at all
Reduce the number until each Project is being used regularly by more than one person on the team
questions.why: Findability is the property that matters, and it is what a count is a poor proxy for. That is the criterion to answer with.
questions.traps: An arbitrary limit ignores the actual need. No limit ignores navigability, and usage frequency is a different question from whether the set is manageable.

questions.stem: A team is setting up a Project and wants to know what to do about questions it cannot answer well.
options: Deal with it once such questions arise
Configure it to attempt every question
Decide now what it should do when it cannot answer, and configure that
Add documents covering as many topics as possible so that there are fewer questions it is unable to answer adequately
questions.why: Defining the out-of-scope behaviour at setup is what makes the boundary visible rather than something users discover through poor answers.
questions.traps: Waiting means users encounter the failure first. Attempting everything produces confident answers outside the knowledge, and broad coverage dilutes.

questions.stem: A team's Project holds a document whose most important content is in footnotes that answers consistently miss.
options: Bring the footnote content into the main text of the document before uploading it
Ask questions that mention the footnotes
Add an instruction to read the footnotes
Upload the document again in a different file format so that the footnotes are more likely to be captured during processing
questions.why: Content positioned as marginal gets treated as marginal. Restructuring the document so the important material sits in the main text is the reliable fix.
questions.traps: Question wording and instructions both work around the document's structure. A format change may not alter how footnotes are represented.

questions.stem: An associate wants their Project to apply one rule strictly and another only as a preference.
options: State both rules and let the model judge
State only the hard requirement
Say which is a hard requirement and which is a preference, since everything stated reads as binding
State the hard rule twice so that it is clearly more important than the preference that is stated only
questions.why: Everything in an instruction set is treated as a requirement unless distinguished. Marking the softer one is what lets the model trade it off appropriately.
questions.traps: Leaving it to judgement produces inconsistent trade-offs. Dropping the preference loses it, and repetition signals emphasis without stating the distinction.

questions.stem: A team's Project knowledge is maintained well but the instructions have not been touched since setup.
options: Leave the instructions entirely alone
Review the instructions on the same cadence as the knowledge
Rewrite the instructions annually
Ask users whether the instructions still seem appropriate for how the Project is being used across the team at the moment
questions.why: Both parts of the configuration drift as usage changes. Extending the existing maintenance cadence to the instructions is the consistent fix.
questions.traps: Leaving them assumes they still fit. An annual rewrite is arbitrary in both timing and scope, and user perception is not a review.

questions.stem: A team is deciding between one Project with all their material and several Projects with subsets of it.
options: Keep everything in one single Project
Split by document type
Split by however many Projects the team can comfortably maintain given the time they have available for keeping each one current
Split by what questions need together, since that is what keeps each Project precise
questions.why: Project boundaries should follow what must be available together to answer a question. That is what makes each one precise without omitting what a question needs.
questions.traps: One Project dilutes every answer. Document type is a property of the material rather than of the questions, and maintenance capacity is a constraint rather than a design principle.

questions.stem: An associate wants to hand a Project over before going on leave and is unsure what the recipient needs to know.
options: Hand over the purpose, the maintenance tasks and the decisions behind the configuration
Give them access and let them work it out
Write a summary of what the Project contains
Arrange a call to walk them through how the Project works so they have seen it in use before taking responsibility for it
questions.why: A handover needs purpose, ongoing tasks and the reasoning behind the setup, because the last of those is what makes safe changes possible.
questions.traps: Access without context leaves them guessing. A contents summary omits the reasoning, and a walkthrough shows what without why.

questions.stem: An HR manager proposes using Claude to screen job applications and produce a shortlist for interview.
options: Applicant data being retained and used for training without candidates' consent
Consumption costs rising sharply as application volume peaks
The model's knowledge cutoff leaving it unaware of recent employment-law changes
Automated screening of people needs human accountability and a bias review before it is used
questions.why: Consequential automated decisions about individuals sit at the centre of this domain: they need an accountable person, a bias review and a route to recourse.
questions.traps: On commercial plans data is not used for training by default, so that is a policy point to confirm rather than the headline risk. Cost is a budget issue, and the cutoff applies to any use.

questions.stem: An associate wants to paste a customer list including names and account numbers into Claude to reformat it.
options: Paste it, since the task is internal and the output will not be shared externally
Remove or replace the identifying fields, since reformatting does not require real identifiers
Paste it and delete the conversation afterwards
Ask Claude not to retain the information
questions.why: Data minimisation is the control: a reformatting task needs the structure, not the identities. Substituting placeholders achieves the task without the disclosure.
questions.traps: Internal use does not exempt personal data from handling rules. Deleting afterwards does not undo the disclosure, and instructions do not govern retention.

questions.stem: A team wants to analyse customer complaints that contain personal details, and the organisation operates under data protection law.
options: Establish the lawful basis and what the privacy notice already told customers before doing anything
Anonymise the complaints and then proceed
Proceed, since analysing complaints improves service for those same customers
Ask the legal team to review the analysis once it has been produced
questions.why: Processing personal data needs a lawful basis and has to be consistent with what people were told. That determines what is permitted before any technical choice.
questions.traps: Anonymisation may be the right control but only once the basis is established. Beneficial purpose is not a lawful basis, and post-hoc legal review follows the processing.

questions.stem: A consultant wants to use one client's material as an example when working on another client's problem.
options: Use it since the two clients are not competitors
Use it with the client's name taken out
Treat the material as covered by the first client's confidentiality unless it is genuinely public
Ask Claude to generalise the example so it no longer resembles the original client's situation
questions.why: Client material is confidential regardless of who else sees the output. Whether it is genuinely public is what determines if it can be reused at all.
questions.traps: Non-competition does not release a confidentiality obligation. Name removal and generalisation both still derive from confidential material.

questions.stem: A team publishes a report drafted with Claude that contains an error, and a customer asks who is responsible.
options: The people who produced and approved the report, since accountability does not transfer to a tool
Claude, since the error originated in the generated text
Nobody in particular, since the error was not deliberate
The reviewer alone, since their role was to catch exactly this kind of problem
questions.why: Accountability attaches to the people who chose to use the tool and approved the output. It cannot be delegated to software.
questions.traps: Attributing responsibility to the tool is the misconception being tested. Diffusing it or narrowing it to one reviewer both misplace where the obligation sits.

questions.stem: A team uses Claude to draft responses that are sent to customers under an employee's name.
options: Disclose it in every single message
Establish what the organisation's policy requires be disclosed, and follow it
Never disclose it, since the employee reviews and sends each message personally
Disclose it only when a customer asks whether a message was written by a person
questions.why: Whether and how to disclose is a policy question with legal and reputational dimensions. Establishing the organisation's position is what makes the practice defensible.
questions.traps: Blanket rules in either direction pre-empt a policy decision. Disclosing only on request treats a standing question as reactive.

questions.stem: A team uses Claude to summarise performance reviews, and notices the summaries describe men and women differently.
options: Instruct the model to use neutral language in the summaries
Remove the names before summarising them
Investigate whether the difference originates in the reviews or in the summarisation
Accept the difference, since the summaries reflect what the original reviews actually said about each person
questions.why: A difference in output could come from the source reviews or be introduced during summarisation, and the response differs completely depending on which. Investigating is the first step.
questions.traps: Neutral language and name removal both treat the symptom before the cause is known. Assuming the source is faithful skips the investigation.

questions.stem: An associate is asked to use Claude for something they suspect breaches the organisation's acceptable use policy.
options: Proceed, since the request came from someone more senior
Proceed but keep a record of who asked
Ask Claude whether the use would be acceptable under a typical acceptable use policy
Check the policy and raise it before proceeding
questions.why: A suspected policy breach is checked against the policy and raised. Seniority of the requester does not change what the policy permits.
questions.traps: Following instructions does not transfer responsibility. A record documents rather than prevents, and the model cannot interpret your organisation's policy.

questions.stem: A team wants to know whether they can use Claude-generated marketing copy commercially.
options: Assume they can, since the output was generated for them
Assume they cannot, since generated content has uncertain ownership
Check the terms that apply to their plan, since that is what governs the position
Ask Claude who owns the output it produces
questions.why: Rights in generated output are set by the terms of the plan being used. Reading them is what answers the question authoritatively.
questions.traps: Both assumptions guess at a documented position. Asking the model produces an unreliable account of a contractual matter.

questions.stem: A team wants to upload a spreadsheet for analysis, and three of its forty columns contain personal data the analysis does not use.
options: Remove the three columns before uploading, since the analysis does not need them
Upload it and instruct the model to ignore those columns
Upload it and delete it again afterwards
Upload it, since the analysis is legitimate and the personal data is incidental to the purpose
questions.why: Sending only what the task needs is the structural control. Columns that are never transmitted cannot be misused, which no instruction guarantees.
questions.traps: An ignore instruction does not prevent transmission. Deletion afterwards does not undo it, and incidental inclusion is still disclosure.

questions.stem: A lending team wants Claude to assess loan applications and produce a recommendation for each one.
options: Automate the recommendations and have a person approve them in bulk
Automate it and audit a monthly sample
Automate the straightforward approvals and route only the refusals to a person for review
Keep an accountable person deciding, with documented reasons that the applicant could be given
questions.why: Lending decisions affect individuals and usually carry a right to an explanation. An accountable decision-maker with documented reasons is what satisfies that.
questions.traps: Bulk approval is a rubber stamp. Sampling audits after the fact, and auto-approving while routing refusals still automates a consequential decision.

questions.stem: An associate wants to use Claude to identify which customers are most likely to leave, using their transaction history.
options: Proceed, since the data is already held by the organisation
Confirm the purpose is compatible with what the data was collected for
Anonymise the transaction history first
Ask customers for consent to the analysis
questions.why: Data collected for one purpose cannot automatically be used for another. Purpose compatibility is the question that determines whether the analysis is lawful.
questions.traps: Possession is not permission. Anonymisation may defeat the analysis, and consent is one possible basis rather than the first question.

questions.stem: A team wants to use Claude on documents covered by legal professional privilege.
options: Proceed, since the analysis is internal to the organisation
Proceed with the client's name removed
Ask the legal team to review the output once the analysis has been completed
Establish whether the disclosure would affect privilege before any material is shared
questions.why: Privilege can be affected by disclosure, and that is a legal question to settle before material is shared rather than after.
questions.traps: Internal use may still constitute disclosure. Name removal does not address privilege, and reviewing output follows the disclosure that matters.

questions.stem: A team is asked to sign off on Claude-generated analysis and is unsure what signing off commits them to.
options: Sign off, since another colleague has already reviewed the work
Sign off with a note that Claude was used in producing it
Establish what sign-off asserts, since it attaches their judgement to the content
Decline to sign off on anything that was produced with a generative tool
questions.why: Sign-off is an accountability act, and knowing what is being asserted determines what has to be checked before signing.
questions.traps: Relying on unspecified prior review is unfounded. A tool disclosure does not limit what is asserted, and refusing categorically forecloses legitimate work.

questions.stem: A team publishes research where Claude was used to analyse the data but not to write the conclusions.
options: Describe the tool's actual role, since readers judge methods by what was done
Do not mention it, since the conclusions are the authors' own
Mention it only in a closing appendix
State that the research was produced with AI assistance
questions.why: Method transparency means describing what the tool actually did, which is what lets a reader evaluate the work.
questions.traps: Omitting it hides part of the method. Burying it in an appendix understates it, and a vague acknowledgement does not tell readers what to evaluate.

questions.stem: A team's Claude-assisted process produces outcomes that differ by postcode, and postcode correlates with ethnicity in their area.
options: Remove postcode from the model's inputs
Investigate whether the difference is justified by the process's legitimate criteria
Accept the difference, since postcode is not a protected characteristic
Add an instruction telling the model not to consider ethnicity in its assessments
questions.why: A proxy variable can produce discriminatory outcomes without the protected characteristic being used. Whether the difference is justified is the question that matters.
questions.traps: Removing postcode may not remove the correlation carried by other fields. The proxy argument is the misconception, and an instruction about ethnicity does not address the proxy.

questions.stem: A team wants to use Claude to generate large volumes of reviews for their own product to post on a retail site.
options: Proceed, since the reviews describe the product accurately
Proceed but mark the reviews as company-written
Generate the reviews and have employees post them under their own accounts
Decline, since fabricated reviews presented as genuine are deceptive regardless of who writes them
questions.why: Fabricated reviews presented as independent customer feedback are deceptive, and that does not change because the content is accurate or because a person posts them.
questions.traps: Accuracy does not cure the misrepresentation of source. Marking them removes the deception but not the described practice, and employee posting compounds it.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to write copy in the distinctive style of a well-known author for a commercial campaign.
options: Proceed, since style itself is not protected
Proceed with an acknowledgement of the author
Consider whether the imitation would mislead or infringe before using it commercially
Ask Claude whether the copy would infringe the author's rights
questions.why: Commercial imitation raises questions of both infringement and misleading association. Considering those before use is what makes the decision informed.
questions.traps: The style argument is a partial truth that ignores passing off and endorsement implications. An acknowledgement may strengthen a false association, and the model cannot give a legal opinion.

questions.stem: A team is unsure whether a particular dataset counts as sensitive under their organisation's classification scheme.
options: Treat it as sensitive just to be safe
Check the classification scheme, since it is what determines the handling requirements
Treat it as non-sensitive since nobody has said otherwise
Ask the data owner for their view on how sensitive the material is
questions.why: The classification scheme is the authority, and consulting it produces the handling requirements directly rather than an estimate of them.
questions.traps: Defaulting either way guesses at a documented position. The data owner's view is useful input but the scheme is what governs.

questions.stem: A school wants Claude to help allocate places to applicants, with staff reviewing the output.
options: Ensure staff can see and change the reasoning, not just the outcome
Have staff approve the allocations as produced
Have staff review a sample of the allocations
Have staff review the allocations that fall outside the expected pattern
questions.why: Meaningful review of a consequential decision requires access to the reasoning, otherwise the review is an approval of an outcome nobody can interrogate.
questions.traps: Approving outputs without reasoning is a rubber stamp. Sampling and exception review both leave most decisions unexamined.

questions.stem: A team receives a request from an individual asking what personal data the organisation holds about them.
options: Ask Claude to search the organisation's systems for the individual's data
Reply that the data is held in systems that cannot easily be searched
Handle it under the organisation's existing process for such requests
Ask the individual to be more specific about what they are looking for
questions.why: Access requests have a defined legal process and timescale. Routing it there is what ensures the response is complete and compliant.
questions.traps: Using the model to search systems it cannot access does not answer the request. Difficulty is not a valid response, and narrowing the request does not discharge the obligation.

questions.stem: An associate wants to check a contract using Claude, and the contract contains a clause restricting disclosure to third parties.
options: Determine whether using the tool constitutes disclosure under that clause
Proceed, since the tool is not a third party in the ordinary sense
Proceed with the counterparty's name removed
Ask the counterparty for permission to use the tool on their contract
questions.why: Whether the clause is engaged is the question, and it turns on how disclosure is defined in that contract rather than on intuition about tools.
questions.traps: Assuming a tool is not a third party is the assumption to test. Name removal does not address the disclosure, and seeking permission presumes the clause applies without checking.

questions.stem: A team's workflow produces an output that nobody in the team fully understands but which has been reliable so far.
options: Continue, since it has been reliable in practice over an extended period
Ensure someone can explain and defend it before it is relied on externally
Add a disclaimer to the output produced
Ask Claude to explain how the output was produced so the team has an account they can give
questions.why: Being able to explain and defend output is part of being accountable for it. Reliability does not substitute for understanding when the output is used externally.
questions.traps: A record of reliability does not equip anyone to answer a challenge. A disclaimer shifts risk, and a model-generated explanation is not an account the team can stand behind.

questions.stem: A team is asked by a customer whether AI was used in preparing the advice they received.
options: Say that a range of tools were used in preparing the advice
Decline to discuss internal processes
Explain that the adviser reviewed everything, without addressing the question that was asked
Answer honestly, since the customer has asked directly
questions.why: A direct question about how advice was produced is answered directly. Evasion damages trust more than the fact being disclosed.
questions.traps: Vague references to tools, refusal, and answering a different question are all forms of evasion of a question the customer is entitled to ask.

questions.stem: An associate notices Claude's suggestions for a job description use language that research associates with fewer applications from women.
options: Change the language, since the effect on applications is the outcome that matters
Keep it, since the wording was not chosen with any intent to exclude anyone
Ask Claude whether the wording is biased
Add a line encouraging applications from underrepresented groups
questions.why: Fairness is assessed on effect rather than intent, and the described effect is exactly what the wording change addresses.
questions.traps: Absence of intent does not remove the effect. Asking the model to assess its own wording is not independent, and an encouraging line does not offset language that suppresses applications.

questions.stem: A team wants to use Claude to analyse publicly available social media posts to build profiles of individual customers.
options: Proceed, since the posts are publicly available
Consider whether compiling profiles from public posts is proportionate and permitted
Proceed but only for customers who have an existing relationship
Anonymise the profiles once they have been built
questions.why: Public availability of individual posts does not make aggregation into profiles permitted or proportionate. That is the question the scenario turns on.
questions.traps: The public-data argument is the misconception being tested. An existing relationship does not authorise profiling, and anonymising after building defeats the stated purpose.

questions.stem: A team wants to publish Claude-generated content under an individual employee's byline.
options: Publish it, since the employee directed and reviewed the work
Publish it with a note that AI was used
Consider whether the byline would misrepresent who created the content
Ask the employee whether they are comfortable with the byline
questions.why: A byline is a claim about authorship. Whether it misrepresents the actual creation process is the question that determines whether it is honest.
questions.traps: Direction and review may or may not amount to authorship, which is the point to consider. A note is one possible remedy, and the employee's comfort does not settle whether it misleads readers.

questions.stem: An associate is working on a task where using real data would be convenient and synthetic data would be sufficient.
options: Use real data, since it produces more realistic results
Use real data with the most sensitive fields removed
Use a small sample of real data rather than the full dataset
Use synthetic data, since it achieves the task without any exposure
questions.why: When synthetic data is sufficient, using it removes the exposure entirely. That is the strongest available control and it costs only convenience.
questions.traps: Realism is not needed when synthetic data suffices. Partial removal and sampling both reduce exposure without eliminating it.

questions.stem: A team uses Claude to draft decisions about benefit eligibility, and applicants can appeal.
options: Give applicants the model's explanation of the decision
Ensure the reasons given to applicants reflect the actual basis for the decision
Tell applicants the decision was made using an automated process
Provide applicants with a standard set of reasons covering the common grounds for refusal
questions.why: An appeal depends on the reasons being the real basis for the decision. Ensuring that correspondence is what makes the appeal meaningful.
questions.traps: A model-generated explanation may not reflect the actual basis. Disclosure of automation and standard reason sets both fall short of giving the real grounds.

questions.stem: A team wants to keep conversation histories containing customer data indefinitely for future reference.
options: Apply the organisation's retention rules, since indefinite retention is rarely permitted
Keep them, since they may be useful and storage is inexpensive
Keep them but restrict who can access them
Keep them for a year and then review whether they are still needed
questions.why: Retention has to follow a defined policy tied to purpose. Indefinite retention of personal data is generally not permitted regardless of utility or storage cost.
questions.traps: Utility and cost are not retention criteria. Access restriction addresses a different risk, and an arbitrary year substitutes a guess for the policy.

questions.stem: An associate's team works for two clients who are direct competitors, using the same shared Project.
options: Keep one Project and instruct the model to keep the clients' material separate
Keep one Project and label each document with its client
Keep one Project and ask people to specify the client in each question
Separate the Projects, since shared context risks one client's material informing the other's work
questions.why: Isolation is structural: material that is not present cannot leak into another client's work. With competitors, that is the standard the situation requires.
questions.traps: Instructions, labels and per-question scoping all rely on correct selection every time, which is not an adequate control between competitors.

questions.stem: A team wants to know who should be accountable for a workflow that spans three departments.
options: Make all three departments jointly accountable
Make the department that initiated the workflow accountable
Name a single accountable owner, since responsibility spread across three departments diffuses
Make whichever department the output affects most accountable for the workflow overall
questions.why: Diffusion across departments is a recognised failure of shared controls. A named owner is what makes accountability real.
questions.traps: Joint accountability is the diffusion being described. Initiation and impact are both arbitrary bases when what matters is who can actually exercise control.

questions.stem: A team's proposal to a client was drafted with Claude, and the client's procurement rules require disclosure of subcontractors.
options: Establish whether the rules cover tool use, since they were written about subcontractors
Disclose it, since transparency is always the safer course
Do not disclose it, since a tool is not a subcontractor
Ask the client informally whether they would want to know about it
questions.why: Whether an obligation applies is determined by reading it. Procurement rules about subcontractors may or may not extend to tools, and that is establishable.
questions.traps: Disclosing reflexively and declining on a definitional argument both skip reading the rule. An informal enquiry does not establish the contractual position.

questions.stem: A team tests their Claude workflow for bias by checking whether it produces different outputs for names associated with different ethnicities.
options: Conclude the workflow is unbiased if the outputs match
Conclude the test is unnecessary since the model is designed to be fair
Recognise this is a useful test and check other attributes and proxies as well
Run the test occasionally rather than as part of the regular process
questions.why: Name-swapping is a genuine test but covers one attribute through one proxy. Extending it to other attributes and proxies is what makes the assessment meaningful.
questions.traps: Passing one narrow test does not establish general fairness. Assuming fairness by design skips testing, and occasional testing does not track changes.

questions.stem: An associate wants to use Claude to write messages that will be sent from accounts appearing to belong to different individuals.
options: Proceed, since the message content is accurate and not harmful
Proceed if the individuals have agreed to it
Proceed but keep a record of which messages were generated
Decline, since messages presented as coming from people who did not write them are deceptive
questions.why: Presenting messages as authored by people who did not write them misrepresents their source, which is the deception regardless of content.
questions.traps: Accurate content does not cure a false attribution. Individual agreement changes the situation materially and is worth distinguishing, but as stated the practice misrepresents authorship. A record does not address the deception.

questions.stem: A team wants to use Claude to summarise a paid research report they subscribe to, and share the summary with colleagues who do not have access.
options: Share it, since a summary is not the original report
Check the subscription terms, since redistribution is what they typically restrict
Share it with attribution to the research provider
Ask the research provider whether they would object to the summary being shared
questions.why: Subscription terms typically govern redistribution and derivative use. Reading them is what determines whether internal sharing is permitted.
questions.traps: Summary status does not automatically escape the terms. Attribution does not grant redistribution rights, and an informal enquiry is weaker than the contract.

questions.stem: A team is asked to process a dataset and cannot determine who owns it or what restrictions apply.
options: Establish ownership and restrictions before processing anything
Process it, since it was provided to the team for that purpose
Process it and note the uncertainty in the output
Process a small sample to see whether anything sensitive appears in the data
questions.why: Unclear provenance and restrictions have to be resolved before processing, because the permitted handling is unknown until they are.
questions.traps: Being given the data does not establish what may be done with it. Noting uncertainty documents rather than resolves, and sampling does not reveal contractual restrictions.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude to help decide which customers receive a service reduction, affecting several thousand people.
options: Automate it using the documented criteria
Automate it and notify affected customers of their right to complain
Document the criteria and keep a person accountable for applying them to individuals
