Automate it for customers below a threshold and review the rest individually
questions.why: Decisions materially affecting thousands of individuals need documented criteria and an accountable person, so that each affected person has a real route to challenge the outcome.
questions.traps: Automating on documented criteria still removes the accountable decision. A complaints route follows the decision, and thresholding automates the majority.

questions.stem: A team member says they are not responsible for an error because Claude produced the text.
options: Accept the explanation, since the error genuinely originated in the generated text
Share the responsibility between the team member and the tool's provider
Treat it as a process failure with no individual responsibility attached to anyone
Explain that using a tool does not transfer responsibility for what is published
questions.why: Responsibility for published work stays with the people who chose to publish it. That is the principle the scenario is testing.
questions.traps: Attributing responsibility to the tool or its provider misplaces it. Treating it as purely systemic removes the accountability that the role carries.

questions.stem: An associate needs to analyse patient records and the organisation has a specific approved process for handling them.
options: Use the process that is most convenient for the analysis being performed
Follow the approved process, since it exists precisely for this category of data
Follow the approved process only for the most sensitive of the records
Ask whether the approved process can be relaxed for this particular analysis
questions.why: An approved handling process for a sensitive data category is the control. Following it is what makes the analysis defensible.
questions.traps: Convenience is not a criterion. Partial application and requesting exemptions both weaken a control designed for exactly this data.

questions.stem: A team wants to transfer customer data to a service hosted in another country for analysis.
options: Transfer it, since the analysis is for the customers' benefit
Transfer only the aggregated data
Transfer the data and document the transfer in the organisation's records
Establish whether the transfer is permitted before any data moves
questions.why: Cross-border transfer of personal data is specifically regulated. Establishing whether it is permitted is the prerequisite to doing it.
questions.traps: Beneficial purpose is not a transfer basis. Aggregation may help but presumes the analysis works on it, and documentation records rather than authorises.

questions.stem: An associate wants to share a Claude conversation with a colleague, and the conversation includes another client's material.
options: Share it, since the colleague is inside the same organisation
Remove or redact the other client's material before sharing anything
Share it and ask the colleague to disregard the unrelated material
Share only the final answer rather than the whole conversation
questions.why: Confidentiality obligations usually restrict disclosure inside the organisation as well. Removing the material is what makes the share compliant.
questions.traps: Internal sharing is still disclosure. Asking someone to disregard what they have seen is not a control, and the final answer may itself derive from the material.

questions.stem: A team's Claude-assisted shortlisting produces a list with no candidates from a particular background, and the applicant pool was mixed.
options: Accept it, since the shortlist was based on merit as assessed by the criteria
Rerun the shortlisting to see whether the result is stable
Investigate the process, since the outcome differs materially from the pool
Add candidates from that background to the shortlist manually
questions.why: A material divergence between pool and outcome is a signal that the process needs examining. That is what fairness monitoring exists to catch.
questions.traps: Assuming merit explains the gap is the assumption to test. A rerun measures stability rather than fairness, and manually adding candidates conceals the process problem.

questions.stem: A team's website says content is written by their expert team, and much of it is now drafted with Claude.
options: Update the statement so it describes how the content is actually produced
Leave it, since experts review everything before it is published
Add a general note about AI use elsewhere on the site
Change the statement only if a reader asks about the content's origin
questions.why: A public statement about how content is produced has to remain true. Updating it is what keeps the claim honest.
questions.traps: Review does not make the original claim accurate. A note elsewhere does not correct the specific statement, and waiting for a challenge leaves a false claim standing.

questions.stem: An associate is asked to use Claude to generate content designed to look like independent journalism about their employer.
options: Proceed, since the content will be factually accurate about the employer
Proceed if the content is labelled as sponsored somewhere on the page
Decline, since content designed to appear independent while being promotional is deceptive
Proceed and let the publisher decide how to present the material to readers
questions.why: Content engineered to read as independent coverage while being promotional misrepresents its source, which is deceptive regardless of factual accuracy.
questions.traps: Accuracy does not cure a misrepresentation of independence. Labelling changes the practice materially, and delegating presentation to a publisher does not remove the intent described.

questions.stem: A team wants to use Claude to produce a work and register it under the organisation's name as original.
options: Register it, since the organisation commissioned and paid for the work
Register it with a note that AI was involved in its production
Ask Claude whether the work can be registered as original
Check what the applicable rules say about generated works before making the claim
questions.why: Whether generated output can be registered as an original work is governed by law that varies by jurisdiction. Checking is what makes the claim defensible.
questions.traps: Commissioning does not determine originality. A note does not resolve the legal question, and the model cannot give a reliable answer on it.

questions.stem: A team uses Claude to rank support tickets by urgency, and one ranked low involved a vulnerable customer in distress.
options: Improve the ranking prompt so distress is weighted more heavily
Add a route that surfaces distress signals regardless of the ranking
Review the lowest-ranked tickets each day
Accept that no ranking system will catch every case correctly every time
questions.why: Cases where a miss causes serious harm need a path that does not depend on the ranking being right. That is a design property rather than a tuning one.
questions.traps: Prompt tuning improves the average and still misses. Reviewing the bottom of the queue is late, and accepting the miss rate ignores the severity.

questions.stem: A team is asked whether they can use Claude on data that a customer supplied under a specific agreement.
options: Read the agreement, since it defines what may be done with the data
Assume permitted uses include analysis
Ask the customers for their permission
Use the data in a way that is consistent with what the customer would probably expect
questions.why: The agreement is the authority on permitted use. Reading it answers the question directly rather than by inference.
questions.traps: Assuming and inferring expectations both guess at a documented position. Seeking permission may be unnecessary if the agreement already permits it.

questions.stem: An associate wants to use real customer names in a test of a Claude workflow.
options: Use real names, since the test needs realistic data to be meaningful
Use fabricated names, since testing does not require real identities
Use real names from customers who have consented to their data being used
Use real names with the surnames removed
questions.why: Testing does not require real identities, so fabricated data removes the exposure entirely at no cost to the test's validity.
questions.traps: Realism does not require real people. Consented data is still personal data used unnecessarily, and partial removal leaves identifiable information.

questions.stem: A team wants to keep using a Project after the client engagement it was built for has ended.
options: Keep it, since the material may be useful for similar work in future
Keep it but restrict access to the original engagement team
Delete the documents and keep the configuration
Establish what the engagement terms require be done with the client's material
questions.why: Post-engagement handling of client material is usually specified in the terms. Establishing that is what determines whether anything may be retained.
questions.traps: Future usefulness is not a retention basis. Access restriction addresses a different risk, and deleting documents presumes an answer the terms may contradict.

questions.stem: A team's workflow has three people involved and none of them considers themselves accountable for the output.
options: Assign accountability explicitly to one of them
Make all three accountable so that responsibility is shared across the workflow
Add a fourth person whose role is to be accountable for the output
Accept that shared workflows have distributed accountability by their nature
questions.why: Explicit assignment to a named person is what prevents responsibility from falling between the people involved.
questions.traps: Shared accountability is the diffusion being described. Adding a person layers on the same problem, and accepting distribution leaves nobody answerable.

questions.stem: A team is asked whether they should tell customers that Claude helps handle their enquiries.
options: Tell them, since customers have a right to know how their enquiries are handled
Do not tell them, since the handling quality is what matters to customers
Decide it as a policy question, weighing customer expectations against the practice
Tell only the customers who seem likely to care about the question
questions.why: Disclosure practice is a policy decision with legal, reputational and expectation dimensions. Deciding it deliberately is what makes it defensible.
questions.traps: Both blanket positions assert a conclusion without weighing the considerations. Selective disclosure by guessed preference is arbitrary and inconsistent.

questions.stem: A team wants to check whether their Claude workflow treats people fairly and is unsure what to measure.
options: Measure whether the same inputs produce the same outputs
Define what fair means for this decision, then measure outcomes against it
Measure whether outcomes are equal across groups
Ask Claude to assess whether its own outputs appear to be fair
questions.why: Fairness has several incompatible definitions and the right one depends on the decision. Choosing it is what makes measurement possible.
questions.traps: Consistency of outputs is a different property. Equal outcomes is one definition among several, and self-assessment is not independent.

questions.stem: An associate wants to use Claude to help identify individuals from fragments of information found online.
options: Decline, since assembling identity from fragments about a private person is intrusive
Proceed, since each fragment is individually public
Proceed if there is a legitimate business reason
Proceed but do not retain the resulting identification
questions.why: Aggregating fragments to identify a private individual is intrusive in a way the individual pieces are not. That aggregation is the concern.
questions.traps: The public-fragments argument is the misconception. A business reason does not authorise it by itself, and non-retention does not undo the identification.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude to produce material closely modelled on a competitor's published guide.
options: Proceed, since the underlying ideas are not protected
Proceed with the competitor's name removed
Proceed and have a lawyer review the result once it is finished
Consider whether the result would reproduce protected expression
questions.why: Copying protected expression rather than ideas is where the line sits. Considering that before producing the material is what avoids the problem.
questions.traps: The idea-expression distinction is real but is exactly what needs checking rather than assuming. Name removal does not address copying, and post-hoc review follows the work.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude to help assess which employees are at risk of leaving, for retention purposes.
options: Proceed, since retention is beneficial for both the organisation and the employees
Proceed with employee names anonymised
Consider what the assessment would be used for and whether employees would be told
Ask HR to review the assessments once they have been produced
questions.why: Assessments about individuals need clarity on use and on whether the person is told. Those determine whether it is a legitimate practice at all.
questions.traps: Beneficial framing does not settle the question. Anonymisation defeats a retention purpose, and post-hoc review follows a decision already taken about the practice.

questions.stem: A team wants to reduce the sensitivity of a dataset before analysis and is considering several techniques.
options: Choose the technique that removes the most information
Choose the technique based on what the analysis actually needs to preserve
Choose whichever technique is quickest to apply
Apply several techniques so the data is protected in more than one way
questions.why: The right technique preserves what the analysis needs while removing what it does not. Starting from the analysis is what makes the choice sound.
questions.traps: Maximum removal may defeat the analysis. Speed is not a criterion, and stacking techniques degrades utility without a rationale.

questions.stem: An associate is unsure whether an anonymised dataset is still personal data.
options: Treat it as non-personal, since the identifiers have been removed
Treat it as personal, since it originated from personal data
Consider whether individuals could be re-identified from it in practice
Ask the data protection team once the analysis has been completed
questions.why: Anonymisation is judged by whether re-identification is reasonably possible, not by whether obvious identifiers were stripped. That is the test to apply.
questions.traps: Removing identifiers does not guarantee anonymity. Origin does not determine current status, and consulting afterwards follows the processing.

questions.stem: A team wants to use Claude on material marked confidential, and the marking was applied years ago by someone who has left.
options: Establish whether the material is still confidential rather than assuming either way
Treat it as confidential indefinitely
Treat it as no longer confidential given the passage of time
Ask a current team member whether they think it is still sensitive
questions.why: Confidentiality has a lifespan that depends on the material and the obligation. Establishing the current position is what resolves it properly.
questions.traps: Assuming permanent confidentiality may block legitimate use. Assuming expiry risks a breach, and a colleague's impression is not the obligation.

questions.stem: A team's Claude-assisted output is challenged and the team cannot reconstruct how it was produced.
options: Explain that the output was produced with AI assistance
Reproduce the output now and present that as the explanation
Accept that generated output cannot always be fully explained
Establish a record of inputs and configuration so future output can be defended
questions.why: Defensibility requires a record of what produced the output. Establishing that is what makes future challenges answerable.
questions.traps: Citing AI assistance is not an explanation. A fresh reproduction may differ, and accepting unexplainability abandons the accountability.

questions.stem: A team is drafting a policy on when Claude use must be disclosed and is starting from what competitors do.
options: Start from what their own stakeholders would expect and what the law requires
Match whatever the competitors have published
Adopt the strictest policy any competitor has
Publish no policy until an industry standard emerges
questions.why: A disclosure policy should follow legal requirements and stakeholder expectations. Competitor practice is context rather than a basis.
questions.traps: Matching or exceeding competitors substitutes their judgement for yours. Waiting for a standard leaves the practice ungoverned meanwhile.

questions.stem: An associate is told their Claude workflow cannot be biased because it does not use any protected characteristics.
options: Agree, since the characteristics are not among the inputs
Suggest testing outcomes across groups to confirm the claim
Explain that proxies can produce biased outcomes without the characteristic being used
Suggest adding the characteristics so bias can be measured directly
questions.why: Correlated proxies reproduce the effect of a characteristic that was never supplied. That is the mechanism the belief overlooks.
questions.traps: Agreeing accepts the misconception. Outcome testing is a good next step but the misconception is what needs correcting first, and adding characteristics is a separate and contested approach.

questions.stem: A team wants to use Claude to automate responses to a regulator's enquiries.
options: Automate the routine enquiries and handle unusual ones manually
Automate the responses and have them reviewed before sending
Automate the drafting and let the regulator know AI was used
Keep a person accountable for what is said to a regulator
questions.why: Statements to a regulator carry personal and organisational accountability. Keeping a person responsible for what is said is what the context requires.
questions.traps: Splitting by routineness still auto-responds to a regulator. Review before sending is closer but frames the system as the responder, and disclosure does not address accountability.

questions.stem: A team wants to feed a licensed database's contents into Claude to answer internal questions.
options: Proceed, since the organisation pays for access to the database
Check whether the licence permits that use of the contents
Proceed for internal use only
Proceed but do not store the outputs
questions.why: Database licences typically restrict how contents may be used and processed. Reading the licence is what establishes whether this use is permitted.
questions.traps: Paying for access does not grant unlimited use. Internal scope and non-retention are both assumptions about terms that have not been read.

questions.stem: A team's Claude-assisted process makes decisions that people can appeal, and appeals are upheld unusually often.
options: Accept it, since the appeal route is working as intended
Make the appeal process more demanding so fewer appeals are lodged
Treat the appeal rate as evidence the process needs examining
Review the appeals more carefully so that fewer of them are upheld
questions.why: A high rate of upheld appeals is direct evidence that the underlying decisions are frequently wrong. That is a signal about the process.
questions.traps: Treating it as the appeal route working ignores what the rate indicates. Making appeals harder and upholding fewer both suppress the signal.

questions.stem: An associate wants to know how long conversation data containing sensitive information is retained.
options: Find out from the applicable terms and settings rather than assuming
Assume it is retained indefinitely
Assume it is deleted when the conversation is deleted
Ask Claude how long the conversation will be retained
questions.why: Retention is determined by the terms and the account configuration. Establishing it factually is what allows the handling decision to be made properly.
questions.traps: Both assumptions guess at a documented position. The model cannot report on the service's retention configuration.

questions.stem: A team wants to use customer data for a purpose the privacy notice does not mention.
options: Proceed, since the customers already agreed to the privacy notice
Update the notice and establish a basis before the new use begins
Proceed and update the notice afterwards
Proceed with data from customers who have not objected to anything
questions.why: A purpose outside what people were told needs the notice updated and a basis established first. Doing it afterwards does not cure the processing.
questions.traps: Prior agreement covers the stated purposes only. Retrospective updating and absence of objection are both after the fact.

questions.stem: A team's Claude output for one client contains a phrase that clearly came from another client's document.
options: Remove the phrase and continue
Apologise to the affected client
Add an instruction preventing the model from mixing client material
Investigate how the material crossed between the two pieces of work
questions.why: A leak between clients indicates a structural problem in how the work is separated. Investigating the mechanism is what prevents recurrence.
questions.traps: Removing the phrase treats one instance. Apologising follows the investigation, and an instruction is a weak control against a structural problem.

questions.stem: A team is asked to demonstrate that their Claude-assisted process is under control.
options: Show the accuracy figures the team has collected
Explain that a person reviews every output before it is used
Show the controls, the records and who is accountable for each part
Describe how the workflow operates from start to finish
questions.why: Demonstrating control means showing the controls themselves, the evidence they operate, and named accountability. That is what an assurance question is asking for.
questions.traps: Accuracy figures are one input. A claim about review is not evidence it operates, and a process description does not demonstrate control.

questions.stem: An associate is writing a report and wants to know whether to say which parts Claude drafted.
options: Disclose every part that was drafted with assistance
Disclose nothing, since the associate takes responsibility for the whole report
Disclose it in a footnote regardless of what readers need
Base it on what the report's readers need in order to evaluate it
questions.why: Disclosure serves the reader's ability to evaluate the work. Starting from that need determines what and how much to say.
questions.traps: Exhaustive disclosure and no disclosure both ignore the reader's actual need. A footnote by default applies a form without asking what it is for.

questions.stem: A team finds their workflow performs less well for customers who write in non-standard English.
options: Ask those customers to write more clearly
Treat the performance gap as a fairness issue affecting those customers
Accept the gap, since the workflow performs well for most customers
Add an instruction telling the model to handle non-standard English carefully
questions.why: A systematic performance gap affecting an identifiable group is a fairness problem, and naming it as such is what triggers the right response.
questions.traps: Asking customers to change puts the burden on those already disadvantaged. Majority performance does not excuse the gap, and an instruction is a tactic rather than the recognition.

questions.stem: A team wants to use Claude to draft a document that will be submitted to a court.
options: Establish what the court requires be disclosed about how documents are prepared
Submit it, since the content is accurate and a lawyer has reviewed it
Submit it with a note that AI was used in its preparation
Ask the court informally whether AI-assisted drafting is acceptable
questions.why: Courts increasingly have specific requirements about AI-assisted filings. Establishing what applies is what makes the submission compliant.
questions.traps: Accuracy and review do not address a disclosure requirement. A voluntary note may not meet the requirement, and an informal enquiry is not the rule.

questions.stem: An associate wants to publish a dataset that Claude helped clean and structure.
options: Publish it, since the cleaning added value to the original data
Consider what rights apply to the underlying data before publishing it
Publish it with an acknowledgement of the tool used
Publish it under a permissive licence so others can use it freely
questions.why: Rights in the underlying data govern whether it can be published at all, and processing does not change that. Establishing them is the prerequisite.
questions.traps: Adding value does not create a right to publish. Tool acknowledgement addresses a different question, and licensing presumes the right to license.

questions.stem: A team's Claude-assisted decisions affect individuals, and the team has never asked whether anyone has been harmed.
options: Assume no harm has occurred since nobody has complained
Review a sample of decisions for signs of harm
Establish a way for affected people to raise problems, and look at what comes back
Ask the team whether they are aware of anyone having been affected badly
questions.why: Harm from consequential decisions is often invisible unless there is a route to report it. Creating that route and examining what arrives is what makes the question answerable.
questions.traps: Absence of complaints is not evidence of no harm when no route exists. Sampling and asking the team both look from inside the process.

questions.stem: A team is deciding how to handle a dataset that contains a small number of sensitive records among many ordinary ones.
options: Apply the sensitive handling to the whole dataset unless the records can be separated
Apply the sensitive handling only to the sensitive records
Apply ordinary handling, since the sensitive records are a small proportion
Remove the sensitive records and process the rest normally
questions.why: A mixed dataset takes the handling of its most sensitive content unless the parts can genuinely be separated. That is the conservative and correct default.
questions.traps: Selective handling within a combined dataset is not achievable in practice. Proportion is not a criterion, and removal may destroy the analysis if those records matter.

questions.stem: A team wants to know whether they need a formal assessment before starting a new Claude-assisted process involving personal data.
options: Carry one out regardless, since it is good practice for any new process
Skip it, since the process uses data the organisation already holds lawfully
Carry one out after the process has been running long enough to see its real effects
Check the criteria that trigger one, since they are defined rather than a matter of judgement
questions.why: Whether a formal impact assessment is required is determined by defined trigger criteria. Checking them answers the question rather than guessing at it.
questions.traps: Doing one reflexively spends effort without establishing necessity. Existing lawful holding does not exempt a new purpose, and a retrospective assessment defeats the point of assessing beforehand.

questions.stem: A team is asked who checked a particular Claude-generated figure before it was published, and nobody can say.
options: Assume it was checked, since the team's process requires checking
Ask the team members whether any of them remembers checking it
Establish a record of who checked what, since accountability needs to be traceable
Check the figure now and confirm that it was correct all along
questions.why: Traceable accountability requires a record of who performed each check. Establishing that is what makes the question answerable in future.
questions.traps: Assuming the process was followed is what the question exposes. Recollection is unreliable, and confirming the figure now does not establish who checked it then.

questions.stem: An associate is asked to use Claude on data belonging to a different department that they have access to but no business need for.
options: Use only the data their own work requires, since access is not the same as need
Use it, since they have been granted access to the system it sits in
Use it and inform the other department afterwards
Use an anonymised extract of the other department's data instead
questions.why: Access is provisioned broadly; the need-to-know principle is what governs use. Confining use to business need is the control.
questions.traps: Having access does not establish need. Informing afterwards follows the use, and anonymising does not create a business need.

questions.stem: A team wants to include real client examples in an internal training document produced with Claude.
options: Include them, since the document is only for internal use
Obtain permission or anonymise thoroughly enough that the client cannot be identified
Include them with the client's name replaced by a letter
Include them and mark the document as confidential
questions.why: Client material used beyond its purpose needs permission or genuine anonymisation. Identifiability rather than naming is the test.
questions.traps: Internal circulation is still use beyond the engagement. Letter substitution rarely defeats identification, and a confidentiality marking does not authorise the use.

questions.stem: A team's process uses Claude to flag transactions as suspicious, and flagged customers have their accounts frozen automatically.
options: Improve the flagging accuracy so fewer legitimate customers are affected
Notify customers promptly when their account is frozen
Review frozen accounts within 24 hours so mistakes are corrected quickly
Separate the flag from the freeze so a person decides on the consequence
questions.why: An automated flag driving an automatic consequential action removes the human decision. Separating detection from action restores it.
questions.traps: Better accuracy reduces frequency without restoring the decision. Notification and rapid review both follow a freeze that has already happened.

questions.stem: A team wants to reduce bias in their workflow and proposes adding an instruction telling Claude to be fair.
options: Recognise that an instruction is not a control, and measure outcomes instead
Add the instruction, since it establishes the expectation clearly
Add the instruction and monitor for complaints
Add a stronger instruction specifying what fairness means in this context
questions.why: Fairness is established by measuring outcomes, not by instructing the model. Recognising that instructions are not controls is the point.
questions.traps: Adding an instruction in any form leaves the outcome unmeasured. Complaint monitoring detects harm after it occurs.

questions.stem: An associate is asked by a colleague whether a document they shared was written with Claude.
options: Say that it was a team effort
Ask why the colleague wants to know
Answer honestly, since there is no reason to conceal it from a colleague
Explain that the associate reviewed it thoroughly before sharing
questions.why: A direct question deserves a direct answer, and evasion creates a problem where none existed.
questions.traps: A vague team-effort answer is misleading. Questioning the motive is evasive, and describing the review answers a different question.

questions.stem: A team wants to use Claude to test whether their own systems can be tricked into revealing customer data.
options: Proceed, since the systems belong to the organisation
Establish authorisation and scope in writing before any testing begins
Proceed on a copy of the systems rather than the live ones
Proceed and report anything that is found to the security team
questions.why: Security testing needs documented authorisation and scope even against your own systems. That is what distinguishes testing from an incident.
questions.traps: Ownership does not authorise an individual to test. A copy narrows the risk but not the authorisation question, and reporting follows unauthorised activity.

questions.stem: A team is drafting a policy on whether generated content may be presented as the organisation's own work.
options: Allow it, since the organisation directed and paid for the work
Prohibit it, since generated content is not original work
Leave it to individual judgement on a case-by-case basis
Decide it deliberately, since the answer affects contracts, marketing and client work
questions.why: Whether generated content may be presented as the organisation's own has contractual and reputational consequences. Deciding it deliberately is what makes practice consistent.
questions.traps: Both blanket positions assert an answer without weighing the consequences. Case-by-case judgement produces inconsistency in exactly the area needing consistency.

questions.stem: A team wants to keep a record of every Claude conversation for audit purposes, and conversations contain personal data.
options: Keep everything, since audit requirements take precedence
Balance the audit need against retention limits and record the justification
Keep everything but restrict access to the audit team
Keep summaries rather than full conversations
questions.why: Competing obligations are resolved by weighing them and documenting the reasoning. That is what makes the retention decision defensible.
questions.traps: Asserting precedence skips the balance. Access restriction addresses a different risk, and summaries may be a good outcome but not the reasoning being tested.

questions.stem: A team wants to know what evidence they would need if a Claude-assisted decision were challenged in a year.
options: Rely on the conversation history being available
Recreate the decision at that point using the same inputs
Keep a note of which decisions were made with assistance
Decide now what to record, since the evidence has to exist before it is needed
questions.why: Evidence for a future challenge has to be captured at the time. Deciding what to record now is what makes it available later.
questions.traps: Conversation history may not persist or may not capture inputs. Recreation produces a new result, and a bare note of tool use is not evidence about the decision.

questions.stem: A team discovers that sensitive data was pasted into Claude by a colleague who did not realise it was restricted.
options: Follow the incident process and address the training gap
Ask the colleague to delete the conversation
Note it informally and remind the team about data handling
Treat it as a minor issue since the data did not leave the organisation
questions.why: A data handling breach follows the incident process, and the underlying cause is a knowledge gap worth addressing. Both parts matter.
questions.traps: Deletion does not undo the disclosure or record the incident. Informal handling bypasses the process, and minimising it skips both the process and the cause.

questions.stem: An associate wants to use Claude to summarise a document marked as restricted to a named group they belong to.
options: Proceed, since the associate is a member of the named group
Proceed with the document's markings removed from the text
Confirm that using the tool keeps the material within the named group
Proceed and avoid sharing the summary outside the group
questions.why: Restriction to a named group constrains where the material may go, which includes systems. Confirming that is what keeps the restriction intact.
questions.traps: Membership authorises the person, not every destination. Removing markings conceals rather than complies, and controlling the summary does not address the input.

questions.stem: A team's Claude-assisted process affects individuals and has been running for a year without anyone reviewing its outcomes.
options: Continue, since no problems have been reported during that time
Review the outcomes now, since consequential processes need periodic assessment
Review the process design rather than its outcomes
Ask the people operating the process whether they have concerns
questions.why: Processes affecting individuals need their actual outcomes examined periodically. A year without review is the gap the scenario identifies.
questions.traps: No reported problems is not evidence of good outcomes. Reviewing design does not reveal what happened, and operator perception is from inside the process.

questions.stem: A team's fairness testing covers the groups they thought of, and someone points out a group they did not consider.
options: Add that group and consider the testing complete
Explain that the original groups were chosen on a reasonable basis
Extend the testing, since the omission is evidence the coverage was incomplete
Test the new group only if there is evidence of a problem affecting them
questions.why: An omission surfacing this way indicates the coverage method missed things. Extending the testing addresses the method rather than the one instance.
questions.traps: Adding one group and stopping repeats the same partial approach. Defending the original selection ignores the finding, and requiring evidence first inverts the purpose of testing.

questions.stem: A team's client asks for a description of the methods used on their engagement, and Claude was used throughout.
options: Describe its use accurately as part of the methods
Mention it only if the client raises AI specifically
Describe the methods without reference to the tools used
Say that standard industry tools were used in the engagement
questions.why: A methods description that omits a tool used throughout is incomplete. Describing it accurately is what the client asked for.
questions.traps: Waiting for a specific question withholds part of the answer. Omitting tools and referring vaguely to industry standards both obscure the method.

questions.stem: An associate is asked to use Claude to produce material that impersonates a named competitor's communications.
options: Proceed, since it is for internal competitive analysis only
Proceed if the material is clearly marked as a simulation
Proceed and destroy the material once the analysis is complete
Decline, since material imitating another organisation's communications is deceptive
questions.why: Producing material that imitates another organisation's communications creates something that functions as an impersonation regardless of intent.
questions.traps: Internal purpose does not change what the material is. Marking changes the situation materially, and destroying it afterwards does not address its creation.

questions.stem: A team wants to use Claude to translate a copyrighted work for internal distribution.
options: Check whether translation and internal distribution are permitted by the licence
Proceed, since translation creates a new work
Proceed, since the distribution is internal
Proceed and credit the original author in the translation
questions.why: Translation is a restricted act and internal distribution is still distribution. The licence determines whether either is permitted.
questions.traps: The new-work argument misstates how translation rights work. Internal scope and attribution both assume permissions that have not been checked.

questions.stem: A team wants to use Claude on data about children, and the organisation has no specific policy on it.
options: Apply the organisation's general data handling policy
Anonymise the data and then proceed
Establish the additional protections that apply, since children's data is treated differently
Ask the parents for consent before processing the data
questions.why: Children's data attracts heightened protection in most regimes. Establishing what applies is the prerequisite to any handling decision.
questions.traps: A general policy does not capture the heightened requirements. Anonymisation and parental consent are possible controls but presume the requirements are known.

questions.stem: A team's process is described in documentation that says a person reviews every output, and in practice reviews are skipped when busy.
options: Update the documentation to describe the review as a target
Align the documentation with what actually happens, or make the practice match
Ask the team to follow the documented process
Accept the gap, since the documentation describes the intended process
questions.why: Documentation asserting a control that does not operate creates false assurance. Closing the gap in either direction is what restores honesty.
questions.traps: Softening the documentation without deciding the control is a partial answer. Instructing compliance without resourcing repeats the failure, and accepting the gap leaves the false assurance.

questions.stem: A team is deciding whether to allow Claude use on a category of data and has no way to monitor what people actually paste.
options: Publish clear guidance and rely on people to follow it
Prohibit all use of Claude for that category of work
Allow it and address problems if they arise
Combine clear guidance with technical limits rather than relying on guidance alone
questions.why: Guidance alone does not constrain behaviour when nothing checks it. Pairing it with technical limits is what makes the control real.
questions.traps: Guidance without enforcement is the gap described. A blanket prohibition forgoes legitimate use, and reactive handling waits for a breach.

questions.stem: An associate realises a Claude conversation they had last week contained material they were not authorised to share.
options: Report it through the incident process rather than handling it privately
Delete the conversation and move on
Mention it to their manager informally
Note it for their own records in case it becomes relevant later
questions.why: An unauthorised disclosure is an incident, and reporting it is what allows the organisation to assess and respond appropriately.
questions.traps: Deletion does not undo the disclosure or trigger assessment. Informal mention and private notes both bypass the process.

questions.stem: A team wants to use Claude to prioritise which safeguarding referrals are reviewed first.
options: Improve the prioritisation prompt so serious cases rank higher
Have a person review the ranking each day
Ensure no referral can be deprioritised beyond a defined time regardless of ranking
Use the ranking only as a suggestion that reviewers may override
questions.why: Safeguarding referrals need a guaranteed floor on how long any case waits, because a ranking error there carries serious consequences.
questions.traps: Prompt improvement and daily review both leave the worst case dependent on the ranking. Advisory framing helps but does not bound the wait.

questions.stem: A team's workflow has been tested for bias once, at launch, eighteen months ago.
options: Rely on the launch test, since the workflow has not been changed
Test again only if a complaint is received
Test again when the workflow is next modified
Test periodically, since inputs, usage and models all change over time
questions.why: Fairness is a property of a system in its current context, and that context drifts. Periodic testing is what tracks it.
questions.traps: An unchanged workflow can still drift as inputs and models change. Complaint-triggered and modification-triggered testing both leave long gaps.

questions.stem: A team is writing a public statement about their use of AI and wants it to be reassuring.
options: Emphasise the human oversight in the process
Make it accurate first, since a reassuring statement that is untrue is worse than none
Keep it general so it does not constrain future practice
Describe the benefits to customers of the approach being taken
questions.why: A public statement about practice has to be true, because an inaccurate reassurance becomes a liability when the practice is examined.
questions.traps: Emphasising oversight, staying general and describing benefits are all presentational choices that do not address accuracy.

questions.stem: An associate wants to use Claude to generate a large number of applications to a scheme with limited places.
options: Proceed, since each application will be genuine and accurate
Proceed but submit them under different names
Consider whether volume submission undermines the scheme and breaches its terms
Proceed and withdraw any that are not needed
questions.why: Mass submission to a scheme with limited places usually breaches its terms and disadvantages other applicants. That is the consideration.
questions.traps: Individual accuracy does not address the volume. Different names compounds the problem, and withdrawal follows the distortion.

questions.stem: A team wants to know whether Claude's output can be used in a product they will sell.
options: Assume it can, since they generated the output themselves
Assume it cannot without a specific commercial licence
Ask a lawyer to advise on the position before proceeding
Check the terms for their plan, since commercial use rights are set there
questions.why: The terms of the plan govern commercial use rights. Reading them answers the question directly and authoritatively.
questions.traps: Both assumptions guess at a documented position. Legal advice is reasonable but starts with the terms.

questions.stem: A team is asked how they would delete an individual's data from their Claude-assisted process if requested.
options: Work out now where personal data ends up in the process
Say the data is not stored by the process
Delete the conversations containing the individual's data
Explain that deletion is handled by the tool provider
questions.why: Answering a deletion request requires knowing where personal data resides across the process. Mapping that is the prerequisite.
questions.traps: Asserting nothing is stored may be wrong. Deleting conversations addresses one location, and deferring to the provider does not discharge the obligation.

questions.stem: A team's manager asks to be shown that the Claude-assisted process is producing correct results.
options: Describe how the process works
Show the verification evidence, since the manager is asking for assurance rather than description
Show them examples of good output
Explain that the team reviews the output before it is used
questions.why: An assurance request is answered with evidence that checking happens and what it found. That is different from describing the process.
questions.traps: A process description, selected examples and a claim about review all describe intent rather than demonstrate results.

questions.stem: An associate is unsure whether a document contains personal data because it uses internal reference numbers rather than names.
options: Treat it as non-personal since no names appear
Treat it as personal only if the linking table is also present
Ask whether anyone could reasonably work out who the numbers refer to
Treat reference numbers that can be linked to individuals as personal data
questions.why: Identifiers that can be linked to individuals are personal data even when the link sits elsewhere. Recognising pseudonymisation as distinct from anonymisation is the point.
questions.traps: Absence of names is not the test. Requiring the linking table alongside misunderstands the rule, and the reasonableness question is closer but the linkability principle is what governs.

questions.stem: A team wants to build a Project holding material from several clients to answer general questions about their sector.
options: Combine it with the client names removed
Combine it and restrict access to senior staff
Do not combine client material, since each client's obligations apply to their own
Ask each client whether they mind their material being combined
questions.why: Each client's confidentiality obligation applies to their material regardless of what else is combined with it. Keeping them separate is the control.
questions.traps: Name removal does not release the obligation. Access restriction is a different control, and seeking permission is worth considering but the default is separation.

questions.stem: A team wants to use Claude to decide which customers are offered a hardship arrangement.
options: Keep the decision with a person, since it affects vulnerable people directly
Automate it using the documented hardship criteria
Automate the offers and route refusals to a person
Automate it and review the decisions weekly
questions.why: Decisions about people in financial hardship affect vulnerable individuals and need an accountable person rather than an automated determination.
questions.traps: Documented criteria do not remove the need for accountability. Asymmetric routing still auto-decides, and weekly review follows the decision.

questions.stem: A team's Claude workflow performs equally well across groups on average but has much higher variance for one group.
options: Accept it, since the average performance is equal across the groups
Treat the variance as a fairness concern in its own right
Investigate whether the variance is caused by smaller sample sizes
Add more examples from that group to the prompt
questions.why: Equal averages with unequal variance means individuals in that group face a less predictable outcome. That is a fairness issue the average conceals.
questions.traps: Equal averages is the misconception being tested. Sample size is one possible explanation, and adding examples is a remedy chosen before the concern is recognised.

questions.stem: An associate is asked to remove a reference to AI assistance from a document before it goes to a client.
options: Remove it, since the person asking is more senior
Refuse to remove the reference
Ask why, since the reason determines whether removing it would mislead
Remove it and keep a record that the reference was there originally
questions.why: Whether removal is appropriate depends on why it is being asked. Establishing that is what distinguishes a formatting preference from concealment.
questions.traps: Complying on seniority and refusing outright both decide without the reason. A private record does not address whether the client is misled.

questions.stem: A team is unsure whether a proposed use is permitted and the policy does not clearly address it.
options: Ask whoever owns the policy, since ambiguity is resolved by the owner
Proceed, since the policy does not prohibit it
Do not proceed, since the policy does not permit it
Proceed and document the reasoning in case it is questioned later
questions.why: Ambiguity in a policy is resolved by the person who owns it. Asking produces an answer and usually improves the policy.
questions.traps: Reading silence as permission or prohibition both substitute a guess. Documented reasoning protects the individual without resolving the question.

questions.stem: A team wants to use Claude to summarise articles from a news service and circulate the summaries internally.
options: Proceed, since summaries are not reproductions
Proceed, since circulation is internal
Proceed and include a link to the original article with each summary
Check the service's terms, since summarising and circulating are usually addressed
questions.why: News service terms typically address both summarisation and internal circulation. Reading them is what establishes whether this is permitted.
questions.traps: The summary argument assumes a conclusion the terms may contradict. Internal scope and linking are both assumptions about permissions not yet checked.

questions.stem: A team wants to profile customers using Claude and is unsure whether individuals have a right to object.
options: Assume no right to object since the profiling is for service improvement
Check what rights apply to profiling in their jurisdiction before starting
Assume a right to object and build an opt-out
Ask customers whether they would want to opt out of profiling
questions.why: Profiling often attracts specific rights including objection. Establishing what applies is the prerequisite to designing the process.
questions.traps: Assuming no right guesses at the law. Building an opt-out may be right but presumes the requirement, and asking customers is not the legal position.

questions.stem: A team is asked whether they can explain a particular Claude-assisted outcome to the person it affected.
options: Explain that the outcome followed the documented process
Provide the person with the inputs that were used
Explain that the outcome was produced with automated assistance
Test whether they can, since being able to explain it is part of using it responsibly
questions.why: Whether an outcome can actually be explained to the person affected is a testable property. Checking it is what reveals whether the process is defensible.
questions.traps: A process reference, raw inputs and a statement about automation are all substitutes for an explanation of this particular outcome.

questions.stem: A team is asked to show that their Claude-assisted process does not disadvantage any group, and they have never collected outcome data by group.
options: Explain that the process does not use any group characteristics as inputs
Point to the fairness instruction included in the configuration
Start collecting outcome data by group, since the question cannot be answered without it
Ask the people operating the process whether they have observed any disparity
questions.why: A claim about disparate impact can only be supported by outcome data broken down by group. Collecting it is what makes the question answerable at all.
questions.traps: Not using group characteristics does not prevent proxy effects. An instruction is not evidence, and operator observation is neither systematic nor independent.

questions.stem: An associate is asked to use Claude to write content that will be presented as a customer testimonial.
options: Write it, since it will describe the product accurately
Decline unless a real customer said it and has agreed to it being used
Write it and have a customer approve the wording afterwards
Write it as a composite drawn from several real customer comments
questions.why: A testimonial asserts that a named customer said something. Fabricating or composing one misrepresents its source regardless of accuracy.
questions.traps: Accuracy does not cure a false attribution. Retrospective approval of words a customer did not say is still a fabrication, and a composite presented as one person's testimonial misrepresents it.

questions.stem: A team wants to use Claude on data they hold under a contract that is silent about processing by third parties.
options: Treat the silence as unresolved and seek clarification before processing
Proceed, since the contract does not prohibit it
Proceed with the data anonymised
Proceed and notify the counterparty afterwards
questions.why: Contractual silence on a material point is an ambiguity to resolve rather than a permission. Seeking clarification is what makes the processing defensible.
questions.traps: Reading silence as permission is the misconception. Anonymisation may not address the contractual question, and notification follows the processing.

questions.stem: A team's automated process produced a decision that was clearly wrong and affected a customer badly.
options: Correct the individual case and apologise to the customer
Correct it, understand why it happened, and check whether others were affected
Correct it and adjust the prompt so the error does not recur
Correct it and add the case to the team's list of known issues
questions.why: A wrong consequential decision needs the individual remedy, a cause analysis, and a check for other affected people, because the same fault may have hit others silently.
questions.traps: Each alternative handles part of it. Correcting one case, tuning the prompt, or logging the issue all omit checking who else was affected.

questions.stem: A team is setting up a new Claude-assisted process and is deciding when to think about accountability.
options: Decide it during the design, since retrofitting accountability rarely works
Decide it once the process is running and its shape is clear
Decide it if a problem arises that requires someone to answer for it
Decide it at the first review of the process after launch
questions.why: Accountability designed in shapes the process, including what gets recorded and who sees what. Added afterwards it is a label rather than a control.
questions.traps: Deferring to after launch, to a problem, or to a review all leave the design decisions already made without it.

questions.stem: A team wants to use Claude to analyse employee communications for signs of dissatisfaction.
options: Proceed, since the purpose is to improve conditions for employees
Proceed with the communications anonymised
Establish the legal basis and what employees were told about monitoring
Inform employees that the analysis is taking place
questions.why: Monitoring employee communications engages specific legal requirements and expectations. Establishing the basis and what people were told is the prerequisite.
questions.traps: Benevolent purpose is not a basis. Anonymisation may defeat the purpose, and informing people is one requirement rather than the whole question.

questions.stem: An associate is leaving the organisation and wants to keep prompts they wrote that reference client work.
options: Keep them, since they wrote them themselves
Keep them with the client-specific parts removed
Keep them and use them only at their next employer's request
Establish what the organisation and the client terms permit them to take
questions.why: What a departing employee may take is governed by their contract and by client terms. Establishing that is what makes the decision defensible.
questions.traps: Authorship does not determine ownership. Removing client parts and limiting future use both assume permissions that have not been checked.

questions.stem: A team's report includes a statistic that Claude produced and that the team verified against the source.
options: Cite Claude as the source of the statistic
Cite the underlying source, since that is where the statistic actually comes from
Cite both Claude and the underlying source
Present the statistic without a citation since it has been verified
questions.why: A verified statistic is cited to its origin. The tool was a route to finding it rather than the source of the fact.
questions.traps: Citing the tool tells a reader nothing checkable. Citing both is misleading about provenance, and omitting the citation removes the reader's ability to verify.

questions.stem: A team's fairness review finds a disparity and the team is unsure whether it is large enough to act on.
options: Act if the disparity is statistically significant
Act if the disparity affects more than a set number of people
Decide the threshold in advance of looking at the result
Discuss it and reach a judgement about whether it warrants action
questions.why: Setting the threshold before seeing the result is what prevents the decision from being shaped by whether acting is convenient.
questions.traps: Significance and headcount are both candidate thresholds but choosing one after seeing the result invites motivated reasoning. Ad-hoc judgement has the same problem.

questions.stem: A team wants to use Claude to respond to online criticism of their organisation using accounts that do not identify the company.
options: Proceed, since the responses will be factually accurate
Proceed if the responses only correct factual errors
Proceed using accounts belonging to employees who agree to it
Decline, since undisclosed corporate responses misrepresent who is speaking
questions.why: Responses from an organisation presented as coming from unaffiliated individuals misrepresent the speaker, which is the deception at issue.
questions.traps: Accuracy and factual correction do not cure the concealed affiliation. Employee accounts make the concealment harder to detect rather than legitimate.

questions.stem: An associate wants to use Claude to produce a work in the style of a specific living artist for internal use.
options: Consider the artist's rights and whether internal use changes the position
Proceed, since internal use does not raise any rights questions
Proceed and credit the artist by name
Proceed but do not retain the work after its internal use has finished
questions.why: Whether internal use affects the position is exactly what needs considering rather than assuming. Rights questions do not automatically disappear at the organisational boundary.
questions.traps: Assuming internal use is exempt is the misconception. Credit may strengthen an association claim, and non-retention follows the creation.

questions.stem: A team is deciding whether to allow Claude use in a department that handles a mixture of sensitive and routine work.
options: Allow it right across the department
Prohibit it across the department
Allow it and ask people to use judgement about the sensitive material
Define which categories of work it may be used for, rather than deciding per department
questions.why: Permission should track the sensitivity of the work rather than the organisational unit, because a mixed department contains both.
questions.traps: Blanket permission or prohibition applies one rule to two categories. Relying on individual judgement without defined categories leaves the boundary unstated.

questions.stem: A team's Claude-assisted process makes decisions about individuals with no human involvement in routine cases.
options: Continue, since a person is available if anyone asks
Continue, since the decisions are routine and low-impact
Establish whether the individuals have a right to human intervention
Add a human review step to a sample of the decisions
questions.why: Fully automated decision-making about individuals attracts specific rights in many regimes, including a right to human intervention. Establishing that is the prerequisite.
questions.traps: Availability on request may not satisfy the requirement. A routine characterisation is the team's judgement rather than the legal test, and sampling does not address individual rights.

questions.stem: A team wants to use anonymised client examples in a public case study produced with Claude.
options: Publish it, since the client's name has been removed
Check whether the client can still be identified from the surrounding detail
Publish it and inform the client afterwards
Publish it with the industry and size details generalised
questions.why: Anonymisation is judged by whether identification remains possible from context. Checking that is the test rather than name removal.
questions.traps: Name removal alone rarely defeats identification. Informing afterwards follows publication, and generalising details is a remedy applied without checking whether it suffices.

questions.stem: A team is designing a process where Claude assesses applications and a person makes the final decision.
options: Ensure the person can reach a different conclusion and has what they need to do so
Ensure the person reviews every assessment before deciding
Ensure the assessments are accurate before they reach the person
Ensure the person records their reasons for each decision
questions.why: Meaningful human decision-making requires the ability to depart from the assessment and the information to justify doing so. Otherwise the review is nominal.
questions.traps: Reviewing every case, improving accuracy and recording reasons are all valuable but none guarantees the person can actually decide differently.

questions.stem: A team's Claude-assisted output is used by another team who assume it has been checked, and it has not.
options: Check everything before it is passed on
Tell the other team that the output is unchecked
Make the checking status explicit so downstream users know what they are receiving
Ask the other team to check the output before they rely on it
questions.why: Downstream assumptions about verification are dangerous when unstated. Making the status explicit is what lets the receiving team act appropriately.
questions.traps: Checking everything may not be feasible. A one-off conversation and a request to check both address this instance rather than making the status a property of the output.

questions.stem: A team is asked whether their AI use needs to be disclosed in a tender response.
options: Disclose it, since transparency improves the chances of winning
Read the tender requirements, since they define what must be disclosed
Do not disclose it, since it is a detail of how the work is done
Ask the procuring organisation informally what they expect
questions.why: Tender requirements define disclosure obligations. Reading them establishes what is required rather than what seems advisable.
questions.traps: Disclosing for advantage and withholding as a detail both guess. An informal enquiry does not establish the formal requirement.

questions.stem: A team wants to know whether their process is fair and has data on outcomes but not on who was affected.
options: Analyse the outcome distribution for unusual patterns
Assume fairness since no group information was used
Ask Claude to assess whether the outcomes appear fair
Recognise that fairness cannot be assessed without knowing who the outcomes affected
questions.why: Fairness is a statement about how outcomes fall across people. Without knowing who was affected, the data cannot support the assessment.
questions.traps: Distribution patterns alone say nothing about groups. Absence of group inputs does not prevent proxy effects, and the model has no access to the missing information.

questions.stem: An associate is asked to use Claude to prepare material for a purpose the organisation's policy explicitly prohibits.
options: Decline and explain the policy position to the person asking
Comply, since the request came through the normal channels
Comply but record that the request was made by someone else
Ask whether an exception can be granted before doing the work
questions.why: An explicit prohibition is declined, and explaining why gives the requester the information they need. Following instructions does not transfer responsibility.
questions.traps: Normal channels do not override a prohibition. A record documents rather than prevents, and seeking an exception before declining treats a clear prohibition as negotiable.

questions.stem: A team wants to fine-tune their understanding of what they can do with generated output and finds the terms ambiguous.
options: Adopt the interpretation most favourable to the organisation
Adopt the most restrictive interpretation
Seek clarification rather than resolving the ambiguity in their own favour
Proceed on their preferred interpretation and document the reasoning
questions.why: Genuine ambiguity in terms is resolved by asking rather than by choosing an interpretation and proceeding on it.
questions.traps: Self-serving and maximally restrictive readings both substitute a choice for an answer. Documented reasoning protects the individual without resolving the position.

questions.stem: A team's staff are pasting varied material into Claude and nobody knows what categories of data are involved.
options: Prohibit all pasting of documents
Find out what is actually being used before designing any controls
Publish guidance on what should not be pasted
Add a warning message reminding people to consider sensitivity before pasting
questions.why: Controls have to match actual practice, and that is currently unknown. Establishing it is what makes the subsequent controls proportionate.
questions.traps: A blanket prohibition and generic guidance are both designed without knowing the exposure. A warning message is a nudge rather than a control.

questions.stem: An associate wants to know whether a particular processing activity needs to be recorded in the organisation's records.
options: Check the criteria, since recording obligations are defined rather than discretionary
Record it, since recording more than necessary is harmless
Do not record it, since it is a routine internal activity
Ask the data protection team to decide once the activity is under way
questions.why: Whether an activity must be recorded follows defined criteria. Checking them produces the answer directly.
questions.traps: Over-recording and under-recording both guess. Consulting after the activity starts follows the obligation it is meant to satisfy.

questions.stem: A team's Project contains client material and a colleague from another engagement asks for access.
options: Grant access, since they are a colleague in the same organisation
Grant them read-only access to it
Grant access and ask them to treat the material as confidential
Establish whether the colleague is permitted access under the client's terms
questions.why: Client confidentiality typically restricts access within the organisation too. Establishing the permitted audience is what governs the decision.
questions.traps: Colleague status is not the test. Read-only access is still access, and an instruction to treat material confidentially does not create authorisation.

questions.stem: A team wants to measure whether their consequential process is working well and proposes tracking its accuracy.
options: Track outcomes for the people affected as well as the process's accuracy
Track accuracy, since a correct decision is a good outcome
Track the number of appeals received
Track how quickly decisions are made
questions.why: A process can be accurate against its criteria while producing poor outcomes for people if the criteria are wrong. Tracking both is what reveals that.
questions.traps: Accuracy against criteria assumes the criteria are right. Appeals and speed are indicators rather than measures of outcome quality.

questions.stem: A team wants to reduce the effort spent on governance for a low-risk Claude use.
options: Apply the same governance as higher-risk uses for consistency
Remove the governance entirely for this use
Scale the governance to the risk, keeping the parts that matter at that level
Apply governance only if the use grows in scale or importance
questions.why: Proportionate governance means keeping the controls that matter at that risk level rather than applying a uniform standard or none.
questions.traps: Uniform governance wastes effort. Removing it entirely leaves the use ungoverned, and deferring until growth leaves a gap meanwhile.

questions.stem: A team publishes content produced with Claude and a reader asks how it was made.
options: Direct them to the organisation's general AI policy
Answer the question accurately
Explain that all content is reviewed by the team before publication
Answer only if the reader has a specific concern about the content
questions.why: A direct question about how something was made deserves an accurate answer. Deflection creates a problem that honesty avoids.
questions.traps: A general policy does not answer the specific question. Describing review answers something else, and gating the answer on the reader's motive is evasive.

questions.stem: A team's process performs well overall and poorly for a small group that makes up two percent of cases.
options: Accept it, since the overall performance is good
Exclude that group from the process
Note the limitation and continue with the process as it currently operates
Treat the small group's experience as mattering regardless of its share
questions.why: Fairness concerns individuals, and a small group's poor experience is not offset by good aggregate performance. That is the principle being tested.
questions.traps: Aggregate performance is the misconception. Excluding the group denies them the service, and noting the limitation continues it unchanged.

questions.stem: An associate is unsure whether a use is acceptable and the organisation has no policy at all.
options: Proceed, since nothing prohibits the use
Do not proceed, since nothing permits the use
Raise the gap, since the absence of a policy is itself the problem to address
Proceed cautiously and stop if anyone objects to what is being done
questions.why: An absent policy is a governance gap worth surfacing, and raising it serves the organisation better than resolving the individual case privately.
questions.traps: Reading absence as permission or prohibition both decide without a basis. Proceeding until someone objects leaves the gap and risks the use.

questions.stem: A team wants to publish a list of prompts they have developed, and some were adapted from a colleague's work.
options: Publish them, since prompts are too short to attract rights
Publish them with a general acknowledgement of the team
Publish only the prompts that were written entirely by the publishing team
Establish who the work belongs to and credit or seek agreement accordingly
questions.why: Adapted work raises both ownership and attribution questions. Establishing the position and acting on it is what makes publication proper.
questions.traps: The brevity argument assumes a legal conclusion. A general acknowledgement does not identify the contributor, and excluding adapted work avoids rather than resolves.

questions.stem: A team is asked to justify why a particular Claude use is safe and points to the fact that nothing has gone wrong.
options: Point to the controls in place rather than to the absence of incidents
Point to the accuracy of the output the process produces
Point to the length of time the use has run without a problem
Point to the fact that a person reviews the output before it is used
questions.why: Safety is demonstrated by the controls that operate, not by an absence of incidents. That distinction is what an assurance question is testing.
questions.traps: Accuracy, elapsed time and a claim about review are all indirect. None of them shows a control operating.

questions.stem: A team wants to know whether they can use Claude on data obtained from a public source.
options: Proceed, since the data is publicly available
Establish whether public availability permits this particular use
Proceed with the data aggregated
Proceed and cite the public source in any output
questions.why: Public availability does not by itself establish that any particular processing is permitted, particularly where personal data is involved.
questions.traps: The public-availability argument is the misconception. Aggregation and citation both address different concerns.

questions.stem: An associate wants to discuss a client problem with Claude to think it through, without sharing documents.
options: Consider whether describing the problem discloses confidential information
Proceed, since no documents are being shared
Proceed with the client's identity withheld
Proceed and delete the conversation afterwards
questions.why: Confidential information can be disclosed through description as readily as through documents. Recognising that is the point.
questions.traps: Treating documents as the only vector is the misconception. Withholding identity may not prevent identification, and deletion follows the disclosure.

questions.stem: A team is asked whether their process should be able to explain its decisions or merely be accurate.
options: Accuracy, since a correct decision does not need further justification
Explainability, since people care more about understanding than about accuracy
Whichever the organisation's policy specifies as the priority
Both, since a decision affecting people needs to be justifiable as well as correct
questions.why: Consequential decisions about people require both correctness and the ability to justify the outcome, because affected people need a route to understand and challenge it.
questions.traps: Treating either as sufficient misses what the other provides. Deferring to policy avoids the substantive question.

questions.stem: A team wants to know what they should do if they discover their Claude-assisted process has been producing wrong results.
options: Deal with it if and when it happens
Establish the response now, including who is told and how affected work is identified
Add more checking so that it does not happen
Ensure the team knows who to escalate to if something goes wrong
questions.why: A response plan decided in advance covers notification, remediation and identifying affected work. Designing it under pressure produces worse decisions.
questions.traps: Waiting until it happens is the pattern being tested. More checking reduces probability without defining a response, and an escalation contact is one part of a plan.

questions.stem: A team is deciding how much detail to give about their AI use in a public statement.
options: Give as little as possible while remaining accurate
Give as much detail as possible to demonstrate openness
Give enough that a reader can understand what is actually happening
Match the level of detail other organisations in the sector provide
questions.why: Disclosure serves a reader's understanding, and that is the standard for how much detail to give.
questions.traps: Minimal and maximal disclosure both optimise something other than understanding. Sector practice is context rather than a standard.

questions.stem: A team's Claude workflow was tested for fairness by the person who built it, and they found no issues.
options: Have someone independent review it, since self-assessment shares the builder's assumptions
Accept the finding, since the builder knows the workflow best
Repeat the test with a larger sample
Ask the builder to test additional groups
questions.why: The blind spots in a fairness assessment are usually the builder's own assumptions, which is exactly what a self-assessment cannot surface.
questions.traps: Familiarity with the workflow is the source of the blind spot. A larger sample and more groups both repeat the same perspective.

questions.stem: An associate finds a way to use Claude that produces good results but that they suspect the organisation would not approve of.
options: Continue, since the results are good and no rule explicitly prohibits it
Continue and stop if anyone raises a concern
Raise it, since a suspected approval problem is worth resolving before it becomes one
Continue but do not mention the method to colleagues
questions.why: A suspected approval problem is resolved by raising it, which either legitimises the practice or stops it before it causes difficulty.
questions.traps: Good results do not settle whether the practice is acceptable. Waiting for objection and concealing the method both compound the exposure.

questions.stem: A team is asked whether Claude-assisted work counts as the organisation's intellectual property under a client contract.
options: Assume it does, since the organisation produced the work
Assume it does not, since generated content has uncertain status
Ask the client what they understand the position to be
Read the contract's IP clause, since it defines what transfers and what does not
questions.why: The contract's IP clause governs what transfers. Reading it produces the answer rather than an inference about it.
questions.traps: Both assumptions guess at a documented position. The client's understanding is useful context but the contract is what governs.

questions.stem: A team is asked to justify why a person rather than the model makes the final call on a decision affecting individuals.
options: Because people are more accurate than models on decisions of this kind
Because a person can be held answerable for the outcome and a system cannot
Because the organisation's policy requires human involvement in such decisions
