Because customers prefer to know that a person was involved in the decision
questions.why: Accountability is the substantive reason: an affected person needs someone answerable who can explain and revisit the decision. Accuracy is a separate and not always favourable comparison.
questions.traps: Accuracy is an empirical claim that may not hold. Policy and customer preference are both real considerations but neither explains why the requirement exists.

questions.stem: An associate's prompt has started producing worse results and nothing about the prompt has changed.
options: Rewrite the prompt from scratch with fresh wording throughout
Look at what else changed, such as the inputs, the settings or the model version
Add more detail to the prompt so it is more robust to whatever has changed
Accept that output quality varies over time and continue as before
questions.why: When output changes and the prompt has not, the cause is elsewhere. Identifying what did change is the diagnosis rather than a guess.
questions.traps: Rewriting discards a prompt that may be fine. More detail treats an undiagnosed cause, and accepting drift abandons a findable explanation.

questions.stem: A prompt produces the right content in the wrong format about one time in five.
options: Ask more firmly for the correct format
Regenerate whenever the format is wrong
Specify the format precisely and validate the output before it is used
Reformat the incorrect responses manually as they arise
questions.why: Precise specification lowers the failure rate and validation catches the remainder. That pairing is what makes format reliable for downstream use.
questions.traps: Firmer wording chases an asymptote. Regenerating and manual reformatting both handle failures rather than preventing them.

questions.stem: A team's answers have got worse since they added more background material to the prompt.
options: Add even more context so the model has a fuller picture
Move to a model with a larger context window
Shorten the questions to compensate for the longer prompt
Check whether the added material is relevant to the questions being asked
questions.why: More context is not automatically better, and irrelevant material competes with what matters. Checking relevance is the direct diagnosis.
questions.traps: Adding more compounds it. A larger window accommodates rather than diagnoses, and shorter questions do not address the added material.

questions.stem: An associate gets different answers to the same question on different days and needs a stable answer.
options: Fix the parts that vary, such as the prompt wording and the context supplied
Ask the question several times and use the most common answer
Ask the question once and record the answer for future use
Accept the variation as a property of generated output
questions.why: Variation usually traces to something that is not being held constant. Fixing those inputs is what produces stability.
questions.traps: Majority voting spends calls to paper over variance. Recording one answer freezes a possibly wrong result, and accepting variation abandons a fixable cause.

questions.stem: A team's prompt is declined by the model and nobody on the team understands what triggered it.
options: Rephrase the prompt until it is accepted
Split the request into smaller parts
Try the request on a different model tier
Read what the response actually says, since it usually identifies the problem
questions.why: The response usually explains the issue, and reading it is faster and more informative than guessing through rephrasings.
questions.traps: Rephrasing until something works may sidestep a legitimate concern without understanding it. Splitting and tier-switching both guess at the cause.

questions.stem: A team's costs have risen and they suspect the prompt has grown over time without anyone noticing.
options: Compare the current prompt against what the task actually requires
Move to a cheaper model tier so each request costs less
Reduce how often the prompt is run across the team each day
Ask for shorter outputs so fewer tokens are generated
questions.why: Prompt bloat is addressed by comparing what is being sent against what the task needs. That removes cost without losing capability.
questions.traps: A cheaper tier pays less for the same waste. Reducing frequency sacrifices work, and output length is a different component.

questions.stem: A team's workflow produces good results for most inputs and consistently poor ones for a particular type.
options: Add an instruction telling the model to handle that type carefully
Examine what is different about that input type
Route that input type to a stronger model tier
Exclude that input type from the workflow
questions.why: A consistent failure on an identifiable subset is a diagnosable pattern. Understanding the difference is what points at the right fix.
questions.traps: An instruction, a stronger tier and exclusion are all responses chosen before the cause is known.

questions.stem: An associate's prompt works well except that it occasionally omits one of the four sections it is meant to produce.
options: Ask for the sections in a different order
Repeat the section list at the end of the prompt
State that each section must appear even when it would be empty
Regenerate whenever a section is missing
questions.why: Sections get dropped when the model judges one to be thin. Stating that an empty section still appears removes that judgement.
questions.traps: Reordering and repetition nudge without deciding. Regeneration handles the failure rather than preventing it.

questions.stem: A team supplies a long document and the model's answers reflect the beginning of it more than the end.
options: Ask questions that direct attention to the relevant part of the document
Supply the document in reverse order
Split the document and ask about each part separately
Ask for longer answers so more of the document is covered
questions.why: Directing the question at the relevant section is the lever that reliably brings the right material into play.
questions.traps: Reversing the order moves the problem. Splitting is a heavier workaround, and length does not redistribute attention.

questions.stem: A team's prompt gives consistent results for one colleague and inconsistent results for another.
options: Ask the second colleague to use the first colleague's wording
Accept that results vary between people
Compare their account settings and any project configuration in use
Ask both to run the prompt several times and compare the averages
questions.why: Account-level configuration applies to every request and is invisible in the prompt. Comparing settings is where an otherwise identical prompt diverges.
questions.traps: Copying wording assumes the prompt differs. Accepting variation skips a systematic cause, and averaging measures rather than explains.

questions.stem: An associate needs Claude to do something it says it cannot do, and the task is legitimate.
options: Insist, explaining that the task is legitimate
Try the same request repeatedly until it succeeds
Report the limitation and abandon the task
Check whether the task can be restructured into something it can do
questions.why: Many limitations are about how a task is framed rather than the task itself. Restructuring is what finds the workable version.
questions.traps: Insisting and repeating both push against the response rather than reframing. Abandoning forgoes a task that may well be achievable.

questions.stem: A team wants to reduce cost and is considering shortening the prompt or shortening the output.
options: Shorten the prompt, since it is sent on every request
Measure which one dominates their token usage before changing either
Shorten the output, since generated tokens usually cost more
Shorten both by roughly the same proportion
questions.why: Which component dominates varies by workload, and measuring is what directs the effort where it pays.
questions.traps: Both assertions are plausible and workload-dependent. Cutting both equally spends effort on the component that may not matter.

questions.stem: A team's results improved after they changed three things at once and they want to know which one helped.
options: Keep all three, since the combination works
Assume the largest change was responsible
Ask Claude which of the three changes it thinks helped most
Change them back one at a time to isolate the effect
questions.why: Isolating one variable at a time is what attributes the improvement. Otherwise the knowledge does not transfer to the next problem.
questions.traps: Keeping the bundle works without producing knowledge. Assuming by size is a guess, and the model cannot report on its own performance differences.

questions.stem: An associate adds an instruction to fix a problem and a different problem appears.
options: Add a third instruction addressing the new problem
Remove the new instruction and accept the original problem
Check whether the new instruction conflicts with an existing one
Reorder the instructions so the new one comes last
questions.why: Instructions interact rather than stack, so a new problem after an addition often signals a conflict. Checking is what resolves it properly.
questions.traps: Stacking a third instruction compounds the interaction. Reverting accepts the original problem, and reordering does not resolve a conflict.

questions.stem: A team pastes a large amount of context and the model appears to ignore a specific instruction within it.
options: Repeat the instruction several times within the pasted material
Move the instruction out of the pasted material so it is not buried in it
Make the instruction longer and more emphatic
Ask the model to confirm it has seen the instruction before proceeding
questions.why: An instruction buried inside a large block of pasted content competes with it. Separating it is what makes it read as an instruction.
questions.traps: Repetition and emphasis both leave it inside the block. A confirmation step adds a round trip without changing the structure.

questions.stem: A team needs identical output from repeated runs and is getting small variations each time.
options: Establish whether identical output is genuinely required, since exact repetition is not the model's default behaviour
Run it once and reuse that output whenever it is needed again
Ask the model to be consistent across the repeated runs
Compare the variations and pick the best one
questions.why: Whether exact reproducibility is required determines the approach entirely, and it is often achievable by caching a validated result rather than by regenerating.
questions.traps: Reusing one output may be right but skips the question. An instruction does not produce determinism, and picking the best each time is manual selection.

questions.stem: A team finds Claude declines a category of request that is central to their workflow.
options: Find wording that avoids triggering the decline
Understand the boundary and design the workflow around what is available
Escalate to the vendor to have the limitation removed
Use a different tool for that part of the workflow
questions.why: Understanding where the boundary sits lets the workflow be designed around it, which is more durable than working against it.
questions.traps: Wording workarounds are fragile and may circumvent a legitimate limit. Escalation is slow, and switching tools is reasonable but follows understanding the boundary.

questions.stem: An associate's prompt includes six examples and the task is a simple two-way classification.
options: Test whether fewer examples hold the accuracy
Keep all six, since accuracy matters more than cost
Add more examples to improve accuracy further
Remove all the examples and rely on the instruction alone
questions.why: Example count has diminishing returns and a binary decision usually saturates early. Measuring where accuracy plateaus finds the cheap point.
questions.traps: Assuming six are needed skips the test. More examples costs more, and removing all of them is as unmeasured as keeping six.

questions.stem: A team's output quality is fine but their reviewers keep rejecting it for reasons the team does not understand.
options: Improve the prompt until the rejections stop
Ask Claude to produce higher-quality output
Ask the reviewers what standard they are applying
Ask a different reviewer to assess the output
questions.why: The rejection criterion is knowledge the reviewers hold. Asking is faster and more accurate than inferring it from rejections.
questions.traps: Iterating against unexplained rejections is a slow search. A general quality instruction has no target, and a different reviewer may apply a different unstated standard.

questions.stem: A prompt that worked well has degraded after a colleague made several edits to it.
options: Rewrite the prompt from scratch rather than tracing the edits
Ask the colleague to explain their edits
Revert to the previous version and forbid further edits
Compare against the previous version to identify what changed
questions.why: A working prompt and a degraded one differ by a known set of edits. Comparing them identifies the cause directly.
questions.traps: Rewriting discards both versions' knowledge. An explanation may not identify which edit caused it, and reverting without diagnosis loses any genuine improvements.

questions.stem: An associate finds their long-running conversation has started ignoring an instruction given at the beginning.
options: Restate the standing constraints, since early instructions fade as a conversation grows
Start a new conversation and re-establish the context there
Ask the model to summarise the constraints agreed so far
Move the instruction to the most recent message
questions.why: Earlier instructions compete with a growing conversation. Restating what must remain true is what keeps a standing constraint in effect.
questions.traps: A fresh start loses accumulated work. A self-summary can omit the same forgotten item, and a single repositioning fades again as the conversation continues.

questions.stem: A team's outputs are consistent within a session and vary noticeably between sessions.
options: Run everything inside one long session to avoid the variation
Accept the between-session variation
Average across several sessions before using the result
Look for something that differs between sessions rather than within them
questions.why: Consistency inside a session and variation across them points at a session-scoped input such as accumulated context or a setting. That is findable.
questions.traps: Forcing single sessions is a workaround. Accepting it abandons the diagnosis, and averaging conceals rather than explains.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude to do something that requires information it does not have access to.
options: Ask more specifically so the model finds the information
Move to a stronger model tier so the gap is closed by capability
Supply the information, since the limitation is about access rather than capability
Ask the model to estimate the information as best it can
questions.why: Missing information is supplied rather than worked around. Distinguishing an access limitation from a capability one is the diagnostic skill here.
questions.traps: Specificity cannot retrieve what is absent. A stronger tier has the same access, and estimation invites invention.

questions.stem: A team's workflow makes two calls where the second only reformats the first's output.
options: Move the second call to a cheaper tier
Ask for the required format in the first call
Combine the two calls into one longer prompt
Run the two calls in parallel so the total time is shorter
questions.why: A separate call purely to reformat is avoidable by specifying the format up front, which removes the call rather than making it cheaper.
questions.traps: A cheaper second call still pays for an avoidable step. Combining prompts is the same idea stated less directly, and parallelism is impossible for dependent calls.

questions.stem: An associate suspects their prompt is the problem but has not compared it against anything.
options: Add more detail to the prompt so it is less open to interpretation
Rewrite the prompt in a different style
Test a deliberately simple version to see whether the problem persists
Ask a colleague to look at the prompt
questions.why: A minimal version isolates whether the prompt is the cause. If the problem persists, the cause is elsewhere and the prompt is exonerated.
questions.traps: Adding detail and restyling both change the prompt without testing whether it is responsible. A colleague's read is opinion rather than a test.

questions.stem: A team's workflow fails on roughly one input in ten and they have not looked at which ones.
options: Add a retry so that failures are attempted a second time before the workflow gives up on the input
Collect the failing cases and look for what they have in common
Move to a stronger model tier so the failures become rarer
Add a review step covering every output the workflow produces
questions.why: Failures are rarely random. Collecting them and looking for a shared property is what turns a rate into a diagnosable pattern.
questions.traps: Retries help only with transient failures. A stronger tier and universal review both respond before the cause is known.

questions.stem: An associate's prompt is two pages long after twenty rounds of case-by-case fixes and new instructions no longer help.
options: Rebuild it around the general rule the fixes share
Continue adding instructions for each new case as it arises
Split it across several shorter prompts run one after another
Move the newest instructions to the top
questions.why: Accretion produces a prompt where instructions compete and dilute. Consolidating around the underlying rule restores the leverage each one has.
questions.traps: Continued accretion created the plateau. Splitting and reordering redistribute a bloated set without simplifying it.

questions.stem: A team's prompt includes a reference document and answers frequently contradict it.
options: Ask the question again using wording that matches the document more closely
Make the reference document shorter so it is easier to use
Ask for the answer twice and compare
Instruct the model to answer from the document and to say when it is silent
questions.why: Supplied documents get blended with general knowledge unless grounding is stated. The instruction is what makes the document authoritative.
questions.traps: Rewording improves retrieval without preventing the blend. Shortening and repeat runs both leave the grounding unstated.

questions.stem: A team's output format is stable in testing and varies in production.
options: Add a stronger format instruction to the prompt so that the model is less likely to deviate from the required structure when it encounters unusual material in production
Compare the production inputs against the test inputs
Validate and reformat the output in production
Test with a larger sample of production inputs before deciding
questions.why: A difference between test and production behaviour usually reflects a difference in the inputs. Comparing them is the direct diagnosis.
questions.traps: A stronger instruction treats an undiagnosed cause. Validation is a good control but not the diagnosis, and more testing measures rather than explains.

questions.stem: An associate finds the model will not produce a specific numeric answer and instead gives a range.
options: Insist on a single figure, explaining that the team needs a specific number in order to make the decision they are currently working through with the information available
Ask for the midpoint of the range and present that as the figure
Check whether the underlying data supports a point answer at all
Move to a stronger model tier so a point answer is produced
questions.why: A range where a point was requested often reflects genuine uncertainty in the inputs. Checking whether a point answer is supportable is the right first question.
questions.traps: Insisting produces false precision. A midpoint discards the uncertainty, and a stronger tier does not create data that is not there.

questions.stem: A team's prompt sends a 40-page appendix that answers have never drawn on.
options: Keep the appendix in case a future question requires it
Move to a cheaper tier so the appendix costs less to send
Compress the appendix into a summary
Remove the appendix and confirm the answers are unaffected
questions.why: Material that never contributes is cost on every request. Removing it and verifying is the direct saving.
questions.traps: Retaining for hypothetical need is how prompts bloat. A cheaper tier pays less for the same waste, and a summary still carries unused content.

questions.stem: A team's results are inconsistent and they have changed the prompt, the tier and the inputs since it started.
options: Return to a known configuration and change one thing at a time
Continue adjusting until the results stabilise, since the combination that works will eventually be found through the process of trying different arrangements
Keep the current configuration and accept the inconsistency
Ask Claude to diagnose the inconsistency itself
questions.why: With three variables changed, nothing is attributable. Returning to a baseline and varying one factor is what makes the investigation interpretable.
questions.traps: Undirected adjustment is the search that has already failed. Keeping the configuration accepts the inconsistency, and the model cannot diagnose its own variability.

questions.stem: An associate's prompt asks for a summary and an assessment, and the assessment is always thin.
options: Ask for a longer assessment so that it receives more attention within the response and the analysis is developed more fully than it currently is
Ask for the assessment first and the summary afterwards
Add an instruction emphasising the assessment
Split them into two requests so each gets a full pass
questions.why: A combined request splits attention between the two tasks. Separating them gives the assessment a full pass over the material.
questions.traps: Length, ordering and emphasis all redistribute attention within a single response rather than changing that it is shared.

questions.stem: A team supplies twelve documents and the model consistently draws on the same three.
options: Upload the nine unused documents again in case they were not processed correctly when they were first added to the material supplied with the prompt
Reduce the set to the three documents that are being used
Ask questions that name the documents the answer should draw on
Ask for longer answers so more of the documents are drawn on
questions.why: Retrieval favours whatever matches the question best. Naming the intended sources is what brings the others into play.
questions.traps: Re-uploading assumes a processing failure. Reducing the set discards material, and length does not change which documents are consulted.

questions.stem: A team gets stable results with short inputs and unstable results with long ones.
options: Ask for shorter answers when the input is long so that the total amount of material being handled at
Investigate whether the long inputs exceed what the model handles reliably here
Split the long inputs into smaller pieces before processing
Move to a stronger tier so long inputs are handled better
questions.why: Instability correlated with input length is a diagnosable pattern about how much material is being handled at once. Investigating that is the direct step.
questions.traps: Shorter answers address the output side. Splitting and tier changes are both remedies chosen before the cause is confirmed.

questions.stem: A team's request is declined and the response explains that the task requires information about a specific private individual.
options: Reconsider whether the task is appropriate given what the response identified
Rephrase the request so that the individual is described
Split the request into smaller parts
Ask a colleague to make the same request
questions.why: The response has identified a substantive concern about a private individual. Reconsidering the task is the appropriate response rather than working around the objection.
questions.traps: Describing rather than naming, splitting the request and having someone else ask are all circumvention of a concern that was raised for a reason.

questions.stem: An associate's workflow runs a verification call on every output and has never measured what it catches.
options: Remove it, since verification calls double the cost of the workflow and the team has no evidence that they are catching anything worth the money being spent
Measure what it catches before deciding whether it earns its cost
Keep it, since verification is always worthwhile
Run the verification on a sample of outputs rather than all
questions.why: Whether the verification is worth its cost depends on what it catches, which is measurable. That measurement is what makes the decision defensible.
questions.traps: Removing and keeping both decide without the evidence. Sampling reduces cost and catch rate together without measuring either.

questions.stem: A team's workflow degrades gradually over months with no single change responsible.
options: Compare current inputs and configuration against what they were originally
Rebuild the workflow from scratch so that it reflects the team's current understanding
Add more review so the degraded output is caught sooner
Accept gradual drift as a normal property of such workflows
questions.why: Gradual degradation is usually accumulated small changes in inputs or configuration. Comparing against the original state is what reveals them.
questions.traps: Rebuilding discards a working system without learning what drifted. More review manages symptoms, and accepting drift abandons the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A prompt produces good output except that it always includes a disclaimer the team does not want.
options: Remove the disclaimer manually from each response before it is used
Ask for shorter output so the disclaimer takes up less room
Ask the model why it includes the disclaimer
Say explicitly that no disclaimer should be included
questions.why: A specific unwanted element is removed by naming it as an exclusion. That is the direct instruction.
questions.traps: Manual removal repeats forever. Shorter output may drop other content, and asking about the cause is a diagnostic detour for a simple exclusion.

questions.stem: A team's answers improved after they removed material from the prompt, which surprised them.
options: Treat it as a coincidence and restore the material, since more context should generally produce better answers and the improvement may not be attributable to the removal
Remove more material until the quality starts to fall
Take it as evidence that some of the material was competing with what mattered
Add the removed material back gradually and watch the effect
questions.why: Improvement after removal is direct evidence that the removed material was interfering. Recognising that is the durable lesson about context.
questions.traps: Dismissing it as coincidence discards a finding. Removing until failure and adding back gradually are both searches that skip the insight.

questions.stem: An associate wants their workflow to behave identically for every user and each user has their own configuration.
options: Ask all the users to align their personal settings so that everyone is working from the same starting point and the workflow behaves the same way for each of them
Document the settings each user is required to configure
Have one person run the workflow for everyone
Move the workflow into shared configuration so personal settings do not apply
questions.why: Account-level settings are invisible inputs to every request. Moving the workflow into shared configuration removes the dependency structurally.
questions.traps: Manual alignment relies on everyone maintaining it. Documentation records the requirement without enforcing it, and single-operator running is a bottleneck.

questions.stem: A team wants an answer the model says it cannot give because the information post-dates what it knows.
options: Ask the question in a way that does not depend on recent information
Move to a newer model whose knowledge extends further forward
Supply the current information, since the limitation is about recency rather than reasoning
Ask the model to estimate what has probably happened since
questions.why: A knowledge cutoff is an information gap that supplying the data closes. Recognising it as such is the diagnostic point.
questions.traps: Reframing to avoid the recency abandons the question. A newer model has a later but still fixed cutoff, and estimation invites invention.

questions.stem: A team's cost is dominated by a small number of very long inputs.
options: Reduce the total number of requests across the whole team
Handle the long inputs differently, since that is where the cost concentrates
Move to a cheaper tier so the long inputs cost less to process
Ask people to submit shorter inputs
questions.why: Cost concentrated in a few large inputs is addressed by treating those inputs differently rather than by uniform reductions affecting the cheap majority.
questions.traps: Cutting overall volume mostly reduces inexpensive requests. A cheaper tier pays less for the same skew, and shorter submissions may not be possible.

questions.stem: An associate's output is poor and they are unsure whether the problem is the prompt or the model.
options: Try the same prompt on a stronger tier to separate the two
Rewrite the prompt to be as clear as possible and see whether the results improve
Move to a stronger tier permanently
Ask a colleague to try the same prompt
questions.why: Running the same prompt on a stronger tier isolates capability from specification. If it still fails, the prompt is the problem.
questions.traps: Rewriting changes the prompt without isolating the variable. Switching permanently spends before diagnosing, and a colleague running the same prompt tests neither.

questions.stem: A team's prompt works on the examples they wrote it against and fails on real inputs.
options: Add the failing real inputs as additional examples in the prompt
Test against real inputs during development rather than curated examples
Make the prompt more general so it covers a wider range
Filter real inputs to resemble the examples
questions.why: Development examples are usually cleaner than reality. Testing against real inputs is what makes the prompt fit its actual job.
questions.traps: Absorbing failures as examples handles each case individually. Generality without testing is a guess, and filtering inputs changes the task.

questions.stem: A team's prompt contains both instructions and reference material with no clear separation.
options: Separate them clearly so the instructions read as instructions
Move the instructions to the end so that they are the most recent thing the model encounters before it begins producing its response to the request
Shorten the reference material so the instructions stand out
Repeat the instructions inside the reference material
questions.why: Instructions blended into reference material compete with it. Clear separation is what makes the instructional content legible as such.
questions.traps: Repositioning and repetition both leave the blend. Shortening the reference reduces volume without clarifying the structure.

questions.stem: A team wants to know whether an apparent improvement is real or normal variation.
options: Adopt the improved version, since the difference was clearly visible in the comparison the team made between the two versions of the prompt they were testing
Ask a colleague to judge which of the two versions is better
Run both versions several times and compare the distributions
Run the improved version once more to confirm the result
questions.why: A single comparison cannot separate a real difference from run-to-run variation. Multiple runs of each is what distinguishes them.
questions.traps: Adopting on one comparison acts on possible noise. Colleague judgement is not measurement, and one more run of one arm is not a comparison.

questions.stem: An associate's workflow depends on behaviour that the model produces most of the time but not reliably.
options: Add an instruction requiring the behaviour so that it happens consistently
Move to a stronger tier so the behaviour becomes reliable
Accept the failures as a limitation
Design the workflow to handle the cases where the behaviour does not occur
questions.why: Depending on unreliable behaviour requires handling the exceptions. Designing for them is what makes the workflow robust.
questions.traps: An instruction reduces the rate without eliminating it. A stronger tier does the same, and accepting failures leaves them unhandled.

questions.stem: A team's workflow is fast enough and costs more than they would like.
options: Reduce the number of requests the workflow makes so that the total cost falls
Keep the current setup since the speed is already adequate
Trade latency for cost, since the speed is not currently being used
Ask for shorter outputs so each request costs less to run
questions.why: Slack on one dimension can be spent to relieve pressure on another. Unused speed is exactly the resource to trade for cost.
questions.traps: Fewer requests reduces the work done. Keeping the setup ignores the cost concern, and shorter outputs may lose content.

questions.stem: A team's workflow works for the person who built it and not for anyone else, and the prompt is identical.
options: Compare everything that differs between them, including settings and project context
Ask the builder to walk the others through how they use it
Have the builder run it for everyone
Rebuild the workflow with the others involved
questions.why: An identical prompt producing different results points at configuration outside the prompt. Comparing everything else is the systematic approach.
questions.traps: A walkthrough may surface a difference by luck. Single-operator running is a bottleneck, and rebuilding starts over without finding the cause.

questions.stem: A team's workflow is accurate and slow, and the slowness is caused by a step nobody has questioned.
options: Move the slow step to a faster model tier so that it completes more quickly
Run the slow step in parallel with the others
Accept the latency as a cost of the current design
Question whether that step is needed at all
questions.why: The cheapest optimisation is removing work that does not need doing. Questioning the step precedes making it faster.
questions.traps: Speeding up or parallelising an unnecessary step optimises waste. Accepting the latency skips the question entirely.

questions.stem: An associate's prompt produces good analysis and poor formatting, and they keep rewriting the whole prompt.
options: Rewrite the prompt from scratch with both the analysis and the formatting requirements described more carefully than they were in the original version
Change only the formatting instruction and leave the rest alone
Add formatting examples to the prompt as well
Reformat the output manually after each run
questions.why: When one aspect works and another does not, changing only the failing part preserves what already works. Wholesale rewriting risks the analysis.
questions.traps: A full rewrite puts the working analysis at risk. Examples may help but are a bigger change than needed, and manual reformatting repeats forever.

questions.stem: A team's answers cite the right document but the wrong section within it.
options: Ask the model to double-check its section references before it produces the final answer
Ask for the answer without a citation
Upload the document again so it is processed freshly
Treat the locator as unverified and check it against the document
questions.why: Correct content with a wrong locator is the characteristic failure, and only checking against the document settles it.
questions.traps: Self-checking uses the process that produced the error. Dropping citations loses traceability, and re-uploading addresses a fault that is not indicated.

questions.stem: A team's prompt gives different results depending on the order documents are attached.
options: Ask people to attach documents in a consistent order so that the results stop varying between different runs of the same workflow by different team members
Accept the variation between the different orderings
Fix the order or remove the dependence, since hidden order effects are a defect
Combine all the documents into one single file
questions.why: Hidden order dependence is a defect. Removing it or making the required order explicit turns invisible variation into a known property.
questions.traps: A convention people must remember is the weakest form of the fix. Accepting it leaves the variation, and combining files changes the input.

questions.stem: An associate needs a task done that the model handles poorly and a colleague could do quickly.
options: Have the colleague do it, since not every task suits the tool
Keep refining the prompt until the model produces acceptable output for the task
Move to a stronger tier so the task is handled better
Split the task into smaller pieces the model can manage
questions.why: Recognising when a task is a poor fit is part of using the tool well. The colleague is the better route here.
questions.traps: Refinement against a poor fit is a slow search. A stronger tier and decomposition both assume the task suits the tool.

questions.stem: A team wants to reduce cost and has identified three candidate changes with different savings and risks.
options: Implement all three at once so that the full saving is realised as quickly as possible and the team can move on to other work
Rank them by saving against risk and start with the best ratio
Implement the largest saving first regardless of its risk
Implement the lowest-risk change first
questions.why: Ranking by return against risk is what makes the sequence defensible rather than driven by one dimension alone.
questions.traps: Implementing all three at once obscures which caused any problem. Size and risk each ignore the other dimension.

questions.stem: A team's failure rate rose sharply on one day and returned to normal the next.
options: Look at what was different about that day's inputs
Add monitoring so that future spikes are detected quickly and the team is alerted when the failure rate rises above its normal level for a sustained period
Ignore it as a transient anomaly that resolved itself
Add a retry so the failing requests are attempted again
questions.why: A one-day spike is a bounded event with a findable cause. Examining that day's inputs is the direct investigation.
questions.traps: Monitoring detects future spikes without explaining this one. Ignoring it discards evidence, and retries treat a symptom.

questions.stem: A prompt works well until the input contains a table, at which point the output degrades noticeably.
options: Add a general instruction telling the model to be careful with structured content
Convert tables to prose before sending
Move to a stronger tier so tables are handled correctly
Handle tables explicitly, since the failure is tied to a specific input feature
questions.why: A failure tied to an identifiable input feature is addressed by handling that feature explicitly. The pattern points directly at the fix.
questions.traps: A general care instruction has no specific target. Conversion loses structure, and a stronger tier is a spend before a targeted fix is tried.

questions.stem: An associate's prompt includes background that was relevant to an earlier version of the task.
options: Leave it, since additional background rarely does any harm and removing material risks losing something that turns out to be relevant to the current version
Update the background to reflect the current task
Remove it, since stale context competes with what currently matters
Move the stale background to the end of the prompt
questions.why: Context that no longer applies competes for attention on every request. Removing it is the direct improvement.
questions.traps: Assuming background is harmless is the misconception. Updating may be right if it is still needed, and repositioning keeps the cost.

questions.stem: A team's workflow is reliable in the morning and less so in the afternoon, and they suspect the time of day.
options: Investigate whether system load in the afternoon is affecting the results that the workflow produces during the busier part of the working day
Look at what differs about afternoon inputs rather than at the clock
Run everything in the morning when results are reliable
Accept the pattern and plan the work around it
questions.why: Time of day is not a mechanism. The likely explanation is a difference in what gets submitted at each time, which is checkable immediately.
questions.traps: Investigating load treats a correlation as causal. Scheduling around it hides the variation, and accepting it abandons a diagnosable problem.

questions.stem: A team wants the model to state a definite conclusion where the evidence genuinely does not support one.
options: Ask for a definite conclusion anyway, since the team needs to make a decision and a hedged answer does not help them choose between the options in front of them
Ask for the most likely conclusion rather than a hedge
Accept the hedged answer, since it reflects the state of the evidence
Move to a stronger tier so a firmer answer is produced
questions.why: A hedge that reflects genuine uncertainty is the correct output. Forcing a definite answer manufactures confidence the evidence does not support.
questions.traps: Insisting produces false certainty. Asking for the most likely conclusion is closer but still presses past the evidence, and a stronger tier does not create data.

questions.stem: An associate's workflow processes every item at the same depth, and most items are straightforward.
options: Move everything to a cheaper tier so that the cost per item falls across the whole workload
Process fewer items so the total cost comes down
Accept the cost as the price of consistent processing
Route straightforward items through a lighter path
questions.why: Matching processing depth to item difficulty is what captures the saving without degrading the hard cases.
questions.traps: A uniform downgrade under-serves the complex items. Processing fewer items reduces the work, and accepting the cost forgoes an available saving.

questions.stem: A team's output is worse than a colleague's on the same task and they cannot see any difference in approach.
options: Compare the two setups systematically rather than looking for a difference by eye
Ask the colleague to explain how they approach the task
Copy the colleague's prompt and use it without changes
Accept the difference between the two sets of results
questions.why: A systematic comparison of prompts, settings and context finds differences that inspection misses. That is the reliable method.
questions.traps: Discussion may surface a difference by luck. Copying works without producing understanding, and accepting the gap forgoes the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A team's prompt has an instruction that has never been tested and may have no effect.
options: Leave it, since it does no harm and may be contributing something that would be lost if it were removed from the prompt
Remove it temporarily and see whether anything changes
Strengthen the wording of the untested instruction
Move the instruction earlier so it carries more weight
questions.why: Removing and comparing is the direct test of whether an instruction does anything. Untested instructions dilute the ones that matter.
questions.traps: Assuming it is harmless ignores the dilution cost. Strengthening and repositioning both act before establishing whether it does anything.

questions.stem: An associate finds that answers improve when they ask about one topic at a time rather than several.
options: Treat it as a coincidence, since a single request covering several topics should produce the same quality of answer as several separate requests would
Ask about several topics but in a longer prompt
Ask about several topics and request longer answers
Take it as a working technique and structure requests around single topics
questions.why: Single-topic requests concentrate attention, and an observed improvement is a technique worth adopting deliberately.
questions.traps: Dismissing the observation discards a finding. Longer prompts and longer answers both keep the attention split.

questions.stem: A team wants reproducible results and is currently regenerating the output each time it is needed.
options: Regenerate each time and compare against the previous version
Accept the variation between the generated versions
Generate once, validate, and reuse the validated output
Average across several generations of the same output
questions.why: When the same output is needed repeatedly, generating once and reusing a validated result is both reproducible and cheaper than regenerating.
questions.traps: Comparing every regeneration is ongoing work for no gain. Accepting variation defeats the requirement, and averaging is not meaningful for text.

questions.stem: A team's prompt occasionally produces a response declining part of the request while completing the rest.
options: Look at which part is being declined and why
Regenerate the response so that a complete answer is produced
Split the request into parts and submit them separately
Remove the part of the request that is being declined
questions.why: Understanding which element triggers the decline is what determines whether the request should be reframed or reconsidered.
questions.traps: Regenerating hopes the decline does not recur. Splitting and removing both act before understanding what is being objected to.

questions.stem: An associate's prompt has grown because each addition seemed small at the time.
options: Remove the most recent additions, since those are the ones that pushed the prompt to its current length and are most likely to be the least necessary of them
Review the whole prompt against what the task needs
Move to a cheaper tier so the longer prompt costs less
Accept the current length as the cost of the additions
questions.why: Incremental growth is only visible against the task's actual requirements. Reviewing the whole prompt against those is what identifies what to cut.
questions.traps: Removing by recency assumes newer means less necessary. A cheaper tier pays less for the same bloat, and accepting it forgoes the saving.

questions.stem: A team's workflow produces good output that their reviewers consistently find unusable.
options: Improve the output quality further so that it meets the standard the reviewers are applying when they assess whether the material is usable for their purposes
Change the reviewers for people with different standards
Find out what the reviewers need that the output does not provide
Ask the reviewers to be rather less demanding
questions.why: Output judged unusable despite being good is missing something specific to the reviewers' need. Finding out what is the direct route.
questions.traps: Improving general quality without knowing the gap is undirected. Changing or pressuring reviewers avoids a legitimate requirement.

questions.stem: A prompt produces the right answer but always adds an unnecessary preamble.
options: Say that the response should begin with the answer and contain no preamble
Ask for shorter responses so that the preamble is compressed along with the rest of the content the model produces in reply to the request
Delete the preamble manually from each response produced
Ask the model to stop being conversational
questions.why: A specific unwanted element is removed by naming it and stating what should replace it. That is the direct instruction.
questions.traps: Shortening compresses the answer too. Manual deletion repeats forever, and a vague instruction about tone is less precise than naming the element.

questions.stem: A team's workflow supplies a document and a set of instructions, and the model follows the document's own instructions instead.
options: Shorten the document so that its own instructional content is less prominent within the material supplied alongside the actual task instructions
Remove the document so its instructions cannot be followed
Repeat the task instructions after the document as well
Make clear which text is the task and which is material to be worked on
questions.why: Documents containing instructions can be read as directives unless the boundary is marked. Making the distinction explicit is what resolves it.
questions.traps: Shortening reduces the surface without marking the boundary. Removing the document loses the material, and repetition competes rather than clarifies.

questions.stem: An associate's results changed after the model was updated and they had not been tracking versions.
options: Rebuild the prompt against the new version so that it is tuned for the current model
Start recording which version produced which results
Revert to the previous model version and stay there
Accept that updates change behaviour
questions.why: Recording versions is what makes future changes attributable. Without it, every update produces an unexplained shift.
questions.traps: Rebuilding may be needed but leaves the same blind spot. Reverting is temporary, and accepting change without tracking it forgoes the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A team wants to know why the model sometimes says it is uncertain and sometimes does not, on similar questions.
options: Ask the model to always state its confidence so that the signal is available consistently across every response the team receives from the workflow
Verify only the answers where uncertainty was expressed
Treat expressed uncertainty as informative when present and uninformative when absent
Ask the question in a consistent way each time
questions.why: Expressed uncertainty is asymmetric: present it means something, absent it means nothing. That asymmetry is the point.
questions.traps: Mandating a confidence statement does not create the missing knowledge. Verifying only flagged answers misses confident errors, and consistent phrasing does not change the asymmetry.

questions.stem: A team's workflow could be made cheaper, faster or more accurate, and they cannot have all three.
options: Improve all three incrementally so that the workflow gets somewhat better on each of the dimensions
Decide which constraint actually binds for this workload
Optimise for accuracy since correctness matters most here
Optimise for cost since the budget is under pressure
questions.why: Optimisation requires knowing which dimension is binding. Identifying that is what makes the trade-off deliberate.
questions.traps: Spreading effort across three dimensions improves none meaningfully. Choosing accuracy or cost by default ignores which one is actually constrained.

questions.stem: An associate has a theory about why their workflow fails and has not tested it.
options: Act on the theory, since it is the most plausible explanation available and testing would take time that could be spent implementing the fix instead
Ask a colleague whether the theory sounds right
Implement a fix that would work regardless of the cause
Test the theory before acting on it
questions.why: An untested theory is a hypothesis. Testing it is usually quick and prevents effort going into a fix for the wrong cause.
questions.traps: Acting untested risks fixing nothing. A colleague's view is opinion, and a cause-agnostic fix is usually a workaround rather than a resolution.

questions.stem: A team's prompt works reliably except when the input it receives is unusually short, where it fails.
options: Handle the short-input case explicitly
Add a general instruction about handling inputs of varying length
Reject short inputs so the failure cannot occur at all
Pad short inputs until they reach a workable length
questions.why: A failure tied to an identifiable input property is addressed by handling that property. The pattern points at the fix.
questions.traps: A general instruction has no specific target. Rejecting short inputs refuses valid work, and padding fabricates content.

questions.stem: An associate supplies a glossary with their prompt and the model still misuses two of the terms.
options: Supply the glossary again in a different format so that the definitions are presented more clearly than they are in the current version being used
Remove the glossary since it is not resolving the terms
Ask the model to confirm it has read the glossary
Check whether those two terms are defined clearly enough in the glossary
questions.why: Two specific terms failing while the rest work points at those definitions rather than at the glossary mechanism. Checking them is the direct step.
questions.traps: Reformatting addresses presentation rather than the definitions. Removing the glossary loses the rest, and a confirmation adds a round trip.

questions.stem: A team's workflow gives one answer when run alone and a different one when run after other work in the same conversation.
options: Run it in a fresh context so prior conversation does not influence it
Ask the model to disregard the earlier conversation when it answers the question that the workflow puts to it during the course of the session
Accept the difference between the two ways of running it
Run it twice and compare the two sets of results
questions.why: Accumulated conversation is an input that changes the result. Isolating the workflow in a fresh context removes that influence.
questions.traps: An instruction to disregard context competes with the context itself. Accepting the difference abandons reproducibility, and comparing measures rather than removes it.

questions.stem: A team finds the model produces a shorter answer than requested when the topic is sensitive.
options: Ask again more forcefully for the full length that was originally specified in the request
Split the request into parts and submit each separately
Consider whether the topic warrants the caution before pressing for length
Move to a different tier that may respond more fully
questions.why: Reduced output on a sensitive topic often reflects a substantive judgement. Considering whether it is warranted comes before pressing past it.
questions.traps: Pressing, splitting and switching tiers are all attempts to get around a response rather than to understand it.

questions.stem: An associate's workflow costs little per run and runs far more often than anyone realised.
options: Reduce the cost per run so that the total falls in proportion to the saving achieved on each individual execution of the workflow
Look at the total, since frequency matters as much as unit cost
Accept the cost since each individual run is inexpensive
Move to a cheaper tier so the frequent runs cost less
questions.why: Total cost is unit cost times frequency, and an unnoticed frequency is the variable that has been overlooked. Examining the total is what reveals it.
questions.traps: Optimising unit cost ignores the frequency that caused the surprise. Accepting it forgoes the finding, and a cheaper tier is one lever chosen before understanding the driver.

questions.stem: A team's workflow began failing after a colleague made an undocumented change.
options: Rebuild the workflow so that its current state is understood by everyone
Revert everything to the last known working backup
Find out what changed, since the timing points directly at it
Add monitoring so future failures are detected sooner
questions.why: A change immediately preceding a failure is the obvious first suspect. Establishing what it was is the fastest route to the cause.
questions.traps: Rebuilding and reverting both act without knowing what changed. Monitoring watches for future problems rather than explaining this one.

questions.stem: A team's instruction to avoid jargon has made the output vague rather than accessible.
options: Ask for simpler language in addition to the existing instruction
Remove the jargon instruction so precision can return
Ask for definitions of any jargon used
Give a list of terms that remain acceptable so precision survives
questions.why: A blanket ban removes vocabulary without supplying replacements, so the model reaches for imprecision. An allowed list keeps the words that carry meaning.
questions.traps: Adding a simplicity instruction compounds the problem. Removing the instruction abandons the goal, and inline definitions are a different technique.

questions.stem: An associate's prompt includes an example that is now inconsistent with the current requirements.
options: Add an instruction explaining that the example is out of date and should not be followed exactly as it is written in the prompt
Update the example, since it demonstrates the pattern the model will follow
Remove all the examples so none of them can mislead
Add a newer example alongside the outdated one
questions.why: Examples demonstrate the target and are followed. An inconsistent one actively teaches the wrong pattern, so it has to be corrected.
questions.traps: A correction note competes with the demonstration. Removing all examples loses the technique, and a second example creates a conflict.

questions.stem: A team measured their workflow at 91% and again at 94% on the same fifty cases a month apart.
options: Treat the difference as within the noise of a fifty-case sample
Conclude that the workflow has improved and record the higher figure as the current level of performance the team can expect from it
Investigate what improved between the two measurements
Average the two figures and report the combined result
questions.why: A three-point difference on fifty cases is well within ordinary variation. Recognising that prevents acting on noise.
questions.traps: Recording the higher figure and investigating an improvement both treat noise as signal. Averaging produces a number without addressing the imprecision.

questions.stem: A team's workflow depends on the model doing something it does reliably today and may not always.
options: Document the dependency so that the team knows what the workflow relies on if problems arise at some point in the future with the behaviour it depends on
Accept the risk since the behaviour is reliable today
Design the workflow so a change in behaviour is detected rather than silent
Test the behaviour periodically to confirm it still holds
questions.why: A dependency on unguaranteed behaviour needs detection, so that a change surfaces as a clear failure rather than as degraded output nobody notices.
questions.traps: Documentation records without detecting. Accepting the risk leaves it silent, and periodic testing is a partial form of the right answer without continuous coverage.

questions.stem: An associate wants to cut cost and the only lever they have considered is the model tier.
options: Move to the cheapest tier that produces acceptable results for the workload
Look at the prompt, the output length and the call pattern as well
Accept the current cost as the price of the workflow
Reduce how much the team uses the workflow each month
questions.why: Cost is driven by tier, input size, output size and frequency. Considering only one lever leaves most of the available saving untouched.
questions.traps: Optimising tier alone is the narrow view being tested. Accepting the cost and cutting usage both forgo capability rather than waste.

questions.stem: A team's workflow produces good results that arrive too late to be useful.
options: Treat timeliness as part of the requirement rather than a separate concern
Improve the output quality further so that the results are more valuable when they do arrive and better justify the time taken to produce them
Accept the delay since the output quality is high
Reduce the scope so the workflow completes sooner
questions.why: Output that arrives after it is needed has failed regardless of quality. Recognising timeliness as part of the requirement is the reframing.
questions.traps: Improving quality optimises the wrong dimension. Accepting the delay leaves the output useless, and scope reduction is a remedy chosen before the reframing.

questions.stem: A team's prompt asks the model to be thorough and the output has become repetitive.
options: Ask for shorter output so that the repetition is reduced along with the overall length of the response the model produces
Ask for less thorough output to reduce the repetition
Remove the repetitive passages manually
Replace the vague instruction with a specific requirement about coverage
questions.why: Thoroughness without a defined target is satisfied by length, which produces repetition. Specifying what must be covered replaces volume with substance.
questions.traps: Shortening compresses the repetition rather than removing it. Asking for less abandons the goal, and manual editing repeats forever.

questions.stem: An associate's workflow supplies context that is correct but written for a different purpose.
options: Supply additional context explaining the current purpose
Rewrite the context around what this task actually needs
Remove the mismatched context from the prompt entirely
Ask more specific questions so the context matters less
questions.why: Context assembled for a different purpose emphasises the wrong things. Rewriting it around the current task is what makes it useful.
questions.traps: Layering explanation on mismatched material adds volume. Removing it loses the information, and specific questions work around the mismatch.

questions.stem: A team's outputs vary and they have never checked whether their inputs vary in the same way.
options: Add an instruction asking for consistent output so that the responses become more uniform across the different runs of the workflow
Accept the variation as inherent to generated output
Run each input several times and compare the results
Check the inputs first, since output variation often traces to input variation
questions.why: Input variation is the most common and most checkable explanation for output variation. Ruling it in or out comes first.
questions.traps: An instruction cannot make varied inputs produce uniform outputs. Accepting the variation skips the check, and repeated runs measure without explaining.

questions.stem: A team wants to know whether a limitation they have hit is about the task or about how they framed it.
options: Try the same framing again to see whether the limitation appears consistently across repeated attempts at the request they are making
Move to a stronger tier so the limitation is not hit
Try a materially different framing of the same task
Ask the model whether the limitation is about the framing
questions.why: Testing a different framing distinguishes a task limitation from a framing one, which determines whether a workaround exists.
questions.traps: Repeating the same framing tests stability rather than the hypothesis. A stronger tier changes a different variable, and self-report is unreliable.

questions.stem: An associate's workflow runs nightly and the results are read once a week.
options: Run it weekly, matching the schedule to how the output is used
Keep the nightly schedule so that the most recent results are always available
Move to a cheaper tier so the nightly runs cost less
Shorten the outputs so each nightly run costs less
questions.why: Six of seven runs produce output nobody reads. Matching the schedule to consumption removes the waste entirely.
questions.traps: Availability arguments justify six wasted runs. A cheaper tier and shorter outputs both reduce the cost of work that should not happen.

questions.stem: A team fixed a recurring problem in their workflow and the same problem returned three weeks later.
options: Apply the same fix again since it resolved the problem last time and can be expected to resolve it again on this occasion as well
Add monitoring so the next recurrence is noticed sooner
Escalate to a stronger tier so the problem stops recurring
Establish whether the original fix addressed the cause or a symptom
questions.why: Recurrence suggests the fix addressed a symptom. Establishing whether the cause was ever found is what breaks the cycle.
questions.traps: Reapplying a symptomatic fix guarantees another recurrence. Monitoring detects the next one, and a tier change is unrelated.

questions.stem: A team's prompt contains two instructions that pull in opposite directions and the output satisfies neither well.
options: Strengthen both instructions so that the model gives more weight to each of them when it produces its response to the request being made
Decide which takes priority and say so
Remove both of the conflicting instructions entirely
Alternate between the two instructions across runs
questions.why: A genuine conflict cannot be resolved by emphasis. Stating the priority is what lets the model trade them off deliberately.
questions.traps: Strengthening both intensifies the conflict. Removing both loses two real requirements, and alternating produces inconsistent behaviour.

questions.stem: An associate finds the model performs better when they describe the situation before asking the question.
options: Treat it as coincidence, since the order in which information appears in a prompt should not affect the quality of the answer that is produced
Describe the situation in rather more detail
Adopt it as a technique and apply it deliberately
Ask the question first and then describe the situation
questions.why: Establishing the situation before the question gives the model context to interpret it against, and an observed improvement is worth applying deliberately.
questions.traps: Dismissing the observation discards a working technique. More detail and reversed ordering both change the technique rather than adopting it.

questions.stem: A team's workflow behaves differently for two inputs that look identical to them.
options: Compare the two inputs precisely rather than by eye
Run both inputs several times to establish whether the difference is consistent or whether it is just ordinary variation between individual runs
Accept the difference between the two apparently identical inputs
Combine the two inputs so they are processed together
questions.why: Inputs that look identical often differ in whitespace, encoding or hidden characters. A precise comparison finds what inspection misses.
questions.traps: Repeated runs establish that the difference is real without explaining it. Accepting it abandons the diagnosis, and combining changes the task.

questions.stem: A team's request is partially completed with a note explaining why the rest was not.
options: Regenerate the request so that a complete response is produced
Read the explanation and decide whether the remaining part should be pursued
Split the request so each part is submitted on its own
Rephrase the part that was not completed
questions.why: The note explains the limitation, and reading it is what tells you whether the remainder is worth pursuing and how.
questions.traps: Regenerating and rephrasing both try to get past an explanation without reading it. Splitting acts before understanding the cause.

questions.stem: An associate has optimised their prompt heavily and further changes make no measurable difference.
options: Continue optimising the prompt since further improvements will eventually be found through additional refinement of the wording and structure
Revert to an earlier version of the optimised prompt
Move to a stronger tier so the plateau is pushed higher
Accept the plateau and look at other parts of the workflow
questions.why: A plateau signals that the remaining gains are elsewhere. Redirecting effort to other parts of the workflow is what makes further progress.
questions.traps: Continued refinement is the sunk-cost path. Reverting rediscovers the same ceiling, and a tier change is a spend chosen without evidence.

questions.stem: A team's workflow has three possible causes for a failure and testing each takes about an hour.
options: Test all three at once so that the answer is found in a single hour
Test them in the order they occur in the workflow
Test the cheapest and most likely cause first
Ask Claude which cause is most likely
questions.why: Ordering diagnostic tests by likelihood and cost is what minimises the expected time to find the cause.
questions.traps: Testing all three simultaneously loses attribution. Workflow order is arbitrary, and the model cannot diagnose a system it cannot observe.

questions.stem: A team's prompt works and nobody knows which parts of it are doing the work.
options: Remove parts one at a time and observe what changes
Leave it alone, since the prompt works and investigating risks breaking something that is currently producing acceptable results for the team
Rewrite it more concisely so the working parts are clearer
Document what each part of it is intended to do
questions.why: Ablation identifies which parts carry the load, which makes the prompt maintainable and often shorter.
questions.traps: Leaving it unexamined accepts unmaintainability. A concise rewrite guesses at what matters, and documenting intent is not the same as testing effect.
